title: 4  Geometry of Representations
text:
4.13 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now measure: length, distance, angle, and similarity. System B has its first complete pipeline: text → vector → similarity → ranked results.
Vectors are still passive objects. Chapter 5 adds matrices, which move vectors from one space to another.

title: 4  Geometry of Representations
text:
Chapter summary

A norm gives length. Distance is the norm of a difference. \(\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_\infty\) differ in their unit balls.
\(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\sum a_ib_i=\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert\cos\theta\).
Cosine similarity compares direction only. It lies in \([-1,1]\) by Cauchy–Schwarz.
Projection splits a vector into an along-part and an orthogonal part.
In an orthonormal basis, the coordinates are dot products.
In high dimension, random vectors are nearly orthogonal.
All pairwise distances come from one matrix product.

title: 4  Geometry of Representations
text:
Exercises

Compute. For \(\mathbf{a}=(1,2,2)\) and \(\mathbf{b}=(2,0,-1)\), find \(\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert_1\), \(\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert_2\), \(\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert_\infty\), \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\), and the angle between them.
Compute. Project \((3,4)\) onto \((1,0)\) and onto \((1,1)\). Check that the remainder is orthogonal in each case.
Prove. Show that \(\lVert\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\rVert^2=\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert^2+\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert^2\) if and only if \(\mathbf{a}\perp\mathbf{b}\).
Prove. Show that cosine similarity is unchanged when \(\mathbf{a}\) is multiplied by a positive scalar. What happens for a negative scalar?
Prove. If \(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\) are unit vectors, show \(\lVert\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\rVert^2=2-2\cos\theta\). What does this say about ranking by distance and ranking by cosine?
Code. Run the Gram–Schmidt function on three nearly parallel vectors. What happens to the numerical orthogonality?
Code. Repeat the angle histogram for vectors with only non-negative entries (like word counts). Does the peak stay at \(90^\circ\)? Explain.
Code. Add "cat pet" queries with a stop-word list. Does the ranking change?
Diagnose. A search system returns the same document for every query. Give two geometric causes from this chapter.
Design. You must search 10 million vectors of dimension 768. How many bytes does the matrix use in float32? How many multiplications does one query need?

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
5.1 The system problem
A model must turn one representation into another. A pixel vector becomes a feature vector. A feature vector becomes class scores. We need a general tool that does this in one step and that can be learned.
The tool is the matrix. A learned matrix is the main kind of parameter in a neural network.
system_map(highlight=["Representation", "Transformation"],
           sublabels={"Representation": "Ch. 3–7", "Transformation": "Part III"});
plt.show()







Figure 5.1: Chapter 5 adds the first transformation to the Representation stage. Part III builds the Transformation stage on it.

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text: How does a model turn one vector into another in a single step, and what can that step never do?

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
5.2 Intuition: a matrix moves space
Imagine a rubber sheet with a square grid drawn on it. A linear transformation stretches, rotates, shears, or flips the sheet. It obeys two rules:

The origin stays where it is.
Grid lines stay straight, parallel, and evenly spaced.

Every such transformation is fully described by where it sends the basis vectors. If we know where \(\mathbf{e}_1=(1,0)\) and \(\mathbf{e}_2=(0,1)\) go, we know where every point goes. We write those two images as the columns of a matrix.

th = np.pi / 6
mats = {
    "scale  diag(2, 0.5)":  np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.5]]),
    "rotate 30°":            np.array([[np.cos(th), -np.sin(th)],
                                       [np.sin(th),  np.cos(th)]]),
    "shear":                 np.array([[1.0, 0.8], [0.0, 1.0]]),
    "reflect over x₂ axis":  np.array([[-1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]]),
    "project onto x₁":       np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]]),
    "rank 1":                np.array([[1.0, 0.5], [2.0, 1.0]]),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(9, 6))
for ax, (name, A) in zip(axes.ravel(), mats.items()):
    warp_grid(ax, A, title=f"{name}\nrank {np.linalg.matrix_rank(A)}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 5.2: Six matrices as transformations of the plane. The blue square is the image of the unit square. The orange and purple arrows are the images of e₁ and e₂: they are the columns of the matrix. The last matrix has rank 1 and flattens the plane onto a line.

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
5.3 The mathematical object
A matrix \(\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is a table with \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns. It defines a function from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^m\):
\[
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x},
\qquad
y_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{ij}x_j.
\tag{5.1}\]
The function is linear: \(\mathbf{A}(a\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{z})=a\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}\).

5.3.1 Two ways to read \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\)
Column view. Write \(\mathbf{A}=[\mathbf{a}_1\ \mathbf{a}_2\ \cdots\ \mathbf{a}_n]\) with columns \(\mathbf{a}_j\). Then
\[
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=x_{1}\mathbf{a}_1+x_{2}\mathbf{a}_2+\dots+x_{n}\mathbf{a}_n.
\tag{5.2}\]
The output is a linear combination of the columns, with the input components as coefficients. This is why the columns are “where the basis vectors go”.
Row view. Each output component is a dot product of one row with \(\mathbf{x}\): \(y_i=\mathbf{A}_{i,:}\cdot\mathbf{x}\). Each row measures one feature of the input.

A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0],
              [0.0, 3.0],
              [1.0, -1.0]])             # (3, 2): maps R^2 -> R^3
x = np.array([4.0, 2.0])                # (2,)

col_view = x[0] * A[:, 0] + x[1] * A[:, 1]          # combination of columns
row_view = np.array([A[i] @ x for i in range(3)])   # one dot product per row
print("A @ x      :", A @ x)
print("column view:", col_view)
print("row view   :", row_view)

A @ x      : [10.  6.  2.]
column view: [10.  6.  2.]
row view   : [10.  6.  2.]




5.3.2 Rotation matrices
The column view lets us write down a matrix for any transformation by asking where \(\mathbf{e}_1\) and \(\mathbf{e}_2\) go. For a counter-clockwise rotation by angle \(\phi\):
\[
\mathbf{e}_{1}\mapsto(\cos\phi,\ \sin\phi),
\qquad
\mathbf{e}_{2}\mapsto(-\sin\phi,\ \cos\phi).
\]
Put these two images in the columns:
\[
\mathbf{R}_\phi=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\phi&-\sin\phi\\ \sin\phi&\cos\phi\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{5.3}\]
Rotations return in Chapter 32: rotary position embeddings rotate pairs of coordinates by an angle that depends on the token position.

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
5.4 Operations

5.4.1 Matrix product is composition
Apply \(\mathbf{B}\) first, then \(\mathbf{A}\). The combined map is one matrix, \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\):
\[
\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{x})=(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\mathbf{x},
\qquad
(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})_{ik}=\sum_jA_{ij}B_{jk}.
\tag{5.4}\]
The shapes must chain: \((m,n)\,(n,p)\to(m,p)\). The inner sizes must match.
The product is not commutative. Rotating then shearing differs from shearing then rotating.

R = mats["rotate 30°"]; S = mats["shear"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.5, 3.6))
warp_grid(axes[0], S @ R, title="shear ∘ rotate   (S @ R)")
warp_grid(axes[1], R @ S, title="rotate ∘ shear   (R @ S)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("S @ R == R @ S :", np.allclose(S @ R, R @ S))







Figure 5.3: Order matters. Left: rotate first, then shear. Right: shear first, then rotate. The product matrices differ, so the results differ.





S @ R == R @ S : False




5.4.2 Transpose
The transpose swaps rows and columns: \((\mathbf{A}^{\intercal})_{ij}=A_{ji}\). For a product, the order reverses:
\[
(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^{\intercal}=\mathbf{B}^{\intercal}\mathbf{A}^{\intercal}.
\tag{5.5}\]






TipDerivation: the transpose of a product



Take one entry. By the definition of the product and the transpose:
\[
\bigl((\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^{\intercal}\bigr)_{ki}=(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})_{ik}=\sum_jA_{ij}B_{jk}=\sum_j(\mathbf{B}^{\intercal})_{kj}(\mathbf{A}^{\intercal})_{ji}=(\mathbf{B}^{\intercal}\mathbf{A}^{\intercal})_{ki}. \qquad\blacksquare
\]


The transpose is also the way to move a matrix across a dot product: \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{b})=(\mathbf{A}^{\intercal}\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{b}\). This is why \(\mathbf{W}^{\intercal}\) appears in backpropagation (Chapter 18).


5.4.3 Inverse
The inverse \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) undoes \(\mathbf{A}\): \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{I}\). It exists only for square matrices that do not collapse space.


5.4.4 Rank
The rank of \(\mathbf{A}\) is the number of independent columns. It is the dimension of the set of all outputs. The last panel of Figure 8.6 has rank 1: its second column is a multiple of the first, so the whole plane lands on a line. Information is lost, and no inverse exists.

A_full = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
A_def  = np.array([[1.0, 0.5], [2.0, 1.0]])
for name, M in [("full rank", A_full), ("rank deficient", A_def)]:
    rank, det = np.linalg.matrix_rank(M), np.linalg.det(M)
    print(f"{name:15s} rank = {rank}   det = {det:.2f}")

full rank       rank = 2   det = 1.00
rank deficient  rank = 1   det = 0.00


The determinant of a \(2\times2\) matrix is the signed area of the image of the unit square. A zero determinant means the area collapsed.


5.4.5 Change of basis
In Chapter 3 we solved for coordinates in a skew basis. The basis vectors are the columns of a matrix \(\mathbf{B}\), and the coordinates are
\[
\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{v}.
\tag{5.6}\]
This is the same equation \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{v}\), solved for \(\mathbf{c}\). Changing the basis is a matrix operation.


5.4.6 Lookup is a matrix product
We can also close the loop on embeddings. The product of a one-hot vector with the embedding matrix selects one row:

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
V, d = 6, 3
E = rng.normal(size=(V, d))               # embedding matrix (V, d)
t = 4
one_hot = np.eye(V)[t]                    # (V,)
print("one_hot @ E == E[t] :", np.allclose(one_hot @ E, E[t]))

one_hot @ E == E[t] : True

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
5.5 Computation: from first principles
We write the product with loops. Then we compare with NumPy. The loop version is the definition. The NumPy version is the one we use.

def matmul_loops(A, B):
    m, n = A.shape
    n2, p = B.shape
    assert n == n2, f"inner sizes differ: {n} vs {n2}"
    C = np.zeros((m, p))
    for i in range(m):
        for k in range(p):
            for j in range(n):
                C[i, k] += A[i, j] * B[j, k]
    return C

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
A, B = rng.normal(size=(40, 50)), rng.normal(size=(50, 30))
assert np.allclose(matmul_loops(A, B), A @ B)
print("loops == NumPy: True")

loops == NumPy: True



sizes = [8, 16, 32, 64, 96]
t_loop, t_np = [], []
for n in sizes:
    A, B = rng.normal(size=(n, n)), rng.normal(size=(n, n))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    matmul_loops(A, B)
    t_loop.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(200): A @ B
    t_np.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) / 200)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.loglog(sizes, t_loop, "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"], label="Python loops")
ax.loglog(sizes, t_np, "o-", color=PALETTE["grad"], label="NumPy  A @ B")
ax.set_xlabel("matrix size n"); ax.set_ylabel("seconds"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
print(f"speed-up at n={sizes[-1]}: {t_loop[-1] / t_np[-1]:,.0f}x")







Figure 5.4: Time for a square matrix product. The Python loop grows with n³ and is about three to five orders of magnitude slower than the optimized library. The library uses vectorized hardware instructions.





speed-up at n=96: 25,631x


A product of \((m,n)\) and \((n,p)\) needs \(mnp\) multiplications and about the same number of additions. Counting these is how we estimate the cost of a model: \(2mnp\) floating-point operations (FLOPs).

5.5.1 Batched products
A matrix product applies the same transformation to many vectors at once. If the rows of \(\mathbf{X}\) are \(B\) input vectors, then \(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{\intercal}\) transforms all of them in one call. This is the form used in every framework:

B_, n_in, n_out = 4, 5, 3
X = rng.normal(size=(B_, n_in))           # (B, n_in)   rows are inputs
W = rng.normal(size=(n_out, n_in))        # (n_out, n_in)
b = rng.normal(size=n_out)                # (n_out,)

Y = X @ W.T + b                           # (B, n_out)
per_row = np.array([W @ X[i] + b for i in range(B_)])
print("batched == one by one:", np.allclose(Y, per_row), "  shape:", Y.shape)

batched == one by one: True   shape: (4, 3)

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
5.6 Solving, not inverting
To find \(\mathbf{x}\) in \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\), the equation suggests \(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}\). Do not compute it this way. Forming the inverse is slower and less accurate than a direct solver. The problem becomes severe when \(\mathbf{A}\) is nearly singular.
We test this on the Hilbert matrix, a standard ill-conditioned example. The condition number measures how much errors are amplified.

from scipy.linalg import hilbert
ns = list(range(2, 13))
err_solve, err_inv, cond = [], [], []
for n in ns:
    H = hilbert(n)
    x_true = np.ones(n)
    rhs = H @ x_true
    err_solve.append(np.linalg.norm(np.linalg.solve(H, rhs) - x_true))
    err_inv.append(np.linalg.norm(np.linalg.inv(H) @ rhs - x_true))
    cond.append(np.linalg.cond(H))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.semilogy(ns, err_solve, "o-", color=PALETTE["grad"], label="solve(A, b)")
ax.semilogy(ns, err_inv, "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"], label="inv(A) @ b")
ax.semilogy(ns, [c * 1e-16 for c in cond], "--", color=PALETTE["neutral"],
            label="cond(A) × 1e-16  (expected scale)")
ax.set_xlabel("matrix size n"); ax.set_ylabel("error in x")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()
print(f"n=12: cond = {cond[-1]:.1e}")







Figure 5.5: Solving A x = b for the Hilbert matrix. The condition number grows very fast with size. Both methods lose accuracy, and the explicit inverse is worse.





n=12: cond = 1.7e+16


The rule of thumb: with condition number \(\kappa\) and machine precision \(\varepsilon\), expect a relative error of about \(\kappa\,\varepsilon\).

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
5.7 Production: PyTorch
PyTorch uses the same shapes. nn.Linear stores \(\mathbf{W}\) with shape (out, in) and computes \(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{\intercal}+\mathbf{b}\).

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

lin = nn.Linear(n_in, n_out)
lin = lin.double()                         # match NumPy's float64
with torch.no_grad():
    lin.weight.copy_(torch.tensor(W)); lin.bias.copy_(torch.tensor(b))

Y_t = lin(torch.tensor(X))
print("nn.Linear == X @ W.T + b :", np.allclose(Y_t.detach().numpy(), Y))
print("weight shape:", tuple(lin.weight.shape))
print("bias shape  :", tuple(lin.bias.shape))
print("parameters  :", sum(p.numel() for p in lin.parameters()))

nn.Linear == X @ W.T + b : True
weight shape: (3, 5)
bias shape  : (3,)
parameters  : 18


Note: \(\mathbf{W}\) has \(n_{\text{out}}\times n_{\text{in}}\) entries, and the bias adds \(n_{\text{out}}\) more. A layer of \(4096\to4096\) has \(16.8\) million weights.

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
5.8 Failure modes
Singular or ill-conditioned matrices. Rank-deficient matrices have no inverse. Nearly rank-deficient ones have a huge condition number and amplify errors. Learned weight matrices can become close to this.
Wrong order or transpose. \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\ne\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\). For square matrices both orders run, and only one is right. Check the shapes of every product (Chapter 2).
Information loss by projection. A layer with \(n_{\text{out}}<n_{\text{in}}\) has rank at most \(n_{\text{out}}\). Whatever lies in the null space is lost. This is intentional in compression and harmful when it removes needed features.
Floating-point accumulation. Summing many products in low precision loses accuracy. Libraries accumulate in higher precision internally. Chapter 34 returns to this.

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
5.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now move vectors: rotate, stretch, project, and change basis, all in one learnable step. A matrix is the basic parameter of a model. The cost of a model is the cost of its matrix products.
A single matrix is still limited. It cannot bend space. Chapter 6 gathers many vectors into tensors, and Chapter 7 studies the structure inside a matrix: eigenvalues and low rank.

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
Chapter summary

A matrix is a linear transformation. Its columns are the images of the basis vectors.
\(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\) is a combination of columns, or one dot product per row.
The matrix product is composition. It is not commutative. Shapes chain as \((m,n)(n,p)\to(m,p)\).
\((\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^{\intercal}=\mathbf{B}^{\intercal}\mathbf{A}^{\intercal}\).
Rank counts independent directions. A rank-deficient matrix loses information.
Coordinates in a basis are \(\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{v}\). Lookup is one-hot × table.
Solve linear systems. Do not form inverses.
A matrix product of \((m,n)(n,p)\) costs \(2mnp\) FLOPs.

title: 5  Matrices: Representing Transformations
text:
Exercises

Compute. Let \(\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). Compute \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\). Describe each as a geometric operation.
Compute. What matrix rotates the plane by \(90^\circ\) counter-clockwise? Check that applying it four times gives \(\mathbf{I}\).
Compute. Find the rank and determinant of \(\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\). Describe what it does to the unit square.
Derive. Show that a rotation matrix satisfies \(\mathbf{R}^{\intercal}\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{I}\). What does this say about lengths and angles?
Derive. Show that \(\text{rank}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\le\min(\text{rank}\,\mathbf{A},\text{rank}\,\mathbf{B})\).
Code. Build a matrix that projects \(\mathbb{R}^3\) onto the plane \(x_3=0\). Apply it twice. What do you notice?
Code. Count the FLOPs in a forward pass of a 784 → 256 → 128 → 10 network on a batch of 64. Which layer dominates?
Code. Measure the product time for sizes \(n=64,\ldots,1024\) and fit the exponent. Is it close to 3?
Diagnose. nn.Linear(10, 20)(x) fails for x.shape == (10, 5). Explain and fix it.
Explain. A \(1000\to10\) layer has rank at most 10. What does that say about what it can represent?

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
text:
6.1 The system problem
So far, one example was one vector. Real systems process many examples at once. They also process data that has more structure than a flat list: images have rows and columns, colours, and frames over time. Text has positions.
The answer is the tensor. Almost every number inside a neural network lives in a tensor.
system_map(highlight=["Data", "Representation"],
           sublabels={"Representation": "Ch. 3–7"});
plt.show()







Figure 6.1: Chapter 6 completes the objects of the Representation stage: vectors, matrices, and now tensors.

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
text: How do batches of images, sequences, and activations fit in one array, and how do operations act on them?

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
text:
6.2 Intuition: a ladder of orders
We already know three objects. A tensor continues the pattern: each new object adds one axis.



Order

col = PALETTE["data"]

def cells(ax, nr, nc, dx=0.0, dy=0.0, alpha=0.9):
    for i in range(nr):
        for j in range(nc):
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((j + dx, -i + dy), 0.9, 0.9,
                                   fc=col, ec="white", alpha=alpha))

titles = ["scalar ()", "vector (d,)", "matrix (m, n)", "tensor (C, m, n)"]
sizes = [(1, 1), (1, 5), (4, 5), (4, 5)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(10, 2.8))
for ax, title, (nr, nc) in zip(axes, titles, sizes):
    if title.startswith("tensor"):
        for k, a in enumerate([0.35, 0.6, 0.9]):          # three stacked sheets
            cells(ax, nr, nc, dx=0.45 * (2 - k), dy=0.35 * (2 - k), alpha=a)
        ax.set_xlim(-0.2, 6.2); ax.set_ylim(-4, 2)
    else:
        cells(ax, nr, nc)
        ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 6); ax.set_ylim(-4, 1.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 6.2: The ladder of tensor orders. Each step adds one axis. A matrix is a row of vectors. A 3-tensor is a stack of matrices.





The ladder has no top. A tensor of any order is a table of numbers with one index per axis.

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
text:
6.3 The mathematical object
A tensor of order \(k\) is a function that assigns one real number to each tuple of \(k\) indices. We write \(\mathcal{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}\times\cdots\times n_k}\) and \(\mathcal{X}_{i_1 i_{2}\cdots i_k}\) for one entry.
The shape \((n_1,\dots,n_k)\) is the key. The number of entries is the product of the sizes:
\[
\text{size}(\mathcal{X}) = n_1\, n_{2}\cdots n_k.
\tag{6.1}\]

6.3.1 Standard layouts








Data
Layout
Axis meaning




Greyscale image
\((H, W)\)
row, column


Colour image
\((H, W, C)\) or \((C, H, W)\)
row, column, channel


Image batch
\((B, C, H, W)\)
example, channel, row, column


Token sequence batch
\((B, T)\) of ids
example, position


Hidden states
\((B, T, d)\)
example, position, feature


Attention scores
\((B, h, T, T)\)
example, head, query position, key position









NoteChannels first or last



Image libraries store colour images as \((H,W,C)\). PyTorch convolutions expect \((B,C,H,W)\). Converting is a permutation of axes. This is a common source of bugs.


We load a real photograph and look at its axes.

from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image
img = load_sample_image("china.jpg")                 # (H, W, C), uint8
print("shape:", img.shape, " dtype:", img.dtype, " entries:", img.size)
print("pixel (100, 200):", img[100, 200], "  -> one vector of C = 3 values")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 2.6))
axes[0].imshow(img); axes[0].set_title("img  (H, W, 3)")
for k, name in enumerate(["R", "G", "B"]):
    axes[k + 1].imshow(img[:, :, k], cmap="gray")        # slice one axis
    axes[k + 1].set_title(f"img[:, :, {k}]  ({name})")
for ax in axes: ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

shape: (427, 640, 3)  dtype: uint8  entries: 819840
pixel (100, 200): [123  47  11]   -> one vector of C = 3 values








Figure 6.3: A colour image is a stack of three matrices. Left to right: the image, then its red, green, and blue channels as separate grey-level images. Each channel is a 2D slice of the 3D tensor.

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
text:
6.4 Operations

6.4.1 Reshape and permute
Reshape changes the shape but keeps the order of the numbers in memory. The total size must stay the same. Permute (transpose) reorders the axes and so changes which numbers sit next to each other.

x = np.arange(24)                       # (24,)
a = x.reshape(2, 3, 4)                  # (2, 3, 4)
b = a.transpose(1, 0, 2)                # (3, 2, 4)  axes permuted
print("a[0, 1, 2] =", a[0, 1, 2], "   b[1, 0, 2] =", b[1, 0, 2])   # same entry
print("a.reshape(6, 4) rows 0-1:\n", a.reshape(6, 4)[:2])

a[0, 1, 2] = 6    b[1, 0, 2] = 6
a.reshape(6, 4) rows 0-1:
 [[0 1 2 3]
 [4 5 6 7]]


Converting an image batch from the library layout to the network layout is one permute:

crops = [img[:100, :100], img[100:200, 100:200]]
batch_hwc = np.stack(crops)                    # (2, 100, 100, 3)
batch_chw = batch_hwc.transpose(0, 3, 1, 2)    # (2, 3, 100, 100)
print(batch_hwc.shape, "->", batch_chw.shape)

(2, 100, 100, 3) -> (2, 3, 100, 100)




6.4.2 Broadcasting
Broadcasting lets an operation combine arrays of different shapes. The rule has two steps.

Align the shapes at the right end. Pad on the left with size 1.
For each axis, the sizes must be equal, or one of them must be \(1\). A size-1 axis is stretched to match.




Left
Right
Result
Valid?




(3, 4)
(4,)
(3, 4)
yes


(3, 1)
(1, 4)
(3, 4)
yes


(B, T, d)
(d,)
(B, T, d)
yes (bias)


(3, 4)
(3,)
—
no: 4 vs 3




col_v = np.array([[10], [20], [30]])        # (3, 1)
row_v = np.array([[1, 2, 3, 4]])            # (1, 4)
out = col_v + row_v                         # (3, 4)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(8.5, 2.6),
                         gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 4, 4]})
titles = ["(3, 1)", "(1, 4)", "sum  (3, 4)"]
for ax, arr, title in zip(axes, [col_v, row_v, out], titles):
    ax.imshow(np.ones_like(arr), cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=2)
    for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(arr):
        ax.text(j, i, str(v), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 6.4: Broadcasting a column (3, 1) and a row (1, 4). Each is stretched along its size-1 axis. The result has shape (3, 4): every pairing of one row entry with one column entry.





Broadcasting is the reason X @ W.T + b works in a layer: the bias of shape (d_out,) is stretched over the batch axis.
One practical use is to normalise each colour channel of an image. We compute a mean per channel and subtract it from every pixel.

x = img.astype(np.float64) / 255.0                  # (H, W, 3)
mean = x.mean(axis=(0, 1), keepdims=True)           # (1, 1, 3)
std = x.std(axis=(0, 1), keepdims=True)             # (1, 1, 3)
z = (x - mean) / std                                # broadcast over H and W
print("mean shape:", mean.shape)
print("z mean per channel:", np.round(z.mean(axis=(0, 1)), 6))
print("z std  per channel:", np.round(z.std(axis=(0, 1)), 3))

mean shape: (1, 1, 3)
z mean per channel: [0. 0. 0.]
z std  per channel: [1. 1. 1.]


The option keepdims=True keeps the reduced axes with size 1. This is what makes the result broadcast correctly.


6.4.3 Reductions
A reduction removes an axis by summing, averaging, or taking a max over it. The axis argument names the axis that disappears.


6.4.4 Contraction and einsum
Matrix product sums over one shared index. A general contraction sums over any shared indices. einsum writes this directly (Chapter 2). A key example is the attention score of Chapter 30:
\[
S_{b,h,t,s}=\sum_{k}Q_{b,t,h,k}\,K_{b,s,h,k}.
\tag{6.2}\]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
B_, T, h, dk = 2, 5, 4, 8
Q = rng.normal(size=(B_, T, h, dk))         # (B, T, h, d_k)
K = rng.normal(size=(B_, T, h, dk))

S = np.einsum("bthd,bshd->bhts", Q, K)      # (B, h, T, T)
S_mm = Q.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3) @ K.transpose(0, 2, 3, 1)   # (B,h,T,dk)@(B,h,dk,T)
print("scores shape:", S.shape, "  equals batched matmul:", np.allclose(S, S_mm))

scores shape: (2, 4, 5, 5)   equals batched matmul: True

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
text:
6.5 Memory: strides, views, and copies
A tensor is stored as one flat block of numbers. The strides say how many bytes to skip to move one step along each axis.

a = np.arange(24, dtype=np.float64).reshape(2, 3, 4)
print("a.strides   :", a.strides, " (bytes per step along each axis)")
t = a.transpose(1, 0, 2)
print("t.strides   :", t.strides, " same memory, permuted strides")
print("t shares memory with a   :", np.shares_memory(a, t))
print("t is C-contiguous        :", t.flags["C_CONTIGUOUS"])
r = t.reshape(6, 4)                  # needs a copy: not contiguous
print("t.reshape shares memory  :", np.shares_memory(t, r))

a.strides   : (96, 32, 8)  (bytes per step along each axis)
t.strides   : (32, 96, 8)  same memory, permuted strides
t shares memory with a   : True
t is C-contiguous        : False
t.reshape shares memory  : False



A view (slice, transpose) shares memory. It is free but changing it changes the original.
A copy has its own memory. It is safe but costs time and space.
Some operations need contiguous memory and make a copy silently.


6.5.1 Memory of activations
The size of a tensor in bytes is its entry count times the bytes per entry. For attention scores, the entry count grows with \(T^2\):
\[
\text{bytes}=B\cdot h\cdot T^{2}\cdot(\text{bytes per number}).
\tag{6.3}\]

Ts = np.array([512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384, 32768, 65536])
bytes_ = 1 * 16 * Ts.astype(float) ** 2 * 2        # B * h * T^2 * 2 bytes (fp16)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.loglog(Ts, bytes_, "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"])
ax.axhline(80e9, ls="--", color=PALETTE["neutral"]); ax.text(600, 95e9, "80 GB")
ax.set_xlabel("sequence length T"); ax.set_ylabel("bytes (one layer)")
plt.show()
print(f"T = 65,536: {bytes_[-1] / 1e9:.0f} GB")







Figure 6.5: Memory for the attention score tensor of one layer (batch 1, 16 heads, 16-bit numbers). It grows with the square of the sequence length. At 64k tokens the score tensor alone exceeds an 80 GB accelerator.





T = 65,536: 137 GB


This is why long-context models need special attention kernels that never form the full \(T\times T\) tensor (Chapter 34).

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
section: 6.6 Patches: reshaping an image into tokens
text:
6.6 Patches: reshaping an image into tokens
Reshape and permute can cut an image into square patches. This is the first step of a Vision Transformer (Chapter 36). We do it with two lines.

P = 16
H, W = 416, 640
crop = img[:H, :W]                                           # (416, 640, 3)
patches = (crop.reshape(H // P, P, W // P, P, 3)    # split rows, columns
               .transpose(0, 2, 1, 3, 4)             # (26, 40, P, P, 3)
               .reshape(-1, P, P, 3))                # (1040, P, P, 3)
print("patches:", patches.shape, "  per patch values:", P * P * 3)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
ax = fig.add_axes([0.05, 0.28, 0.9, 0.7]); ax.imshow(crop)
for i in range(0, H + 1, P): ax.axhline(i - 0.5, color="white", lw=0.4)
for j in range(0, W + 1, P): ax.axvline(j - 0.5, color="white", lw=0.4)
ax.axis("off")
for k, idx in enumerate([0, 300, 520, 800, 1030]):
    pa = fig.add_axes([0.1 + k * 0.17, 0.03, 0.12, 0.2])
    pa.imshow(patches[idx])
    pa.set_xticks([]); pa.set_yticks([]); pa.grid(False)
    pa.set_title(f"patch {idx}", fontsize=8)
plt.show()

patches: (1040, 16, 16, 3)   per patch values: 768








Figure 6.6: Patchification by reshape and permute. A 416×640 image becomes a grid of 26×40 patches of size 16×16. Each patch is a small image and later becomes one token.





Each patch contains \(16\times16\times3=768\) numbers. A linear layer maps it to a token embedding. The whole image becomes a sequence of \(26\times40=1040\) tokens, each a vector.

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
text:
6.7 From first principles to production
PyTorch tensors follow the same rules. Two differences matter in practice: view fails on non-contiguous data, and tensors can live on a GPU and track gradients.

import torch

xt = torch.arange(24.0).reshape(2, 3, 4)
tt = xt.permute(1, 0, 2)                               # view with new strides
print("permute is contiguous:", tt.is_contiguous())
try:
    tt.view(6, 4)                                      # needs contiguous memory
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("view failed:", str(e)[:60], "...")
print("reshape works:", tuple(tt.reshape(6, 4).shape))
print("contiguous().view:", tuple(tt.contiguous().view(6, 4).shape))

S_t = torch.einsum("bthd,bshd->bhts", torch.tensor(Q), torch.tensor(K))
print("einsum matches NumPy:", np.allclose(S_t.numpy(), S))

permute is contiguous: False
view failed: view size is not compatible with input tensor's size and str ...
reshape works: (6, 4)
contiguous().view: (6, 4)
einsum matches NumPy: True

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
text:
6.8 Failure modes

6.8.1 Silent broadcasting in a loss
Predictions of shape (B, 1) and targets of shape (B,) look compatible. They are not what we want:

B_ = 4
y_pred = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0], [4.0]])        # (B, 1)
y_true = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])      # (B,)  predictions perfect

wrong = np.mean((y_pred - y_true) ** 2)                # broadcast to (B, B)!
right = np.mean((y_pred[:, 0] - y_true) ** 2)
print("(y_pred - y_true).shape =", (y_pred - y_true).shape)
print(f"wrong loss = {wrong:.3f}    correct loss = {right:.3f}")

(y_pred - y_true).shape = (4, 4)
wrong loss = 2.500    correct loss = 0.000


A perfect model reports a non-zero loss. The code runs without any error. Always check the shape of the loss inputs.


6.8.2 Integer overflow in image data
Images are stored as 8-bit unsigned integers. Arithmetic wraps around:

a = np.array([200], dtype=np.uint8)
b = np.array([100], dtype=np.uint8)
print("uint8: 200 + 100 =", (a + b)[0], "   float: ", float(a[0]) + float(b[0]))

uint8: 200 + 100 = 44    float:  300.0


Convert to float before arithmetic.


6.8.3 Other failures

Wrong axis in a reduction. mean(axis=0) and mean(axis=1) give different shapes. State the shape you expect.
View modified in place. Changing a slice changes the original array.
Out of memory. Activation memory grows with \(B\), \(T\), depth, and (for attention) \(T^2\).
Layout mismatch. Passing \((H,W,C)\) where \((C,H,W)\) is expected can run and give nonsense.

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
text:
6.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now hold batches and structured data: images with rows, columns, and channels, sequences with positions, and the hidden states of a deep network. It has the tools to reshape them, combine them by broadcasting, and contract them with einsum.
The data is still treated as raw numbers. Chapter 7 looks inside these arrays for structure that allows a smaller description.

title: 6  Tensors and High-Dimensional Data
text:
Chapter summary

A tensor is an array with \(k\) axes. The shape lists the sizes.
Standard layouts: image \((H,W,C)\) or \((B,C,H,W)\), sequences \((B,T,d)\), attention \((B,h,T,T)\).
Reshape keeps the memory order. Permute reorders axes.
Broadcasting: align at the right, sizes equal or 1.
einsum expresses any contraction.
Views share memory. Copies do not. Strides describe the layout.
Attention-score memory grows as \(T^2\).
Typical failures: silent broadcasting, integer overflow, wrong layout, out of memory.

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text:
7.1 The system problem
A digit image has 64 numbers. A word embedding has hundreds. A weight matrix in a language model has millions.
Do we need all of these numbers? Often a few directions carry most of what matters. The other directions hold small variations or noise.
The tools of this chapter find those directions. They answer three practical questions: how to compress data, how to visualise it in 2D, and how to update a huge model with few parameters.
system_map(highlight=["Data", "Representation"],
           sublabels={"Representation": "Ch. 3–7"});
plt.show()







Figure 7.1: Chapter 7 finishes the Representation stage. Vectors, matrices, and tensors hold the data. Eigen-analysis finds the structure inside.

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text: Can a 64-number image be described by far fewer numbers without losing what matters?

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text:
7.2 Eigenvectors: directions that survive
A matrix usually changes the direction of a vector. For a few special directions it does not. It only stretches or flips them.
\[
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\,\mathbf{v},\qquad \mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}.
\tag{7.1}\]
The vector \(\mathbf{v}\) is an eigenvector. The number \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue.
Worked example. Take \(\mathbf{S}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\). We need \((\mathbf{S}-\lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}\) with \(\mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf{0}\). This needs \(\det(\mathbf{S}-\lambda\mathbf{I})=0\):
\[
(2-\lambda)^2-1=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda_1=3,\ \lambda_2=1.
\]
For \(\lambda_1=3\): \(\mathbf{v}_{1}\propto(1,1)\). For \(\lambda_2=1\): \(\mathbf{v}_{2}\propto(1,-1)\). The matrix stretches the diagonal direction by 3 and leaves the anti-diagonal direction unchanged.

S = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(S)                  # symmetric: eigh, ascending order
print("eigenvalues:", vals)
print("eigenvectors (columns):\n", np.round(vecs, 3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 4.6))
warp_grid(ax, S, title="S = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]")
for k, col in zip([1, 0], [PALETTE["loss"], PALETTE["grad"]]):
    v = vecs[:, k]
    ax.plot([-3 * v[0], 3 * v[0]], [-3 * v[1], 3 * v[1]], color=col, lw=2,
            label=f"λ = {vals[k]:.0f}")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.show()

eigenvalues: [1. 3.]
eigenvectors (columns):
 [[-0.707  0.707]
 [ 0.707  0.707]]








Figure 7.2: A symmetric matrix as a transformation. The eigenvectors (red lines) are the only directions that keep their orientation. The grid is stretched by 3 along the diagonal and by 1 along the anti-diagonal.





For a symmetric matrix (\(\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{S}^{\intercal}\)) a strong result holds. We state it without proof.






ImportantSpectral theorem



A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues. It has \(n\) eigenvectors that are orthonormal. So \(\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^{\intercal}\) with \(\mathbf{V}\) orthogonal and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) diagonal.

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text:
7.3 The covariance matrix
How do we describe the shape of a data cloud? One number per feature (its spread) is not enough. Two features can vary together.
Take \(N\) data points \(\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^d\), stored as rows of \(\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}\). First centre the data by subtracting the mean: \(\mathbf{X}_c=\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\). The sample covariance matrix is
\[
\mathbf{S}=\frac{1}{N}\mathbf{X}_c^{\intercal}\mathbf{X}_c,
\qquad
S_{jk}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_{ij}-\mu_j)(x_{ik}-\mu_k).
\tag{7.2}\]

The diagonal \(S_{jj}\) is the variance of feature \(j\).
The off-diagonal \(S_{jk}\) is positive when features \(j\) and \(k\) rise together, and negative when one rises as the other falls.
\(\mathbf{S}\) is symmetric and \(d\times d\).

Chapter 21 gives the probabilistic meaning of covariance. Here we use it as a computed object.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [1.2, 0.6]])                       # shapes the cloud
X2 = rng.normal(size=(400, 2)) @ A.T + np.array([3.0, 2.0])  # (400, 2)

mu = X2.mean(axis=0)                           # (2,)
Xc = X2 - mu                                   # centred
Scov = Xc.T @ Xc / len(X2)                     # (2, 2)
lam, V = np.linalg.eigh(Scov)                  # ascending

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 4.2))
ax.scatter(*X2.T, s=10, alpha=0.5, color=PALETTE["data"])
for k, col in [(1, PALETTE["model"]), (0, PALETTE["loss"])]:
    draw_arrow(ax, 2 * np.sqrt(lam[k]) * V[:, k], origin=mu, color=col, lw=3)
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("feature 1"); ax.set_ylabel("feature 2")
plt.show()
print("covariance:\n", np.round(Scov, 2))
print("eigenvalues (variance along each axis):", np.round(lam, 2))







Figure 7.3: A correlated 2D data cloud. The eigenvectors of its covariance matrix (arrows) point along the long and short axes of the cloud. Their lengths are proportional to the standard deviation along each axis.





covariance:
 [[4.02 2.42]
 [2.42 1.82]]
eigenvalues (variance along each axis): [0.26 5.58]

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text:
7.4 PCA: the best directions
Principal component analysis (PCA) answers: in which direction does the data vary most? For a unit vector \(\mathbf{u}\), the data projected on it has coordinates \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{x}_i\). The variance of these is
\[
\frac1N\sum_i(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{c,i})^2=\mathbf{u}^{\intercal}\mathbf{S}\,\mathbf{u}.
\tag{7.3}\]






TipDerivation: the best direction is the top eigenvector



We want the unit vector \(\mathbf{u}\) that maximises \(\mathbf{u}^{\intercal}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{u}\).
By the spectral theorem, \(\mathbf{S}\) has orthonormal eigenvectors \(\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_d\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_{1}\ge\dots\ge\lambda_{d}\ge0\). Write \(\mathbf{u}=\sum_ic_{i}\mathbf{v}_i\). Because \(\mathbf{u}\) has unit length, \(\sum_ic_i^2=1\). Then
\[
\mathbf{u}^{\intercal}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{u}=\sum_{i}\lambda_i\,c_i^2.
\]
This is a weighted average of the eigenvalues, with weights \(c_i^2\) that sum to 1. A weighted average cannot exceed the largest value. So \(\mathbf{u}^{\intercal}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{u}\le\lambda_1\), with equality exactly when \(\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{v}_1\).
The best direction is \(\mathbf{v}_1\), and the variance it captures is \(\lambda_1\). The same argument, restricted to vectors orthogonal to \(\mathbf{v}_1\), gives \(\mathbf{v}_2\) with variance \(\lambda_2\), and so on. \(\blacksquare\)


The procedure is:

Centre the data.
Compute \(\mathbf{S}\).
Find its eigenvectors, sorted by eigenvalue.
Keep the top \(k\). Project: \(\mathbf{z}_i=\mathbf{V}_k^{\intercal}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\).
Reconstruct if needed: \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{V}_{k}\mathbf{z}_i\).

The fraction of variance kept by \(k\) components is \(\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_{i}\big/\sum_{i}\lambda_i\).

def pca_fit(X):
    mu = X.mean(axis=0)
    Xc = X - mu
    S = Xc.T @ Xc / len(X)
    lam, V = np.linalg.eigh(S)
    order = np.argsort(lam)[::-1]              # largest first
    return mu, lam[order], V[:, order]

def pca_transform(X, mu, V, k):
    return (X - mu) @ V[:, :k]                 # (N, k)

def pca_inverse(Z, mu, V):
    k = Z.shape[1]
    return mu + Z @ V[:, :k].T                 # (N, d)


7.4.1 PCA on digits
We now apply it to the \(8\times8\) digits of Chapter 3: 1,797 vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^{64}\).

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
digits = load_digits()
X, y = digits.data, digits.target                    # (1797, 64)

mu, lam, V = pca_fit(X)
Z2 = pca_transform(X, mu, V, 2)                      # (1797, 2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.6))
sc = ax.scatter(*Z2.T, c=y, cmap="tab10", s=8)
ax.set_xlabel("component 1"); ax.set_ylabel("component 2")
ax.legend(*sc.legend_elements(), title="digit", fontsize=7,
          loc="upper left", ncol=2)
plt.show()
print(f"variance kept by 2 components: {lam[:2].sum() / lam.sum():.1%}")







Figure 7.4: The digit dataset projected from 64 dimensions to 2 with PCA. Classes are not given to the method, yet they form visible groups. The first two components keep only a part of the variance, so the groups overlap.





variance kept by 2 components: 28.5%


How many components are enough? The scree plot shows the eigenvalues. The cumulative curve shows the fraction of variance kept.

ratio = lam / lam.sum()
cum = np.cumsum(ratio)
k90 = int(np.searchsorted(cum, 0.90)) + 1

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2))
ax1.bar(range(1, 65), lam, color=PALETTE["data"])
ax1.set_xlabel("component"); ax1.set_ylabel("eigenvalue")
ax2.plot(range(1, 65), cum, color=PALETTE["model"])
guide = dict(ls=":", color=PALETTE["neutral"])
ax2.axhline(0.9, **guide); ax2.axvline(k90, **guide)
ax2.set_xlabel("number of components k"); ax2.set_ylabel("cumulative variance")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("components for 90% of variance:", k90, "of 64")







Figure 7.5: Left: eigenvalues of the digit covariance (the scree plot). They fall quickly. Right: cumulative variance kept. About 20 components keep 90% of the variance.





components for 90% of variance: 21 of 64



idx = 12
ks = [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(ks) + 1, figsize=(10, 1.9))
for ax, k in zip(axes, ks):
    Zk = pca_transform(X[idx:idx + 1], mu, V, k)
    rec = pca_inverse(Zk, mu, V)[0].reshape(8, 8)
    ax.imshow(rec, cmap="gray_r", vmin=0, vmax=16)
    ax.set_title(f"k = {k}", fontsize=9)
axes[-1].imshow(X[idx].reshape(8, 8), cmap="gray_r", vmin=0, vmax=16)
axes[-1].set_title("original", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes: ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 7.6: Reconstructing one digit from k principal components. With 2 components the digit is a blur. With 10 it is recognisable. With 30 it is close to the original. The original has 64 numbers.

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text:
7.5 SVD: the general factorisation
The eigen-decomposition works for symmetric square matrices. The singular value decomposition (SVD) works for every matrix \(\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\):
\[
\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\intercal},
\tag{7.4}\]
with \(\mathbf{U}\) (\(m\times m\)) and \(\mathbf{V}\) (\(n\times n\)) orthogonal, and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) diagonal with \(\sigma_{1}\ge\sigma_{2}\ge\dots\ge0\), the singular values.
The geometry is clear: rotate (by \(\mathbf{V}^{\intercal}\)), stretch along the axes (by \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\)), rotate (by \(\mathbf{U}\)). The image of the unit circle is an ellipse whose semi-axes are the singular values.

M = np.array([[2.0, 0.6], [1.0, 1.4]])
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M)
t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
circle = np.stack([np.cos(t), np.sin(t)])

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.8))
setup_2d(ax1, xlim=(-3, 3), ylim=(-3, 3)); ax1.set_title("input: unit circle")
ax1.plot(*circle, color=PALETTE["data"])
for k, col in enumerate([PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["prob"]]):
    draw_arrow(ax1, Vt[k], color=col, lw=2.5, label=f"v{k+1}",
               label_offset=(0.1, 0.1))
setup_2d(ax2, xlim=(-3, 3), ylim=(-3, 3)); ax2.set_title("output: M · circle")
ax2.plot(*(M @ circle), color=PALETTE["data"])
for k, col in enumerate([PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["prob"]]):
    draw_arrow(ax2, s[k] * U[:, k], color=col, lw=2.5,
               label=f"σ{k+1}u{k+1}", label_offset=(0.1, 0.1))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("singular values:", np.round(s, 3))
print("check  U Σ Vᵀ = M :", np.allclose(U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt, M))







Figure 7.7: SVD as rotate–stretch–rotate. The unit circle (left) maps to an ellipse (right). The right singular vectors v₁, v₂ are the input directions. They map to the semi-axes σ₁u₁ and σ₂u₂.





singular values: [2.566 0.857]
check  U Σ Vᵀ = M : True



7.5.1 SVD and PCA are the same computation
For centred data \(\mathbf{X}_c=\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\intercal}\). Then
\[
\mathbf{S}=\frac1N\mathbf{X}_c^{\intercal}\mathbf{X}_c=\mathbf{V}\,\frac{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^2}{N}\,\mathbf{V}^{\intercal}.
\tag{7.5}\]
So the right singular vectors \(\mathbf{V}\) are the principal directions, and the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{S}\) are \(\sigma_i^2/N\). SVD is the numerically preferred way to do PCA because it never forms \(\mathbf{X}_c^{\intercal}\mathbf{X}_c\).

Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)       # (1797,64) (64,) (64,64)
print("eigenvalues from SVD match covariance:", np.allclose(s ** 2 / len(X), lam))
cos = np.abs(np.sum(Vt.T * V, axis=0))                  # |cosine| per component
print("directions match up to sign (first 5):", np.round(cos[:5], 6))

eigenvalues from SVD match covariance: True
directions match up to sign (first 5): [1. 1. 1. 1. 1.]




7.5.2 Best low-rank approximation
Keep only the top \(k\) terms of the SVD:
\[
\mathbf{A}_k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_i\,\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_i^{\intercal}.
\tag{7.6}\]






ImportantEckart–Young theorem (statement)



Among all matrices of rank at most \(k\), \(\mathbf{A}_k\) is closest to \(\mathbf{A}\) in Frobenius norm. The error is \[
\lVert\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}_{k}\rVert_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2.
\]


The error is exactly the energy in the discarded singular values. We verify it numerically below. The proof that no other rank-\(k\) matrix does better needs more tools. We omit it.


7.5.3 Compressing an image
A greyscale image is a matrix. If its singular values fall fast, a low-rank approximation stores it in far fewer numbers.

from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image
gray = load_sample_image("china.jpg").astype(float).mean(axis=2)     # (427, 640)
Ug, sg, Vtg = np.linalg.svd(gray, full_matrices=False)

def rank_k(k):
    return (Ug[:, :k] * sg[:k]) @ Vtg[:k]          # sum of k rank-1 terms

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(11, 2.4))
axes[0].imshow(gray, cmap="gray"); axes[0].set_title("original")
for ax, k in zip(axes[1:], [1, 5, 20, 50]):
    ax.imshow(rank_k(k), cmap="gray"); ax.set_title(f"rank {k}")
for ax in axes: ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 7.8: Low-rank approximations of a photograph. The original has rank 427. Rank 5 keeps the coarse layout. Rank 20 is clearly recognisable. Rank 50 is visually close to the original.






m, n = gray.shape
ks = np.arange(1, 201)
total = np.sum(sg ** 2)
rel_err = np.sqrt(np.array([np.sum(sg[k:] ** 2) for k in ks]) / total)
storage = ks * (m + n + 1) / (m * n)            # k (m + n + 1) numbers

# check the Eckart–Young error formula at k = 20
direct = np.linalg.norm(gray - rank_k(20)) / np.linalg.norm(gray)
print(f"k=20: relative error from formula {rel_err[19]:.4f}, direct {direct:.4f}")

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2))
ax1.semilogy(ks, rel_err, color=PALETTE["loss"])
ax1.set_xlabel("rank k"); ax1.set_ylabel("relative error ‖A − A_k‖ / ‖A‖")
ax2.plot(ks, storage, color=PALETTE["data"])
ax2.set_xlabel("rank k"); ax2.set_ylabel("storage / original")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"k=50: storage {storage[49]:.1%}, relative error {rel_err[49]:.1%}")

k=20: relative error from formula 0.1364, direct 0.1364








Figure 7.9: Error and storage as the rank grows. Left: relative error falls fast. Right: storage as a fraction of the original. Rank 50 stores about 20% of the numbers and has an error of about 10%.





k=50: storage 19.5%, relative error 10.3%

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
section: 7.6 Low rank in modern AI: LoRA
text:
7.6 Low rank in modern AI: LoRA
The weight matrices of large models have millions of entries. Fine-tuning a model for a new task changes them. Updating every entry is expensive: it needs gradients and optimizer state for every weight.
Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) freezes the pre-trained matrix \(\mathbf{W}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) and learns only a low-rank update:
\[
\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{W}_0+\Delta\mathbf{W},
\qquad
\Delta\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A},
\qquad
\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\ \mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d},\ r\ll d.
\tag{7.7}\]
The update has rank at most \(r\). It has \(2dr\) parameters instead of \(d^2\).

d = 4096
ranks = [1, 4, 8, 16, 64]
full = d * d
lora = [2 * d * r for r in ranks]
for r, p in zip(ranks, lora):
    print(f"r = {r:3d}: {p:>9,d} parameters   ({p / full:.2%} of full)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
ax.bar(["full"] + [f"r={r}" for r in ranks], [full] + lora,
       color=[PALETTE["loss"]] + [PALETTE["grad"]] * len(ranks))
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_ylabel("trainable parameters")
plt.show()

r =   1:     8,192 parameters   (0.05% of full)
r =   4:    32,768 parameters   (0.20% of full)
r =   8:    65,536 parameters   (0.39% of full)
r =  16:   131,072 parameters   (0.78% of full)
r =  64:   524,288 parameters   (3.12% of full)








Figure 7.10: Trainable parameters for one 4096×4096 matrix. The full update has 16.8 million. A rank-8 LoRA update has 65,536: under 0.4% of the full count.





The method works if the update is approximately low rank. This is an assumption about the task, not a law. We can test the idea on a toy update: a rank-4 matrix plus noise.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
dd, true_r = 256, 4
low_rank = rng.normal(size=(dd, true_r)) @ rng.normal(size=(true_r, dd))
delta = low_rank + 0.05 * rng.normal(size=(dd, dd))    # rank 4 plus noise
Ud, sd, Vtd = np.linalg.svd(delta)
rel = [np.sqrt(np.sum(sd[r:] ** 2) / np.sum(sd ** 2)) for r in range(0, 21)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 3.4))
ax.semilogy(range(0, 21), np.maximum(rel, 1e-3), "o-",
            color=PALETTE["model"])
ax.axvline(true_r, ls="--", color=PALETTE["neutral"])
ax.set_xlabel("rank r of the approximation")
ax.set_ylabel("relative error")
plt.show()
print(f"relative error  r=3: {rel[3]:.3f}  r=4: {rel[4]:.3f}  r=8: {rel[8]:.3f}")







Figure 7.11: How much of a synthetic update is captured by a rank-r approximation. The true update has rank 4 plus noise. The error drops sharply at r = 4 and then flattens. Adding more rank mostly fits noise.





relative error  r=3: 0.453  r=4: 0.025  r=8: 0.024


LoRA initialises \(\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}\), so \(\Delta\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{0}\) at the start. The model begins exactly as the pre-trained one.

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text:
7.7 From first principles to production
Libraries provide the same decompositions. We confirm they agree with our code.

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import torch

skl = PCA(n_components=10).fit(X)
print("sklearn variance ratio matches ours:",
      np.allclose(skl.explained_variance_ratio_, (lam / lam.sum())[:10]))

Ut, st, Vht = torch.linalg.svd(torch.tensor(Xc), full_matrices=False)
print("torch singular values match NumPy:", np.allclose(st.numpy(), s))

# a LoRA layer in PyTorch: frozen W0 + trainable low-rank update
class LoRALinear(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_out, r):
        super().__init__()
        self.W0 = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(d_out, d_in),
                                     requires_grad=False)
        self.A = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(r, d_in) * 0.01)
        self.B = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d_out, r))      # B = 0 at start
    def forward(self, x):
        return x @ self.W0.T + (x @ self.A.T) @ self.B.T

layer = LoRALinear(512, 512, r=8)
x_in = torch.randn(4, 512)
print("output equals frozen layer at start:",
      torch.allclose(layer(x_in), x_in @ layer.W0.T))
n_train = sum(p.numel() for p in layer.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
print("trainable parameters:", n_train, "  frozen:", layer.W0.numel())

sklearn variance ratio matches ours: True
torch singular values match NumPy: True
output equals frozen layer at start: True
trainable parameters: 8192   frozen: 262144

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text:
7.8 Failure modes

7.8.1 Forgetting to centre
Without centring, the first “principal component” points at the mean, not at the direction of largest spread.

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
Xoff = rng.normal(size=(500, 2)) * [1.0, 0.3] + np.array([10.0, 10.0])
ev, evec = np.linalg.eigh(Xoff.T @ Xoff / len(Xoff))
pc1_uncentred = evec[:, -1]
mean_dir = Xoff.mean(axis=0) / np.linalg.norm(Xoff.mean(axis=0))
print("PC1 without centring vs mean direction, |cos| =",
      round(abs(pc1_uncentred @ mean_dir), 4))
_, _, evec_c = pca_fit(Xoff)
print("PC1 with centring: ", np.round(np.abs(evec_c[:, 0]), 3),
      " (spread is along axis 0)")

PC1 without centring vs mean direction, |cos| = 1.0
PC1 with centring:  [1.    0.018]  (spread is along axis 0)




7.8.2 Features on different scales
PCA maximises variance. A feature measured in large units has a large variance and dominates. Standardise features first, unless the scale carries meaning (Chapter 3).


7.8.3 Sign and ties
Eigenvectors are defined up to sign: \(\mathbf{v}\) and \(-\mathbf{v}\) are both valid. Two eigenvalues that are nearly equal give directions that are unstable under small data changes. Do not interpret such directions individually.


7.8.4 Nonlinear structure
PCA is linear. It finds flat subspaces. Data on a curved surface can have no good linear summary.

from sklearn.datasets import make_circles
Xcir, ycir = make_circles(n_samples=600, factor=0.4, noise=0.04, random_state=0)
mu_c, lam_c, V_c = pca_fit(Xcir)
z1 = pca_transform(Xcir, mu_c, V_c, 1)[:, 0]

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2))
ax1.scatter(*Xcir.T, c=ycir, cmap="coolwarm", s=8); ax1.set_aspect("equal")
ax1.set_title("data")
style = dict(bins=30, alpha=0.6)
ax2.hist(z1[ycir == 0], color=PALETTE["loss"], label="outer ring", **style)
ax2.hist(z1[ycir == 1], color=PALETTE["data"], label="inner ring", **style)
ax2.set_title("projection on PC1"); ax2.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 7.12: Two concentric circles. The two classes are clearly separate in 2D, but no single threshold on the first principal component separates them: the inner ring projects inside the range of the outer ring. Linear compression misses nonlinear structure. Autoencoders (Chapter 38) can handle it.

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text:
7.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now find structure. It can rank directions by how much variation they carry, compress data to a few of them, and describe a large matrix by a small one. This closes Part II: the system can represent the world as vectors, matrices, and tensors, measure them, and simplify them.
Part III turns to transformation. A model must not just hold representations. It must change them, step by step, into something useful. Chapter 8 starts with the general notion of a function.

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text:
Chapter summary

An eigenvector keeps its direction under a matrix: \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\).
The covariance matrix \(\mathbf{S}=\frac1N\mathbf{X}_c^{\intercal}\mathbf{X}_c\) describes the shape of a data cloud.
PCA keeps the top eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{S}\). They maximise the variance of the projection.
SVD factors any matrix as rotate–stretch–rotate: \(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{\intercal}\).
The best rank-\(k\) approximation drops the small singular values. Its error is \(\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2\).
LoRA trains \(\Delta\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\) with \(2dr\ll d^2\) parameters.
Always centre. Standardise features when scales differ. PCA cannot find nonlinear structure.

title: 7  Structure Hidden in Data
text:
Exercises

Compute. Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\). What is its rank?
Compute. For the points \((1,2),(3,4),(5,6),(7,8)\), centre the data and compute the covariance matrix by hand. What is the first principal direction?
Derive. Show that the trace of \(\mathbf{S}\) equals the sum of its eigenvalues. What does it say about the total variance?
Derive. Using Equation 7.4, show that the columns of \(\mathbf{V}\) are eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{A}^{\intercal}\mathbf{A}\) and that \(\sigma_i^2\) are the eigenvalues.
Derive. A LoRA update uses \(r=8\) on a \(d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}\) matrix. Give the parameter count. For which shapes is LoRA not a saving?
Code. Run PCA on the digits restricted to classes 3, 5, and 8. Plot the 2D projection. Do the classes separate better than with all ten?
Code. Find the smallest \(k\) such that the digit reconstructions have mean squared error below 1. Compare with the 90%-variance rule.
Code. Compress each of the three colour channels of the sample photo at rank 30. Recombine them. Compare storage and quality with the greyscale case.
Diagnose. A team runs PCA on a table with columns “income in dollars” and “age in years”. The first component is almost exactly the income axis. Explain, and fix it.
Explain. Why would a fine-tuning update be approximately low rank, when the model itself needed many parameters to learn the original task?

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text:
8.1 The system problem
Part II built objects: vectors, matrices, tensors. Part III builds the machinery that acts on them. Before we study particular layers, we need the general idea precisely, because every later chapter uses it.
system_map(highlight=["Representation", "Transformation"],
           sublabels={"Transformation": "Ch. 8–12"});
plt.show()







Figure 8.1: Part III builds the Transformation stage. This chapter gives its vocabulary.

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text: What is a model, exactly, and what can we do with functions to build bigger models from smaller ones?

title: 8  Functions as Machines
section: 8.2 Intuition: a function is a machine
text:
8.2 Intuition: a function is a machine
A function is a machine with one input slot and one output slot. You put an input in. One output comes out. The same input always gives the same output.
A machine may be simple (add one) or large (a language model). From outside, both have the same form. This is why the language of functions is the right language for AI systems.

fig = box_flow(["x", "f₁", "f₂", "f₃", "ŷ"],
               colors=[PALETTE["data"], PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["model"],
                       PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["prob"]], figsize=(8, 1.3))
plt.show()







Figure 8.2: Three machines in a chain. Each takes a vector and returns a vector. The chain is again one machine.

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text:
8.3 The mathematical object
A function \(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\) assigns to every \(x\in\mathcal{X}\) exactly one \(f(x)\in\mathcal{Y}\).








Term
Meaning
Example: \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\)




Domain \(\mathcal{X}\)
allowed inputs
all real numbers


Codomain \(\mathcal{Y}\)
where outputs are declared to live
all real numbers


Range (image)
outputs that actually occur
\([0,\infty)\)


Graph
the set of pairs \((x,f(x))\)
a parabola



In AI the inputs and outputs are vectors, so most functions have the form \(f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^m\). A function of this kind is just \(m\) scalar functions that share the same input. Chapter 17 studies how to differentiate such functions.

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text:
8.4 Operations on functions

8.4.1 Composition
Given \(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\) and \(g:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{Z}\), the composition \(g\circ f\) applies \(f\) first:
\[
(g\circ f)(x)=g\bigl(f(x)\bigr).
\tag{8.1}\]
The codomain of \(f\) must match the domain of \(g\). For vector functions this is the shape rule of Chapter 2: the output size of \(f\) must equal the input size of \(g\).
Composition is associative: \(h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f\). So we may write \(h\circ g\circ f\) with no brackets.






TipProof of associativity



Apply both sides to any \(x\): \[
\bigl(h\circ(g\circ f)\bigr)(x)=h\bigl((g\circ f)(x)\bigr)=h\bigl(g(f(x))\bigr)=(h\circ g)\bigl(f(x)\bigr)=\bigl((h\circ g)\circ f\bigr)(x).\ \blacksquare
\]


Composition is not commutative: \(g\circ f\neq f\circ g\) in general.
A neural network is a composition of layer functions:
\[
f_\theta=f_{L}\circ f_{L-1}\circ\dots\circ f_1.
\tag{8.2}\]
We now build composition in code and test associativity.

def compose(*fs):
    """compose(h, g, f)(x) == h(g(f(x)))  -- the rightmost function runs first."""
    def composed(x):
        for f in reversed(fs):
            x = f(x)
        return x
    return composed

f = lambda x: 0.5 * x ** 2 - 1.0
g = np.tanh
h = lambda x: 3.0 * x + 2.0

xs = np.linspace(-3, 3, 7)
left  = compose(h, compose(g, f))(xs)
right = compose(compose(h, g), f)(xs)
print("associative:", np.allclose(left, right))
print("commutative:", np.allclose(compose(g, f)(xs), compose(f, g)(xs)))

associative: True
commutative: False



x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, f(x), color=PALETTE["data"], label="f(x) = x²/2 − 1")
ax.plot(x, g(x), color=PALETTE["prob"], label="g(x) = tanh x")
ax.plot(x, compose(g, f)(x), color=PALETTE["model"], lw=2.5, label="g∘f")
ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 3.5); ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_xlabel("x")
plt.show()







Figure 8.3: Composition on the real line. f squeezes and shifts, g = tanh saturates. The composite g∘f combines both: it is flat where f is large.







8.4.2 Identity and inverse
The identity \(\text{id}(x)=x\) does nothing. An inverse \(f^{-1}\) undoes \(f\):
\[
f^{-1}\circ f=\text{id}.
\tag{8.3}\]
Not every function has one. Two properties decide it.








Property
Definition
Meaning




Injective (one-to-one)
\(f(a)=f(b)\Rightarrow a=b\)
different inputs give different outputs


Surjective (onto)
every \(y\in\mathcal{Y}\) is some \(f(x)\)
every output is reached


Bijective
both
an inverse exists









TipWhy a non-injective function has no inverse



Suppose \(f(a)=f(b)=y\) with \(a\ne b\). A left inverse \(g\) would need \(g(y)=g(f(a))=a\) and also \(g(y)=g(f(b))=b\). But \(a\ne b\). No single value \(g(y)\) can do both. \(\blacksquare\)


For compositions, inverses undo in reverse order: \((g\circ f)^{-1}=f^{-1}\circ g^{-1}\). You take off your shoes before your socks only if you put on socks before shoes. This is the same pattern as \((\mathbf{AB})^{\intercal}=\mathbf{B}^{\intercal}\mathbf{A}^{\intercal}\) in Chapter 5.


8.4.3 Linear and nonlinear
A function is linear if \(f(a\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{y})=af(\mathbf{x})+bf(\mathbf{y})\). Matrices are exactly the linear functions on vectors (Chapter 5). All other functions are nonlinear. We study the simplest linear case in Chapter 9 and the nonlinear case in Chapter 10.

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text:
8.5 Parameterized families
A model is not one function. It is a family of functions, selected by parameters \(\theta\):
\[
\mathcal{F}=\{f_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}.
\tag{8.4}\]
In code, a parameterized function is a closure: a function that returns a function.

def make_f(a, b, c):
    """Return the function f_theta with theta = (a, b, c)."""
    return lambda x: a * np.tanh(b * x) + c

x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 300)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for theta in [(1.0, 1.0, 0.0), (2.0, 0.5, 0.0), (1.0, 4.0, 0.0),
              (1.0, 1.0, 1.5), (-1.5, 1.0, 0.0)]:
    ax.plot(x, make_f(*theta)(x), label=f"θ = {theta}")
ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.set_xlabel("x")
plt.show()







Figure 8.4: One family, many functions. f_θ(x) = a·tanh(b·x) + c. Changing the three parameters changes height, steepness, and offset. Learning picks one curve.






8.5.1 The loss is a function of the parameters
There are two ways to look at \(f_\theta(x)\).

Fix \(\theta\) and vary \(x\): a function of the input. This is inference.
Fix the data \(x\) and vary \(\theta\): a function of the parameters. This is what training optimises.

The loss \(L(\theta)=\frac1N\sum_{i}\ell(f_\theta(x_i),y_i)\) is of the second kind. The data is held fixed. The parameters are the argument. This switch of viewpoint is the core of learning.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
xd = rng.uniform(-2, 2, 30)
yd = 2.0 * xd + 1.0 + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 30)

def loss(a, b):                      # data (xd, yd) is fixed inside
    pred = a * xd[:, None, None] + b           # (30, 200, 200)
    return np.mean((pred - yd[:, None, None]) ** 2, axis=0)

A_, B_ = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1, 5, 200), np.linspace(-3, 5, 200))
Lz = loss(A_, B_)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.2))
cs = ax.contour(A_, B_, Lz, levels=15, cmap="viridis")
ax.plot([2], [1], "*", color=PALETTE["loss"], ms=14)
ax.set_xlabel("slope a"); ax.set_ylabel("offset b")
plt.show()







Figure 8.5: The loss as a function of the parameters (a, b) of a line. Contours show L(a, b) for fixed data. The minimum sits near the true values (2, 1). Chapters 16 and 17 show how to move downhill on this surface.

title: 8  Functions as Machines
section: 8.6 Geometry: what maps do to space
text:
8.6 Geometry: what maps do to space
For maps of the plane, we can see the function by watching what it does to a grid. Linear maps keep grid lines straight (Chapter 5). Nonlinear maps bend them. Maps that lose information fold or flatten them.
We compare four maps \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^2\).








Map
Rule
Invertible?




Bend
\((x,y)\mapsto(x,\ y+0.4x^2)\)
yes: \(v\mapsto v-0.4u^2\)


Squash
\((x,y)\mapsto(\tanh x,\ \tanh y)\)
yes, onto \((-1,1)^2\)


Fold
\((x,y)\mapsto(|x|,\ y)\)
no: \(x\) and \(-x\) collide


ReLU
\((x,y)\mapsto(\max(0,x),\max(0,y))\)
no: a whole quadrant collapses




maps = {
    "bend":   lambda x, y: (x, y + 0.4 * x ** 2),
    "squash": lambda x, y: (np.tanh(x), np.tanh(y)),
    "fold":   lambda x, y: (np.abs(x), y),
    "ReLU":   lambda x, y: (np.maximum(0, x), np.maximum(0, y)),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 3.0))
for ax, (name, fn) in zip(axes, maps.items()):
    ok = name in ("bend", "squash")              # invertible maps in green
    warp_fn(ax, fn, extent=2.0, title=name,
            color=PALETTE["grad"] if ok else PALETTE["loss"])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 8.6: Four maps of the plane. Bend and squash keep every point distinct and can be undone. Fold maps two points to one. ReLU collapses three quadrants onto the axes. Information is lost.





We confirm in code that the first two can be undone and the last two cannot.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
P = rng.uniform(-2, 2, size=(1000, 2))                      # random points

bend_inv   = lambda u, v: (u, v - 0.4 * u ** 2)
squash_inv = lambda u, v: (np.arctanh(u), np.arctanh(v))

for name, fwd, inv in [("bend", maps["bend"], bend_inv),
                       ("squash", maps["squash"], squash_inv)]:
    u, v = fwd(P[:, 0], P[:, 1]); xr, yr = inv(u, v)
    print(f"{name:7s} round-trip error: {np.max(np.abs(xr - P[:, 0])):.1e}")

# fold: both x and -x give the same output, so no inverse can recover the sign
u1, _ = maps["fold"](np.array([1.5]), np.array([0.0]))
u2, _ = maps["fold"](np.array([-1.5]), np.array([0.0]))
print("fold:   f(1.5, 0) and f(-1.5, 0) first coordinates:", u1[0], u2[0])

bend    round-trip error: 0.0e+00
squash  round-trip error: 1.1e-15
fold:   f(1.5, 0) and f(-1.5, 0) first coordinates: 1.5 1.5

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text:
8.7 Computation: models are callables
A model is a function in the programming sense, too. In PyTorch, nn.Sequential is literally composition:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
f1, f2, f3 = nn.Linear(4, 8), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(8, 2)

seq = nn.Sequential(f1, f2, f3)                           # f3 ∘ f2 ∘ f1
x_in = torch.randn(5, 4)

by_hand = f3(f2(f1(x_in)))
print("Sequential == f3(f2(f1(x)))  :", torch.allclose(seq(x_in), by_hand))
print("shape rule: 4 -> 8 -> 8 -> 2, output:", tuple(seq(x_in).shape))

Sequential == f3(f2(f1(x)))  : True
shape rule: 4 -> 8 -> 8 -> 2, output: (5, 2)


Shape mismatches are composition errors: the output size of one layer must equal the input size of the next.

try:
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 8), nn.Linear(6, 2))(x_in)    # 8 != 6
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", str(e)[:70], "...")

RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (5x8 and 6x2) ...

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text:
8.8 Information loss on purpose
A classifier maps 64 pixel values to one of 10 labels. This map is many-to-one by design. Millions of different images get the same label. The classifier is not invertible, and it should not be: it throws away everything except class evidence.

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
digits = load_digits()
X, y = digits.data, digits.target

means = np.array([X[y == c].mean(axis=0) for c in range(10)])           # (10, 64)
Xn = X / np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True)
Mn = means / np.linalg.norm(means, axis=1, keepdims=True)
pred = (Xn @ Mn.T).argmax(axis=1)           # f: R^64 -> {0..9}

print(f"accuracy of this simple classifier: {np.mean(pred == y):.3f}")
same = np.where(pred == 3)[0]
print(f"images mapped to class 3: {len(same)}; distinct pixel vectors: "
      f"{len({tuple(r) for r in X[same]})}")

accuracy of this simple classifier: 0.906
images mapped to class 3: 167; distinct pixel vectors: 167


The consequence is general: a trained classifier cannot recover its input from its output. Information has been discarded. Each layer in a network may add information-losing steps such as ReLU or pooling.

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text:
8.9 Failure modes
Outside the domain. Some functions are defined only on part of \(\mathbb{R}\). log(0), sqrt(-1), and 1/0 give -inf, nan, or inf. These values spread through a whole computation.

with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
    print("log(0)    =", np.log(0.0))
    print("sqrt(-1)  =", np.sqrt(-1.0))
    print("1/0       =", np.float64(1.0) / 0.0)
    print("0 * log(0) =", 0.0 * np.log(0.0), "  (needs a convention, Ch. 15)")

log(0)    = -inf
sqrt(-1)  = nan
1/0       = inf
0 * log(0) = nan   (needs a convention, Ch. 15)


Discontinuous functions. floor, argmax, and thresholds jump. Small input changes can give large output changes. Their derivative is zero almost everywhere, so gradients cannot flow through them. This is why classifiers output probabilities (via softmax, Chapter 24) and not the argmax during training.
Loss of invertibility. Do not assume that a hidden representation can be mapped back to the input. Some architectures (normalising flows, Chapter 43) are built to stay invertible. Most are not.
Hidden dependence on parameters. A function that looks like it only depends on \(x\) may depend on global state (random seeds, dropout, batch statistics). Then equal inputs give different outputs. Mathematical functions have no such hidden state. Code must be careful to match them.

title: 8  Functions as Machines
section: 8.10 Where this appears in modern AI
text:
8.10 Where this appears in modern AI



Idea
Where




Function \(f_\theta:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^m\)
every model


Composition
layer stacks, residual blocks, whole Transformers


Parameterized family
the model class; fine-tuning changes \(\theta\)


Loss as a function of \(\theta\)
training objective

pooling, ReLU, classification heads


Invertible maps
normalising flows; reversible layers
