log, sqrt, division need safe forms

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text:
8.11 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system now has the vocabulary of transformation: a model is a function, a network is a composition, a family is selected by parameters, and training views the loss as a function of the parameters. We know that a map may lose information and when it may be undone.
We have not yet chosen which functions to compose. The simplest building block is the linear function. Chapter 9 studies it.

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text:
Chapter summary

A function \(f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\) gives one output for each input. Domain, codomain, and range describe it.
Composition \(g\circ f\) applies \(f\) first. It is associative and not commutative.
An inverse exists only for bijections. Inverses of compositions reverse the order.
A model is a parameterized family \(f_\theta\). In code it is a closure.
Training treats the loss as a function of \(\theta\) with the data fixed.
Maps of the plane can be pictured by their effect on a grid: bend, squash, fold, collapse.
A network is \(f_{L}\circ\dots\circ f_1\), and shape mismatches are composition errors.
Invalid domains (log 0) and jumps (argmax) break computation and gradients.

title: 8  Functions as Machines
text:
Exercises

Compose. For \(f(x)=2x+1\) and \(g(x)=x^2\), compute \(g\circ f\) and \(f\circ g\). Show they are different.
Invert. Find the inverse of \(f(x)=\frac{x-3}{2}\). Verify \(f^{-1}\circ f=\text{id}\).
Classify. Is \(f(x)=x^3\) injective? Surjective on \(\mathbb{R}\)? Is \(f(x)=e^x\) surjective onto \(\mathbb{R}\)?
Prove. If \(f\) and \(g\) are injective, then \(g\circ f\) is injective.
Prove. Show that ReLU applied element-wise on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is not injective for any \(n\ge1\).
Code. Write make_layer(W, b, act) that returns the function \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto\text{act}(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b})\). Compose three layers and check the shapes.
Code. Add the “swirl” map \((x,y)\mapsto(x\cos r-y\sin r,\ x\sin r+y\cos r)\) with \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) to the grid figure. Is it invertible?
Code. Plot \(L(a)\) for a one-parameter model \(f_a(x)=a\,x\) on the data of this chapter. Where is its minimum?
Diagnose. A function f(x) returns different values for the same x on two calls. List three possible causes in a deep learning program.
Explain. Why is it acceptable that a classifier is not invertible? Give one example in which an invertible model is required.

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text:
9.1 The system problem
Part II gave us vectors and matrices. Part III asks how a model transforms a representation into another one. The simplest transformation that can be learned is a matrix plus a shift.
system_map(highlight=["Representation", "Transformation"],
           sublabels={"Transformation": "Ch. 8–12"});
plt.show()







Figure 9.1: Chapter 9 adds the first learnable transformation to the Transformation stage.

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text: What can \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}\) do, and why is it the main building block of neural networks despite its limits?

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text:
9.2 What linear means
A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear if for all vectors \(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}\) and scalars \(a,b\):
\[
f(a\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{z})=a\,f(\mathbf{x})+b\,f(\mathbf{z}).
\tag{9.1}\]
Two special cases carry the idea: additivity \(f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{z})=f(\mathbf{x})+f(\mathbf{z})\) and homogeneity \(f(a\mathbf{x})=af(\mathbf{x})\). One consequence: \(f(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}\).
Every matrix gives a linear function. The reverse also holds: a linear function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a matrix whose columns are \(f(\mathbf{e}_1),\dots,f(\mathbf{e}_n)\) (Chapter 5).
We test linearity numerically. The test samples random inputs and checks Equation 9.1.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def is_linear(f, n, trials=100, tol=1e-9):
    for _ in range(trials):
        x, z = rng.normal(size=n), rng.normal(size=n)
        a, b = rng.normal(size=2)
        if not np.allclose(f(a * x + b * z), a * f(x) + b * f(z), atol=tol):
            return False
    return True

W = rng.normal(size=(3, 4)); bias = rng.normal(size=3)
tests = {
    "W x":              lambda x: W @ x,
    "W x + b":          lambda x: W @ x + bias,
    "ReLU(W x)":        lambda x: np.maximum(0, W @ x),
    "x ⊙ x  (square)":  lambda x: x * x,
    "sum of x":         lambda x: np.array([x.sum()]),
}
for name, f in tests.items():
    n = 4
    print(f"{name:18s} linear: {is_linear(f, n)}")

W x                linear: True
W x + b            linear: False
ReLU(W x)          linear: False
x ⊙ x  (square)    linear: False
sum of x           linear: True


Note that \(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}\) fails the test. It is affine, not linear, because \(f(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{b}\ne\mathbf{0}\). In machine learning we call it a “linear layer”, and the context decides what is meant.

9.2.1 The bias trick
An affine map can be written as a linear map in one more dimension. Append a constant \(1\) to the input and a column \(\mathbf{b}\) to the matrix:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{W}&\mathbf{b}\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}.
\tag{9.2}\]

x = rng.normal(size=4)
W_aug = np.hstack([W, bias[:, None]])            # (3, 5)
x_aug = np.append(x, 1.0)                        # (5,)
print("bias trick matches:", np.allclose(W_aug @ x_aug, W @ x + bias))

bias trick matches: True


This is why we may study \(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}\) and treat the bias as a weight on a constant input.

title: 9  Linear Transformations
section: 9.3 Geometry: what a layer does to space
text:
9.3 Geometry: what a layer does to space
Chapter 7 showed that any matrix is rotate–stretch–rotate (SVD). A linear layer adds one more step: translate by \(\mathbf{b}\).

W2 = np.array([[1.6, 0.5], [0.3, 0.9]]); b2 = np.array([1.2, 0.8])
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(W2)
t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200); C = np.stack([np.cos(t), np.sin(t)])
steps = [("input: circle", C),
         ("rotate  Vᵀ", Vt @ C),
         ("stretch  Σ", np.diag(s) @ Vt @ C),
         ("rotate  U, shift  b", U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt @ C + b2[:, None])]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 3.0))
for ax, (title, pts) in zip(axes, steps):
    setup_2d(ax, xlim=(-2.5, 3.5), ylim=(-2.5, 3.5), xlabel="", ylabel="")
    ax.plot(*pts, color=PALETTE["data"], lw=2); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
draw_arrow(axes[3], b2, color=PALETTE["model"], lw=2.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("singular values (stretch factors):", np.round(s, 3))







Figure 9.2: Anatomy of an affine layer on the plane. The unit circle is rotated by Vᵀ (no visible change), stretched by Σ along the axes, rotated by U, and shifted by b. The result is an ellipse.





singular values (stretch factors): [1.786 0.722]


Four things cannot happen in a linear layer:

Straight lines never become curves.
Parallel lines stay parallel.
The origin moves only by the shift \(\mathbf{b}\).
A rank-deficient \(\mathbf{W}\) flattens space onto a lower-dimensional subspace. Information is lost for good.

title: 9  Linear Transformations
section: 9.4 Hyperplanes: each output is a boundary
text:
9.4 Hyperplanes: each output is a boundary
Consider one output of a layer: \(y=\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b\). The set where \(y=0\) is a hyperplane: a line in 2D, a plane in 3D, and a flat \((n-1)\)-dimensional surface in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The vector \(\mathbf{w}\) is normal (perpendicular) to it. The sign of \(y\) tells on which side a point lies.






TipDerivation: signed distance to a hyperplane



Let \(H=\{\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b=0\}\). Take any point \(\mathbf{p}\in H\). The unit normal is \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{w}/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\). The signed distance of \(\mathbf{x}\) from \(H\) is the length of the projection of \(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p}\) onto \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}\) (Chapter 4):
\[
d(\mathbf{x})=\hat{\mathbf{w}}\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p})=\frac{\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{p}}{\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert}=\frac{\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b}{\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert},
\]
because \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{p}=-b\) for \(\mathbf{p}\in H\). \(\blacksquare\)


So the output \(y\) is the signed distance to the boundary, scaled by \(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\). A linear classifier decides by the sign of \(y\).

9.4.1 A linear classifier: the perceptron
The perceptron is the oldest learning rule. For each misclassified point, move the boundary towards it: \(\mathbf{w}\leftarrow\mathbf{w}+y_{i}\mathbf{x}_i\), where \(y_{i}\in\{-1,+1\}\). We use the bias trick, so \(b\) is part of \(\mathbf{w}\).

def perceptron(X, y, epochs=50):
    Xa = np.hstack([X, np.ones((len(X), 1))])        # bias trick, (N, d+1)
    w = np.zeros(Xa.shape[1])
    for _ in range(epochs):
        mistakes = 0
        for xi, yi in zip(Xa, y):
            if yi * (w @ xi) <= 0:                   # wrong side (or on boundary)
                w += yi * xi
                mistakes += 1
        if mistakes == 0:
            break
    return w

from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
Xb, yb = make_blobs(n_samples=120, centers=[[-1.5, -1.0], [1.5, 1.2]],
                    cluster_std=0.9, random_state=0)
yb = 2 * yb - 1                                       # labels in {-1, +1}
w = perceptron(Xb, yb)
acc = np.mean(np.sign(np.hstack([Xb, np.ones((len(Xb), 1))]) @ w) == yb)
print("weights (w1, w2, b):", np.round(w, 2), "  accuracy:", acc)

weights (w1, w2, b): [ 2.68  0.7  -1.  ]   accuracy: 1.0



fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.2))
ax.scatter(*Xb[yb == -1].T, color=PALETTE["data"], s=14, label="class −1")
ax.scatter(*Xb[yb == 1].T, color=PALETTE["model"], s=14, label="class +1")
xs = np.linspace(-4, 4, 50)
line = lambda c: (c - w[0] * xs - w[2]) / w[1]          # w1 x1 + w2 x2 + b = c
ax.plot(xs, line(0), color="black", lw=2)
for c in (-1, 1):
    ax.plot(xs, line(c), "--", color=PALETTE["neutral"], lw=1)
draw_arrow(ax, w[:2] / np.linalg.norm(w[:2]) * 1.5, origin=(0, -w[2] / w[1]),
           color=PALETTE["loss"], lw=2.5)
ax.set_xlim(-4, 4); ax.set_ylim(-4, 4); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.show()







Figure 9.3: A linear classifier in 2D. The line is the hyperplane w·x + b = 0. The arrow w is normal to it and points to the positive side. The dashed lines show distance 1/‖w‖ on each side.







9.4.2 What a single hyperplane cannot do: XOR
XOR is true when exactly one input is true. Its four points \((0,0),(1,1)\mapsto-1\) and \((0,1),(1,0)\mapsto+1\) cannot be separated by one line. No choice of \(\mathbf{w},b\) works.






TipProof that no line separates XOR



Suppose \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b\) is positive at \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\), and negative at \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\). Adding the two positive conditions: \(w_1+w_2+2b>0\). Adding the two negative ones: \(w_1+w_2+2b<0\). Contradiction. \(\blacksquare\)



Xx = np.array([[0, 0], [1, 1], [0, 1], [1, 0]], dtype=float)
yx = np.array([-1, -1, 1, 1])
Xxa = np.hstack([Xx, np.ones((4, 1))])
best = 0.0
w_x = np.zeros(3)
for epoch in range(200):
    for xi, yi in zip(Xxa, yx):
        if yi * (w_x @ xi) <= 0:
            w_x += yi * xi
    best = max(best, np.mean(np.sign(Xxa @ w_x) == yx))
print(f"best accuracy over 200 epochs: {best:.2f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.6, 3.4))
for pt, lab in zip(Xx, yx):
    ax.scatter(*pt, s=160, color=PALETTE["model"] if lab == 1 else PALETTE["data"])
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 1.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 1.5); ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$"); ax.set_ylabel("$x_2$")
plt.show()

best accuracy over 200 epochs: 0.50








Figure 9.4: XOR is not linearly separable. The perceptron never settles: its accuracy on the four points never exceeds 75%, however long it trains. In this run the best value is 50%.

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text:
9.5 A linear classifier for digits
For many classes, we use one hyperplane per class: \(\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{10\times64}\). The score vector is \(\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}\), and the prediction is the largest score. We fit \(\mathbf{W}\) by least squares against one-hot targets. This is a closed-form solve (Chapter 5). We do not need gradients yet.

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
digits = load_digits()
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(digits.data / 16.0, digits.target,
                                      test_size=0.25, random_state=0,
                                      stratify=digits.target)
A_tr = np.hstack([Xtr, np.ones((len(Xtr), 1))])        # bias trick, (N, 65)
T = np.eye(10)[ytr]                                    # one-hot targets, (N, 10)
Wls = np.linalg.lstsq(A_tr, T, rcond=None)[0]          # (65, 10)

A_te = np.hstack([Xte, np.ones((len(Xte), 1))])
pred = (A_te @ Wls).argmax(axis=1)
print(f"test accuracy of the linear classifier: {np.mean(pred == yte):.3f}")
print("parameters:", Wls.size)

test accuracy of the linear classifier: 0.938
parameters: 650


A linear model recognises most digits. Each row of \(\mathbf{W}\) is a template: it scores an image by how well it matches a pixel pattern.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 10, figsize=(11, 1.5))
for c, ax in enumerate(axes):
    ax.imshow(Wls[:64, c].reshape(8, 8), cmap="RdBu_r",
              vmin=-1.2, vmax=1.2)
    ax.set_title(str(c), fontsize=10); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 9.5: The ten rows of the linear classifier as 8×8 images. Red pixels raise the score of the class, blue pixels lower it. Each class has a recognisable template.

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text:
9.6 Cost: parameters and FLOPs
A layer from \(n_{\text{in}}\) to \(n_{\text{out}}\) has \(n_{\text{out}}n_{\text{in}}+n_{\text{out}}\) parameters. It needs about \(2\,n_{\text{out}}n_{\text{in}}\) FLOPs per input vector: one multiply and one add per weight.

def layer_cost(n_in, n_out):
    params = n_out * n_in + n_out
    flops = 2 * n_out * n_in
    return params, flops

rows = [("digits classifier", 64, 10),
        ("MNIST classifier", 784, 10),
        ("hidden layer", 784, 256),
        ("transformer projection", 4096, 4096),
        ("LLM MLP up-projection", 4096, 16384)]
print(f"{'layer':26s} {'params':>14s} {'FLOPs / vector':>16s}")
for name, n_in, n_out in rows:
    p, f = layer_cost(n_in, n_out)
    print(f"{name:26s} {p:14,d} {f:16,d}")

layer                              params   FLOPs / vector
digits classifier                     650            1,280
MNIST classifier                    7,850           15,680
hidden layer                      200,960          401,408
transformer projection         16,781,312       33,554,432
LLM MLP up-projection          67,125,248      134,217,728

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text:
9.7 Stacked linear layers collapse
What if we stack two linear layers? The result is again one linear layer.
\[
\mathbf{W}_2(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}_1)+\mathbf{b}_2=(\mathbf{W}_{2}\mathbf{W}_1)\mathbf{x}+(\mathbf{W}_{2}\mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_2).
\tag{9.3}\]

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
W1, b1 = rng.normal(size=(5, 4)), rng.normal(size=5)
W2, b2 = rng.normal(size=(3, 5)), rng.normal(size=3)
x = rng.normal(size=4)

two_layers = W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2
one_layer = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2)
print("two layers == one layer:", np.allclose(two_layers, one_layer))

two layers == one layer: True


Depth gives no new power without something between the layers. Chapter 10 adds it.

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text:
9.8 From first principles to production
nn.Linear is this layer. We load our least-squares weights into it and check that it gives the same predictions.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

lin = nn.Linear(64, 10).double()
with torch.no_grad():
    lin.weight.copy_(torch.tensor(Wls[:64].T))        # (10, 64)
    lin.bias.copy_(torch.tensor(Wls[64]))             # (10,)
out = lin(torch.tensor(Xte))
print("same predictions as NumPy:", bool((out.argmax(1).numpy() == pred).all()))

same predictions as NumPy: True

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text:
9.9 Failure modes
Not linearly separable. XOR is the smallest example. Real data is often not separable in the raw feature space. A richer representation or a nonlinearity is needed.
Collinear features. If one feature is a combination of others, the least-squares problem has no unique answer and the normal equations \(\mathbf{A}^{\intercal}\mathbf{A}\) are singular.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.normal(size=(50, 2))
A_col = np.column_stack([a, a[:, 0] + a[:, 1]])        # third column = sum of first two
print("rank of A:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(A_col), " columns:", A_col.shape[1])
print("condition number of AᵀA: %.1e" % np.linalg.cond(A_col.T @ A_col))

rank of A: 2  columns: 3
condition number of AᵀA: 1.9e+16


lstsq returns the minimum-norm solution and is safe. Solving the normal equations by hand is not.
Features at different scales. The weights on large-scale features are tiny and on small-scale features are huge. Standardise first (Chapter 3).
A boundary is only a sign. The raw output \(y\) is a distance times \(\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\). It is not a probability. Chapter 24 turns scores into probabilities.

title: 9  Linear Transformations
section: 9.10 Where this appears in modern AI
text:
9.10 Where this appears in modern AI







Place
Linear layer role




MLP in a Transformer
two large linear layers (up and down projection)


Attention
\(\mathbf{W}_Q,\mathbf{W}_K,\mathbf{W}_V,\mathbf{W}_O\) are linear maps


Classification head
one linear layer from features to class scores


Token output head
linear map from hidden state to vocabulary scores


\(1\times1\) convolution
a linear layer applied at every pixel


LoRA (Chapter 7)
a low-rank update to a linear layer


Most model parameters
live in linear layers; most FLOPs are matrix products

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text:
9.11 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system has its first learnable transformation: an affine layer that rotates, stretches, projects, and shifts, and whose rows are hyperplane tests. It is cheap, differentiable, and runs fast on hardware.
It has a hard limit. Any stack of linear layers is one linear layer. The system still cannot compute XOR. Chapter 10 adds the missing ingredient.

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text:
Chapter summary

A function is linear if \(f(a\mathbf{x}+b\mathbf{z})=af(\mathbf{x})+bf(\mathbf{z})\). Matrices are exactly the linear maps.
\(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}\) is affine. The bias trick appends a 1 to the input.
A layer is rotate–stretch–rotate–shift. It never bends space.
Each output is a hyperplane. \(y/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\) is the signed distance.
A perceptron learns a hyperplane by moving it towards mistakes. It cannot learn XOR.
A layer has \(n_{\text{out}}n_{\text{in}}+n_{\text{out}}\) parameters and about \(2n_{\text{out}}n_{\text{in}}\) FLOPs.
Stacked linear layers collapse into one.

title: 9  Linear Transformations
text:
Exercises

Test. Which are linear? (a) \(f(x)=3x\), (b) \(f(x)=3x+1\), (c) \(f(x,y)=x-2y\), (d) \(f(x,y)=xy\), (e) \(f(\mathbf{x})=\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\).
Compute. The hyperplane is \(2x_1-x_2+3=0\). Find the unit normal and the signed distance of \((1,1)\).
Compute. Use the bias trick to write \(f(x_1,x_2)=4x_1-x_2+7\) as one matrix–vector product.

Derive. Show that two parallel hyperplanes \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b_1=0\) and \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b_2=0\) are \(|b_1-b_2|/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\) apart.
Code. Fit a linear classifier on digits using only classes 3 and 8. Plot the template \(\mathbf{w}_3-\mathbf{w}_8\).
Code. Compute the rank of the \(10\times64\) digit weight matrix. Is it full rank?
Code. Count the parameters and FLOPs of a 784 → 512 → 512 → 10 network of linear layers. Show it collapses to one \(10\times784\) matrix.
Diagnose. A model has three linear layers and no activations. Training loss stops at the same value as a one-layer model. Explain.
Design. Add two features to the XOR inputs so that one hyperplane separates them. Which features?

title: 10  Nonlinearity and Expressiveness
text:
10.1 The system problem
Chapter 9 ended with a problem. A stack of linear layers is equal to one linear layer. XOR cannot be learned. Curved boundaries cannot be learned.
The change is small: apply a simple fixed nonlinear function to each number between the layers.
system_map(highlight=["Representation", "Transformation"],
           sublabels={"Transformation": "Ch. 8–12"});
plt.show()







Figure 10.1: Chapter 10 adds nonlinearity to the Transformation stage.

title: 10  Nonlinearity and Expressiveness
text: Why does a stack of linear layers equal one linear layer, and what is the smallest change that fixes it?

title: 10  Nonlinearity and Expressiveness
text:
10.2 The collapse, once more
Chapter 9 showed \(\mathbf{W}_2(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{x})=(\mathbf{W}_{2}\mathbf{W}_1)\mathbf{x}\). By induction, any depth reduces to a single matrix. The reason is that the product of matrices is a matrix.
The fix: insert a function \(\sigma\) that is not linear, applied element by element:
\[
\mathbf{h}=\sigma(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}_1),\qquad
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{W}_{2}\mathbf{h}+\mathbf{b}_2.
\tag{10.1}\]
Now \(\mathbf{y}\) is not a matrix times \(\mathbf{x}\), because \(\sigma\) sits between the two matrices.

title: 10  Nonlinearity and Expressiveness
text:
10.3 A gallery of activations
Five activations appear in almost all models.









Name
Formula
Range
Where used




ReLU
\(\max(0,z)\)
\([0,\infty)\)
CNNs, many MLPs


Sigmoid
\(\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\)
\((0,1)\)
gates, binary outputs


Tanh
\(\dfrac{e^z-e^{-z}}{e^z+e^{-z}}\)
\((-1,1)\)
RNNs, small networks


GELU
\(z\,\Phi(z)\)
\(\approx[-0.17,\infty)\)
Transformers (BERT, GPT)


SiLU (swish)
\(z\,\sigma(z)\)
\(\approx[-0.28,\infty)\)
modern LLM MLPs (SwiGLU)



Here \(\Phi\) is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. GELU weights its input by the probability that a standard normal variable is smaller than it.
We define them and their derivatives. Then we check each derivative against a finite difference, as in Chapter 1.

from scipy.special import erf

def Phi(z):                                   # normal CDF
    return 0.5 * (1.0 + erf(z / np.sqrt(2.0)))

def phi(z):                                   # normal density
    return np.exp(-0.5 * z ** 2) / np.sqrt(2.0 * np.pi)

sig = lambda z: 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))

ACTS = {   # name: (function, derivative)
    "ReLU":    (lambda z: np.maximum(0, z),   lambda z: (z > 0) * 1.0),
    "sigmoid": (sig,                          lambda z: sig(z) * (1 - sig(z))),
    "tanh":    (np.tanh,                      lambda z: 1 - np.tanh(z) ** 2),
    "GELU":    (lambda z: z * Phi(z),         lambda z: Phi(z) + z * phi(z)),
    "SiLU":    (lambda z: z * sig(z),         lambda z: sig(z) + z * sig(z) * (1 - sig(z))),
}

z = np.linspace(-4, 4, 801)
eps = 1e-6
for name, (f, df) in ACTS.items():
    fd = (f(z + eps) - f(z - eps)) / (2 * eps)
    mask = np.abs(z) > 1e-3                   # skip the ReLU kink at 0
    print(f"{name:8s} max |derivative - finite difference| = "
          f"{np.max(np.abs(fd - df(z))[mask]):.1e}")

ReLU     max |derivative - finite difference| = 1.4e-10
sigmoid  max |derivative - finite difference| = 1.3e-10
tanh     max |derivative - finite difference| = 7.3e-11
GELU     max |derivative - finite difference| = 4.8e-10
SiLU     max |derivative - finite difference| = 5.7e-10



cols = [PALETTE[k] for k in ["data", "model", "prob", "grad", "loss"]]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(11, 4.2), sharex=True)
for j, (name, (f, df)) in enumerate(ACTS.items()):
    axes[0, j].plot(z, f(z), color=cols[j], lw=2); axes[0, j].set_title(name)
    axes[1, j].plot(z, df(z), color=cols[j], lw=2)
    for i in (0, 1):
        axes[i, j].axhline(0, color="#9CA3AF", lw=0.6)
        axes[i, j].set_ylim(-1.3, 2.0 if i == 0 else 1.3)
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("σ(z)"); axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("σ′(z)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 10.2: Five activations (top) and their derivatives (bottom). ReLU has a constant gradient of 1 for positive input and 0 otherwise. Sigmoid and tanh have gradients that vanish at both ends. GELU and SiLU are smooth versions of ReLU with a small dip below zero.

title: 10  Nonlinearity and Expressiveness
text:
10.4 Solving XOR by hand
We now solve the problem that a linear model cannot. With two ReLU units we can set the weights by hand.
\[
h_1=\text{ReLU}(x_1+x_2),\qquad
h_2=\text{ReLU}(x_1+x_2-1),\qquad
y=h_1-2h_2.
\tag{10.2}\]

relu = lambda z: np.maximum(0, z)
pts = np.array([[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]], dtype=float)

W1 = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]]); b1 = np.array([0.0, -1.0])
W2 = np.array([1.0, -2.0])
h = relu(pts @ W1.T + b1)                  # (4, 2)
y = h @ W2                                 # (4,)
for p, hh, yy in zip(pts, h, y):
    print(f"x = {p}   h = {hh}   y = {yy:+.0f}")

x = [0. 0.]   h = [0. 0.]   y = +0
x = [1. 0.]   h = [1. 0.]   y = +1
x = [0. 1.]   h = [1. 0.]   y = +1
x = [1. 1.]   h = [2. 1.]   y = +0


The four points give \(0,1,1,0\). XOR is solved. The hidden layer bends the plane: it maps \((1,1)\) to a point where a line can separate it from \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\).

title: 10  Nonlinearity and Expressiveness
section: 10.5 How a ReLU network represents a function
text:
10.5 How a ReLU network represents a function
A network with ReLU units is a piecewise linear function. Each unit is linear on each side of its hyperplane, and the sum of such functions is linear on each region.

10.5.1 Width: pieces side by side
In one dimension, a sum of shifted ReLUs makes a polyline:
\[
f(x)=y_0+\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_i\,\text{ReLU}(x-t_i).
\tag{10.3}\]
The knots \(t_i\) are where the slope changes, and \(c_i\) is the change in slope. We can choose them to match any target function at the knots. With \(k\) units, the function has \(k+1\) linear pieces. Here we approximate \(\sin\).

def relu_interpolant(target, a, b, k):
    """k ReLU units at equal spacing that interpolate `target` at k+1 points."""
    knots = np.linspace(a, b, k + 1)
    vals = target(knots)
    slopes = np.diff(vals) / np.diff(knots)              # slope on each piece
    c = np.diff(slopes, prepend=0.0)                     # slope changes
    def f(x):
        out = vals[0] + 0.0 * x
        for ci, ti in zip(c, knots[:-1]):
            out = out + ci * np.maximum(0, x - ti)
        return out
    return f

xs = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 1000)
ks = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]
errs = [np.max(np.abs(relu_interpolant(np.sin, 0, 2 * np.pi, k)(xs) - np.sin(xs)))
        for k in ks]

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))
ax1.plot(xs, np.sin(xs), color="black", lw=2, label="sin x")
for k, col in zip([2, 4, 8], [PALETTE["loss"], PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["grad"]]):
    ax1.plot(xs, relu_interpolant(np.sin, 0, 2 * np.pi, k)(xs), color=col, label=f"k = {k}")
ax1.legend(fontsize=8); ax1.set_xlabel("x")
ax2.loglog(ks, errs, "o-", color=PALETTE["data"], label="max error")
ax2.loglog(ks, [errs[0] * (ks[0] / k) ** 2 for k in ks], "--",
           color=PALETTE["neutral"], label="∝ 1/k²")
ax2.set_xlabel("number of ReLU units k"); ax2.set_ylabel("max |error|"); ax2.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("errors:", [f"{e:.4f}" for e in errs])







Figure 10.3: Approximating sin(x) with k ReLU units placed at equal spacing. With k = 2 the fit is rough. With k = 8 it is close. The maximum error falls roughly with 1/k²: doubling the width cuts the error by about four.





errors: ['1.0000', '0.2105', '0.0704', '0.0188', '0.0048', '0.0012']


This construction is the core of the universal approximation idea: a network with one hidden layer of enough units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded interval to any accuracy. The theorem says that such a network exists. It does not say how to find it, how large it must be, or that training will find it.


10.5.2 Regions in higher dimension
In 2D, each hidden unit has a boundary line \(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+b=0\). Together, \(n\) lines cut the plane into regions. In each region the on/off pattern of the units is fixed, so the network is affine there.
\(n\) lines in general position make at most \(1+n+\binom{n}{2}\) regions. We count the regions of random networks by the number of distinct activation patterns.

def count_regions(n, rng, grid=500, lim=3.0):
    W = rng.normal(size=(n, 2)); b = rng.normal(scale=0.6, size=n)
    g = np.linspace(-lim, lim, grid)
    P = np.stack(np.meshgrid(g, g), -1).reshape(-1, 2)
    codes = (P @ W.T + b > 0)                         # (G, n) on/off pattern
    keys = codes.dot(1 << np.arange(n))               # pattern as one integer
    uniq, inv = np.unique(keys, return_inverse=True)
    return len(uniq), inv.reshape(grid, grid)

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.8))
for ax, n in zip(axes, [3, 8]):
    n_reg, labels = count_regions(n, rng)
    ax.imshow(labels, extent=(-3, 3, -3, 3), origin="lower", cmap="tab20")
    ax.set_title(f"{n} units: {n_reg} regions (max {1 + n + n * (n - 1) // 2})")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 10.4: Linear regions of a random one-hidden-layer ReLU network in 2D. Each colour is one on/off pattern of the hidden units. Inside a region the network is affine. Three units reach the maximum of 7 regions. Eight units give 20 in this window, below the maximum of 37, because some lines cross outside it.







10.5.3 Depth: pieces multiply
Width adds pieces. Composition multiplies them. Take the tent map on \([0,1]\), built from two ReLUs:
\[
\text{tent}(x)=2\,\text{ReLU}(x)-4\,\text{ReLU}\!\left(x-\tfrac12\right).
\tag{10.4}\]
It rises from 0 to 1 on \([0,\frac12]\) and falls back on \([\frac12,1]\). Composing it with itself \(k\) times gives a sawtooth with \(2^k\) teeth, using only \(2k\) ReLU units.

tent = lambda x: 2 * np.maximum(0, x) - 4 * np.maximum(0, x - 0.5)
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 2001)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 2.6))
y = x.copy()
for k, ax in enumerate(axes, start=1):
    y = tent(y)                                       # one more composition
    ax.plot(x, y, color=PALETTE["model"], lw=1.4)
    slopes = np.sign(np.diff(y))
    pieces = 1 + int(np.sum(slopes[1:] != slopes[:-1]))
    ax.set_title(f"depth {k}:  {pieces} pieces,  {2 * k} units", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xticks([0, 1]); ax.set_yticks([0, 1])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 10.5: Depth multiplies linear pieces. Each additional tent layer doubles the number of teeth while adding only two hidden units. A one-hidden-layer network would need about 2^k units for the same function.





Real networks do not build sawtooths. The lesson is general: depth gives a number of regions that grows exponentially with the number of layers, while width grows it only polynomially.

Smoothness. ReLU has a kink at 0, where the derivative is undefined. Libraries use 0 or 1 there, and this almost never matters. GELU and SiLU are smooth, which can help optimisation of very deep Transformers.
Why not use sigmoid everywhere? Its maximum derivative is \(0.25\), so the backward signal shrinks by at least \(4\times\) per layer (Chapter 18).

text:
10.7 From first principles to production
PyTorch implements these functions and their derivatives. We check that they agree with ours.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

zt = torch.tensor(z, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
pairs = {"ReLU": F.relu, "sigmoid": torch.sigmoid, "tanh": torch.tanh,
         "GELU": F.gelu, "SiLU": F.silu}
for name, fn in pairs.items():
    out = fn(zt)
    grad, = torch.autograd.grad(out.sum(), zt)       # derivative at every point
    f_np, df_np = ACTS[name]
    mask = np.abs(z) > 1e-3
    print(f"{name:8s} value diff {np.max(np.abs(out.detach().numpy() - f_np(z))):.1e}"
          f"   derivative diff {np.max(np.abs(grad.numpy() - df_np(z))[mask]):.1e}")

title: 10  Nonlinearity and Expressiveness
text:
10.8 Failure modes

10.8.1 Saturation
For sigmoid and tanh, large \(|z|\) gives a nearly flat curve. The derivative is almost zero. The backward signal dies, and the weights below that unit hardly change.

for zv in [0.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0]:
    print(f"z = {zv:4.1f}   sigmoid'(z) = {ACTS['sigmoid'][1](np.array(zv)):.2e}")

z =  0.0   sigmoid'(z) = 2.50e-01
z =  2.0   sigmoid'(z) = 1.05e-01
z =  5.0   sigmoid'(z) = 6.65e-03
z = 10.0   sigmoid'(z) = 4.54e-05




10.8.2 Dead ReLUs
If a ReLU unit gets \(z\le0\) for every input, its output and its gradient are both zero. Its weights stop changing. The unit is dead for good.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(-1, 1, size=(1000, 2))
w_dead, b_dead = np.array([1.0, 1.0]), -10.0         # bias far too negative
z_unit = X @ w_dead + b_dead
print("fraction of inputs with the unit active:", np.mean(z_unit > 0))
print("gradient of the unit w.r.t. its weights: ",
      np.mean((z_unit > 0)[:, None] * X, axis=0))

fraction of inputs with the unit active: 0.0
gradient of the unit w.r.t. its weights:  [0. 0.]


Common causes are a too-large learning rate and a poor initialisation. Remedies: smaller learning rates, careful initialisation (Chapter 20), and “leaky” variants (\(\max(0.01z,z)\)).


10.8.3 Nonlinearity at the output
The last layer usually has no activation, or one matched to the loss: a sigmoid for binary outputs, a softmax for classes (Chapter 24). A ReLU at the output would forbid negative predictions.


10.8.4 Too little or too much
A network with too few nonlinear units underfits. One with too many can fit noise. This trade-off is the subject of Part VII.

10.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now represent curved boundaries and nonlinear functions. The key is one fixed nonlinear function between linear layers. Width adds linear pieces side by side, and depth multiplies them.
We have the two ingredients, \(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}\) and \(\sigma\). Chapter 11 assembles them into a complete network and trains it.

title: 10  Nonlinearity and Expressiveness
text:
Chapter summary

Linear layers collapse. A nonlinearity between them prevents this.
ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, GELU, and SiLU differ in range, smoothness, and gradient.
Two ReLU units solve XOR by hand.
A ReLU network is piecewise linear. \(k\) units in 1D make \(k+1\) pieces. \(n\) units in 2D make up to \(1+n+\binom n2\) regions.
Depth multiplies pieces. A \(k\)-fold composition of the tent map has \(2^k\) pieces.
Universal approximation says a good network exists. It does not say that training finds it.
Sigmoid and tanh saturate. ReLU units can die.

title: 11  Neural Networks as Function Composition
text:
11.2 The mathematical object
An MLP with \(L\) layers computes
\[
\mathbf{a}_0=\mathbf{x},\qquad
\mathbf{a}_l=\sigma(\mathbf{W}_{l}\mathbf{a}_{l-1}+\mathbf{b}_l)\ \ (l<L),\qquad
\mathbf{z}_L=\mathbf{W}_{L}\mathbf{a}_{L-1}+\mathbf{b}_L.
\tag{11.1}\]
In words, it is \(f=f_{L}\circ\dots\circ f_1\) with each \(f_l\) an affine map followed by \(\sigma\). The last layer has no \(\sigma\). It outputs scores (logits).
The vectors \(\mathbf{a}_1,\dots,\mathbf{a}_{L-1}\) are the hidden representations. Each layer changes the representation into a new one.

11.2.1 Shapes and parameters
For layer sizes \(n_0,n_1,\dots,n_L\), layer \(l\) has \(\mathbf{W}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{l}\times n_{l-1}}\) and \(\mathbf{b}_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_l}\):
\[
\#\text{parameters}=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\bigl(n_l\,n_{l-1}+n_{l}\bigr).
\tag{11.2}\]

def n_params(sizes):
    return sum(n_out * n_in + n_out for n_in, n_out in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:]))

for name, sizes in [("digits MLP", [64, 32, 10]),
                    ("MNIST MLP", [784, 256, 128, 10]),
                    ("2-layer, width 4096", [4096, 4096, 4096])]:

text:
11.3 A forward pass in NumPy
We write the forward pass for any depth. We keep the shape convention: a batch has shape (N, d), and a weight has shape (d_out, d_in).

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def init(sizes, rng):
    """He initialisation: weights ~ N(0, 2 / fan_in)."""
    return [(rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2.0 / n_in), (n_out, n_in)), np.zeros(n_out))
            for n_in, n_out in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:])]

def forward(params, X, trace=False):
    a = X                                          # (N, n_0)
    for l, (W, b) in enumerate(params):
        z = a @ W.T + b                            # (N, n_l)
        last = (l == len(params) - 1)
        a = z if last else np.maximum(0, z)        # ReLU on hidden layers
        if trace:
            print(f"layer {l + 1}: W {W.shape}  ->  output {a.shape}")
    return a

params = init([64, 32, 16, 10], rng)
out = forward(params, rng.normal(size=(5, 64)), trace=True)

layer 1: W (32, 64)  ->  output (5, 32)
layer 2: W (16, 32)  ->  output (5, 16)
layer 3: W (10, 16)  ->  output (5, 10)


The pattern is the same as in Chapter 2: the batch axis passes through unchanged, and only the feature axis changes.

title: 11  Neural Networks as Function Composition
section: 11.4 Training: gradients as a black box
text:
11.4 Training: gradients as a black box
To train, we need \(\nabla_\theta L\). We have not yet derived how to compute it for a deep network. That is Chapter 18. For this chapter, PyTorch provides it:

loss.backward() computes \(\partial L/\partial\theta\) for every parameter.
optimizer.step() applies \(\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\,\nabla_\theta L\). This is the update of Chapter 1. Better optimisers are the subject of Chapter 19.


import torch
import torch.nn as nn

def fit(model, X, y, loss_fn, steps, lr):
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)    # θ ← θ − η ∇L
    for _ in range(steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(model(X), y)
        loss.backward()                                  # Chapter 18 explains this
        opt.step()
    return loss.item()

text:
11.5 Experiment 1: a spiral
We build a 2D problem that no hyperplane can solve: two interleaved spirals. We compare a linear model and MLPs of growing size.

def spiral(n=200, noise=0.2, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t = np.sqrt(r.uniform(0, 1, n)) * 3 * np.pi / 1.5 + 0.3
    X, y = [], []
    for c in (0, 1):
        th = t + c * np.pi
        pts = np.stack([t * np.cos(th), t * np.sin(th)], 1) / (3 * np.pi / 1.5)
        X.append(pts + r.normal(0, noise / 3, (n, 2))); y += [c] * n
    return np.vstack(X).astype(np.float32), np.array(y, dtype=np.float32)

Xs, ys = spiral()
Xs_t, ys_t = torch.tensor(Xs), torch.tensor(ys).unsqueeze(1)
print("data:", Xs.shape, " labels:", ys.shape)

data: (400, 2)  labels: (400,)



specs = {
    "linear":        lambda: nn.Linear(2, 1),
    "2-4-1":         lambda: nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 4), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(4, 1)),
    "2-16-1":        lambda: nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 16), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(16, 1)),
    "2-16-16-1":     lambda: nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 16), nn.Tanh(),
                                           nn.Linear(16, 16), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(16, 1)),
}

models, results = {}, []
for name, make in specs.items():

11.5.1 Seeing the untangling
A network with a 2-unit hidden layer lets us look at its hidden representation. The input is 2D, so is the hidden layer. The second space is a bent copy of the first. We plot both.

torch.manual_seed(0)
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 16), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(16, 2), nn.Tanh(),
                    nn.Linear(2, 1))
loss = fit(net, Xs_t, ys_t, bce, steps=6000, lr=0.5)
acc = ((net(Xs_t) > 0).float() == ys_t).float().mean().item()
print(f"bottleneck network: loss {loss:.3f}, accuracy {acc:.3f}")

with torch.no_grad():
    H = net[:4](Xs_t).numpy()                            # hidden layer, (400, 2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.5, 3.8))
for ax, P, title in zip(axes, [Xs, H], ["input space", "hidden space (2 units)"]):
    ax.scatter(*P[ys == 0].T, s=8, color=PALETTE["data"])
    ax.scatter(*P[ys == 1].T, s=8, color=PALETTE["model"])
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_aspect("equal")

11.6 Experiment 2: digits, the first complete System A
We now build the whole classifier for \(8\times8\) digits: 64 pixels \(\to\) 32 hidden units \(\to\) 10 scores. We train it with cross-entropy and test it on images it has not seen.

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

D = load_digits()
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(D.data / 16.0, D.target, test_size=0.25,
                                      random_state=0, stratify=D.target)
Xtr_t, Xte_t = (torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32) for a in (Xtr, Xte))
ytr_t, yte_t = torch.tensor(ytr), torch.tensor(yte)

def test_acc(model, X=Xte_t, y=yte_t):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (model(X).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()

torch.manual_seed(0)
linear_clf = nn.Linear(64, 10)
mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 10))
ce = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
for name, m in [("linear", linear_clf), ("MLP 64-32-10", mlp)]:
    loss = fit(m, Xtr_t, ytr_t, ce, steps=600, lr=0.5)
    n = sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())
    print(f"{name:14s} params {n:5d}  train loss {loss:.3f}  test accuracy {test_acc(m):.3f}")

linear         params   650  train loss 0.155  test accuracy 0.958
MLP 64-32-10   params  2410  train loss 0.040  test accuracy 0.976


The MLP is more accurate than the linear model. The gain is small on this easy data. The linear model already reads digits well (Chapter 9).

11.6.1 What the hidden units learned
Each hidden unit has 64 incoming weights. Shown as an image, they form a feature detector: the pixel pattern that makes the unit fire. After short training the patterns are mixed, and no single unit has a simple meaning.

Wh = mlp[0].weight.detach().numpy()                      # (32, 64)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(10, 2.8))
for ax, w in zip(axes.ravel(), Wh[:16]):
    lim = np.abs(w).max()
    ax.imshow(w.reshape(8, 8), cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-lim, vmax=lim)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 11.4: Sixteen of the 32 hidden units, shown as 8×8 weight images. Red weights excite the unit, blue weights inhibit it. The patterns are noisy, not clean stroke detectors: training was short and started from random weights. The output layer combines the 32 unit responses into class scores.







11.6.2 Budget

parts = {"W₁": mlp[0].weight.numel(), "b₁": mlp[0].bias.numel(),
         "W₂": mlp[2].weight.numel(), "b₂": mlp[2].bias.numel()}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3))
ax.bar(parts.keys(), parts.values(), color=PALETTE["model"])
for i, v in enumerate(parts.values()):
    ax.text(i, v, f"{v:,}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("parameters")
plt.show()
print("total:", sum(parts.values()), " formula:", n_params([64, 32, 10]))







Figure 11.5: Where the parameters are. In the digits MLP, the first layer holds 86% of the parameters. In wide models, a layer’s parameter count grows with the product of its two widths.

text:
11.8 Failure modes

11.8.1 The same architecture can fail to train
We train a 9-layer ReLU network on the digits with the same data, loss, and optimiser. The only difference is the initial weights.

def deep_net(he_init):
    layers = [nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU()]
    for _ in range(8):
        layers += [nn.Linear(32, 32), nn.ReLU()]
    net = nn.Sequential(*layers, nn.Linear(32, 10))
    if he_init:
        for mod in net:
            if isinstance(mod, nn.Linear):
                nn.init.kaiming_normal_(mod.weight, nonlinearity="relu")
                nn.init.zeros_(mod.bias)
    return net

def fit_curve(model, steps, lr):
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr); hist = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        opt.zero_grad(); loss = ce(model(Xtr_t), ytr_t); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        hist.append(loss.item())
    return hist

torch.manual_seed(0); h_default = fit_curve(deep_net(False), 600, 0.1)
torch.manual_seed(0); net_he = deep_net(True); h_he = fit_curve(net_he, 600, 0.1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(h_default, color=PALETTE["loss"], label="default init")
ax.plot(h_he, color=PALETTE["grad"], label="He init")
ax.set_xlabel("step"); ax.set_ylabel("training loss"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
print(f"default init: final loss {h_default[-1]:.3f}")
print(f"He init:      final loss {h_he[-1]:.4f}, test accuracy {test_acc(net_he):.3f}")







Figure 11.6: The same 9-layer ReLU network trained with two different initialisations. With PyTorch’s default, the loss stays at ln 10 ≈ 2.30: the network does not learn. With He initialisation, it learns. The architecture is identical. Chapters 18 and 20 explain why.





default init: final loss 2.302
He init:      final loss 0.0026, test accuracy 0.953




11.8.2 Other failures

Wrong head and loss. A softmax output with a squared-error loss, or a ReLU on the final layer of a regression model, can train badly or never work. Match them as in the table above.
No nonlinearity. Forgetting the activation gives a linear model with extra parameters (Chapter 10).
Shape mismatch. The output size of a layer must equal the input size of the next. Shape errors appear at the first forward pass.
Overfitting. A network with enough parameters can fit noise. The training accuracy is then no guide to test accuracy (Part VII).
Standardisation. Inputs with very different scales slow or break training (Chapter 3).

11.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system is now a complete model: input → affine → nonlinearity → … → scores. System A runs from pixels to class, and its parameters are learned from data. We also see why composition works: early layers bend space, and later layers read off the result.
Two parts are still borrowed: the loss (we named cross-entropy, Chapter 14 explains it) and the gradient (PyTorch computed it, Chapter 18 derives it). First, Chapter 12 adds a transformation designed for images.

title: 11  Neural Networks as Function Composition
text:
Chapter summary

An MLP is \(f_{L}\circ\dots\circ f_1\) with affine layers and activations. The last layer outputs scores.
Parameters: \(\sum_l(n_ln_{l-1}+n_l)\).
The head and the loss must match the task.
Hidden units are learned feature detectors. Hidden layers re-represent the input.
On the spiral, more units and layers give a boundary that follows the data.
System A: a 64-32-10 MLP reaches about 97% test accuracy on digits.
Initialisation can decide whether a deep network trains at all.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.1 The system problem
A dense layer from a \(64\times64\) image to 64 hidden units needs \(4096\times64\) weights. For a \(1000\times1000\) photo it would need a billion. A dense layer also treats every pixel as unrelated to its neighbours. It must learn “an edge here” again for every position.
Images have two properties that a dense layer ignores:
system_map(highlight=["Representation", "Transformation"],
           sublabels={"Transformation": "Ch. 8–12"});
plt.show()







Figure 12.1: Chapter 12 closes Part III with a transformation designed for images.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
Locality. Useful patterns (edges, corners) are made of nearby pixels.
Translation. A pattern means the same thing wherever it appears.


How can a layer use locality and translation, so that it needs few parameters and finds a pattern anywhere?

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.2 Intuition: a sliding pattern detector
Take a small grid of weights, the kernel, for example \(3\times3\). Place it on the image. Multiply each weight with the pixel below it and add the nine products. This number says how well the patch matches the kernel pattern. Slide the kernel one step. Repeat. The grid of results is a feature map.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.3 The mathematical object
For an image \(I\) and a kernel \(K\) of size \(k\times k\), the output at position \((i,j)\) is
\[
(I\star K)_{ij}=\sum_{u=0}^{k-1}\sum_{v=0}^{k-1}I_{i+u,\,j+v}\;K_{uv}.
\tag{12.1}\]






NoteConvolution or correlation?



Equation 12.1 is strictly cross-correlation. True mathematical convolution flips the kernel first. Deep learning libraries compute Equation 12.1 and call it “convolution”. Since the kernel is learned, the flip makes no difference to what the network can represent.



12.3.1 Size, stride, and padding
With input size \(n\), kernel size \(k\), padding \(p\) (zeros added at each border), and stride \(s\) (step between positions), the output size is
\[
n_{\text{out}}=\left\lfloor\frac{n+2p-k}{s}\right\rfloor+1.
\tag{12.2}\]

12.3.2 Channels
Images have \(C_{\text{in}}\) channels. A layer has \(C_{\text{out}}\) kernels, each of shape \((C_{\text{in}},k,k)\). The weight tensor has shape \((C_{\text{out}},C_{\text{in}},k,k)\), and
\[
\#\text{params}=C_{\text{out}}\,(C_{\text{in}}k^2+1).
\tag{12.3}\]
The count does not depend on the image size. A \(3\times3\) layer with 64 input and 64 output channels always has \(64\cdot(64\cdot9+1)=36{,}928\) parameters, for any image.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.4 Derivation: translation equivariance
Let \(T_\tau\) shift an image by \(\tau\) pixels: \((T_\tau I)_{i}=I_{i-\tau}\). Ignoring borders (1D for clarity):
\[
(T_\tau I\star K)_i=\sum_uI_{i+u-\tau}K_u=(I\star K)_{i-\tau}=T_\tau(I\star K)_i.
\tag{12.4}\]
Shifting the input and then convolving gives the same result as convolving and then shifting. The operation is translation equivariant.
The reason is that the same kernel is used at every position. A dense layer has a separate weight for every pair of positions. It has no such property.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.5 Computation: from first principles
We write the definition with loops. It is slow and exact.

def conv2d_loops(img, K, stride=1, pad=0):
    img = np.pad(img, pad)
    k = K.shape[0]
    n_h = (img.shape[0] - k) // stride + 1
    n_w = (img.shape[1] - k) // stride + 1
    out = np.zeros((n_h, n_w))
    for i in range(n_h):
        for j in range(n_w):
            patch = img[i * stride:i * stride + k, j * stride:j * stride + k]
            out[i, j] = np.sum(patch * K)              # dot product of patch and kernel
    return out

img = np.arange(64.0).reshape(8, 8)
K = np.array([[1.0, 0.0, -1.0]] * 3)                  # a vertical-edge kernel
for pad, stride in [(0, 1), (1, 1), (1, 2)]:
    print(f"pad={pad} stride={stride}: output shape",
          conv2d_loops(img, K, stride, pad).shape)

pad=0 stride=1: output shape (6, 6)
pad=1 stride=1: output shape (8, 8)
pad=1 stride=2: output shape (4, 4)


The shapes match Equation 12.2.

12.5.1 Convolution as a matrix product (im2col)
Chapter 6 introduced strided views. A sliding window view gives all patches as one array. Then convolution is one contraction. This is the “im2col” idea behind fast implementations.

from numpy.lib.stride_tricks import sliding_window_view

def conv2d_fast(img, K):
    k = K.shape[0]
    windows = sliding_window_view(img, (k, k))          # (H-k+1, W-k+1, k, k), a view
    return np.einsum("ijuv,uv->ij", windows, K)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
test_img = rng.normal(size=(20, 20)); test_K = rng.normal(size=(5, 5))
print("fast == loops:", np.allclose(conv2d_fast(test_img, test_K),
                                    conv2d_loops(test_img, test_K)))

fast == loops: True


To see the matrix, we build it. For a 1D signal of length 8 and a kernel of length 3, the convolution is a \(6\times8\) matrix. Each row is the kernel, shifted by one:

n, k = 8, 3
kern = np.array([1.0, 2.0, -1.0])
M = np.zeros((n - k + 1, n))
for i in range(n - k + 1):
    M[i, i:i + k] = kern                                 # same kernel, shifted

sig = rng.normal(size=n)
print("matrix product == sliding window:",
      np.allclose(M @ sig, np.correlate(sig, kern, mode="valid")))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.2))
ax.imshow(M, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-2, vmax=2)
for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(M):
    ax.text(j, i, f"{v:g}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("input position"); ax.set_ylabel("output position"); ax.grid(False)
plt.show()

matrix product == sliding window: True








Figure 12.2: A 1D convolution as a matrix. Each row holds the same three weights, shifted by one place. Most entries are zero. A dense layer would have 48 free parameters here. The convolution has 3.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.6 Kernels as feature detectors
Different kernels detect different patterns. We apply five classic ones to a photograph.

from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image
photo = load_sample_image("china.jpg").astype(float).mean(axis=2)[:300, 150:550]

kernels = {
    "blur":      np.ones((5, 5)) / 25.0,
    "Sobel x":   np.array([[1, 0, -1], [2, 0, -2], [1, 0, -1]], dtype=float),
    "Sobel y":   np.array([[1, 2, 1], [0, 0, 0], [-1, -2, -1]], dtype=float),
    "Laplacian": np.array([[0, 1, 0], [1, -4, 1], [0, 1, 0]], dtype=float),
}
resp = {name: conv2d_fast(photo, K) for name, K in kernels.items()}
h = min(r.shape[0] for r in resp.values()); w = min(r.shape[1] for r in resp.values())
mag = np.hypot(resp["Sobel x"][:h, :w], resp["Sobel y"][:h, :w])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 5.2))
panels = [("input", photo)] + [(n, r) for n, r in resp.items()] + [("edge strength", mag)]
for ax, (title, im) in zip(axes.ravel(), panels):
    ax.imshow(im, cmap="gray"); ax.set_title(title); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 12.3: Classic hand-designed kernels on a photograph. Blur averages neighbours. The two Sobel kernels respond to horizontal and vertical edges. The Laplacian responds to any rapid change. The last panel is the edge strength. A CNN learns such kernels from data instead.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.7 Equivariance, tested
We check Equation 12.4 numerically. We shift the image, convolve, and compare with the shifted feature map. Borders break the symmetry, so we compare only the interior.

img = photo[:120, :160]
Kx = kernels["Sobel x"]
shift = 7

shifted_input = np.roll(img, shift, axis=1)                       # shift right by 7
out_of_shifted = conv2d_fast(shifted_input, Kx)
shifted_out = np.roll(conv2d_fast(img, Kx), shift, axis=1)

inner = (slice(None), slice(shift + 2, -2))                       # skip wrapped columns
diff = np.max(np.abs(out_of_shifted[inner] - shifted_out[inner]))
print(f"conv(shift(x)) vs shift(conv(x)), interior max difference: {diff:.1e}")

conv(shift(x)) vs shift(conv(x)), interior max difference: 0.0e+00


The difference is exactly zero in the interior. Convolution commutes with translation.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.8 Pooling
Max pooling replaces each \(p\times p\) block by its maximum. It halves the resolution (for \(p=2\)) and gives some tolerance to small shifts: a feature that moves by one pixel inside a block gives the same pooled value.
\[
\text{pool}(F)_{ij}=\max_{0\le u,v<p}F_{pi+u,\,pj+v}.
\tag{12.5}\]

def max_pool(F, p=2):
    H, W = (F.shape[0] // p) * p, (F.shape[1] // p) * p
    return F[:H, :W].reshape(H // p, p, W // p, p).max(axis=(1, 3))

F = np.zeros((6, 6)); F[2, 2] = 1.0          # one active feature
F_shift = np.roll(F, 1, axis=1)              # moved by one pixel, still in its block
print("same block -> pooled maps equal:",
      np.array_equal(max_pool(F), max_pool(F_shift)))
F_far = np.roll(F, 2, axis=1)                # moved to the next block
print("next block -> pooled maps equal:",
      np.array_equal(max_pool(F), max_pool(F_far)))

same block -> pooled maps equal: True
next block -> pooled maps equal: False


Pooling gives tolerance only for shifts that stay inside a block. Larger or different shifts change the result. This will matter below.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.9 A CNN for digits
We build a small CNN: \(8\times8\) image \(\to\) 8 kernels of size \(3\times3\) \(\to\) ReLU \(\to\) \(2\times2\) max pool \(\to\) linear layer to 10 classes. We train it with the same tools as in Chapter 11, and compare it with the MLP.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

D = load_digits()
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(D.data / 16.0, D.target, test_size=0.25,
                                      random_state=0, stratify=D.target)
Xtr_t, Xte_t = (torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32) for a in (Xtr, Xte))
ytr_t, yte_t = torch.tensor(ytr), torch.tensor(yte)

class SmallCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(1, 8, kernel_size=3)       # (1, 8, 8) -> (8, 6, 6)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(8 * 3 * 3, 10)               # after 2x2 pooling: (8, 3, 3)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = torch.relu(self.conv(x.view(-1, 1, 8, 8)))
        x = torch.max_pool2d(x, 2)
        return self.fc(x.flatten(1))

def train(model, steps, lr=0.5):
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    ce = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    for _ in range(steps):
        opt.zero_grad(); ce(model(Xtr_t), ytr_t).backward(); opt.step()
    return model

def acc(model, X, y):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (model(X).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()

torch.manual_seed(0)
mlp = train(nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 10)), 600)
torch.manual_seed(0)
cnn = train(SmallCNN(), 800)

n_params = lambda m: sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())
print(f"MLP 64-32-10 : {n_params(mlp):5d} parameters, test accuracy {acc(mlp, Xte_t, yte_t):.3f}")
print(f"CNN          : {n_params(cnn):5d} parameters, test accuracy {acc(cnn, Xte_t, yte_t):.3f}")

MLP 64-32-10 :  2410 parameters, test accuracy 0.973
CNN          :   810 parameters, test accuracy 0.973


The CNN reaches the same accuracy with about a third of the parameters. On this tiny dataset that is the whole benefit. On large images the saving is far greater.

Kl = cnn.conv.weight.detach().numpy()[:, 0]               # (8, 3, 3)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 8, figsize=(10, 1.6))
for ax, kk in zip(axes, Kl):
    lim = np.abs(kk).max()
    ax.imshow(kk, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-lim, vmax=lim)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 12.4: The eight 3×3 kernels learned by the CNN. Each is a small pattern detector found by training, like the Sobel kernels but chosen for digit recognition.






12.9.1 Equivariance is not invariance
A classifier should give the same label for a shifted digit. This is invariance. Convolution gives equivariance: the feature map moves with the input. Only the later layers and pooling can turn this into invariance, and they do so only partly.
We test it. We shift every test image by one pixel to the right and measure accuracy.

def shift_images(X, dx):
    im = X.reshape(-1, 8, 8)
    out = np.roll(im, dx, axis=2)
    out[:, :, :dx] = 0.0                               # clear wrapped column
    return torch.tensor(out.reshape(len(X), -1), dtype=torch.float32)

Xshift = shift_images(Xte, 1)
print(f"{'':6s} {'original':>9s} {'shifted by 1 px':>16s}")
for name, m in [("MLP", mlp), ("CNN", cnn)]:
    print(f"{name:6s} {acc(m, Xte_t, yte_t):9.3f} {acc(m, Xshift, yte_t):16.3f}")

        original  shifted by 1 px
MLP        0.973            0.429
CNN        0.973            0.498


Both models lose much of their accuracy under a one-pixel shift. The CNN is not much better than the MLP here. In an \(8\times8\) image, one pixel is a large move, and the model has seen no shifted examples. What helps in practice is data augmentation (training on shifted copies), more pooling, and depth (Chapter 35).

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.10 Production: PyTorch
nn.Conv2d has weight shape \((C_{\text{out}},C_{\text{in}},k,k)\) and computes cross-correlation, as in Equation 12.1. We check it against our code.

import torch.nn.functional as F

x_t = torch.tensor(test_img).view(1, 1, 20, 20)           # (N, C, H, W)
k_t = torch.tensor(test_K).view(1, 1, 5, 5)               # (C_out, C_in, k, k)
out_t = F.conv2d(x_t, k_t)[0, 0].numpy()
print("F.conv2d == our implementation:",
      np.allclose(out_t, conv2d_fast(test_img, test_K)))

layer = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
print("weight shape:", tuple(layer.weight.shape),
      "  parameters:", n_params(layer), "  formula:", 64 * (64 * 9 + 1))

F.conv2d == our implementation: True
weight shape: (64, 64, 3, 3)   parameters: 36928   formula: 36928

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.11 Failure modes
Border effects. A “valid” convolution shrinks the image. Zero padding adds artificial edges at the border. Equivariance holds exactly only away from the borders.
Aliasing from stride. A stride larger than 1 samples the signal sparsely. A fast oscillation can turn into a slow one or a constant. Blur before subsampling.

signal = np.array([1.0, -1.0] * 8)                         # fastest possible oscillation
strided = signal[::2]                                      # stride-2 sampling
blurred = np.convolve(signal, [0.5, 0.5], mode="valid")[::2]
print("stride 2 without blur:", strided[:6], " <- looks like a constant")
print("stride 2 after blur  :", blurred[:6])

stride 2 without blur: [1. 1. 1. 1. 1. 1.]  <- looks like a constant
stride 2 after blur  : [0. 0. 0. 0. 0. 0.]


Invariance is not given for free. See the shift test above.
Flip versus no flip. SciPy’s convolve2d flips the kernel. PyTorch does not. For a non-symmetric kernel, the two give different (mirrored) results. Check the library.

from scipy.signal import convolve2d, correlate2d
a = rng.normal(size=(6, 6)); kk = np.array([[1.0, 2.0], [0.0, -1.0]])
print("correlate2d == our conv:", np.allclose(correlate2d(a, kk, mode="valid"),
                                              conv2d_fast(a, kk)))
print("convolve2d  == our conv:", np.allclose(convolve2d(a, kk, mode="valid"),
                                              conv2d_fast(a, kk)))

correlate2d == our conv: True
convolve2d  == our conv: False


Receptive field too small. A single \(3\times3\) layer sees only 9 pixels. To recognise a large object, the network must stack layers or pool. We compute receptive fields in Chapter 35.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
12.13 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system has a transformation that uses the structure of the data: few shared parameters, local patterns, and equivariance to translation. System A now has a proper image classifier, and the same kernels can be viewed as feature detectors or as a structured matrix.
This closes Part III. The system can transform: linear layers, nonlinearities, composition, and structured layers. In Part IV, we ask how it can measure: how similar two things are and how wrong a prediction is.

title: 12  Convolution and Structured Transformations
text:
Chapter summary

A convolution slides a kernel and takes a dot product at each position: \((I\star K)_{ij}=\sum I_{i+u,j+v}K_{uv}\).
Output size: \(\lfloor(n+2p-k)/s\rfloor+1\). Parameters: \(C_{\text{out}}(C_{\text{in}}k^2+1)\).
It is translation equivariant. The proof is one line because the kernel is shared.
It equals a matrix product with a banded, repeated matrix.
Pooling gives limited shift tolerance. Equivariance is not invariance.
A small CNN matches an MLP on digits with fewer parameters.
Watch for borders, aliasing, and the flip convention.
