title: 20  The Geometry and Dynamics of Learning
text:
20.4 Saddles and local minima
At a critical point, the Hessian classifies the point (Chapter 17). For a minimum we need all eigenvalues positive. How likely is that?
For a random symmetric matrix, the fraction that is positive definite falls extremely fast with the dimension.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
print(f"{'dimension':>10s} {'fraction with all eigenvalues > 0':>36s}")
for d in [1, 2, 4, 8]:
    ok = 0
    for _ in range(3000):
        A = rng.normal(size=(d, d)); H = (A + A.T) / 2
        ok += np.all(np.linalg.eigvalsh(H) > 0)
    print(f"{d:10d} {ok / 3000:36.4f}")

 dimension    fraction with all eigenvalues > 0
         1                               0.4787
         2                               0.1577
         4                               0.0017
         8                               0.0000


This is a toy model, not a statement about real networks. It does suggest why, in high dimension, a critical point with some negative eigenvalue (a saddle) is far more likely than a minimum. Saddles are escapable: gradient descent moves away along the negative-curvature direction, even from a tiny perturbation.

f = lambda x, y: x ** 2 - y ** 2 + y ** 4 / 4
grad = lambda p: np.array([2 * p[0], -2 * p[1] + p[1] ** 3])
p = np.array([1.5, 1e-6]); path = [p.copy()]
for _ in range(120):
    p = p - 0.1 * grad(p); path.append(p.copy())
path = np.array(path)
near = np.sum(np.linalg.norm(path, axis=1) < 0.1)

gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-2, 2, 300), np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 300))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 4.4))
ax.contour(gx, gy, f(gx, gy), levels=20, cmap="viridis")
ax.plot(*path.T, "o-", ms=3, color=PALETTE["loss"], lw=1)
ax.plot(0, 0, "kx", ms=10); ax.plot([0, 0], [np.sqrt(2), -np.sqrt(2)], "*", color=PALETTE["grad"], ms=14)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
print(f"steps within distance 0.1 of the saddle: {near}; final point {np.round(path[-1], 2)}")







Figure 20.4: Escaping a saddle. f(x, y) = x² − y² + y⁴/4 has a saddle at the origin and minima at y = ±√2. Started almost exactly on the ridge (y = 10⁻⁶), gradient descent first slides along x towards the saddle, spends many steps near it, then drops into one of the minima.





steps within distance 0.1 of the saddle: 51; final point [0.   1.41]
crumbs: 20  The Geometry and Dynamics of Learning

title: 20  The Geometry and Dynamics of Learning
text:
20.5 Initialisation
Weights start random. How large should they be? If too small, the signal shrinks layer by layer. If too large, it grows. Either way the gradient suffers (Chapter 18).






TipDerivation: variance-preserving initialisation



Take one layer \(z=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_ja_j\) with \(n\) inputs. Let the weights be independent with mean \(0\) and variance \(\sigma_w^2\), independent of the inputs \(a_j\), which have \(\mathbb{E}[a_j^2]=q\). Then (Chapter 15 primer) \[
\text{Var}(z)=\sum_{j}\text{Var}(w_ja_j)=n\,\sigma_w^2\,q.
\]

Linear or tanh near zero: \(q=\text{Var}(z_{\text{prev}})\). To keep \(\text{Var}(z)=\text{Var}(z_{\text{prev}})\) we need \(\sigma_w^2=1/n\) (Xavier/Glorot uses the average of fan-in and fan-out).
ReLU: it zeroes the negative half of a symmetric input, so \(q=\tfrac12\text{Var}(z_{\text{prev}})\). We need \(\sigma_w^2=2/n\) (He initialisation). \(\blacksquare\)




rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, L = 256, 40
x0 = rng.normal(size=(64, n))
def activation_std(scale_fn):
    a = x0; out = []
    for _ in range(L):
        W = rng.normal(0, scale_fn(n), size=(n, n))
        a = np.maximum(0, a @ W.T); out.append(a.std())
    return out

variants = {"std = 0.01": lambda n: 0.01,
            "std = 1": lambda n: 1.0,
            "He: √(2/n)": lambda n: np.sqrt(2 / n)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.5))
for (name, fn), c in zip(variants.items(), [PALETTE["data"], PALETTE["loss"], PALETTE["grad"]]):
    s = activation_std(fn)
    ax.semilogy(range(1, L + 1), s, color=c, lw=2, label=name)
    print(f"{name:12s} activation std at layer 40: {s[-1]:.2e}")
ax.set_xlabel("layer"); ax.set_ylabel("std of activations"); ax.legend()
plt.show()

std = 0.01   activation std at layer 40: 7.65e-39
std = 1      activation std at layer 40: 6.06e+41
He: √(2/n)   activation std at layer 40: 2.68e-01








Figure 20.5: Activation scale through 40 ReLU layers of width 256, for three initial weight scales. Too small (0.01): the signal vanishes. Too large (standard normal): it explodes. He initialisation (std = √(2/n)) keeps it roughly constant.
crumbs: 20  The Geometry and Dynamics of Learning

title: 20  The Geometry and Dynamics of Learning
text:
20.6 Normalisation
Initialisation sets the scale at the start. Training changes weights, and the scale can drift. A normalisation layer fixes the scale at every step.
For a vector \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) (one token’s features), LayerNorm subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation:
\[
\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\frac{\mathbf{x}-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}},\qquad\mu=\frac1d\sum_ix_i,\quad\sigma^2=\frac1d\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2,
\tag{20.3}\]
followed by a learned scale and shift, \(\gamma\odot\hat{\mathbf{x}}+\beta\). RMSNorm (used in Llama-style models, Chapter 32) skips the mean:
\[
\text{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\mathbf{x}}{\sqrt{\frac1d\sum_ix_i^2+\epsilon}}\odot\mathbf{g}.
\tag{20.4}\]
Both make the output invariant to the scale of the input: \(\text{LN}(c\,\mathbf{x})=\text{LN}(\mathbf{x})\) for \(c>0\).

20.6.1 The backward pass of LayerNorm
LayerNorm is a function of the whole vector. For the output \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) with upstream gradient \(\hat{\mathbf{g}}=\partial L/\partial\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) (and \(\epsilon\to0\), no \(\gamma,\beta\)):
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{x}}=\frac{1}{\sigma}\Bigl(\hat{\mathbf{g}}-\overline{\hat{g}}\,\mathbf{1}-\overline{\hat{g}\odot\hat{x}}\;\hat{\mathbf{x}}\Bigr),
\tag{20.5}\]
where overlines denote the mean over the \(d\) components. The gradient is projected so it has zero mean and no component along \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\): the two directions the normalisation removes. We check it numerically (the habit of Chapters 1 and 18).

def ln_forward(x, eps=1e-12):
    mu = x.mean(); var = ((x - mu) ** 2).mean()
    return (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps), np.sqrt(var + eps)

def ln_backward(x, g):
    xh, sigma = ln_forward(x)
    return (g - g.mean() - (g * xh).mean() * xh) / sigma

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x, g = rng.normal(size=8), rng.normal(size=8)
loss = lambda x: np.dot(g, ln_forward(x)[0])              # a scalar test loss
analytic = ln_backward(x, g)
numeric = np.array([(loss(x + 1e-6 * e) - loss(x - 1e-6 * e)) / 2e-6 for e in np.eye(8)])
print("max |analytic − numeric|:", np.abs(analytic - numeric).max())
print("scale invariance: LN(5x) == LN(x):", np.allclose(ln_forward(5 * x)[0], ln_forward(x)[0]))

max |analytic − numeric|: 5.434097616330291e-10
scale invariance: LN(5x) == LN(x): True




20.6.2 What normalisation buys
We repeat the 40-layer experiment with standard-normal weights (the bad setting) and add LayerNorm after each layer.

def run_net(use_ln):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    a = rng.normal(size=(64, 256)); out = []
    for _ in range(40):
        W = rng.normal(0, 1.0, size=(256, 256))           # deliberately too large
        a = np.maximum(0, a @ W.T)
        if use_ln:
            a = (a - a.mean(1, keepdims=True)) / np.sqrt(a.var(1, keepdims=True) + 1e-6)
        out.append(a.std())
    return out
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.4))
ax.semilogy(run_net(False), color=PALETTE["loss"], lw=2, label="no normalisation")
ax.semilogy(run_net(True), color=PALETTE["grad"], lw=2, label="LayerNorm")
ax.set_xlabel("layer"); ax.set_ylabel("std of activations"); ax.legend()
plt.show()







Figure 20.6: The same badly initialised 40-layer ReLU network, with and without LayerNorm after each layer. Without it, the activation scale grows by many orders of magnitude. With it, the scale is pinned and the network remains usable.





Normalisation also changes the geometry of the loss. It removes sensitivity to the scale of each layer’s weights, which improves conditioning in practice. The precise reason is still debated. What we measure reliably is that deep networks train with larger learning rates and less careful initialisation when normalised.
crumbs: 20  The Geometry and Dynamics of Learning

title: 20  The Geometry and Dynamics of Learning
text:
20.7 Gradient clipping
Occasionally a batch produces a huge gradient. One huge step can destroy the model. Global-norm clipping rescales the whole gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold \(c\):
\[
\mathbf{g}\leftarrow\mathbf{g}\cdot\min\!\Bigl(1,\ \frac{c}{\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert}\Bigr).
\tag{20.6}\]
The direction is kept. Only the length is bounded.

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
D = load_digits()
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(D.data / 16.0, D.target, test_size=0.25,
                                      random_state=0, stratify=D.target)
Xt, yt = torch.tensor(Xtr, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(ytr)

def train_clip(lr, clip=None, steps=100):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    m = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 32),
                      nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 10))
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), lr=lr); hist = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(m(Xt), yt); loss.backward()
        if clip:
            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(m.parameters(), clip)
        opt.step(); hist.append(loss.item())
    return hist

h_free, h_clip = train_clip(1.0), train_clip(1.0, clip=1.0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 3.4))
ax.plot(h_free, color=PALETTE["loss"], lw=1.6, label="no clipping")
ax.plot(h_clip, color=PALETTE["grad"], lw=2, label="clip global norm to 1")
ax.set_xlabel("step"); ax.set_ylabel("training loss"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
print(f"no clipping: lowest loss {min(h_free):.3f}, final {h_free[-1]:.3f}")
print(f"clipping   : lowest loss {min(h_clip):.3f}, final {h_clip[-1]:.3f}")







Figure 20.7: Training the digits MLP with SGD at a learning rate of 1.0 for 100 steps, with and without gradient clipping (global norm 1). Without clipping, the loss falls and then bounces back up. With clipping, each step is bounded and the loss falls steadily.





no clipping: lowest loss 0.369, final 3.307
clipping   : lowest loss 0.132, final 0.132


Clipping is a safety rail, not a cure for a learning rate that is far too high. It bounds the size of an update but not the direction errors that come from curvature.

title: 20  The Geometry and Dynamics of Learning
text:
20.8 Failure modes
Exploding activations. Weights too large, or no normalisation in a deep network. Signs: nan loss in the first steps, gradient norm in the thousands.
Vanishing signal. Weights too small or saturating activations. The loss stays at its initial value (for 10 classes, \(\ln10=2.30\)). Chapter 11 showed a case.
Dead units. ReLUs with very negative pre-activations never recover (Chapter 10).
Normalisation at tiny batch size. BatchNorm computes statistics over the batch. With a batch of 2 they are noisy. LayerNorm and RMSNorm use one example only and avoid this.
Low precision. In 16-bit arithmetic, activations above about 65,000 overflow. Normalisation and loss scaling are needed (Chapter 34).
Stability depends on the largest curvature, which can change during training (a sudden “edge-of-stability” rise). A learning rate that worked at the start may not later. Warmup and decay (Chapter 19) manage this.

title: 20  The Geometry and Dynamics of Learning
text:
20.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system now understands when learning works. The step size must respect the steepest curvature (\(\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}\)). The speed is limited by the condition number. Initialisation and normalisation keep signal scale under control, and clipping bounds a single bad step.
This closes Part V. The system can learn: it has a loss, a gradient, an optimiser, and a theory of stability.
\[
x\to f_\theta(x)\to L\to\nabla_\theta L\to\theta'.
\]
All the numbers so far came from data we treated as certain. Real data is noisy, and models must express doubt. Part VI develops the mathematics of uncertainty.

title: 20  The Geometry and Dynamics of Learning
text:
Chapter summary

A convex loss has no bad local minima. Neural-network losses are not convex.
GD on a quadratic is stable for \(\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}\) and needs about \(\kappa\) steps.
Saddles dominate in high dimension. Gradient descent escapes them slowly.
He initialisation: \(\text{Var}(w)=2/n_{\text{in}}\) for ReLU. Xavier: \(1/n\) (or \(2/(n_{\text{in}}+n_{\text{out}})\)).
LayerNorm and RMSNorm pin activation scale. Their output is scale-invariant.
Global-norm clipping bounds the step without changing the gradient direction.

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text:
21.1 The system problem
Everything so far treated data as exact. In the real world, it is not. Pixels have sensor noise. Labels are sometimes wrong. A model that reads “this is a 3” is usually more or less sure. Words in a sentence are uncertain until they are written.
Probability is that language. This chapter gives its vocabulary. Chapters 22–25 turn it into models and losses.
system_map(highlight=["Data", "Uncertainty"],
           sublabels={"Uncertainty": "Ch. 21–25"});
plt.show()







Figure 21.1: Part VI builds the Uncertainty stage of the system.
crumbs: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text: How do we write down “I am not sure” so that it can be computed with?
crumbs: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text:
21.2 Random variables and distributions
A random variable \(X\) is a quantity whose value depends on chance. Its distribution assigns probabilities to values.
Discrete variables take countable values (a die, a class label). The probability mass function (PMF) is \(p(x)=P(X=x)\). It satisfies \(p(x)\ge0\) and \(\sum_xp(x)=1\).
Continuous variables take values on a line (a height, a pixel intensity). Their probability density function (PDF) \(p(x)\) gives probability by area: \[
P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^bp(x)\,dx.
\tag{21.1}\] A density can exceed 1. Only the area must be at most 1.
The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is \(F(x)=P(X\le x)\). It rises from 0 to 1 for both kinds.

from scipy.stats import norm
faces = np.arange(1, 7); pmf = np.array([0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 5))
axes[0, 0].bar(faces, pmf, color=PALETTE["data"]); axes[0, 0].set_title("PMF  p(x)")
axes[0, 1].step(np.r_[0, faces, 7], np.r_[0, np.cumsum(pmf), 1], where="post", color=PALETTE["model"])
axes[0, 1].set_title("CDF  F(x)")
xs = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
axes[1, 0].plot(xs, norm.pdf(xs), color=PALETTE["data"])
mask = (xs >= -1) & (xs <= 1)
axes[1, 0].fill_between(xs[mask], norm.pdf(xs[mask]), color=PALETTE["data"], alpha=0.35)
axes[1, 0].set_title("PDF  p(x)")
axes[1, 1].plot(xs, norm.cdf(xs), color=PALETTE["model"])
axes[1, 1].set_title("CDF  F(x)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"P(-1 <= X <= 1) = F(1) - F(-1) = {norm.cdf(1) - norm.cdf(-1):.4f}")







Figure 21.2: The three descriptions of a distribution. Top: a discrete variable (a biased die): PMF and CDF. Bottom: a continuous variable (standard normal): PDF and CDF. The shaded area of the PDF is the probability that X lies in [−1, 1]; it equals the rise of the CDF over that interval.





P(-1 <= X <= 1) = F(1) - F(-1) = 0.6827
crumbs: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text:
21.3 Expectation and variance
The expectation (mean) is the probability-weighted average:
\[
\mathbb{E}[f(X)]=\sum_xp(x)f(x)\quad\text{or}\quad\int p(x)f(x)\,dx.
\tag{21.2}\]
It is linear: \(\mathbb{E}[aX+bY+c]=a\,\mathbb{E}[X]+b\,\mathbb{E}[Y]+c\), whether or not \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.
The variance measures the spread around the mean \(\mu\):
\[
\text{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(X-\mu)^{2}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2,
\qquad\text{std}(X)=\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}.
\tag{21.3}\]






TipWhy \(\text{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2\)



Expand the square and use linearity: \(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]=\mathbb{E}[X^2-2\mu X+\mu^2]=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-2\mu\,\mathbb{E}[X]+\mu^2=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2.\) \(\blacksquare\)


Two scaling rules follow: \(\text{Var}(aX+c)=a^2\,\text{Var}(X)\), and the standard deviation scales by \(|a|\).
crumbs: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text:
21.4 Two variables: joint, marginal, covariance
For two variables, the joint distribution \(p(x,y)\) gives the probability of each pair. The marginal sums out the other variable:
\[
p(x)=\sum_yp(x,y).
\tag{21.4}\]
\(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if \(p(x,y)=p(x)\,p(y)\) for all pairs.
The covariance measures linear co-movement:
\[
\text{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[XY]-\mu_{X}\mu_Y.
\tag{21.5}\]
The correlation \(\rho=\text{Cov}(X,Y)/(\sigma_{X}\sigma_Y)\) lies in \([-1,1]\) (by Cauchy–Schwarz, Chapter 4). The variance of a sum depends on it:
\[
\text{Var}(X+Y)=\text{Var}(X)+\text{Var}(Y)+2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y).
\tag{21.6}\]
For independent variables \(\text{Cov}=0\) and variances add. This is the rule used in Chapter 20 for initialisation.

21.4.1 The covariance matrix
For a random vector \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d\), the covariance matrix has entries \(\Sigma_{jk}=\text{Cov}(x_j,x_k)\). The sample covariance of Chapter 7, \(\mathbf{S}=\frac1N\mathbf{X}_c^{\intercal}\mathbf{X}_c\), is the estimate of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) from \(N\) samples. The eigenvectors of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) are the axes of the distribution’s ellipse. This is why PCA works.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200); circ = np.stack([np.cos(t), np.sin(t)])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.4))
for ax, rho in zip(axes, [0.0, 0.8, -0.8]):
    C = np.array([[1.0, rho], [rho, 1.0]])
    Xs = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], C, size=800)
    S = np.cov(Xs.T, bias=True)
    lam, V = np.linalg.eigh(S)
    ax.scatter(*Xs.T, s=5, alpha=0.4, color=PALETTE["data"])
    ax.plot(*(V @ (2 * np.sqrt(lam)[:, None] * circ)), color=PALETTE["loss"], lw=2)
    ax.set_xlim(-4, 4); ax.set_ylim(-4, 4); ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_title(f"ρ = {rho:+.1f}   sample ρ̂ = {S[0, 1] / np.sqrt(S[0, 0] * S[1, 1]):+.2f}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 21.3: Samples from three 2D Gaussians with correlation ρ = 0, +0.8, −0.8. The ellipse is the 2σ contour computed from the sample covariance. Positive covariance tilts the cloud up; negative tilts it down.







21.4.2 Uncorrelated is not independent
Correlation sees only linear dependence. Take \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and \(Y=X^2\). \(Y\) is a deterministic function of \(X\), so the two are strongly dependent. Yet their covariance is \(\mathbb{E}[X^3]-\mathbb{E}[X]\,\mathbb{E}[X^2]=0\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = rng.normal(size=200_000); y = x ** 2
print(f"corr(X, X²) = {np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]:+.4f}   (≈ 0, yet Y is a function of X)")
big = np.abs(x) > 1.5
print(f"mean of Y when |X| > 1.5: {y[big].mean():.2f};  overall mean of Y: {y.mean():.2f}")

corr(X, X²) = -0.0054   (≈ 0, yet Y is a function of X)
mean of Y when |X| > 1.5: 3.92;  overall mean of Y: 1.00

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text:
21.5 Estimating from data: joint tables
We estimate a joint distribution of two binary pixels in the digits data (on if brightness \(>8\)) by counting.

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
D = load_digits()
A = (D.data[:, 27] > 8).astype(int); B = (D.data[:, 28] > 8).astype(int)   # neighbouring pixels
joint = np.zeros((2, 2))
for a_, b_ in zip(A, B):
    joint[a_, b_] += 1
joint /= joint.sum()
pa, pb = joint.sum(axis=1), joint.sum(axis=0)             # marginals
print("joint p(a, b):\n", np.round(joint, 3))
print("marginals  p(a) =", np.round(pa, 3), "  p(b) =", np.round(pb, 3))
print("product    p(a) p(b):\n", np.round(np.outer(pa, pb), 3))
print(f"largest |joint − product| = {np.abs(joint - np.outer(pa, pb)).max():.3f}  -> not independent")

joint p(a, b):
 [[0.239 0.217]
 [0.118 0.426]]
marginals  p(a) = [0.456 0.544]   p(b) = [0.357 0.643]
product    p(a) p(b):
 [[0.163 0.293]
 [0.194 0.35 ]]
largest |joint − product| = 0.076  -> not independent


Neighbouring pixels are strongly dependent, as expected for images.
crumbs: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text:
21.6 Law of large numbers
Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be independent with the same mean \(\mu\). The sample mean \(\bar{X}_n=\frac1n\sum_{i\le n}X_i\) converges to \(\mu\) as \(n\) grows. This is the law of large numbers.
It makes Monte Carlo estimation work: to estimate \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\), average \(f\) over samples. The error shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{n}\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, 20000)
running = np.cumsum(rolls) / np.arange(1, len(rolls) + 1)

truth = np.exp(0.5)                       # E[e^X] for X ~ N(0, 1)
ns = np.unique(np.logspace(1, 5, 20).astype(int))
errs = []
for n in ns:
    e = [abs(np.exp(rng.normal(size=n)).mean() - truth) for _ in range(100)]
    errs.append(np.mean(e))

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.3))
ax1.plot(running, color=PALETTE["data"]); ax1.axhline(3.5, ls="--", color=PALETTE["neutral"])
ax1.set_xscale("log"); ax1.set_xlabel("number of rolls"); ax1.set_ylabel("running mean")
ax2.loglog(ns, errs, "o-", color=PALETTE["model"], label="mean |error|")
ax2.loglog(ns, errs[0] * np.sqrt(ns[0] / ns), "--", color=PALETTE["neutral"], label="∝ 1/√n")
ax2.set_xlabel("samples n"); ax2.set_ylabel("error"); ax2.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 21.4: Left: the running average of die rolls settles at 3.5. Right: the Monte Carlo error in estimating E[eˣ] for X ~ N(0,1) falls as 1/√n, a straight line of slope −½ on a log-log plot. To gain one more digit of accuracy requires 100 times as many samples.
crumbs: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text:
21.7 Central limit theorem
The sample mean not only converges. Its error is approximately Gaussian, whatever the original distribution (if the variance is finite):
\[
\bar{X}_n\;\approx\;\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
\tag{21.7}\]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 2.8), sharey=False)
for ax, n in zip(axes, [1, 2, 5, 30]):
    means = rng.exponential(1.0, size=(20000, n)).mean(axis=1)
    ax.hist(means, bins=60, density=True, color=PALETTE["data"], alpha=0.6)
    xs = np.linspace(means.min(), np.quantile(means, 0.999), 300)
    ax.plot(xs, norm.pdf(xs, 1, 1 / np.sqrt(n)), color=PALETTE["loss"], lw=2)
    skew = np.mean(((means - means.mean()) / means.std()) ** 3)
    ax.set_title(f"n = {n}\nskewness {skew:.2f}", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 21.5: The central limit theorem. Samples are exponential (strongly skewed). The histogram of the mean of n samples becomes a bell curve as n grows. The curve is the Gaussian N(1, 1/n) predicted by the theorem.





The skewness falls as \(2/\sqrt{n}\). For \(n=30\), a Gaussian is a good description. This is why Gaussian noise is the default model of aggregated errors, and why batch averages behave well.

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
section: 21.8 Heavy tails: when averages do not settle
text:
21.8 Heavy tails: when averages do not settle
The law of large numbers needs a finite mean. The Cauchy distribution has tails so heavy that its mean does not exist. Its sample mean never settles. It has the same distribution as one sample, however large \(n\) is.

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 20000
g = rng.normal(size=n); c = rng.standard_cauchy(size=n)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.3))
ax.plot(np.cumsum(g) / np.arange(1, n + 1), color=PALETTE["data"], label="Gaussian")
ax.plot(np.cumsum(c) / np.arange(1, n + 1), color=PALETTE["loss"], label="Cauchy")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_ylim(-5, 5); ax.legend()
ax.set_xlabel("number of samples"); ax.set_ylabel("running mean")
plt.show()







Figure 21.6: Running mean of 20,000 samples. For a Gaussian (blue) it converges to 0. For a Cauchy variable (red) it keeps jumping, because occasional huge samples dominate the sum.





Real data, such as losses, gradient norms, or word frequencies, can be heavy-tailed. Check before trusting an average.

from scipy import stats

      "  empirical:", round(np.mean(x <= 3.0), 4))

M = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[2.0, 1.2], [1.2, 1.0]], size=100_000)

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text:
21.10 Failure modes
Assuming independence. The variance of a mean is \(\sigma^2/n\) only for independent samples. Correlated samples (neighbouring pixels, consecutive frames, duplicates) give far less information than \(n\) independent ones.
Heavy tails. No finite mean or variance. Averages and standard deviations mislead. Use medians and quantiles.
Correlation read as causation or independence. Zero correlation does not mean independence (shown above). Nonzero correlation does not mean cause.
Too few samples. The central limit theorem is an approximation. For small \(n\) or skewed data, Gaussian error bars are wrong.
Estimating a covariance with too few samples. For \(N<d\), the sample covariance matrix is singular (rank at most \(N-1\)). Whitening (Chapter 13) then fails.

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text:
21.12 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now describe uncertainty: distributions, expectations, spread, and joint behaviour. It can estimate these from data and knows that averages converge at a \(1/\sqrt{n}\) rate, with Gaussian error, unless the tails are too heavy.
It cannot yet update beliefs with evidence, or turn a score into a probability. Chapter 22 adds conditioning and Bayes’ rule.

title: 21  Probability as a Language of Uncertainty
text:
Chapter summary

A random variable has a distribution: PMF, PDF, CDF.
\(\mathbb{E}[X]\) is linear. \(\text{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mu^2\).
Covariance measures linear co-movement. Independent implies uncorrelated, not the reverse.
\(\text{Var}(X+Y)=\text{Var}(X)+\text{Var}(Y)+2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)\).
Sample means converge (LLN) with Gaussian error \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) (CLT).
Heavy tails break both: the Cauchy mean never settles.

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
22.1 The system problem
Chapter 21 described how uncertain quantities are distributed. A system must also update what it believes when it sees evidence. A spam filter sees words and must decide the class. A language model sees the first words of a sentence and must predict the next.
system_map(highlight=["Data", "Uncertainty"],
           sublabels={"Uncertainty": "Ch. 21–25"});
plt.show()







Figure 22.1: Chapter 22 adds conditioning and updating to the Uncertainty stage.

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text: How should evidence change belief, and how does a joint distribution break into steps we can compute?

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
22.2 Conditional probability
The probability of \(A\) given \(B\) restricts attention to the cases where \(B\) holds:
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A,B)}{P(B)},\qquad P(B)>0.
\tag{22.1}\]
Rearranged, this is the product rule:
\[
P(A,B)=P(A\mid B)\,P(B)=P(B\mid A)\,P(A).
\tag{22.2}\]
We compute a conditional from a joint table. For the two neighbouring digit pixels of Chapter 21 (call them \(A\) and \(B\), on if brightness is above 8):

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
D = load_digits()
A = (D.data[:, 27] > 8).astype(int); B = (D.data[:, 28] > 8).astype(int)
joint = np.array([[np.mean((A == a) & (B == b)) for b in (0, 1)] for a in (0, 1)])
pA = joint.sum(axis=1)
cond = joint / pA[:, None]                       # P(B = b | A = a), rows sum to 1
print("P(B=1)              =", round(joint[:, 1].sum(), 3))
print("P(B=1 | A=0)        =", round(cond[0, 1], 3))
print("P(B=1 | A=1)        =", round(cond[1, 1], 3), "  <- knowing A changes the belief about B")

P(B=1)              = 0.643
P(B=1 | A=0)        = 0.476
P(B=1 | A=1)        = 0.783   <- knowing A changes the belief about B

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
22.3 The chain rule
Apply the product rule repeatedly. For any \(n\) variables,
\[
P(x_1,\dots,x_n)=P(x_1)\,P(x_{2}\mid x_1)\,P(x_{3}\mid x_1,x_2)\cdots P(x_{n}\mid x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})=\prod_{t=1}^{n}P(x_{t}\mid x_{<t}).
\tag{22.3}\]






TipDerivation by induction



For \(n=2\) it is Equation 22.2. Suppose it holds for \(n-1\) variables. Treat \((x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})\) as one event \(A\) and \(x_n\) as \(B\). Then \(P(A,B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)\), which is \(P(x_{n}\mid x_{<n})\prod_{t<n}P(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\). \(\blacksquare\)


This is exact. It makes no assumption. It says that the probability of a sequence is the product of the probability of each element given the ones before it. Chapter 33 builds language models on it: the whole model is a machine for \(P(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\).
We build the smallest word-level language model from the Zen of Python text (Chapter 15): a bigram model, where each word depends only on the previous one. Then we compute the probability of a sentence using the chain rule.

import io, codecs, contextlib
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
    import this
text = codecs.decode(this.s, "rot13").lower()
words = "".join(c if c.isalpha() else " " for c in text).split()
vocab = sorted(set(words)); V = len(vocab)
ix = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
ids = np.array([ix[w] for w in words])
print(f"{len(words)} words, vocabulary {V}")

alpha = 0.1                                       # add-alpha smoothing
C = np.full((V, V), alpha)
np.add.at(C, (ids[:-1], ids[1:]), 1)              # bigram counts
P_next = C / C.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)         # P(next | previous), rows sum to 1
P_first = (np.bincount(ids, minlength=V) + alpha)
P_first = P_first / P_first.sum()                 # P(first word)

def sentence_prob(sentence):
    w = [ix[t] for t in sentence.split()]
    p = P_first[w[0]]
    for a, b in zip(w[:-1], w[1:]):
        p *= P_next[a, b]                         # chain rule, one factor per word
    return p

for s in ["beautiful is better than ugly", "ugly is better than beautiful"]:
    print(f"P('{s}') = {sentence_prob(s):.2e}")
print("rows of P(next|prev) sum to 1:", np.allclose(P_next.sum(axis=1), 1))
print("all two-word sequences sum to 1:",
      np.isclose((P_first[:, None] * P_next).sum(), 1.0))

147 words, vocabulary 87
P('beautiful is better than ugly') = 9.72e-06
P('ugly is better than beautiful') = 8.03e-08
rows of P(next|prev) sum to 1: True
all two-word sequences sum to 1: True


The model assigns a much higher probability to the first sentence, which appears in the text, than to the reordered version. Note the last line: the probabilities of all two-word sequences sum to 1. The chain rule gives a valid distribution.

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
22.4 Bayes’ theorem
Equate the two forms of the product rule and divide:
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)},\qquad
P(B)=\sum_aP(B\mid a)\,P(a).
\tag{22.4}\]








Term
Name
Meaning




\(P(A)\)
prior
belief before the evidence


\(P(B\mid A)\)
likelihood
how likely the evidence is if \(A\) is true


\(P(A\mid B)\)
posterior
belief after the evidence


\(P(B)\)
evidence (marginal)
how likely the evidence is overall



In a diagnosis problem, the cause is the disease and the evidence is the test. We usually know \(P(\text{test}\mid\text{disease})\) from lab studies. We want \(P(\text{disease}\mid\text{test})\).

22.4.1 The base-rate trap
A disease affects 1% of people. A test detects it in 90% of sick people (sensitivity). It is negative in 95% of healthy people (specificity). A person tests positive. How likely are they to be sick?
Most people guess about 90%. The right answer is far lower.
\[
P(\text{sick}\mid+)=\frac{0.90\cdot0.01}{0.90\cdot0.01+0.05\cdot0.99}\approx0.154.
\]
The reason is simple in counts. In 2,000 people, 20 are sick and 18 test positive. Among the 1,980 healthy, 5% (99) also test positive. Of 117 positives, only 18 are sick.

n, prev, sens, spec = 2000, 0.01, 0.90, 0.95
sick = int(n * prev); healthy = n - sick
tp = int(round(sick * sens)); fn = sick - tp
fp = int(round(healthy * (1 - spec))); tn = healthy - fp
print(f"sick {sick}: positive {tp}, negative {fn};  healthy {healthy}: positive {fp}, negative {tn}")
print(f"P(sick | positive) = {tp / (tp + fp):.3f}")

codes = np.array([0] * tn + [1] * fn + [2] * fp + [3] * tp)       # 0 healthy-neg ... 3 sick-pos
grid = codes.reshape(40, 50)
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap
cmap = ListedColormap(["#E5E7EB", "#9CA3AF", PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["loss"]])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
ax.imshow(grid, cmap=cmap, aspect="auto"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
labels = [("healthy, negative", "#E5E7EB"), ("sick, negative (missed)", "#9CA3AF"),
          ("healthy, positive (false alarm)", PALETTE["model"]), ("sick, positive", PALETTE["loss"])]
for i, (lab, c) in enumerate(labels):
    ax.plot([], [], "s", color=c, label=lab)
ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02), ncol=2, fontsize=8, frameon=False)
plt.show()

sick 20: positive 18, negative 2;  healthy 1980: positive 99, negative 1881
P(sick | positive) = 0.154








Figure 22.2: 2,000 people, one square each. Sick people are a small group (1%). The test catches 90% of them, but it also flags 5% of the much larger healthy group. A positive result is therefore mostly a false alarm: 18 of the 117 positives are sick (15%).





We confirm it by simulation.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N = 2_000_000
is_sick = rng.random(N) < prev
positive = np.where(is_sick, rng.random(N) < sens, rng.random(N) < 1 - spec)
print(f"simulated P(sick | positive) = {is_sick[positive].mean():.3f}  (Bayes: {tp / (tp + fp):.3f})")

simulated P(sick | positive) = 0.153  (Bayes: 0.154)

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
22.5 Updating beliefs: the Beta–Binomial model
Bayes’ theorem can be applied again and again as data arrives. The posterior after one observation is the prior for the next.
Take a coin with unknown heads probability \(\theta\). We flip it \(n\) times and see \(k\) heads. The likelihood is \(\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}\). Use a Beta prior, \(p(\theta)\propto\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\). By Bayes,
\[
p(\theta\mid k)\;\propto\;\underbrace{\theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{n-k}}_{\text{likelihood}}\;\underbrace{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}_{\text{prior}}=\theta^{a+k-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-k-1}.
\tag{22.5}\]
The posterior is again a Beta, with parameters \((a+k,\ b+n-k)\). The prior is conjugate: the update only adds the counts. The posterior mean is \(\frac{a+k}{a+b+n}\). Think of \(a,b\) as “pseudo-counts” of heads and tails.

from scipy.stats import beta
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
flips = (rng.random(100) < 0.7).astype(int)
ths = np.linspace(0, 1, 400)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4), sharey=True)
for ax, (a0, b0), title in zip(axes, [(1, 1), (20, 20)], ["flat prior Beta(1, 1)", "strong prior Beta(20, 20)"]):
    for n_obs, c in zip([0, 1, 5, 20, 100], ["#9CA3AF", PALETTE["data"], PALETTE["prob"], PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["loss"]]):
        k = flips[:n_obs].sum()
        ax.plot(ths, beta.pdf(ths, a0 + k, b0 + n_obs - k), color=c, lw=2, label=f"n = {n_obs}")
    ax.axvline(0.7, ls="--", color="black", lw=0.8); ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("θ")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8); axes[0].set_ylabel("posterior density")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for (a0, b0) in [(1, 1), (20, 20)]:
    k = flips[:10].sum()
    print(f"prior Beta({a0},{b0}), after 10 flips ({k} heads): posterior mean {(a0 + k) / (a0 + b0 + 10):.3f}")







Figure 22.3: Beliefs about a coin’s heads probability after 0, 1, 5, 20, and 100 flips (true value 0.7). The flat prior gives way to a narrow peak near the truth. Left: a flat prior Beta(1,1). Right: a strong prior Beta(20,20) that expects a fair coin: it needs more data to move.





prior Beta(1,1), after 10 flips (8 heads): posterior mean 0.750
prior Beta(20,20), after 10 flips (8 heads): posterior mean 0.560


With little data the prior dominates. With much data the likelihood dominates and the prior is forgotten. This is how Bayesian reasoning behaves, and it is the idea behind regularisation (Chapter 25).

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
22.6 Naive Bayes: a spam filter
Chapter 1 opened with a spam filter. We can now build one. Let \(c\) be the class (spam or ham) and \(\mathbf{w}=(w_1,\dots,w_m)\) the words of a message. By Bayes,
\[
P(c\mid\mathbf{w})\;\propto\;P(c)\,P(\mathbf{w}\mid c).
\]
The likelihood \(P(\mathbf{w}\mid c)\) of a whole message is hard to estimate. Naive Bayes assumes the words are independent given the class:
\[
P(\mathbf{w}\mid c)\approx\prod_{j=1}^{m}P(w_{j}\mid c).
\tag{22.6}\]
Each factor is a word frequency in that class, with add-one smoothing:
\[
P(w\mid c)=\frac{\text{count}(w,c)+1}{\sum_{w'}\text{count}(w',c)+|V|}.
\tag{22.7}\]
We compute in log space (sums, not products), to avoid underflow.

spam = ["win a free prize now", "free money click here now", "claim your free gift card today",
        "limited offer win cash prize", "urgent your account is suspended click here",
        "cheap pills online buy now", "you have won a free vacation claim now",
        "exclusive deal buy cheap watches today", "congratulations you won cash click now",
        "earn money fast work from home", "free entry win a prize text now",
        "final notice claim your cash prize"]
ham = ["are we still meeting for lunch today", "please review the report before the meeting",
       "can you send me the notes from class", "dinner at my place on friday",
       "the project deadline is moved to next week", "thanks for your help with the presentation",
       "i will call you after the meeting", "let us go for a walk this evening",
       "did you see the game last night", "happy birthday hope you have a great day",
       "the report is attached please review it", "see you at the office tomorrow morning"]

vocab_nb = sorted({w for m in spam + ham for w in m.split()})
ix_nb = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab_nb)}
def counts(msgs):
    c = np.zeros(len(vocab_nb))
    for m in msgs:
        for w in m.split():
            c[ix_nb[w]] += 1
    return c

cs, ch = counts(spam), counts(ham)
logp_w = {"spam": np.log((cs + 1) / (cs.sum() + len(vocab_nb))),
          "ham":  np.log((ch + 1) / (ch.sum() + len(vocab_nb)))}
log_prior = {"spam": np.log(len(spam) / (len(spam) + len(ham))),
             "ham":  np.log(len(ham) / (len(spam) + len(ham)))}

def p_spam(message):
    known = [ix_nb[w] for w in message.split() if w in ix_nb]       # ignore unseen words
    s = log_prior["spam"] + sum(logp_w["spam"][i] for i in known)
    h = log_prior["ham"] + sum(logp_w["ham"][i] for i in known)
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(h - s))                                   # normalise two classes

tests = [("free cash prize waiting for you", "spam"), ("claim your free vacation now", "spam"),
         ("please send the report before lunch", "ham"), ("are you free for dinner tomorrow", "ham"),
         ("win money now", "spam"), ("meeting notes attached for review", "ham")]
print(f"{'message':40s} {'P(spam)':>8s}  truth")
for m, truth in tests:
    print(f"{m:40s} {p_spam(m):8.3f}  {truth}")

message                                   P(spam)  truth
free cash prize waiting for you             0.958  spam
claim your free vacation now                0.999  spam
please send the report before lunch         0.002  ham
are you free for dinner tomorrow            0.135  ham
win money now                               0.991  spam
meeting notes attached for review           0.008  ham


Which words carry the decision? The log-odds of a word is \(\ln\frac{P(w\mid\text{spam})}{P(w\mid\text{ham})}\).

lo = logp_w["spam"] - logp_w["ham"]
order = np.argsort(lo)
pick = np.r_[order[:10], order[-10:]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.2))
ax.barh([vocab_nb[i] for i in pick], lo[pick],
        color=[PALETTE["loss"] if v > 0 else PALETTE["data"] for v in lo[pick]])
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.8); ax.set_xlabel("log-odds  ln P(w|spam) − ln P(w|ham)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 22.4: Words ranked by their log-odds of spam against ham. Positive values (red) point to spam: ‘now’, ‘free’, ‘win’, ‘prize’, ‘claim’. Negative values (blue) point to ham: ‘the’, ‘you’, ‘meeting’, ‘report’.






22.6.1 When the independence assumption fails
Words are not independent. In “free cash prize”, the three words are all signs of the same thing. Naive Bayes counts each as new evidence. The posterior becomes over-confident.
We can see it by repeating a message. Repeating it adds no information, but multiplies the likelihood ratios.

msg = "are you free for dinner tomorrow"           # truly ham, contains one spammy word
for reps in [1, 2, 4, 8]:
    print(f"message repeated {reps}x: P(spam) = {p_spam(' '.join([msg] * reps)):.4f}")
msg2 = "free prize for the report"                 # mixed evidence
print()
for reps in [1, 2, 4, 8]:
    print(f"mixed message repeated {reps}x: P(spam) = {p_spam(' '.join([msg2] * reps)):.4f}")

message repeated 1x: P(spam) = 0.1347
message repeated 2x: P(spam) = 0.0237
message repeated 4x: P(spam) = 0.0006
message repeated 8x: P(spam) = 0.0000

mixed message repeated 1x: P(spam) = 0.2762
mixed message repeated 2x: P(spam) = 0.1271
mixed message repeated 4x: P(spam) = 0.0208
mixed message repeated 8x: P(spam) = 0.0004


Evidence that is only repeated pushes the probability towards 0 or 1. Naive Bayes is often a good classifier (the ranking is right) and a poor probability estimator (the numbers are too extreme). Chapter 24 shows how to calibrate probabilities.

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
22.7 Production
scikit-learn provides the same classifier. We check that it matches ours.

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB

cv = CountVectorizer(vocabulary=vocab_nb, token_pattern=r"\b\w+\b")
Xtr = cv.transform(spam + ham); ytr = np.array([1] * len(spam) + [0] * len(ham))
nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
Xq = cv.transform([m for m, _ in tests])
ours = np.array([p_spam(m) for m, _ in tests])
print("sklearn P(spam):", np.round(nb.predict_proba(Xq)[:, 1], 3))
print("ours           :", np.round(ours, 3))
print("match:", np.allclose(nb.predict_proba(Xq)[:, 1], ours))

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
22.8 Failure modes
Base-rate neglect. A good test applied to a rare condition gives mostly false positives. Always ask: what is the prior?
Zero counts. A word never seen in spam gives \(P(w\mid\text{spam})=0\) and kills the whole product. Smoothing (add-one or add-\(\alpha\)) fixes this.
Violated independence. Strongly dependent features give over-confident posteriors (shown above).
Prior sensitivity. With little data, the posterior depends on the prior (Figure 40.4). State the prior and test how much the conclusion changes.
Underflow. A product of many small probabilities underflows to 0. Work with log-probabilities.
Conditioning on rare events. If \(P(B)\) is tiny, estimates of \(P(A\mid B)\) come from few samples and are unreliable.

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
22.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now condition and update: it can ask what a piece of evidence implies, break a joint distribution into steps by the chain rule, and combine a prior with a likelihood. It has the equation \(P(x_{1:n})=\prod_tP(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\) that language models are built on.
Next, Chapter 23 lists the few distributions that appear almost everywhere: Bernoulli, categorical, Gaussian, and their relatives.

title: 22  Conditional Probability and Bayes
text:
Chapter summary

\(P(A\mid B)=P(A,B)/P(B)\). The product rule: \(P(A,B)=P(A\mid B)P(B)\).
Chain rule: \(P(x_{1:n})=\prod_tP(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\). It is exact.
Bayes: posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) prior.
With a rare condition, a positive test is mostly a false alarm.
The Beta prior is conjugate to the Binomial: the update adds counts.
Naive Bayes multiplies per-word likelihoods. Smoothing avoids zeros. Dependent features make it over-confident.

The categorical distribution is the output of every classifier and every language model: a vector \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) of \(K\) non-negative numbers that sum to one (the softmax of Chapter 24 produces it). rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pi = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05])
cum = np.cumsum(pi)

def sample_categorical(pi_cum, n):
    u = rng.random(n)
    return np.searchsorted(pi_cum, u)             # first index with cum >= u

draws = sample_categorical(cum, 100_000)
print("target   :", pi)
print("empirical:", np.round(np.bincount(draws, minlength=4) / len(draws), 3))

title: 23  Probability Distributions Used in AI
text:
23.3 The Gaussian
The Gaussian (normal) distribution has density
\[
\mathcal{N}(x;\mu,\sigma^2)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
\tag{23.1}\]
Its mean is \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). About 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of the mass lie within \(1\sigma\), \(2\sigma\), \(3\sigma\) of the mean.
Three facts make the Gaussian the workhorse.

Central limit theorem (Chapter 21): sums of many small independent effects are approximately Gaussian.
Closure: a sum of independent Gaussians is Gaussian, with means and variances added. Any affine map of a Gaussian is Gaussian.
Maximum entropy: among all distributions with a given mean and variance, the Gaussian has the largest entropy. It assumes the least beyond those two numbers.


rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.normal(1.0, 2.0, 500_000)
b = rng.normal(-3.0, 1.5, 500_000)
s = a + b
print(f"sum: mean {s.mean():.3f} (expect {1.0 - 3.0}),  var {s.var():.3f} (expect {4.0 + 2.25})")
within = [np.mean(np.abs(a - 1.0) < k * 2.0) for k in (1, 2, 3)]
print("fraction within 1, 2, 3 sigma:", np.round(within, 4))

sum: mean -1.996 (expect -2.0),  var 6.254 (expect 6.25)
fraction within 1, 2, 3 sigma: [0.6817 0.9545 0.9972]



23.3.1 The multivariate Gaussian
For \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) with mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) (positive definite),
\[
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{1/2}}\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\intercal}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\Bigr).
\tag{23.2}\]
The exponent is half the squared Mahalanobis distance of Chapter 13. The contours are ellipses with axes along the eigenvectors of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\).






TipDerivation: mean and covariance of a linear map



Let \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}\). By linearity of expectation, \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}]=\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{b}\). The deviation is \(\mathbf{y}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{y}]=\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\). Then \[
\text{Cov}(\mathbf{y})=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^{\intercal}\mathbf{A}^{\intercal}\bigr]=\mathbf{A}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\,\mathbf{A}^{\intercal}.
\] For a Gaussian \(\mathbf{x}\), \(\mathbf{y}\) is also Gaussian, so these two numbers describe it fully. \(\blacksquare\)


This gives the standard way to sample: take \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\), find a matrix \(\mathbf{L}\) with \(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^{\intercal}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) (the Cholesky factor), and set \(\mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\). Then \(\text{Cov}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{L}\mathbf{I}\mathbf{L}^{\intercal}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
A = np.array([[2.0, 0.5], [0.0, 0.8]]); b = np.array([3.0, 1.0])
eps = rng.normal(size=(2000, 2))
y = eps @ A.T + b
S_pred = A @ A.T
S_emp = np.cov(y.T, bias=True)
print("predicted covariance A Aᵀ:\n", np.round(S_pred, 2))
print("sample covariance:\n", np.round(S_emp, 2))

L = np.linalg.cholesky(S_pred)
y2 = rng.normal(size=(200_000, 2)) @ L.T + b                  # Cholesky sampling
print("Cholesky sampling covariance:\n", np.round(np.cov(y2.T), 2))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.5, 3.6))
axes[0].scatter(*eps.T, s=4, alpha=0.4, color=PALETTE["data"]); axes[0].set_title("ε ~ N(0, I)")
axes[1].scatter(*y.T, s=4, alpha=0.4, color=PALETTE["model"]); axes[1].set_title("y = A ε + b")
for ax in axes: ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axhline(0, c="#9CA3AF", lw=0.5); ax.axvline(0, c="#9CA3AF", lw=0.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

title: 23  Probability Distributions Used in AI
text:
23.5 Changing variables
If \(Y=g(X)\) for a monotone, differentiable \(g\), the density of \(Y\) is
\[
p_Y(y)=p_{X}\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)\,\Bigl|\frac{d\,g^{-1}(y)}{dy}\Bigr|.
\tag{23.3}\]
The factor \(|dg^{-1}/dy|\) accounts for how \(g\) stretches the axis. In several dimensions it is \(|\det\mathbf{J}_{g^{-1}}|\) (the Jacobian of Chapter 17). This formula is the basis of normalising flows.
Example: if \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and \(Y=e^X\), then \(g^{-1}(y)=\ln y\) and \(p_Y(y)=\frac{1}{y}\mathcal{N}(\ln y;0,1)\), the log-normal density.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
y = np.exp(rng.normal(size=400_000))
lo, hi = 0.5, 2.0
emp = np.mean((y > lo) & (y < hi))
from scipy.integrate import quad
formula = quad(lambda t: stats.norm.pdf(np.log(t)) / t, lo, hi)[0]
print(f"P({lo} < Y < {hi}): simulated {emp:.4f}, from the change-of-variables density {formula:.4f}")

P(0.5 < Y < 2.0): simulated 0.5106, from the change-of-variables density 0.5118

title: 23  Probability Distributions Used in AI
text:
23.6 The reparameterisation trick
Models often need a gradient of an expectation with respect to a distribution’s parameters:
\[
\nabla_\mu\,\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)}\bigl[f(z)\bigr].
\]
The sample \(z\) is random, so it is not obvious how to differentiate through it. The reparameterisation trick writes the sample as a deterministic function of the parameters and parameter-free noise:
\[
z=\mu+\sigma\,\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).
\tag{23.4}\]
Now \(\mathbb{E}[f(z)]=\mathbb{E}_\epsilon[f(\mu+\sigma\epsilon)]\), and the gradient moves inside the expectation: \(\nabla_\mu\mathbb{E}[f]=\mathbb{E}_\epsilon[f'(\mu+\sigma\epsilon)]\). This is a sample average of ordinary derivatives. It is used in VAEs (Chapter 40) and in the diffusion training objective (Chapter 41).
There is another way: the score-function (REINFORCE) estimator, \(\mathbb{E}[f(z)\,\nabla_\mu\ln p(z)]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[f(z)\frac{z-\mu}{\sigma^2}\bigr]\). It works for any distribution but has a far higher variance. We compare them for \(f(z)=z^2\). The true gradient is \(\nabla_\mu\mathbb{E}[z^2]=\nabla_\mu(\mu^2+\sigma^2)=2\mu\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
mu, sigma, n, reps = 1.0, 1.0, 100, 3000
eps = rng.normal(size=(reps, n))
z = mu + sigma * eps
reparam = (2 * z).mean(axis=1)                          # mean of f'(z) = 2z
score = (z ** 2 * (z - mu) / sigma ** 2).mean(axis=1)    # mean of f(z) (z - mu)/sigma^2
print(f"true gradient: {2 * mu}")
print(f"reparameterised: mean {reparam.mean():.3f}, std {reparam.std():.3f}")
print(f"score function : mean {score.mean():.3f}, std {score.std():.3f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.3))
ax.hist(score, bins=80, alpha=0.6, color=PALETTE["loss"], label="score function", density=True)
ax.hist(reparam, bins=80, alpha=0.7, color=PALETTE["grad"], label="reparameterised", density=True)
ax.axvline(2, color="black", ls="--"); ax.set_xlabel("estimate"); ax.legend()
plt.show()

true gradient: 2.0
reparameterised: mean 2.001, std 0.204
score function : mean 2.000, std 0.552








Figure 23.4: Two unbiased estimators of d/dμ E[z²] at μ = 1, σ = 1 (true value 2), from 100 samples each, repeated 3000 times. The reparameterised estimator is concentrated near the truth. The score-function estimator has a much larger spread.

title: 23  Probability Distributions Used in AI
text:
23.7 KL divergence between Gaussians
Chapter 15 defined \(D_{\text{KL}}\). For two univariate Gaussians it has a closed form. For the case that matters in VAEs, a Gaussian against the standard normal:
\[
D_{\text{KL}}\bigl(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\,\Vert\,\mathcal{N}(0,1)\bigr)=\tfrac12\bigl(\mu^2+\sigma^2-1-\ln\sigma^{2}\bigr).
\tag{23.5}\]






TipDerivation



\(D_{\text{KL}}=\mathbb{E}_p[\ln p(z)-\ln q(z)]\) with \(\ln p(z)=-\tfrac12\ln(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{(z-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\) and \(\ln q(z)=-\tfrac12\ln2\pi-\tfrac12z^2\). Under \(p\), \(\mathbb{E}[(z-\mu)^2]=\sigma^2\) and \(\mathbb{E}[z^2]=\mu^2+\sigma^2\). So \[
D_{\text{KL}}=-\tfrac12\ln\sigma^2-\tfrac12+\tfrac12(\mu^2+\sigma^2)=\tfrac12(\mu^2+\sigma^2-1-\ln\sigma^2).\ \blacksquare
\] For a diagonal multivariate Gaussian, sum this over the coordinates.



mu, sigma = 0.8, 0.6
closed = 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + sigma ** 2 - 1 - np.log(sigma ** 2))
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
z = rng.normal(mu, sigma, 2_000_000)
mc = np.mean(stats.norm.logpdf(z, mu, sigma) - stats.norm.logpdf(z, 0, 1))
print(f"closed form {closed:.5f}   Monte Carlo {mc:.5f}")

closed form 0.51083   Monte Carlo 0.51137

text:
23.8 Production
torch.distributions bundles these with sampling and log-densities. rsample is the reparameterised sample (gradients flow). sample is not (gradients stop).

import torch
from torch.distributions import Normal, Categorical, MultivariateNormal, kl_divergence

mu_t = torch.tensor(0.8, requires_grad=True)
sd_t = torch.tensor(0.6, requires_grad=True)
d = Normal(mu_t, sd_t)

z = d.rsample((50_000,))                       # reparameterised: z = mu + sd * eps
(z ** 2).mean().backward()
print(f"rsample gradient d/dmu E[z²]: {mu_t.grad.item():.3f}  (truth 2·mu = {2 * 0.8})")
print("sample() keeps gradients:", d.sample((3,)).requires_grad)

print("closed-form KL matches torch:",
      np.isclose(kl_divergence(Normal(0.8, 0.6), Normal(0.0, 1.0)).item(), closed))
print("Categorical log_prob:", Categorical(torch.tensor(pi)).log_prob(torch.tensor(2)).item(),
      "  ln(0.15) =", round(float(np.log(0.15)), 4))
mvn = MultivariateNormal(torch.tensor(b), covariance_matrix=torch.tensor(S_pred))
print("MVN log_prob at mean:", round(mvn.log_prob(torch.tensor(b)).item(), 4),
      "  formula:", round(float(-np.log(2 * np.pi) - 0.5 * np.log(np.linalg.det(S_pred))), 4))

title: 23  Probability Distributions Used in AI
text:
23.9 Failure modes
Density is not probability. A density can exceed 1. Only its integral is a probability. Comparing a density to a probability is a type error.
Variance collapse. A maximum-likelihood Gaussian fitted to one point has likelihood growing without limit as \(\sigma\to0\). Models that learn their own variance need a floor or a prior.

x0, mu0 = 0.7, 0.7                                    # one data point, mean placed on it
for s in [1.0, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001]:
    print(f"sigma = {s:6.3f}   log-likelihood = {stats.norm.logpdf(x0, mu0, s):7.2f}")

sigma =  1.000   log-likelihood =   -0.92
sigma =  0.100   log-likelihood =    1.38
sigma =  0.010   log-likelihood =    3.69
sigma =  0.001   log-likelihood =    5.99


Wrong tails. A Gaussian noise model assigned to heavy-tailed data lets rare large errors dominate the fit. Use a Laplace or Student-\(t\) model, or a robust loss (Chapter 14).
Underflow. Densities of many variables are tiny products. Use log_prob always. Compare log-densities, and avoid exponentiating.
Not positive definite. A sampled or learned covariance may fail to be positive definite. Parameterise through a Cholesky factor or a diagonal.
Discrete versus continuous. The pixel intensity is an integer in 0–255. A continuous model assigns it a density. Dequantisation (adding small noise) is needed to compare likelihoods fairly.

23.11 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system has a vocabulary of distributions: the discrete ones for classes, the Gaussian for continuous noise and latents, and tools to transform them and sample from them. It can differentiate through random samples (reparameterisation) and measure the distance between Gaussians in closed form.

title: 23  Probability Distributions Used in AI
text:
Chapter summary

Bernoulli, binomial, categorical, multinomial are the discrete workhorses. The categorical is the output of classifiers and language models.
The Gaussian is closed under affine maps: \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{b},\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{A}^{\intercal})\).
Sample a Gaussian as \(\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) with \(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^{\intercal}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\).
Laplace and Student-\(t\) have heavier tails and correspond to robust losses.
Change of variables multiplies the density by \(|dg^{-1}/dy|\).
Reparameterisation \(z=\mu+\sigma\epsilon\) gives low-variance gradients through samples.
\(D_{\text{KL}}(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\Vert\mathcal{N}(0,1))=\frac12(\mu^2+\sigma^2-1-\ln\sigma^2)\).

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.1 The system problem
The last layer of a network produces numbers such as \((2.3,-0.7,4.1)\). These can be negative, they do not sum to 1, and they are not probabilities. Yet we compute losses on probabilities (Chapter 15), sample from them (Chapter 33), and report them to users.
system_map(highlight=["Transformation", "Uncertainty"],
           sublabels={"Uncertainty": "Ch. 21–25"});
plt.show()







Figure 24.1: Chapter 24 connects the Transformation stage’s output to the Uncertainty stage.

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text: A network outputs unconstrained numbers. How do we turn them into valid, trustworthy probabilities?

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.2 Sigmoid: two classes
For one logit \(z\), the sigmoid gives the probability of the positive class:
\[
\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\in(0,1).
\tag{24.1}\]
The inverse is the logit (log-odds): \(z=\ln\frac{p}{1-p}\). A logit of 0 means 50%. A logit of 2 means 88%. A logit of 5 means 99.3%.

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.3 Softmax: many classes
For \(K\) logits \(\mathbf{z}\), the softmax is
\[
p_i=\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_i=\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}e^{z_j}}.
\tag{24.2}\]
It is positive, sums to 1, and keeps the order of the logits. Exponentiating makes a gap in logits into a ratio of probabilities: \(p_i/p_j=e^{z_i-z_j}\).
Properties:

Shift invariance. \(\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z}+c\mathbf{1})=\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})\). Only differences of logits matter.
Two classes reduce to the sigmoid. \(\text{softmax}(z_1,z_2)_1=\sigma(z_1-z_2)\).
Monotone. A larger logit gives a larger probability.


24.3.1 Temperature
Dividing the logits by a temperature \(T>0\) changes the sharpness:
\[
p_i^{(T)}=\frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_je^{z_j/T}}.
\tag{24.3}\]
As \(T\to0\) the distribution approaches a one-hot vector at the largest logit (argmax). As \(T\to\infty\) it approaches uniform. At \(T=1\) it is the ordinary softmax.

def softmax(z, T=1.0):
    z = np.asarray(z, float) / T
    z = z - z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)           # stable: subtract the maximum
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def entropy_bits(p):
    p = p[p > 0]; return -np.sum(p * np.log2(p))

logits = np.array([3.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.0, -1.0])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 2.6), sharey=True)
for ax, T in zip(axes, [0.25, 1.0, 3.0, 10.0]):
    p = softmax(logits, T)
    ax.bar(range(5), p, color=PALETTE["model"])
    ax.set_title(f"T = {T}\nentropy {entropy_bits(p):.2f} bits", fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_ylabel("probability")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 24.2: Softmax of the same five logits at four temperatures. Low temperature concentrates the mass on the largest logit. High temperature spreads it out. Entropy (in bits) rises with T.

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.4 Computing softmax safely
The exponential overflows for large logits. In 32-bit floats, \(e^{89}\) is already infinity. Because softmax is shift-invariant, we subtract the maximum first. Then the largest exponent is 0, and nothing overflows.
For the loss we need \(\ln p_i=z_i-\ln\sum_je^{z_j}\). The second term is the log-sum-exp:
\[
\text{LSE}(\mathbf{z})=m+\ln\sum_je^{z_j-m},\qquad m=\max_jz_j.
\tag{24.4}\]

z = np.array([1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0])
with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    naive = np.exp(z) / np.exp(z).sum()
print("naive softmax :", naive)
print("stable softmax:", np.round(softmax(z), 4))

def log_softmax(z):
    m = z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return z - (m + np.log(np.exp(z - m).sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)))
print("log-softmax   :", np.round(log_softmax(z), 4))

naive softmax : [nan nan nan]
stable softmax: [0.09   0.2447 0.6652]
log-softmax   : [-2.4076 -1.4076 -0.4076]


Never compute log(softmax(z)). Use log_softmax. Libraries fuse the log-softmax with the loss (cross_entropy takes logits) for this reason.

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.5 The Jacobian of softmax
For backpropagation we need \(\partial p_i/\partial z_j\).






TipDerivation



Write \(p_i=e^{z_i}/S\) with \(S=\sum_ke^{z_k}\). Then \(\partial S/\partial z_j=e^{z_j}\).

If \(i=j\): \(\dfrac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_i}=\dfrac{e^{z_i}S-e^{z_i}e^{z_i}}{S^2}=p_i(1-p_i)\).
If \(i\ne j\): \(\dfrac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j}=\dfrac{-e^{z_i}e^{z_j}}{S^2}=-p_ip_j\).

Together, \[
\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j}=p_i(\delta_{ij}-p_j),\qquad\mathbf{J}=\text{diag}(\mathbf{p})-\mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}^{\intercal}.\ \blacksquare
\]


The rows of \(\mathbf{J}\) sum to zero (the probabilities always sum to 1). Where one \(p_i\) is near 1, every entry of \(\mathbf{J}\) is near 0: softmax saturates, as the sigmoid does (Chapter 10).

24.5.1 Cross-entropy on logits
The loss for true class \(c\) is \(\ell=-\ln p_c\). Its gradient with respect to the logits follows from the Jacobian:
\[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_j}=-\frac{1}{p_c}\,\frac{\partial p_c}{\partial z_j}=-\frac{1}{p_c}\,p_c(\delta_{cj}-p_j)=p_j-\delta_{cj}.
\]
In vector form,
\[
\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}\ell=\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y},
\tag{24.5}\]
with \(\mathbf{y}\) the one-hot label. The gradient is the prediction minus the target. We verify the Jacobian and this gradient numerically.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
z = rng.normal(size=5); c = 2
p = softmax(z)
J = np.diag(p) - np.outer(p, p)
eps = 1e-6
J_num = np.stack([(softmax(z + eps * e) - softmax(z - eps * e)) / (2 * eps)
                  for e in np.eye(5)], axis=1)
print("max |analytic − numeric| Jacobian:", np.abs(J - J_num).max())
print("rows sum to zero:", np.allclose(J.sum(axis=1), 0))

loss = lambda z: -np.log(softmax(z)[c])
g_num = np.array([(loss(z + eps * e) - loss(z - eps * e)) / (2 * eps) for e in np.eye(5)])
y = np.eye(5)[c]
print("max |(p − y) − numeric gradient|:", np.abs((p - y) - g_num).max())

max |analytic − numeric| Jacobian: 2.923021547029947e-11
rows sum to zero: True
max |(p − y) − numeric gradient|: 9.871489736745787e-11

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.6 The probability simplex
Three-class probabilities live on a triangle, the simplex: all \((p_1,p_2,p_3)\) with \(p_{i}\ge0\) and \(\sum p_i=1\). Corners are certain outcomes. The centre is the uniform distribution. Softmax maps all of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) onto the interior.

corners = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.0], [0.5, np.sqrt(3) / 2]])
to_xy = lambda P: P @ corners
g = np.linspace(0, 1, 120)
U, V = np.meshgrid(g, g)
mask = U + V <= 1
P = np.stack([U[mask], V[mask], 1 - U[mask] - V[mask]], axis=1)
XY = to_xy(P)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.9))
sc = axes[0].scatter(*XY.T, c=P.max(axis=1), s=4, cmap="viridis")
axes[0].set_title("largest probability"); plt.colorbar(sc, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.04)
zz = np.stack(np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3, 3, 13), np.linspace(-3, 3, 13)), -1).reshape(-1, 2)
zz = np.c_[zz, np.zeros(len(zz))]
for T, col in [(1.0, PALETTE["data"]), (0.3, PALETTE["loss"])]:
    axes[1].scatter(*to_xy(softmax(zz, T)).T, s=10, color=col, label=f"T = {T}")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8); axes[1].set_title("softmax of a logit grid")
for ax in axes:
    t = np.vstack([corners, corners[:1]]); ax.plot(*t.T, color="black", lw=1)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 24.3: Softmax maps the plane of logit differences onto the probability triangle. Left: contours of the largest class probability. Right: softmax outputs for a grid of logits; low temperature pushes points towards the corners. The corners are certain predictions that no finite logit reaches.

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.7 Calibration
A model is calibrated if, among predictions with confidence 80%, about 80% are correct. Softmax outputs are not guaranteed to be calibrated. Deep networks trained to low cross-entropy on their training data are often over-confident on new data.
We measure it with a reliability diagram: bin predictions by confidence and plot the accuracy in each bin. A calibrated model lies on the diagonal. The expected calibration error (ECE) is the weighted average gap:
\[
\text{ECE}=\sum_{b}\frac{n_b}{N}\,\bigl|\text{acc}(b)-\text{conf}(b)\bigr|.
\tag{24.6}\]
We build an over-confident model on purpose: a flexible network trained on noisy labels for many steps.

import torch, torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=3000, n_features=10, n_informative=4, n_classes=3,
                           n_clusters_per_class=2, flip_y=0.15, class_sep=1.0, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xrest, ytr, yrest = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=0)
Xval, Xte, yval, yte = train_test_split(Xrest, yrest, test_size=0.6, random_state=0)
T_ = lambda a: torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32)
Xtr_t, Xval_t, Xte_t = T_(Xtr), T_(Xval), T_(Xte)
ytr_t = torch.tensor(ytr)

torch.manual_seed(0)
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(),
                    nn.Linear(128, 3))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=0.01)
for _ in range(600):
    opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(Xtr_t), ytr_t).backward(); opt.step()

with torch.no_grad():
    logits_val, logits_te = net(Xval_t).numpy(), net(Xte_t).numpy()

def ece(probs, labels, bins=10):
    conf = probs.max(1); pred = probs.argmax(1); correct = (pred == labels)
    edges = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, bins + 1); total = 0.0; rows = []
    for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        m = (conf > lo) & (conf <= hi)
        if m.sum():
            rows.append((conf[m].mean(), correct[m].mean(), m.sum()))
            total += m.mean() * abs(correct[m].mean() - conf[m].mean())
    return total, rows

p_te = softmax(logits_te)
e_before, rows_before = ece(p_te, yte)
print(f"test accuracy {np.mean(p_te.argmax(1) == yte):.3f}   mean confidence {p_te.max(1).mean():.3f}"
      f"   ECE {e_before:.3f}")

test accuracy 0.660   mean confidence 0.957   ECE 0.297


The model’s average confidence is higher than its accuracy. This is over-confidence.

24.7.1 Temperature scaling
The simplest repair is to divide all logits by one number \(T\) found on a held-out validation set by minimising the cross-entropy:
\[
T^*=\arg\min_T\;-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\ln\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_i/T)_{y_i}.
\tag{24.7}\]
Since \(T\) rescales all logits equally, the argmax is unchanged. Accuracy stays the same. Only the confidence changes.

from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar
nll = lambda T: -np.mean(log_softmax(logits_val / T)[np.arange(len(yval)), yval])
T_star = minimize_scalar(nll, bounds=(0.2, 200), method="bounded").x
p_te_T = softmax(logits_te, T_star)
e_after, rows_after = ece(p_te_T, yte)
print(f"fitted temperature T* = {T_star:.2f}")
print(f"ECE before {e_before:.3f}  ->  after {e_after:.3f}")
print(f"accuracy before {np.mean(p_te.argmax(1) == yte):.3f}, "
      f"after {np.mean(p_te_T.argmax(1) == yte):.3f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.8))
for ax, rows, title in zip(axes, [rows_before, rows_after],
                           [f"raw softmax (ECE {e_before:.3f})", f"T = {T_star:.2f} (ECE {e_after:.3f})"]):
    conf = np.array([r[0] for r in rows]); acc = np.array([r[1] for r in rows])
    ax.bar(conf, acc, width=0.07, color=PALETTE["model"], edgecolor="white")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--", color="black"); ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("confidence"); ax.set_ylabel("accuracy"); ax.set_xlim(0.3, 1.02); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

fitted temperature T* = 10.09
ECE before 0.297  ->  after 0.057
accuracy before 0.660, after 0.660








Figure 24.4: Reliability diagrams on the test set. Left: the raw softmax. Bars below the diagonal mean the model is more confident than accurate. Right: after temperature scaling with one parameter fitted on the validation set, the bars follow the diagonal. Accuracy is identical in both.

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.8 Label smoothing
A related idea acts at training time. Instead of a one-hot target, use \(y_k=1-\varepsilon\) for the true class and \(\varepsilon/(K-1)\) for the others. This discourages logits from growing without limit, since a one-hot target is reached only by an infinite logit gap. Smoothing usually improves calibration and is common in classification and translation models.

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.9 Production
PyTorch fuses log-softmax and cross-entropy. We check that our code matches.

import torch.nn.functional as F
logits_t = torch.tensor(rng.normal(size=(6, 5)) * 4)
labels_t = torch.tensor([0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 0])

print("softmax        :", torch.allclose(F.softmax(logits_t, 1), torch.tensor(softmax(logits_t.numpy()))))
print("log_softmax    :", torch.allclose(F.log_softmax(logits_t, 1), torch.tensor(log_softmax(logits_t.numpy()))))
ours = -log_softmax(logits_t.numpy())[np.arange(6), labels_t.numpy()].mean()
print("cross_entropy  :", np.isclose(F.cross_entropy(logits_t, labels_t).item(), ours))

eps_ls, K = 0.1, 5
target = np.full((6, K), eps_ls / (K - 1)); target[np.arange(6), labels_t.numpy()] = 1 - eps_ls
ours_ls = -(target * log_softmax(logits_t.numpy())).sum(1).mean()
print("label smoothing:", np.isclose(F.cross_entropy(logits_t, labels_t, label_smoothing=eps_ls * K / (K - 1)).item(), ours_ls))

softmax        : True
log_softmax    : True
cross_entropy  : True
label smoothing: True

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.10 Failure modes
Overflow. exp of a large logit is infinite. Always subtract the maximum, or use library functions.
Saturation. If one class has a very large logit, \(\mathbf{J}\approx\mathbf{0}\) and the gradient vanishes. It is harmless when the prediction is right and harmful when it is confidently wrong (the cross-entropy gradient \(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y}\) remains large in that case, which is why we pair softmax with cross-entropy).
Over-confidence. Low training loss does not give calibrated probabilities. Always check a reliability diagram before using probabilities in decisions.
Distribution shift. Calibration fitted on one distribution may not hold on another (Chapter 27).
Ties in argmax. Equal logits make the argmax arbitrary. In float16, many logits may be equal after rounding.
Wrong activation for the task. Softmax for multi-label tasks (several classes can be true at once) is wrong. Use an independent sigmoid per class.
Temperature misuse. A temperature that is fitted for calibration (a post-hoc scale) is not the same as sampling temperature in generation, though the formula is identical (Chapter 33).

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
24.12 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now express its output as a probability distribution: logits become probabilities through sigmoid or softmax, with a temperature control, a stable computation, a clean gradient (\(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y}\)), and a way to check and repair calibration.
The loss function, cross-entropy, was assumed in Chapters 14 and 15. Chapter 25 explains where it comes from: it is what maximum likelihood estimation gives.

title: 24  From Scores to Probabilities
text:
Chapter summary

Sigmoid: \(\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\). Softmax: \(p_i=e^{z_i}/\sum_je^{z_j}\). Two-class softmax is a sigmoid of the logit difference.
Softmax is shift-invariant. Temperature \(T\) rescales the logits.
Compute with the max-subtraction and log-sum-exp trick.
\(\partial p_i/\partial z_j=p_i(\delta_{ij}-p_j)\). The cross-entropy gradient on logits is \(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{y}\).
Calibration: confidence should match accuracy. Measure with reliability diagrams and ECE.
Temperature scaling fixes confidence without changing predictions.

text:

title: 25  Statistical Estimation
text:
25.1 The system problem
We used squared error, cross-entropy, and weight decay without saying where they come from. They looked like design choices. They are not arbitrary.
The answer is a single principle: choose the parameters under which the observed data is most probable.
system_map(highlight=["Measurement", "Learning", "Uncertainty"],
           sublabels={"Uncertainty": "Ch. 21–25"});
plt.show()







Figure 25.1: Chapter 25 closes Part VI and links the Uncertainty stage to the Learning stage.

title: 25  Statistical Estimation
text: Why are cross-entropy and mean squared error the right losses, and why does weight decay appear?

title: 25  Statistical Estimation
text:
25.2 Likelihood and maximum likelihood
A probabilistic model gives the probability (or density) of data \(\mathcal{D}\) for each setting of the parameters \(\theta\): \(p(\mathcal{D}\mid\theta)\). Seen as a function of \(\theta\), with the data fixed, it is the likelihood \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\).
For independent examples, it is a product, so we work with its logarithm:
\[
\ell(\theta)=\ln\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ln p(y_{i}\mid x_i;\theta).
\tag{25.1}\]
The maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE) is
\[
\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}}=\arg\max_\theta\ \ell(\theta)=\arg\min_\theta\ \underbrace{-\frac1N\sum_{i}\ln p(y_{i}\mid x_i;\theta)}_{\text{negative log-likelihood (NLL)}}.
\tag{25.2}\]
Maximising the likelihood is the same as minimising the negative log-likelihood, which is a loss function.

25.2.1 Example: a coin
We flip a coin \(n=10\) times and see \(k=7\) heads. For heads probability \(\theta\), \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}\) and \(\ell(\theta)=k\ln\theta+(n-k)\ln(1-\theta)\). Setting the derivative to zero:
\[
\frac{k}{\theta}-\frac{n-k}{1-\theta}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\hat\theta=\frac{k}{n}.
\]
The MLE is the observed frequency.

k, n = 7, 10
th = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 400)
L = th ** k * (1 - th) ** (n - k)
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2))
ax1.plot(th, L, color=PALETTE["data"], lw=2); ax1.axvline(k / n, ls="--", color=PALETTE["loss"])
ax1.set_xlabel("θ"); ax1.set_ylabel("likelihood")
ax2.plot(th, np.log(L), color=PALETTE["model"], lw=2); ax2.axvline(k / n, ls="--", color=PALETTE["loss"])
ax2.set_xlabel("θ"); ax2.set_ylabel("log-likelihood")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"numerical argmax: {th[np.argmax(L)]:.3f}   closed form k/n = {k / n}")







Figure 25.2: Likelihood (left) and log-likelihood (right) of a coin’s heads probability after 7 heads in 10 flips. Both peak at θ = 0.7. The log is easier to work with: it turns a product into a sum and has the same maximiser.





numerical argmax: 0.700   closed form k/n = 0.7




25.2.2 Example: a Gaussian
For \(y_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the log-likelihood is \(-\frac N2\ln(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2\). The derivative in \(\mu\) gives \(\hat\mu=\frac1N\sum_iy_i\), the sample mean. The derivative in \(\sigma^2\) gives \(\hat\sigma^2=\frac1N\sum_i(y_i-\hat\mu)^2\). (This variance estimate is slightly biased low, as Chapter 26 shows.)

title: 25  Statistical Estimation
text:
25.3 From likelihood to loss
The likelihood of a model that predicts \(y\) from \(x\) depends on what we assume about the randomness in \(y\).

25.3.1 Gaussian noise gives squared error
Suppose \(y=f_\theta(x)+\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\). Then \(p(y\mid x;\theta)=\mathcal{N}(y;f_\theta(x),\sigma^2)\) and
\[
-\ln p(y_{i}\mid x_i;\theta)=\frac{(y_i-f_\theta(x_i))^2}{2\sigma^2}+\frac12\ln(2\pi\sigma^2).
\tag{25.3}\]
The second term does not depend on \(\theta\). Summing over examples, the NLL is the mean squared error scaled by \(1/2\sigma^2\), plus a constant. Minimising MSE is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N = 50
x = rng.uniform(-2, 2, N); y = 2 * x + 1 + rng.normal(0, 0.5, N)
sigma = 0.5

def nll(a, b):                                    # sum over examples of -ln N(y; a x + b, sigma²)
    r = y - (a * x + b)
    return np.sum(0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi * sigma ** 2) + r ** 2 / (2 * sigma ** 2))
mse = lambda a, b: np.mean((y - (a * x + b)) ** 2)

print(f"{'(a, b)':>12s} {'NLL':>9s} {'MSE':>8s} {'NLL − N/(2σ²)·MSE':>20s}")
for a, b in [(0.0, 0.0), (1.0, 0.5), (2.0, 1.0), (3.0, -1.0)]:
    print(f"{str((a, b)):>12s} {nll(a, b):9.2f} {mse(a, b):8.3f} "
          f"{nll(a, b) - N / (2 * sigma ** 2) * mse(a, b):20.3f}")
print(f"constant N/2·ln(2πσ²) = {N / 2 * np.log(2 * np.pi * sigma ** 2):.3f}")

      (a, b)       NLL      MSE    NLL − N/(2σ²)·MSE
  (0.0, 0.0)    767.53    7.562               11.290
  (1.0, 0.5)    229.33    2.180               11.290
  (2.0, 1.0)     36.73    0.254               11.290
 (3.0, -1.0)    519.36    5.081               11.290
constant N/2·ln(2πσ²) = 11.290


The last column is the same for every \((a,b)\). The NLL and the MSE differ only by a scale and a constant, so they have the same minimiser.


25.3.2 Categorical outputs give cross-entropy
For classification, the model outputs a probability vector \(\mathbf{q}_\theta(x)\) over \(K\) classes. The likelihood of the label \(y_i\) is \(q_{\theta,y_i}(x_i)\), so
\[
\text{NLL}=-\frac1N\sum_{i}\ln q_{\theta,y_i}(x_i).
\tag{25.4}\]
This is the cross-entropy loss of Chapters 14 and 24. The cross-entropy of Chapter 15 makes the link exact. Let \(\hat{p}\) be the empirical distribution of the data. Then
\[
\text{NLL}=H(\hat{p},q_\theta)=H(\hat{p})+D_{\text{KL}}(\hat{p}\Vert q_\theta).
\]
Since \(H(\hat{p})\) does not depend on \(\theta\), maximum likelihood is the same as minimising the KL divergence from the data distribution to the model. We verify the identity for a discrete example.

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
labels = rng.choice(3, size=1000, p=[0.6, 0.3, 0.1])
p_hat = np.bincount(labels, minlength=3) / len(labels)          # empirical distribution
q = np.array([0.5, 0.35, 0.15])                                  # some model
nll_cat = -np.mean(np.log(q[labels]))                            # mean NLL
H = -np.sum(p_hat * np.log(p_hat)); KL = np.sum(p_hat * np.log(p_hat / q))
print(f"NLL = {nll_cat:.5f};   H(p̂) + KL(p̂‖q) = {H + KL:.5f}")
print(f"the q that minimises NLL is q = p̂ = {np.round(p_hat, 3)};  its NLL equals H(p̂) = {H:.5f}")

NLL = 0.92875;   H(p̂) + KL(p̂‖q) = 0.92875
the q that minimises NLL is q = p̂ = [0.596 0.296 0.108];  its NLL equals H(p̂) = 0.90916

fig = box_flow(["probability model\np(y | x; θ)", "likelihood\n∏ p(yᵢ | xᵢ; θ)", "loss\n−Σ ln p(yᵢ | xᵢ; θ)",
                "optimisation\nθ ← θ − η∇L"],
