title: 30  The Mathematics of Attention
text:
30.3 Intuition: soft lookup
A Python dictionary maps a key to a value. A lookup returns the value of the key that equals the query. A soft lookup compares the query with every key, and returns a blend of values weighted by how well each key matches.
This is the idea of semantic search (Chapters 4 and 13): the key is the embedding of a document, the query is the embedding of a question. Attention does it inside the network, for every token at once.
Take a query \(\mathbf{q}\), keys \(\mathbf{k}_1,\dots,\mathbf{k}_T\), values \(\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_T\):
\[
s_j=\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}_j,\qquad
a_j=\frac{e^{s_j}}{\sum_ie^{s_i}},\qquad
\mathbf{o}=\sum_ja_j\,\mathbf{v}_j.
\tag{30.1}\]
The scores come from the dot product (Chapter 4). The weights come from the softmax (Chapter 24): non-negative and summing to one. The output is a convex combination of the values.

import math
keys   = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [0.7, 0.7]]
values = [[10.0, 0.0], [0.0, 10.0], [5.0, 5.0]]
query  = [0.9, 0.1]                                   # close to the first key

scores = [sum(q * k for q, k in zip(query, key)) for key in keys]
m = max(scores)                                       # stable softmax
exps = [math.exp(s - m) for s in scores]
weights = [e / sum(exps) for e in exps]
output = [sum(w * v[c] for w, v in zip(weights, values)) for c in range(2)]
print("scores :", [round(s, 3) for s in scores])
print("weights:", [round(w, 3) for w in weights], " sum =", round(sum(weights), 6))
print("output :", [round(o, 3) for o in output])

scores : [0.9, 0.1, 0.7]
weights: [0.441, 0.198, 0.361]  sum = 1.0
output : [6.214, 3.786]


The query is closest to the first key, so the output leans towards the first value. Sharper queries give a harder lookup.

title: 30  The Mathematics of Attention
section: 30.4 From tokens to queries, keys and values
text:
30.4 From tokens to queries, keys and values
In a Transformer, queries, keys, and values all come from the same token matrix \(\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}\) (hence “self-attention”), through three learned linear maps (Chapter 9):
\[
\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_Q,\qquad
\mathbf{K}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_K,\qquad
\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_V,
\tag{30.2}\]
with \(\mathbf{W}_Q,\mathbf{W}_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_k}\) and \(\mathbf{W}_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_v}\). Each token plays three roles: what it asks (query), what it offers for matching (key), and what it hands over (value). Separate maps let a token ask for one thing and offer another.
For all tokens at once, all scores form one matrix product:
\[
\mathbf{S}=\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\intercal}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times T},\qquad
\mathbf{A}=\text{softmax}_{\text{rows}}(\mathbf{S}),\qquad
\mathbf{O}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_v}.
\tag{30.3}\]
Row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) is the distribution of attention that token \(i\) pays to every token.

def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    """Q, K: (T, d_k); V: (T, d_v); mask: (T, T) bool, True = allowed."""
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[-1])                   # (T, T) scores
    if mask is not None:
        S = np.where(mask, S, -np.inf)                   # forbid masked pairs
    A = softmax(S, axis=-1)                              # (T, T) rows sum to 1
    return A @ V, A                                      # (T, d_v)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
T, d, dk = 6, 16, 8
X = rng.normal(size=(T, d))
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(size=(d, dk)) / np.sqrt(d) for _ in range(3))
O, A = attention(X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv)
print("output shape:", O.shape, "  attention shape:", A.shape)
print("rows of A sum to 1:", np.allclose(A.sum(axis=1), 1.0))

output shape: (6, 8)   attention shape: (6, 6)
rows of A sum to 1: True
crumbs: Part VIII — Putting the Mathematical Systems Together

title: 30  The Mathematics of Attention
text:
30.5 Why divide by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)






TipDerivation: the variance of a dot product



Suppose the components of \(\mathbf{q}\) and \(\mathbf{k}\) are independent, with mean 0 and variance 1. Each product \(q_ik_i\) has mean 0 and variance \(\mathbb{E}[q_i^2]\,\mathbb{E}[k_i^2]=1\). The dot product is a sum of \(d_k\) independent such terms. Variances of independent terms add (Chapter 21): \[
\text{Var}(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k})=d_k.
\] So the standard deviation of a score grows like \(\sqrt{d_k}\). Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) gives a score of variance 1. \(\blacksquare\)


Why does it matter? The softmax is sensitive to the scale of its input (temperature, Chapter 24). When scores have a large variance, the largest one dominates, the weights become almost one-hot, and the Jacobian of the softmax is near zero: gradients vanish (Chapter 18).

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
dks = [1, 4, 16, 64, 256, 1024]
var_raw, var_scaled, ent_raw, ent_scaled = [], [], [], []
for dk_ in dks:
    q = rng.normal(size=(20000, dk_)); k = rng.normal(size=(20000, dk_))
    s = (q * k).sum(axis=1)
    var_raw.append(s.var()); var_scaled.append((s / np.sqrt(dk_)).var())
    Q_ = rng.normal(size=(2000, dk_)); K_ = rng.normal(size=(16, dk_))     # 16 keys
    for scale, store in [(1.0, ent_raw), (1 / np.sqrt(dk_), ent_scaled)]:
        P = softmax(Q_ @ K_.T * scale)
        H = -(P * np.log(P + 1e-300)).sum(axis=1)
        store.append(H.mean() / np.log(16))

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))
ax1.loglog(dks, var_raw, "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"], label="q·k")

title: 30  The Mathematics of Attention
text:
30.6 Masks
Some pairs must not interact. In a language model that predicts the next token, position \(i\) must not see positions \(j>i\) (they are the answers). A causal mask sets those scores to \(-\infty\) before the softmax. Since \(e^{-\infty}=0\), they receive weight 0, and the remaining weights renormalise.
\[
\tilde S_{ij}=\begin{cases}S_{ij}&j\le i\\-\infty&j>i\end{cases}
\tag{30.4}\]

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
T, dk = 8, 16
Qm, Km, Vm = (rng.normal(size=(T, dk)) for _ in range(3))
causal = np.tril(np.ones((T, T), dtype=bool))
_, A_full = attention(Qm, Km, Vm)
_, A_caus = attention(Qm, Km, Vm, mask=causal)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.5, 3.6))
for ax, A_, title in zip(axes, [A_full, A_caus], ["bidirectional", "causal mask"]):
    im = ax.imshow(A_, cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=0.6)
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("key position j"); ax.set_ylabel("query position i"); ax.grid(False)
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes, fraction=0.03)
plt.show()
print("upper triangle of causal weights is zero:", np.allclose(np.triu(A_caus, 1), 0))
print("rows still sum to 1:", np.allclose(A_caus.sum(axis=1), 1))







Figure 30.4: Attention weights for 8 tokens with random queries and keys. Left: bidirectional attention (every token sees all). Right: causal attention: the upper triangle is exactly zero, and each row still sums to 1.





upper triangle of causal weights is zero: True
rows still sum to 1: True

title: 30  The Mathematics of Attention
text:
30.7 Multi-head attention
One attention layer computes one distribution of weights per token. Multi-head attention runs \(h\) lookups in parallel, each in its own lower-dimensional subspace, and concatenates the results. Each head can attend to a different relation (previous word, a matching bracket, a subject).
With model width \(d\) and \(d_h=d/h\):
\[
\text{head}_m=\text{Attention}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_Q^{(m)},\ \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_K^{(m)},\ \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_V^{(m)}),\qquad
\text{MHA}(\mathbf{X})=\bigl[\text{head}_1;\dots;\text{head}_{h}\bigr]\mathbf{W}_O.
\tag{30.5}\]
In practice the \(h\) projections are one big matrix. The result is reshaped (Chapter 6) from \((T,d)\) to \((h,T,d_h)\), so all heads run as one batched matrix product.

def mha(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, h, causal=False):
    T, d = X.shape; dh = d // h
    def split(M):                                        # (T, d) -> (h, T, dh)
        return M.reshape(T, h, dh).transpose(1, 0, 2)
    Q, K, V = split(X @ Wq), split(X @ Wk), split(X @ Wv)
    S = Q @ K.transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(dh)           # (h, T, T)
    if causal:
        S = np.where(np.tril(np.ones((T, T), bool)), S, -np.inf)
    A = softmax(S)
    heads = A @ V                                        # (h, T, dh)
    concat = heads.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(T, d)      # (T, d)
    return concat @ Wo, A

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
T, d, h = 6, 32, 4
X = rng.normal(size=(T, d))
Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo = (rng.normal(size=(d, d)) / np.sqrt(d) for _ in range(4))
out, A = mha(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, h)

# the same computation head by head, with plain slices
dh = d // h
manual = []
for m in range(h):
    sl = slice(m * dh, (m + 1) * dh)
    o_m, _ = attention(X @ Wq[:, sl], X @ Wk[:, sl], X @ Wv[:, sl])
    manual.append(o_m)
out_loop = np.concatenate(manual, axis=1) @ Wo
print("batched reshape version equals the loop over heads:", np.allclose(out, out_loop))
print("output (T, d):", out.shape, "  attention (h, T, T):", A.shape)
print("parameters of MHA: 4 d² =", 4 * d * d)

output (T, d): (6, 32)   attention (h, T, T): (4, 6, 6)
parameters of MHA: 4 d² = 4096

30.8 Properties
Convex combinations. Each output row is a weighted average of value vectors. It lies inside the convex hull of the values (the smallest convex set containing them).

from scipy.spatial import ConvexHull
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Vv = rng.normal(size=(6, 2)) * 2
Kk = rng.normal(size=(6, 4)); Qq = rng.normal(size=(300, 4)) * 1.5
W = softmax(Qq @ Kk.T / 2)
Out = W @ Vv
hull = ConvexHull(Vv)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 4.2))
poly = np.vstack([Vv[hull.vertices], Vv[hull.vertices][:1]])
ax.plot(*poly.T, "--", color="black")
ax.scatter(*Out.T, s=8, color=PALETTE["model"], alpha=0.6)
ax.scatter(*Vv.T, s=70, color="black"); ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
inside = np.all(hull.equations[:, :2] @ Out.T + hull.equations[:, 2:3] <= 1e-9, axis=0)
print("fraction of outputs inside the hull:", inside.mean())







Figure 30.5: Attention outputs lie inside the convex hull of the values. Black points: six value vectors in 2D. Orange points: outputs for 300 random queries. Every output is a weighted average of the values, so none leaves the hull (dashed).





fraction of outputs inside the hull: 1.0


Permutation equivariance. Attention has no notion of position. If we shuffle the input tokens, the outputs are shuffled in the same way. The model must therefore be given positions (Chapter 31).

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
T, d = 7, 16
X = rng.normal(size=(T, d)); W3 = [rng.normal(size=(d, d)) / np.sqrt(d) for _ in range(3)]
perm = rng.permutation(T)
run = lambda X_: attention(X_ @ W3[0], X_ @ W3[1], X_ @ W3[2])[0]
print("attention(P X) == P attention(X):", np.allclose(run(X[perm]), run(X)[perm]))

attention(P X) == P attention(X): True


Cost. The score matrix has \(T^2\) entries. Time is \(O(T^2d)\) and score memory is \(O(T^2)\) (Chapter 6). Doubling the context length multiplies the attention cost by four.

title: 30  The Mathematics of Attention
text:
30.9 The backward pass
Training needs \(\partial L/\partial\mathbf{Q}\), \(\partial L/\partial\mathbf{K}\), \(\partial L/\partial\mathbf{V}\). Using the rules of Chapter 18 and the softmax Jacobian of Chapter 24:






TipDerivation



Let \(\mathbf{G}=\partial L/\partial\mathbf{O}\) be the upstream gradient. From \(\mathbf{O}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\) (a matrix product, Chapter 5): \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{V}}=\mathbf{A}^{\intercal}\mathbf{G},\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{A}}=\mathbf{G}\mathbf{V}^{\intercal}.
\] Row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) is a softmax of row \(i\) of \(\mathbf{S}\). With Jacobian \(\text{diag}(\mathbf{a})-\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\intercal}\) (Chapter 24), for each row: \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{ij}}=a_{ij}\Bigl(\frac{\partial L}{\partial A_{ij}}-\sum_{m}a_{im}\frac{\partial L}{\partial A_{im}}\Bigr).
\] Finally, from \(\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\intercal}/\sqrt{d_k}\): \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{Q}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{S}}\,\mathbf{K},\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{K}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Bigl(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf{S}}\Bigr)^{\!\intercal}\mathbf{Q}.\ \blacksquare
\]


We check these formulas against automatic differentiation.

import torch
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
T, dk, dv = 5, 8, 6
Qn, Kn, Vn = rng.normal(size=(T, dk)), rng.normal(size=(T, dk)), rng.normal(size=(T, dv))
G = rng.normal(size=(T, dv))                                  # upstream gradient dL/dO

def backward_manual(Q, K, V, G):
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[1]); A = softmax(S)
    dV = A.T @ G
    dA = G @ V.T
    dS = A * (dA - (A * dA).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))      # softmax Jacobian, row-wise
    dQ = dS @ K / np.sqrt(K.shape[1])
    dK = dS.T @ Q / np.sqrt(K.shape[1])
    return dQ, dK, dV

Qt, Kt, Vt = (torch.tensor(a, requires_grad=True) for a in (Qn, Kn, Vn))
St = Qt @ Kt.T / np.sqrt(dk)
Ot = torch.softmax(St, dim=-1) @ Vt
Ot.backward(torch.tensor(G))
for name, mine, ref in zip(["dQ", "dK", "dV"], backward_manual(Qn, Kn, Vn, G),
                           [Qt.grad, Kt.grad, Vt.grad]):
    print(f"{name}: max |manual − autograd| = {np.abs(mine - ref.numpy()).max():.1e}")

dQ: max |manual − autograd| = 3.3e-16
dK: max |manual − autograd| = 3.3e-16
dV: max |manual − autograd| = 2.2e-16

title: 30  The Mathematics of Attention

30.10 From first principles to production
PyTorch fuses the whole operation into one function that never has to store the full \(T\times T\) matrix on suitable hardware (Chapter 34). We check that it equals ours, with and without the causal mask.

import torch.nn.functional as F
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
T, dk = 10, 16
Qn, Kn, Vn = (rng.normal(size=(1, 2, T, dk)) for _ in range(3))            # (batch, heads, T, d_k)
Qt, Kt, Vt = (torch.tensor(a) for a in (Qn, Kn, Vn))
for causal in (False, True):
    ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(Qt, Kt, Vt, is_causal=causal).numpy()
    mask = np.tril(np.ones((T, T), bool)) if causal else None
    ours = np.stack([[attention(Qn[0, h], Kn[0, h], Vn[0, h], mask)[0] for h in range(2)]])
    print(f"causal = {causal!s:5s}: matches F.scaled_dot_product_attention:", np.allclose(ref, ours))

mha_layer = torch.nn.MultiheadAttention(embed_dim=64, num_heads=8, batch_first=True)
print("nn.MultiheadAttention parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in mha_layer.parameters()),
      "  4d² + 4d =", 4 * 64 * 64 + 4 * 64)

title: 30  The Mathematics of Attention
text:
30.12 Failure modes
Saturated softmax. Without \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\), scores are large and the weights are nearly one-hot. Gradients vanish (Figure 34.4). Large learned query and key norms can cause the same effect during training.
Fully masked rows. If all entries of a row are \(-\infty\), the softmax gives \(0/0=\text{NaN}\). This happens with padding masks. Add a safe value or skip such rows.

S_bad = np.full((1, 4), -np.inf)
with np.errstate(invalid="ignore"):
    print("softmax of an all-masked row:", softmax(S_bad))

softmax of an all-masked row: [[nan nan nan nan]]


Quadratic cost. Memory for the score matrix grows with \(T^2\) (Figure 6.5 of Chapter 6). Long contexts need restructured computation (Chapter 34).
No notion of order. Attention is permutation-equivariant. Without positional information, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” look the same.
Numerical precision. In 16-bit arithmetic, the exponentials and sums need float32 accumulation.

title: 30  The Mathematics of Attention
text:
30.14 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now let every element of a sequence read from every other with content-dependent weights. Attention is a soft lookup built entirely from dot products, a softmax, and weighted averages, with a variance-preserving scale, optional masks, and several heads.
Attention alone is not a model. It has no position, no non-linearity, and no depth. Chapter 31 combines it with an MLP, residual connections, and normalisation into the Transformer block.

title: 30  The Mathematics of Attention
text:
Chapter summary

Attention is a soft key–value lookup: \(\text{softmax}(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\intercal}/\sqrt{d_k})\mathbf{V}\).
\(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V}\) are linear projections of the tokens.
The scale \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps \(\text{Var}(s)=1\) and prevents softmax saturation.
A mask adds \(-\infty\) before the softmax. The causal mask makes the weights lower-triangular.
Multi-head attention splits \(d\) into \(h\) subspaces by reshape and concatenates the heads.
Outputs lie in the convex hull of the values. Attention is permutation-equivariant. Cost is \(O(T^2d)\).

title: 31  The Mathematics of the Transformer
text:
31.3 Embeddings and positions
Token ids become vectors by lookup in an embedding matrix \(\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}\) (Chapters 3, 5). Attention cannot distinguish positions: shuffling tokens shuffles outputs (Chapter 30). Positional information is therefore added to each token vector.
Two common choices:

Learned: a table \(\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{\max}\times d}\) of parameters.
Sinusoidal (the original Transformer): a fixed function of position,

\[
\text{PE}(p,2i)=\sin\!\bigl(p\,\omega_{i}\bigr),\quad
\text{PE}(p,2i+1)=\cos\!\bigl(p\,\omega_{i}\bigr),\qquad
\omega_i=10000^{-2i/d}.
\tag{31.2}\]






TipDerivation: a shift is a linear map



For one frequency \(\omega\), the pair \((\sin\omega p,\cos\omega p)\) is a point on a circle. By the angle-addition formulas, \[
\begin{pmatrix}\sin\omega(p+k)\\\cos\omega(p+k)\end{pmatrix}=
\begin{pmatrix}\cos\omega k&\sin\omega k\\-\sin\omega k&\cos\omega k\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\sin\omega p\\\cos\omega p\end{pmatrix}.
\] The matrix is a rotation (Chapter 5) that depends only on the offset \(k\), not on \(p\). The full encoding is a stack of such pairs, so \(\text{PE}(p+k)=\mathbf{M}_k\,\text{PE}(p)\) for a fixed block-diagonal \(\mathbf{M}_k\). A model can therefore learn relations such as “the token \(k\) steps before”. \(\blacksquare\)



def sinusoidal(T, d):
    p = np.arange(T)[:, None]; i = np.arange(d // 2)[None, :]
    ang = p * 10000.0 ** (-2 * i / d)
    PE = np.zeros((T, d)); PE[:, 0::2] = np.sin(ang); PE[:, 1::2] = np.cos(ang)
    return PE

d, T = 32, 64
PE = sinusoidal(T, d)
def shift_matrix(k, d):
    M = np.zeros((d, d))
    for i in range(d // 2):
        w = 10000.0 ** (-2 * i / d)
        M[2*i:2*i+2, 2*i:2*i+2] = [[np.cos(w * k), np.sin(w * k)], [-np.sin(w * k), np.cos(w * k)]]
    return M
k, p = 5, 17
print("PE(p + k) == M_k PE(p):", np.allclose(shift_matrix(k, d) @ PE[p], PE[p + k]))

PE(p + k) == M_k PE(p): True



PEL = sinusoidal(256, 64)
offsets = np.arange(0, 100)
sim = [np.mean([PEL[p] @ PEL[p + k] for p in range(0, 100, 10)]) for k in offsets]
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
im = ax1.imshow(PE, aspect="auto", cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax1.set_xlabel("dimension"); ax1.set_ylabel("position p"); ax1.grid(False)
ax2.plot(offsets, np.array(sim) / sim[0], color=PALETTE["model"], lw=2)
ax2.set_xlabel("offset k"); ax2.set_ylabel("PE(p)·PE(p+k), normalised")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

title: 31  The Mathematics of the Transformer
text:
31.4 The sub-layers
Attention sub-layer (Chapter 30): \(\text{MHA}(\text{LN}(\mathbf{x}))\).
MLP sub-layer (Chapter 11): applied to each token independently with the same weights:
\[
\text{MLP}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{W}_2\,\text{GELU}(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}_1)+\mathbf{b}_2,\qquad\mathbf{W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{4d\times d},\ \mathbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times4d}.
\tag{31.3}\]
Attention mixes across positions. The MLP transforms each position. The two alternate.
Pre-norm block (the modern default):
\[
\mathbf{x}'=\mathbf{x}+\text{MHA}(\text{LN}(\mathbf{x})),\qquad
\mathbf{x}''=\mathbf{x}'+\text{MLP}(\text{LN}(\mathbf{x}')).
\tag{31.4}\]
The original post-norm block applied \(\text{LN}\) after the addition: \(\text{LN}(\mathbf{x}+\text{MHA}(\mathbf{x}))\).

31.4.1 Why residual connections






TipDerivation: an identity path for the gradient



For \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}+F(\mathbf{x})\), the Jacobian is \(\partial\mathbf{y}/\partial\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{I}+\partial F/\partial\mathbf{x}\) (Chapter 17). Through \(L\) blocks, the backward signal (Chapter 18) is multiplied by \[
\prod_{l=1}^{L}\bigl(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{J}_{l}\bigr)=\mathbf{I}+\sum_{l}\mathbf{J}_l+\sum_{l<m}\mathbf{J}_{m}\mathbf{J}_l+\cdots.
\] There is a term \(\mathbf{I}\): the gradient of the loss with respect to an early layer always contains a direct, unattenuated path from the output. Without the skip, the factor is \(\prod_{l}\mathbf{J}_l\) and shrinks or grows exponentially. \(\blacksquare\)



import torch, torch.nn as nn
torch.manual_seed(0)
L_, dd = 24, 64
Ws = [torch.randn(dd, dd) / math.sqrt(dd) * 0.7 for _ in range(L_)]
def grad_norms(skip):
    x = torch.randn(32, dd, requires_grad=True); h = x; hs = []
    for W in Ws:
        h = h + torch.tanh(h @ W) if skip else torch.tanh(h @ W)
        h.retain_grad(); hs.append(h)
    (h ** 2).mean().backward()
    return [t.grad.norm().item() for t in hs]
g_skip, g_plain = grad_norms(True), grad_norms(False)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
ax.semilogy(range(1, L_ + 1), g_plain, "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"], label="no residual")
ax.semilogy(range(1, L_ + 1), g_skip, "o-", color=PALETTE["grad"], label="residual")
ax.set_xlabel("block index (1 = nearest the input)"); ax.set_ylabel("‖∂L/∂h‖"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
print(f"gradient at block 1 / gradient at block 24:  no residual {g_plain[0] / g_plain[-1]:.1e},  residual {g_skip[0] / g_skip[-1]:.1f}")







Figure 31.4: Gradient norm reaching each block of a 24-block stack at initialisation, with and without a residual connection. Each block is x → tanh(Wx). Without the skip (red), the gradient decays exponentially towards the input. With it (green), it does not decay: the identity path carries it, and it even grows slightly.





gradient at block 1 / gradient at block 24:  no residual 1.3e-03,  residual 6.1

title: 31  The Mathematics of the Transformer
text:
31.5 Counting parameters
With width \(d\), an attention sub-layer has \(4d^2\) weights (Chapter 30). The MLP has \(d\cdot4d+4d\cdot d=8d^2\). So one block has about \(12d^2\) parameters. Adding biases and LayerNorm scales gives exactly \(12d^2+13d\).
\[
N_{\text{params}}\approx\underbrace{12\,L\,d^2}_{\text{blocks}}+\underbrace{V\,d}_{\text{embedding}}\;(+\,V\,d\text{ if the output head is not tied}).
\tag{31.5}\]
For \(d=4096\), \(L=32\): \(12\cdot32\cdot4096^{2}\approx6.4\times10^9\) parameters in the blocks.

title: 31  The Mathematics of the Transformer
text:
31.6 A complete model in PyTorch
We write the whole Transformer as three small classes: about 40 lines. It uses causal self-attention (a decoder). The pre flag selects pre- or post-norm.

class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, h, pre=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.h, self.pre = h, pre
        self.ln1, self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.qkv, self.o = nn.Linear(d, 3 * d), nn.Linear(d, d)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * d, d))

    def attn(self, x):
        B, T, d = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        split = lambda t: t.view(B, T, self.h, d // self.h).transpose(1, 2)   # (B, h, T, dh)
        q, k, v = split(q), split(k), split(v)
        S = q @ k.transpose(-1, -2) / math.sqrt(d // self.h)
        S = S.masked_fill(~torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool)), float("-inf"))
        A = S.softmax(-1)
        out = (A @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, d)
        return self.o(out), A

    def forward(self, x):
        if self.pre:
            a, A = self.attn(self.ln1(x)); x = x + a
            x = x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x))
        else:
            a, A = self.attn(x); x = self.ln1(x + a)
            x = self.ln2(x + self.mlp(x))
        return x, A

class TinyLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, V, T, d=64, h=4, L=2, pre=True, use_pos=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.E, self.P, self.use_pos = nn.Embedding(V, d), nn.Embedding(T, d), use_pos
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([Block(d, h, pre) for _ in range(L)])
        self.ln, self.head = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.Linear(d, V, bias=False)

    def forward(self, idx):
        x = self.E(idx)
        if self.use_pos:
            x = x + self.P(torch.arange(idx.shape[1]))
        attn = []
        for b in self.blocks:
            x, A = b(x); attn.append(A)
        return self.head(self.ln(x)), attn

V_, T_, d_, h_, L2 = 16, 12, 64, 4, 2
model = TinyLM(V_, T_, d_, h_, L2)
n_actual = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
n_formula = V_ * d_ + T_ * d_ + L2 * (12 * d_ ** 2 + 13 * d_) + 2 * d_ + V_ * d_
print(f"parameters: counted {n_actual:,}, formula {n_formula:,}, equal: {n_actual == n_formula}")

parameters: counted 102,912, formula 102,912, equal: True



31.6.1 Pre-norm versus post-norm
The block order changes how well deep models train. We train the copy task (defined in the next section) with 2 and 8 blocks, at two learning rates, without warmup, for both orders. One seed each.

Vc, halfc = 16, 6
def copy_batch(B):
    a = torch.randint(0, Vc - 1, (B, halfc)); sep = torch.full((B, 1), Vc - 1)
    return torch.cat([a, sep, a], dim=1)

def train_copy(pre, L, lr, steps=600, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = TinyLM(Vc, 12, d=64, h=4, L=L, pre=pre)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(m.parameters(), lr=lr); hist = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        x = copy_batch(128)
        logits, _ = m(x[:, :-1])
        loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, Vc), x[:, 1:].reshape(-1))
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); hist.append(loss.item())
    return np.array(hist)

curves = {}
print(f"{'order':10s} {'blocks':>6s} {'lr':>7s} {'final loss':>11s}")
for pre in (True, False):
    for L in (2, 8):
        for lr in (3e-3, 1e-2):
            h = train_copy(pre, L, lr)
            curves[(pre, L, lr)] = h
            print(f"{'pre-norm' if pre else 'post-norm':10s} {L:6d} {lr:7.3f} {h[-30:].mean():11.3f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
ax.plot(curves[(False, 8, 1e-2)], color=PALETTE["loss"], label="post-norm")
ax.plot(curves[(True, 8, 1e-2)], color=PALETTE["grad"], label="pre-norm")
ax.set_xlabel("step"); ax.set_ylabel("training loss"); ax.legend()
plt.show()

order      blocks      lr  final loss
pre-norm        2   0.003       1.133
pre-norm        2   0.010       1.132
pre-norm        8   0.003       1.131
pre-norm        8   0.010       1.132
post-norm       2   0.003       1.132
post-norm       2   0.010       1.131
post-norm       8   0.003       1.131
post-norm       8   0.010       2.769








Figure 31.5: Training loss of an 8-block model on the copy task at learning rate 0.01, with no warmup. Pre-norm (green) reaches the loss floor. Post-norm (red) does not learn within the same 600 steps. At learning rate 0.003, or with 2 blocks, both orders train. One seed per curve: this shows that post-norm is more fragile, not a law.





The original Transformer used post-norm and needed a long learning-rate warmup. With pre-norm, the residual stream is never normalised in place, so the identity path of the residual connection stays intact (see the derivation above). This is why pre-norm became the default.

text:
31.7 Training: learning to copy
We train a small Transformer on a synthetic task that requires attention. Each sequence is six random symbols, a separator, then the same six symbols again. The model reads left to right and predicts the next token. The first half is unpredictable (random). The second half is a copy of the first, and can only be predicted by looking back six positions: at the position of the separator, the next token equals the token at position 0.

V, half = 16, 6                      # symbols 0..14, separator 15
def make_batch(B):
    a = torch.randint(0, V - 1, (B, half))
    sep = torch.full((B, 1), V - 1)
    return torch.cat([a, sep, a], dim=1)                      # length 13

torch.manual_seed(0)
lm = TinyLM(V, 12, d=64, h=4, L=2)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(lm.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
losses = []
t0 = time.time()
for step in range(1500):
    x = make_batch(128); inp, tgt = x[:, :-1], x[:, 1:]
    logits, _ = lm(inp)
    loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, V), tgt.reshape(-1))
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); losses.append(loss.item())

x = make_batch(2000); inp, tgt = x[:, :-1], x[:, 1:]
with torch.no_grad():
    pred = lm(inp)[0].argmax(-1)
acc_first = (pred[:, :half] == tgt[:, :half]).float().mean().item()
acc_copy = (pred[:, half:] == tgt[:, half:]).float().mean().item()
floor = (half - 1) * math.log(V - 1) / (2 * half)            # loss if only the copy part is learned
print(f"trained in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; final loss {np.mean(losses[-50:]):.3f}  "
      f"(floor if the copy half is perfect: {floor:.3f})")
print(f"accuracy on the random first half: {acc_first:.3f};  on the copied second half: {acc_copy:.3f}")

trained in 15 s; final loss 1.130  (floor if the copy half is perfect: 1.128)
accuracy on the random first half: 0.224;  on the copied second half: 1.000


The loss reaches its theoretical floor: the copy half is predicted perfectly, and the random half costs \(\ln15\) per token, which cannot be reduced. The model learned an algorithm.

x = make_batch(1)
with torch.no_grad():
    _, attn = lm(x[:, :-1])
layer = 0                                                  # first block
heads = attn[layer][0]                                    # (h, T, T)
score = [np.mean([heads[m, i, i - 6].item() for i in range(6, 12)]) for m in range(4)]
best = int(np.argmax(score))
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
ax1.plot(losses, color=PALETTE["loss"]); ax1.axhline(floor, ls="--", color="black")
ax1.set_xlabel("step"); ax1.set_ylabel("training loss")
ax2.imshow(heads[best].numpy(), cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1)
ax2.set_xlabel("key position"); ax2.set_ylabel("query position"); ax2.grid(False)
ax2.set_title(f"block {layer + 1}, head {best + 1}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"head {best + 1}: average weight on the position 6 steps back (positions 6-11): {score[best]:.2f}")







Figure 31.6: What the model learned. Left: training loss falls to the floor (dashed). Right: the attention weights of one head of the first block, on one input. From the separator onwards, each position attends to the position exactly six steps back (the bright off-diagonal): it looks up the token to copy.

title: 31  The Mathematics of the Transformer
text:
31.10 Failure modes
No positional information. A model without positions is blind to order. We confirm this below.

torch.manual_seed(1)
one_layer = TinyLM(V, 12, d=64, h=4, L=1, use_pos=False).eval()   # no positional information
idx = torch.randint(0, V, (1, 8)); perm = torch.randperm(7)
shuffled_prefix = torch.cat([idx[:, :7][:, perm], idx[:, 7:]], dim=1)   # same tokens, other order
with torch.no_grad():
    first = one_layer(idx)[0][0, -1]
    second = one_layer(shuffled_prefix)[0][0, -1]
print("last-token logits identical when only the order of earlier tokens changes:",
      torch.allclose(first, second, atol=1e-5))

last-token logits identical when only the order of earlier tokens changes: True


Post-norm fragility. Deep post-norm models are hard to train without warmup (Figure 31.5).
Wrong mask in training. If the model can see the future during training, the loss falls to zero and the model is useless at generation. Always verify that the upper triangle of the attention is zero.
Context-length limits. The positional table has a fixed size. Sinusoidal encodings extrapolate in form but not necessarily in behaviour (Chapter 32).
Cost. Attention is \(O(T^2d)\) and the MLP is \(O(Td^2)\). For small \(d\) and long \(T\), attention dominates. For large \(d\) and short \(T\), the MLP dominates, and it holds two thirds of the parameters.

title: 32  Decoder-only Language Models
text:
32.4 RoPE: positions as rotations
Chapter 31 added a position vector to the input. Rotary position embedding (RoPE) instead rotates the query and key vectors inside each attention layer, by an angle that grows with position.
Split a vector into pairs of coordinates. Treat each pair as a point in a plane. For position \(m\), rotate the \(i\)-th pair by the angle \(m\theta_i\), with \(\theta_i=10000^{-2i/d_h}\):
\[
\mathbf{R}_{m}=\text{blockdiag}\Bigl(\begin{pmatrix}\cos m\theta_i&-\sin m\theta_i\\\sin m\theta_i&\cos m\theta_{i}\end{pmatrix}\Bigr)_{i=0}^{d_h/2-1}.
\tag{32.1}\]
Queries and keys at position \(m\) and \(n\) become \(\mathbf{R}_{m}\mathbf{q}\) and \(\mathbf{R}_{n}\mathbf{k}\).






TipDerivation: the score depends only on the offset



Rotation matrices satisfy \(\mathbf{R}_m^{\intercal}=\mathbf{R}_{-m}\) and \(\mathbf{R}_{a}\mathbf{R}_b=\mathbf{R}_{a+b}\) (Chapter 5: a rotation by \(a\) then by \(b\) is a rotation by \(a+b\)). So \[
(\mathbf{R}_{m}\mathbf{q})\cdot(\mathbf{R}_{n}\mathbf{k})=\mathbf{q}^{\intercal}\mathbf{R}_m^{\intercal}\mathbf{R}_n\,\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{q}^{\intercal}\mathbf{R}_{n-m}\,\mathbf{k}.
\] The attention score depends on the content \(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k}\) and on the relative offset \(n-m\), and not on the absolute positions. \(\blacksquare\)


Rotations preserve length (Chapter 4), so RoPE changes no norms. It carries only angle information.

def rope(x, positions, base=10000.0):
    """x: (T, d) with d even; positions: (T,) -> rotated x."""
    T, d = x.shape
    theta = base ** (-np.arange(0, d, 2) / d)                   # (d/2,)
    ang = positions[:, None] * theta[None, :]                   # (T, d/2)
    c, s = np.cos(ang), np.sin(ang)
    x1, x2 = x[:, 0::2], x[:, 1::2]
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    out[:, 0::2] = x1 * c - x2 * s
    out[:, 1::2] = x1 * s + x2 * c
    return out

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d = 16
q, k = rng.normal(size=d), rng.normal(size=d)
score = lambda m, n: rope(q[None], np.array([m]))[0] @ rope(k[None], np.array([n]))[0]
print("score(m=3,  n=8)      =", round(score(3, 8), 6))
print("score(m=40, n=45)     =", round(score(40, 45), 6), " (same offset 5)")
print("score(m=100, n=105)   =", round(score(100, 105), 6), " (same offset 5)")
print("score(m=3,  n=9)      =", round(score(3, 9), 6), " (offset 6: different)")
print("norm preserved:", np.isclose(np.linalg.norm(rope(q[None], np.array([37]))[0]), np.linalg.norm(q)))

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
v = np.array([[1.0, 0.0]])

t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 100)
ax1.plot(np.cos(t), np.sin(t), color="#D1D5DB")

for m, p in enumerate(pts): ax1.annotate(str(m), p * 1.12, ha="center", fontsize=9)
ax1.set_aspect("equal"); ax1.set_title("one pair rotated by m·θ")
x_ = rng.normal(size=64)

title: 32  Decoder-only Language Models
text:
32.5 RMSNorm
LayerNorm (Chapter 20) subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation. RMSNorm divides only by the root mean square:
\[
\text{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\mathbf{x}}{\sqrt{\tfrac1d\sum_ix_i^2+\epsilon}}\odot\mathbf{g}.
\tag{32.2}\]
It has no mean statistic and no bias, so it is cheaper, and it is as effective in practice. For a vector with zero mean it equals LayerNorm without its shift.

def layernorm(x, eps=1e-6):
    mu = x.mean(-1, keepdims=True); v = x.var(-1, keepdims=True)
    return (x - mu) / np.sqrt(v + eps)

def rmsnorm(x, eps=1e-6):
    return x / np.sqrt((x ** 2).mean(-1, keepdims=True) + eps)

x = rng.normal(size=(4, 64))
x0 = x - x.mean(-1, keepdims=True)                         # zero-mean rows
print("equal when the mean is zero  :", np.allclose(layernorm(x0), rmsnorm(x0), atol=1e-4))
xs = x + 5.0                                                # large common offset
print("differ when there is an offset:", not np.allclose(layernorm(xs), rmsnorm(xs), atol=1e-2))
print("RMS of the output is 1       :", np.round(np.sqrt((rmsnorm(xs) ** 2).mean(-1)), 3))

differ when there is an offset: True

title: 32  Decoder-only Language Models
text:
32.6 SwiGLU
A gated linear unit multiplies two projections of the input element-wise: one passes through an activation and acts as a gate for the other. With the SiLU activation (Chapter 10), the MLP becomes
\[
\text{SwiGLU}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{W}_{2}\Bigl(\text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{x})\odot(\mathbf{W}_{3}\mathbf{x})\Bigr),\qquad\text{SiLU}(z)=z\,\sigma(z).
\tag{32.3}\]
It has three matrices instead of two. To keep the parameter count of the standard MLP (\(2\cdot d\cdot4d=8d^2\)), the hidden size is reduced to \(\frac83d\):
\[
3\cdot d\cdot\tfrac83d=8d^2.
\]
The gate lets the network switch features on and off per token, a multiplicative interaction that a plain MLP only approximates. Empirically it gives a better loss at equal parameters.

d = 4096
hid_std = 4 * d
hid_glu = int(8 * d / 3)
print(f"standard MLP: 2 · d · 4d = {2 * d * hid_std:,}")
print(f"SwiGLU (hidden {hid_glu}): 3 · d · h = {3 * d * hid_glu:,}")
print("difference: {:.2%}".format(abs(3 * d * hid_glu - 2 * d * hid_std) / (2 * d * hid_std)))

difference: 0.01%

section: 32.7 Grouped-query attention and the KV cache
text:
32.7 Grouped-query attention and the KV cache
During generation, the keys and values of all past tokens are needed at every step. Recomputing them is wasteful. The KV cache stores them. Each new token only computes its own \(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k},\mathbf{v}\), appends \(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{v}\) to the cache, and attends over the cache.
The cache holds \(2\cdot L\cdot T\cdot n_{\text{kv}}\cdot d_h\) numbers. It grows with the context length and can dominate memory. Grouped-query attention (GQA) uses fewer key/value heads \(n_{\text{kv}}\) than query heads \(h\). Several query heads share one key/value head. It shrinks the cache by \(h/n_{\text{kv}}\) with a small loss in quality.

def kv_bytes(L, T, n_kv, dh, bytes_per=2):
    return 2 * L * T * n_kv * dh * bytes_per

L_, h_, dh_, T_ = 32, 32, 128, 8192                       # a 7B-class shape, 8k context, fp16
for name, n_kv in [("multi-head (32 KV heads)", 32), ("GQA (8 KV heads)", 8), ("multi-query (1 KV head)", 1)]:
    print(f"{name:26s} KV cache per sequence: {kv_bytes(L_, T_, n_kv, dh_) / 2**30:6.2f} GiB")

multi-head (32 KV heads)   KV cache per sequence:   4.00 GiB
GQA (8 KV heads)           KV cache per sequence:   1.00 GiB
multi-query (1 KV head)    KV cache per sequence:   0.12 GiB

title: 32  Decoder-only Language Models
text:
32.8 A minimal Llama block
We assemble everything in PyTorch: RMSNorm, RoPE, grouped-query causal attention, SwiGLU, residual connections. It follows the structure of Figure 32.2.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, eps=1e-6):
        super().__init__(); self.g = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d)); self.eps = eps
    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps) * self.g

def rope_cache(dh, T, base=10000.0):
    theta = base ** (-torch.arange(0, dh, 2).float() / dh)
    ang = torch.arange(T).float()[:, None] * theta[None, :]          # (T, dh/2)
    return ang.cos(), ang.sin()

def apply_rope(x, cos, sin):                                         # x: (B, heads, T, dh)
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]
    return torch.stack([x1 * cos - x2 * sin, x1 * sin + x2 * cos], dim=-1).flatten(-2)

class LlamaBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, n_heads, n_kv, hidden):
        super().__init__()
        self.h, self.n_kv, self.dh = n_heads, n_kv, d // n_heads
        self.wq = nn.Linear(d, n_heads * self.dh, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(d, n_kv * self.dh, bias=False)
        self.wv = nn.Linear(d, n_kv * self.dh, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(n_heads * self.dh, d, bias=False)
        self.w1 = nn.Linear(d, hidden, bias=False)       # gate branch
        self.w3 = nn.Linear(d, hidden, bias=False)       # linear branch
        self.w2 = nn.Linear(hidden, d, bias=False)       # down projection
        self.n1, self.n2 = RMSNorm(d), RMSNorm(d)

    def _qkv(self, x, cos, sin):
        B, T, _ = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T, self.h, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T, self.n_kv, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T, self.n_kv, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)
        return apply_rope(q, cos, sin), apply_rope(k, cos, sin), v

    def _mlp(self, x):
        return self.w2(F.silu(self.w1(x)) * self.w3(x))

    def forward(self, x, cos, sin):
        B, T, d = x.shape
        q, k, v = self._qkv(self.n1(x), cos[:T], sin[:T])
        rep = self.h // self.n_kv                              # query heads per KV head
        k, v = k.repeat_interleave(rep, dim=1), v.repeat_interleave(rep, dim=1)
        a = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
        x = x + self.wo(a.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, d))
        return x + self._mlp(self.n2(x))

    def step(self, x_t, pos, cache, cos, sin):
        """One-token forward with a KV cache. x_t: (B, 1, d)."""
        B, _, d = x_t.shape
        q, k, v = self._qkv(self.n1(x_t), cos[pos:pos + 1], sin[pos:pos + 1])
        cache["k"] = k if cache.get("k") is None else torch.cat([cache["k"], k], dim=2)
        cache["v"] = v if cache.get("v") is None else torch.cat([cache["v"], v], dim=2)
        rep = self.h // self.n_kv
        K, Vv = cache["k"].repeat_interleave(rep, 1), cache["v"].repeat_interleave(rep, 1)
        a = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, K, Vv)           # one query: no mask needed
        x_t = x_t + self.wo(a.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, 1, d))
        return x_t + self._mlp(self.n2(x_t))

torch.manual_seed(0)
d, h, n_kv, hid = 64, 8, 2, 176                                # hidden ≈ 8d/3 rounded
blk = LlamaBlock(d, h, n_kv, hid)
cos, sin = rope_cache(d // h, 64)
X = torch.randn(2, 10, d)
Y = blk(X, cos, sin)
print("output shape:", tuple(Y.shape))

n_counted = sum(p.numel() for p in blk.parameters())
n_formula = (2 * d * d + 2 * d * n_kv * (d // h)) + 3 * d * hid + 2 * d
print(f"parameters: counted {n_counted:,}, formula {n_formula:,}, equal: {n_counted == n_formula}")

output shape: (2, 10, 64)
parameters: counted 44,160, formula 44,160, equal: True



32.8.1 Checks
Causality. Changing a future token must not change earlier outputs.
KV cache. Decoding one token at a time with a cache must give exactly the same outputs as the full forward pass.

X2 = X.clone(); X2[:, 7:] += torch.randn(2, 3, d)              # change tokens 7..9
Y2 = blk(X2, cos, sin)
print("outputs at positions 0..6 unchanged by a change in the future:",
      torch.allclose(Y[:, :7], Y2[:, :7], atol=1e-6))

cache, outs = {}, []
for t in range(X.shape[1]):
    outs.append(blk.step(X[:, t:t + 1], t, cache, cos, sin))
Y_cached = torch.cat(outs, dim=1)
print("KV-cache decoding equals the full forward pass:", torch.allclose(Y, Y_cached, atol=1e-5))
print("cache shapes (B, n_kv, T, d_h):", tuple(cache["k"].shape))

# attention score count: recompute everything each step vs cached
T = 1000
no_cache = sum(t * t for t in range(1, T + 1)); with_cache = sum(t for t in range(1, T + 1))
print(f"query–key score computations to generate {T} tokens: "
      f"without cache {no_cache:,}, with cache {with_cache:,}  (×{no_cache / with_cache:.0f})")

section: 32.9 Weight tying and the output head
text:
32.9 Weight tying and the output head
The output layer maps a hidden vector \(\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) to \(V\) scores. If we reuse the embedding matrix, the logits are
\[
\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{h}\,\mathbf{E}^{\intercal}\in\mathbb{R}^V,\qquad z_t=\mathbf{h}\cdot\mathbf{e}_t.
\tag{32.4}\]
The score of token \(t\) is the dot product of the final representation with that token’s embedding (Chapter 4). Embedding and output share one matrix and the model saves \(Vd\) parameters. After softmax this is the next-token distribution (Chapter 24).

title: 32  Decoder-only Language Models
text:
32.10 Counting a full model
Putting the pieces together, for width \(d\), \(L\) blocks, \(h\) query heads of size \(d_h=d/h\), \(n_{\text{kv}}\) key/value heads, and hidden size \(f\):
\[
N\approx Vd+L\Bigl(\underbrace{2d^2+2\,d\,n_{\text{kv}}d_h}_{\text{attention}}+\underbrace{3\,d\,f}_{\text{SwiGLU}}+\underbrace{2d}_{\text{norms}}\Bigr)+d.
\tag{32.5}\]

def llama_params(V, d, L, h, n_kv, f):
    dh = d // h
    per_block = 2 * d * d + 2 * d * n_kv * dh + 3 * d * f + 2 * d
    return V * d + L * per_block + d

N7 = llama_params(V=32000, d=4096, L=32, h=32, n_kv=32, f=11008)
print(f"7B-class configuration: {N7 / 1e9:.2f} billion parameters")
print(f"  embedding: {32000 * 4096 / 1e6:.0f} M;  blocks: {(N7 - 32000 * 4096) / 1e9:.2f} B")
print(f"forward FLOPs per token ≈ 2N = {2 * N7 / 1e9:.1f} GFLOP")

title: 32  Decoder-only Language Models
text:
32.12 Failure modes
RoPE beyond the training length. Rotation angles for positions never seen in training put queries and keys in configurations the model did not learn. Quality falls sharply past the trained context. Methods that rescale positions (position interpolation) exist for this reason.
Position precision. Position indices stored in 16-bit floats lose exactness:

pos = torch.arange(250, 270, dtype=torch.float32)
print("float32:", pos[:8].tolist())
print("bfloat16:", pos.to(torch.bfloat16)[:8].float().tolist(), " <- distinct positions collide")

float32: [250.0, 251.0, 252.0, 253.0, 254.0, 255.0, 256.0, 257.0]
bfloat16: [250.0, 251.0, 252.0, 253.0, 254.0, 255.0, 256.0, 256.0]  <- distinct positions collide


Compute RoPE angles in float32.
Norm epsilon. In 16-bit arithmetic, \(\epsilon=10^{-6}\) can vanish in the sum, and the reciprocal square root may overflow for tiny inputs. Models normalise in float32.
GQA grouping. If \(h\) is not a multiple of \(n_{\text{kv}}\), heads cannot be grouped. If the repeat uses the wrong order (repeat instead of repeat_interleave), query heads read the wrong KV head and the model silently degrades.
Cache memory. The KV cache grows linearly with context and batch size and often limits the number of simultaneous requests.

32.14 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



System C is now a modern language-model architecture: tokens \(\to\) embeddings \(\to\) (RMSNorm, RoPE-attention, SwiGLU) \(\times\,N\to\) logits \(=\mathbf{h}\mathbf{E}^{\intercal}\) \(\to\) softmax. Every change from Chapter 31 was an application of earlier mathematics: rotations, norms, element-wise gating, and reuse of cached tensors.
The model gives a distribution over the next token. Chapter 33 shows how a distribution becomes a sentence, and how the whole model is trained by the chain rule of probability.

title: 32  Decoder-only Language Models
text:
Chapter summary

RoPE rotates query/key pairs by \(m\theta_i\). The score depends on content and the offset \(n-m\).
RMSNorm: \(\mathbf{x}/\text{RMS}(\mathbf{x})\odot\mathbf{g}\), no mean subtraction.
SwiGLU: \(\mathbf{W}_2(\text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{x})\odot\mathbf{W}_{3}\mathbf{x})\), hidden size \(\frac83d\) for equal parameters.
GQA shares KV heads and shrinks the cache by \(h/n_{\text{kv}}\). The cache has \(2LTn_{\text{kv}}d_h\) numbers.
Tied head: \(\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{h}\mathbf{E}^{\intercal}\).
A 7B-class model: about \(12d^2L\) block parameters, \(2N\) FLOPs per token.

title: 33  Autoregressive Generation and Sampling
text:
33.2 The factorisation
The probability of a text \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) is, by the chain rule (Chapter 22):
\[
P_\theta(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}P_\theta(x_{t}\mid x_{<t}).
\tag{33.1}\]
This is exact: no independence assumption is made. The model \(f_\theta\) computes each factor from the prefix: its softmax output (Chapter 24) is the categorical distribution \(P_\theta(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\).

33.2.1 Training: maximum likelihood
Maximum likelihood (Chapter 25) maximises \(\ln P_\theta\) of the training text. Taking the negative log of Equation 33.1 and averaging over positions gives the cross-entropy loss:
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n}\ln P_\theta(x_{t}\mid x_{<t}).
\tag{33.2}\]
This is the same cross-entropy as in Chapter 14. The only difference is that the “label” at each position is the next token of the text itself. All \(n\) factors are computed in one forward pass, thanks to the causal mask (Chapter 30). This is called teacher forcing: the model is always fed the true prefix.
The exponential of the loss is the perplexity (Chapter 15). It is the effective number of tokens the model hesitates between.
crumbs: Part VIII — Putting the Mathematical Systems Together

title: 33  Autoregressive Generation and Sampling
text:
33.3 A small language model
We train a character-level Transformer (Chapter 31) on a text of 300,000 characters: the documentation shipped with Python, lower-cased, using 29 symbols (letters, space, ., ,, newline). The model is small (3 blocks, width 96) so that it trains in under a minute on a CPU.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from pydoc_data import topics

raw = " ".join(topics.topics[k] for k in sorted(topics.topics)).lower()
keep = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz .,\n")
text = " ".join("".join(c if c in keep else " " for c in raw).split())[:300_000]
chars = sorted(set(text)); V = len(chars)
ix = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(chars)}
data = torch.tensor([ix[c] for c in text])
n_train = int(0.9 * len(data))
train_data, val_data = data[:n_train], data[n_train:]
print(f"{len(text):,} characters; vocabulary {V}: {''.join(chars)!r}")
print("sample:", repr(text[:100]))

300,000 characters; vocabulary 29: ' ,.abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz'
sample: 'the assert statement assert statements are a convenient way to insert debugging assertions into a pr'



T_ctx, d_model, n_heads, n_layers = 64, 96, 4, 3

class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1, self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model), nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.qkv, self.o = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model), nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d_model, 4 * d_model), nn.GELU(),
                                 nn.Linear(4 * d_model, d_model))
    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, _ = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(self.ln1(x)).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        sp = lambda t: t.view(B, T, n_heads, d_model // n_heads).transpose(1, 2)
        a = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(sp(q), sp(k), sp(v), is_causal=True)
        x = x + self.o(a.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, d_model))
        return x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x))

class CharLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.E, self.P = nn.Embedding(V, d_model), nn.Embedding(T_ctx, d_model)
        nn.init.normal_(self.E.weight, std=0.02); nn.init.normal_(self.P.weight, std=0.02)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([Block() for _ in range(n_layers)])
        self.ln = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
    def forward(self, idx):
        x = self.E(idx) + self.P(torch.arange(idx.shape[1]))
        for b in self.blocks:
            x = b(x)
        return self.ln(x) @ self.E.weight.T            # tied output head: logits = h Eᵀ

def get_batch(src, B=64):
    starts = torch.randint(0, len(src) - T_ctx - 1, (B,))
    return torch.stack([src[s:s + T_ctx + 1] for s in starts])

torch.manual_seed(0)
lm = CharLM()
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(lm.parameters(), lr=3e-3, weight_decay=0.01)
hist, t0 = [], time.time()
for step in range(1500):
    b = get_batch(train_data)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(lm(b[:, :-1]).reshape(-1, V), b[:, 1:].reshape(-1))
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); hist.append(loss.item())

title: 33  Autoregressive Generation and Sampling
text:
33.4 Scoring versus generating
Scoring a given text needs one forward pass: the causal mask lets every position compute its next-token distribution at once. Generating needs one pass per token, because each token depends on the previous one. We check that the two give the same log-probability.

@torch.no_grad()
def seq_logprob_parallel(ids):
    logits = lm(ids[None, :-1])[0]                                # one pass
    lp = F.log_softmax(logits, dim=-1)
    return lp[torch.arange(len(ids) - 1), ids[1:]].sum().item()

@torch.no_grad()
def seq_logprob_sequential(ids):
    total = 0.0
    for t in range(1, len(ids)):                                   # one pass per token
        lp = F.log_softmax(lm(ids[None, :t])[0, -1], dim=-1)
        total += lp[ids[t]].item()
    return total

ids = val_data[:40]
print(f"parallel (teacher-forcing) log P: {seq_logprob_parallel(ids):.4f}")
print(f"sequential, token by token     : {seq_logprob_sequential(ids):.4f}")

sequential, token by token     : -51.3990

title: 33  Autoregressive Generation and Sampling
text:
33.5 Decoding
The model fixes \(P_\theta(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\). A decoding rule chooses the next token from it. The rule is not part of the model, and has a large effect on the text.







Rule
Next token




Greedy
\(\arg\max_xp(x)\)


Temperature \(T\)
sample from \(p_T(x)\propto p(x)^{1/T}\) (softmax of \(\mathbf{z}/T\), Chapter 24)


Top-\(k\)
keep the \(k\) most likely tokens, renormalise, sample


Top-\(p\) (nucleus)
keep the smallest set whose probability sums to at least \(p\), renormalise, sample



Temperature changes the shape: low \(T\) sharpens, high \(T\) flattens. Top-\(k\) and top-\(p\) cut off the unreliable tail, since sampling from the tail produces nonsense tokens with small but non-zero probability at every step.

def next_token_probs(logits, temperature=1.0, top_k=None, top_p=None):
    z = logits / max(temperature, 1e-8)
    p = F.softmax(z, dim=-1)
    if top_k is not None:
        kth = torch.topk(p, top_k).values[-1]
        p = torch.where(p >= kth, p, torch.zeros_like(p))
    if top_p is not None:
        sp, si = torch.sort(p, descending=True)
        cum = torch.cumsum(sp, dim=-1)
        keep = cum - sp < top_p                         # keep tokens until mass >= top_p
        mask = torch.zeros_like(p, dtype=torch.bool); mask[si[keep]] = True
        p = torch.where(mask, p, torch.zeros_like(p))
    return p / p.sum()

@torch.no_grad()
def generate(prompt, n=300, greedy=False, **kw):
    ids = torch.tensor([ix[c] for c in prompt])
    for _ in range(n):
        logits = lm(ids[None, -T_ctx:])[0, -1]
        if greedy:
            nxt = logits.argmax()
        else:
            nxt = torch.multinomial(next_token_probs(logits, **kw), 1)[0]
        ids = torch.cat([ids, nxt.view(1)])
    return "".join(chars[i] for i in ids.tolist())

torch.manual_seed(1)
prompt = "the function "
for name, kw in [("greedy", dict(greedy=True)), ("T = 0.7", dict(temperature=0.7)),
                 ("T = 1.0", dict(temperature=1.0)), ("T = 1.5", dict(temperature=1.5)),
                 ("top-p 0.9", dict(top_p=0.9)), ("top-k 5", dict(top_k=5))]:
    print(f"{name:10s}: {generate(prompt, 150, **kw)!r}")

Greedy decoding falls into a loop (here, “the same as the same as the same as…”). Pure sampling at \(T=1\) is varied and often garbled. Truncation methods give a middle ground. This is typical, and it is why chat models use temperature around 0.7 with nucleus sampling.

33.5.1 Measuring it
We quantify two things over 20 samples of 300 characters for each rule: the fraction of repeated 8-grams (repetition) and the average log-probability the model assigns to its own text (how “likely” the output is).

def stats(kw, n_samples=20, n=300):
    reps, lps = [], []
    for _ in range(n_samples):
        s = generate("the function ", n, **kw)
        grams = [s[i:i + 8] for i in range(len(s) - 8)]
        seen, rep = set(), 0
        for g in grams:
            rep += g in seen; seen.add(g)
        reps.append(rep / len(grams))
        ids = torch.tensor([ix[c] for c in s])
        lps.append(seq_logprob_parallel(ids[-(T_ctx + 1):]) / T_ctx)
    return np.mean(reps), np.mean(lps)

torch.manual_seed(2)
settings = {"greedy": dict(greedy=True), "T=0.5": dict(temperature=0.5), "T=1.0": dict(temperature=1.0),
            "T=1.5": dict(temperature=1.5), "top-p 0.9": dict(top_p=0.9), "top-k 5": dict(top_k=5)}
res = {k: stats(v, n_samples=1 if k == "greedy" else 20) for k, v in settings.items()}
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))

for k in names: print(f"{k:10s} repeats {res[k][0]:.2f}   mean log P {res[k][1]:.2f}")

Greedy decoding repeats the most. Right: average log-probability per character that the model assigns to the text it generated. Lower temperature gives more ‘likely’ text; high temperature gives text the model itself finds unlikely.

33.5.2 Entropy and temperature on real model output
Chapter 24 showed that entropy rises with \(T\) for a fixed set of logits. We confirm it for the model’s actual next-token distribution, and look at how many tokens a nucleus of \(p=0.9\) actually contains.

@torch.no_grad()
def ent_bits(p):
    p = p[p > 0]; return -(p * p.log2()).sum().item()

ax2.set_xlabel("tokens in the top-p = 0.9 nucleus"); ax2.set_ylabel("number of positions")

title: 33  Autoregressive Generation and Sampling
text:
33.6 Production
PyTorch provides torch.topk, torch.multinomial, and torch.cumsum. We check our nucleus implementation against a direct, slower one.

def nucleus_reference(p, top_p):
    order = np.argsort(-p); cum = 0.0; keep = []
    for j in order:
        keep.append(j); cum += p[j]
        if cum >= top_p:
            break
    out = np.zeros_like(p); out[keep] = p[keep]
    return out / out.sum()

ok = True
for _ in range(100):
    z = torch.randn(V) * 3
    mine = next_token_probs(z, top_p=0.8).numpy()
    ref = nucleus_reference(F.softmax(z, -1).numpy(), 0.8)
    ok &= np.allclose(mine, ref, atol=1e-6)
print("top-p implementation matches the reference on 100 random distributions:", ok)
print("temperature 1 and no truncation leaves the distribution unchanged:",
      torch.allclose(next_token_probs(logits), F.softmax(logits, -1)))

top-p implementation matches the reference on 100 random distributions: True
temperature 1 and no truncation leaves the distribution unchanged: True


In production, generation uses the KV cache (Chapter 32), so each new token costs one attention step over the cache and not a full recomputation.

title: 33  Autoregressive Generation and Sampling
text:
33.7 Failure modes
Repetition loops. Greedy and low-temperature decoding return to the same high-probability continuation (see above). Remedies are sampling, repetition penalties, and nucleus truncation.
Exposure bias. In training the model always sees the true prefix. At generation it sees its own samples. An early mistake puts it in a context it never saw. The mismatch can compound over long outputs.
Tail sampling. At \(T=1\) without truncation, each step has a small chance of sampling a bad token. Over hundreds of tokens, this accumulates.
Degenerate settings. \(T\to0\) is greedy. Top-\(p\) near 0 keeps one token. \(T=0\) exactly divides by zero: implementations clamp it.
Miscalibration. A language model’s probabilities need not be calibrated (Chapter 24). A sequence with a high probability is not necessarily a good one: the most probable text is often generic or repetitive.
Likelihood is not quality. Perplexity measures prediction of held-out text. It does not measure truthfulness, helpfulness, or safety.
Cost. Each token needs a forward pass. Generating \(n\) tokens takes \(n\) sequential steps, which cannot be parallelised across time for one sequence.

title: 33  Autoregressive Generation and Sampling
text:
33.9 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



System C is complete as a language model: it is trained by maximum likelihood with the chain rule, evaluated by perplexity, and used to generate text by sampling from its next-token distribution under a chosen decoding rule. The central equation \(P(x_{1:n})=\prod_tP(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\) connects probability (Part VI), the architecture (Chapters 30–32), and learning (Part V).
Next we ask what limits such models: how parameters, data, and compute scale, how to add parameters without adding compute (mixtures of experts), and how numerical precision constrains training. That is Chapter 34.

title: 33  Autoregressive Generation and Sampling
text:
Chapter summary

\(P(x_{1:n})=\prod_tP(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\) is exact. The model supplies each factor.
Training minimises \(-\frac1n\sum_{t}\ln P_\theta(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\) with teacher forcing. Perplexity is its exponential.
Scoring is one parallel pass. Generation is sequential, one token per pass.
Decoding: greedy, temperature, top-\(k\), top-\(p\). Entropy rises with temperature.
Greedy repeats. Pure sampling is noisy. Truncated sampling balances them.
Exposure bias, tail sampling, and the difference between likelihood and quality are the main caveats.

title: 34  Mixture-of-Experts, Scale and Numerical Precision
text:
34.2 Mixture of experts
In a dense Transformer block, one MLP processes every token. An MoE layer replaces it with \(E\) expert MLPs and a small router. For each token \(\mathbf{x}\):

The router computes probabilities \(\mathbf{p}=\text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_{r}\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^E\) (Chapter 24).
The top-\(k\) experts are chosen. Their weights are renormalised: \(g_i=p_i/\sum_{j\in\text{top-}k}p_j\).
The output is the weighted sum of the chosen experts:

\[
\mathbf{y}=\sum_{i\in\text{top-}k(\mathbf{x})}g_i(\mathbf{x})\,\text{Expert}_i(\mathbf{x}).
\tag{34.1}\]
Each token touches \(k\) of the \(E\) experts. The model has \(E\) times the MLP parameters of a dense block, but each token pays for only \(k\) of them.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

class MoE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, n_experts=4, k=1, hidden=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.E, self.k = n_experts, k
        self.router = nn.Linear(d, n_experts, bias=False)
        self.experts = nn.ModuleList([nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, hidden), nn.GELU(),
                                                    nn.Linear(hidden, d)) for _ in range(n_experts)])

    def forward(self, x):                                    # x: (tokens, d)
        p = F.softmax(self.router(x), dim=-1)                # (tokens, E)
        topv, topi = p.topk(self.k, dim=-1)
        g = topv / topv.sum(-1, keepdim=True)                # renormalised gate weights
        out = torch.zeros_like(x)
        for e in range(self.E):
            sel = (topi == e)                                # (tokens, k) bool
            rows = sel.any(-1)
            if rows.any():
                w = (g * sel).sum(-1)[rows].unsqueeze(-1)
                out[rows] += w * self.experts[e](x[rows])    # only routed tokens are computed
        f = F.one_hot(topi[:, 0], self.E).float().mean(0)   # fraction of tokens whose top choice is e
        aux = self.E * (f * p.mean(0)).sum()                 # load-balancing loss
        return out, aux, f

m = MoE(d=8, n_experts=8, k=2)
x = torch.randn(1000, 8)
y, aux, f = m(x)
print("output shape:", tuple(y.shape))
dense_params = sum(p.numel() for p in nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(8, 32), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(32, 8)).parameters())
moe_params = sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())
print(f"one expert: {dense_params} params; MoE total: {moe_params} params "
      f"(×{moe_params / dense_params:.1f});  active per token: {m.k} experts + router")

output shape: (1000, 8)
one expert: 552 params; MoE total: 4480 params (×8.1);  active per token: 2 experts + router



34.2.1 Active versus total parameters
For a realistic block, the accounting is simple. We compare dense and MoE versions of a Mixtral-style configuration.

def moe_model_params(V, d, L, h, n_kv, f, E=1, k=1):
    dh = d // h
    attn = 2 * d * d + 2 * d * n_kv * dh
    expert = 3 * d * f                                       # SwiGLU
    router = d * E if E > 1 else 0
    total = V * d + L * (attn + E * expert + router + 2 * d) + d
    active = V * d + L * (attn + k * expert + router + 2 * d) + d
    return total, active

dense = moe_model_params(32000, 4096, 32, 32, 8, 14336)
moe = moe_model_params(32000, 4096, 32, 32, 8, 14336, E=8, k=2)
print(f"dense : total {dense[0] / 1e9:5.1f} B   active {dense[1] / 1e9:5.1f} B")
print(f"MoE   : total {moe[0] / 1e9:5.1f} B   active {moe[1] / 1e9:5.1f} B   (8 experts, top-2)")
print(f"MoE has {moe[0] / dense[0]:.1f}x the parameters for {moe[1] / dense[1]:.1f}x the per-token compute")

dense : total   7.1 B   active   7.1 B
MoE   : total  46.6 B   active  12.7 B   (8 experts, top-2)
MoE has 6.5x the parameters for 1.8x the per-token compute


The memory to hold the model follows the total. The compute per token follows the active parameters. MoE trades memory for compute.


34.2.2 Load balancing
If a router prefers one expert, that expert gets most tokens and the others learn little. In a distributed system with experts on different devices, it also leaves devices idle. A standard remedy is an auxiliary loss. Let \(f_i\) be the fraction of tokens whose top choice is expert \(i\), and \(P_i\) the mean router probability for expert \(i\):
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}=E\sum_{i=1}^{E}f_i\,P_i.
\tag{34.2}\]
When routing is uniform (\(f_i=P_i=1/E\)), \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}=1\). When all tokens go to one expert (\(f=P=\text{one-hot}\)), it is \(E\). By Cauchy–Schwarz, for \(f=P\) the sum \(\sum f_i^2\) is smallest at the uniform distribution, so the loss pushes towards balance. It is added to the training loss with a small coefficient.

E = 8
uniform = np.full(E, 1 / E)
print("uniform routing        : aux =", round(E * np.sum(uniform * uniform), 3))
one_hot = np.eye(E)[0]
print("all tokens to expert 0 : aux =", round(E * np.sum(one_hot * one_hot), 3))
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
vals = [E * np.sum(q * q) for q in rng.dirichlet(np.ones(E), size=1000)]
print("random routing (f = P) : min over 1000 draws =", round(min(vals), 3), "(never below 1)")

uniform routing        : aux = 1.0
all tokens to expert 0 : aux = 8.0
random routing (f = P) : min over 1000 draws = 1.098 (never below 1)




34.2.3 An experiment: does the balance loss work?
We build a task with four clusters of tokens, each with its own linear target map, and train an MoE with four experts and top-1 routing, with and without the balance loss.

def run_moe(aux_coef, seed):
    torch.manual_seed(seed); d = 8
    cent = torch.randn(4, d) * 3; maps = torch.randn(4, d, d) / math.sqrt(d)
    moe = MoE(d, n_experts=4, k=1, hidden=32)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(moe.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
    def data(n):
        c = torch.randint(0, 4, (n,)); x = cent[c] + torch.randn(n, d)
        return x, torch.einsum("bij,bj->bi", maps[c], x)
    for _ in range(600):
        x, y = data(256)
        out, aux, _ = moe(x)
        loss = F.mse_loss(out, y) + aux_coef * aux
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        x, y = data(4000); out, _, f = moe(x)
    return F.mse_loss(out, y).item(), f.numpy()

coefs = [0.0, 0.01, 0.1]
results = {c: [run_moe(c, s) for s in (0, 1)] for c in coefs}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.2), sharey=True)
for ax, c in zip(axes, coefs):
    for s, (err, f) in enumerate(results[c]):
        ax.bar(np.arange(4) + 0.4 * s - 0.2, f, 0.38, color=[PALETTE["data"], PALETTE["model"]][s],
               label=f"seed {s}: MSE {err:.2f}")
    ax.axhline(0.25, ls="--", color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_title(f"balance coefficient {c}"); ax.set_xlabel("expert"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("fraction of tokens")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for c in coefs:
    print(f"coefficient {c:5.2f}: usage seed0 {np.round(results[c][0][1], 2)}, seed1 {np.round(results[c][1][1], 2)};"
          f"  MSE {results[c][0][0]:.3f}, {results[c][1][0]:.3f}")







Figure 34.2: Expert usage after training an MoE (4 experts, top-1) on a four-cluster task, for balance-loss coefficients 0, 0.01, and 0.1 (two seeds each). Without the loss, the load is uneven (one expert is almost unused). With even a small coefficient it is nearly uniform. The test error (legend) is higher with the balance loss: forcing balance cost accuracy in this small task.





coefficient  0.00: usage seed0 [0.39 0.02 0.3  0.28], seed1 [0.02 0.42 0.2  0.36];  MSE 0.064, 0.044
coefficient  0.01: usage seed0 [0.26 0.26 0.24 0.24], seed1 [0.23 0.29 0.24 0.24];  MSE 0.125, 0.175
coefficient  0.10: usage seed0 [0.26 0.25 0.25 0.24], seed1 [0.24 0.28 0.24 0.24];  MSE 0.122, 0.171


Without the balance loss, some experts are used far less than others (in both seeds, one expert receives about 2% of the tokens). Even a small coefficient (\(0.01\)) makes the load almost uniform, and a tenfold larger one changes little. In this small task, forcing uniform routing also made the model less accurate (MSE about 0.12–0.18 against 0.04–0.06): the router can no longer assign each token freely to its best expert. Real systems accept this cost because balanced load is needed for hardware efficiency, and they use a small coefficient.

title: 34  Mixture-of-Experts, Scale and Numerical Precision
text:
34.3 The cost of training: \(C\approx6ND\)
For a dense model with \(N\) parameters trained on \(D\) tokens, the compute is about \(6ND\) floating-point operations.






TipDerivation



Consider one linear layer with weight matrix of \(N_\ell\) entries, applied to \(B\) tokens. A matrix product of \((B,n_{\text{in}})\) with \((n_{\text{in}},n_{\text{out}})\) costs \(2Bn_{\text{in}}n_{\text{out}}=2BN_\ell\) FLOPs (Chapter 5).

Forward: \(2BN_\ell\).
Backward (Chapter 18): the input gradient \(\mathbf{G}\mathbf{W}^{\intercal}\) costs \(2BN_\ell\), and the weight gradient \(\mathbf{X}^{\intercal}\mathbf{G}\) costs another \(2BN_\ell\). Total \(4BN_\ell\).

Per token and per parameter: \(2+4=6\) FLOPs. Summing over all weights and all \(D\) tokens gives \(C\approx6ND\). (Attention score computation adds a smaller \(T\)-dependent term.) \(\blacksquare\)



def train_flops(N, D):
    return 6 * N * D

print(f"{'model':>10s} {'tokens':>10s} {'FLOPs':>10s} {'A100-class GPU-days at 40% util.':>34s}")
peak = 312e12                                  # bf16 peak FLOP/s of one A100-class accelerator
for N, D in [(125e6, 2.5e9), (7e9, 1e12), (70e9, 2e12)]:
    C = train_flops(N, D)
    days = C / (0.4 * peak) / 86400
    print(f"{N:10.1e} {D:10.1e} {C:10.1e} {days:34,.0f}")

     model     tokens      FLOPs   A100-class GPU-days at 40% util.
   1.2e+08    2.5e+09    1.9e+18                                  0
   7.0e+09    1.0e+12    4.2e+22                              3,895
   7.0e+10    2.0e+12    8.4e+23                             77,902


Training a 7B-parameter model on a trillion tokens needs about \(4\times10^{22}\) FLOPs, which is thousands of GPU-days. Inference costs about \(2N\) FLOPs per token, a third of one training token’s forward and backward.

34.3.1 Where the FLOPs go: context length
Per token, the dense layers cost about \(2\cdot12d^2=24d^2\) FLOPs per block. Attention over a context of length \(T\) adds \(4Td\) (scores and weighted values). They are equal at \(T\approx6d\).

d = 4096
Ts = np.logspace(2, 6, 100)
share = 4 * Ts * d / (4 * Ts * d + 24 * d * d)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.4))
ax.semilogx(Ts, share, color=PALETTE["model"], lw=2)
ax.axvline(6 * d, ls="--", color=PALETTE["neutral"]); ax.axhline(0.5, ls=":", color=PALETTE["neutral"])
ax.set_xlabel("context length T"); ax.set_ylabel("attention share of FLOPs")
plt.show()
for T in (2048, 8192, 32768, 131072):
    print(f"T = {T:7d}: attention share {4 * T * d / (4 * T * d + 24 * d * d):.2f}")







Figure 34.3: Share of the forward FLOPs per token spent on attention scores and values, as the context length T grows, for width d = 4096. Below about 8k tokens, the dense layers dominate. At T = 6d ≈ 24,576 the two are equal. Beyond that, attention dominates.





T =    2048: attention share 0.08
T =    8192: attention share 0.25
T =   32768: attention share 0.57
T =  131072: attention share 0.84

title: 34  Mixture-of-Experts, Scale and Numerical Precision
text:
34.4 Scaling laws
Empirically, the test loss of language models falls as a power law in parameters, data, and compute, when the other factors are not the bottleneck:
\[
L(N)\approx\Bigl(\frac{N_c}{N}\Bigr)^{\alpha}+L_\infty.
\tag{34.3}\]
On a log–log plot, loss minus the floor is a straight line with slope \(-\alpha\). Published large-scale studies find exponents of the order \(0.05\)–\(0.1\): a tenfold increase in size reduces the reducible loss by only a modest factor. Such laws let one predict, from small runs, how a larger run will behave.
We run a miniature version with the character model of Chapter 33, at six widths. Every run has 2 blocks and 1,000 steps at the same learning rate. This is a demonstration of the method, not a measurement of a law.

from pydoc_data import topics
raw = " ".join(topics.topics[k] for k in sorted(topics.topics)).lower()
keep = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz .,\n")
text = " ".join("".join(c if c in keep else " " for c in raw).split())[:300_000]
chars = sorted(set(text)); Vc = len(chars); ixc = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(chars)}
data = torch.tensor([ixc[c] for c in text]); ntr = int(0.9 * len(data))
tr, va = data[:ntr], data[ntr:]
Tc = 64

class SBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, H=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.H = H
        self.l1, self.l2 = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.qkv, self.o = nn.Linear(d, 3 * d), nn.Linear(d, d)
        self.m = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * d, d))
    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, d = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(self.l1(x)).chunk(3, -1)
        sp = lambda t: t.view(B, T, self.H, d // self.H).transpose(1, 2)
        a = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(sp(q), sp(k), sp(v), is_causal=True)
        x = x + self.o(a.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, d))
        return x + self.m(self.l2(x))

class SLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, L=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.E, self.P = nn.Embedding(Vc, d), nn.Embedding(Tc, d)
        nn.init.normal_(self.E.weight, std=0.02); nn.init.normal_(self.P.weight, std=0.02)
        self.b = nn.ModuleList([SBlock(d) for _ in range(L)]); self.ln = nn.LayerNorm(d)
    def forward(self, i):
        x = self.E(i) + self.P(torch.arange(i.shape[1]))
        for b in self.b:
            x = b(x)
        return self.ln(x) @ self.E.weight.T

def batch(src, B=64):
    st = torch.randint(0, len(src) - Tc - 1, (B,))
    return torch.stack([src[s:s + Tc + 1] for s in st])

widths = [16, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128]
Ns, losses = [], []
for d in widths:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    lm = SLM(d); Ns.append(sum(p.numel() for p in lm.parameters()))
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(lm.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
    for _ in range(1000):
        b = batch(tr)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(lm(b[:, :-1]).reshape(-1, Vc), b[:, 1:].reshape(-1))
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        torch.manual_seed(1); b = batch(va, 512)
        losses.append(F.cross_entropy(lm(b[:, :-1]).reshape(-1, Vc), b[:, 1:].reshape(-1)).item())
    print(f"width {d:4d}: {Ns[-1]:8,d} parameters, validation loss {losses[-1]:.3f}")

width   16:    8,080 parameters, validation loss 1.776
width   32:   28,448 parameters, validation loss 1.410
width   48:   61,104 parameters, validation loss 1.287
width   64:  106,048 parameters, validation loss 1.245
width   96:  232,800 parameters, validation loss 1.183
width  128:  408,704 parameters, validation loss 1.243



from scipy.optimize import curve_fit
Ns_a, L_a = np.array(Ns, float), np.array(losses)
pl = lambda N, A, a, c: A * N ** (-a) + c
popt, _ = curve_fit(pl, Ns_a[:5], L_a[:5], p0=[5.0, 0.3, 1.0], maxfev=20000)
grid = np.logspace(np.log10(Ns_a.min()), np.log10(Ns_a.max()), 100)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.6))
ax.semilogx(Ns_a, L_a, "o", color=PALETTE["loss"], ms=7, label="measured")
ax.semilogx(grid, pl(grid, *popt), "--", color="black", label=f"power-law fit (α = {popt[1]:.2f})")
ax.set_xlabel("parameters N"); ax.set_ylabel("validation loss (nats/char)"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
print(f"fitted: A = {popt[0]:.2f}, alpha = {popt[1]:.2f}, floor L_inf = {popt[2]:.2f}  (five points: not reliable)")







Figure 34.4: Validation loss against parameter count for six widths of the character model (1,000 steps each). Loss falls as the model grows, with diminishing returns. The largest model does not follow the trend: with the same step count and learning rate it is under-trained. The dashed curve is a power-law fit to the first five points; with so few points it only illustrates the method.





fitted: A = 186.11, alpha = 0.62, floor L_inf = 1.10  (five points: not reliable)


Two lessons. Bigger is better with diminishing returns. And scaling laws need the other resources (data, steps, learning rate) to grow with the model. Compute-optimal scaling studies tune all of them together.
