title: 34  Mixture-of-Experts, Scale and Numerical Precision
text:
34.5 Numerical precision
A floating-point number has a sign, an exponent (range), and a mantissa (resolution). The three common training formats split 16 or 32 bits differently.

print(f"{'format':10s} {'bits':>5s} {'exp':>4s} {'mant':>5s} {'machine eps':>12s} {'max':>10s} {'min normal':>12s}")
for name, dt, e, m in [("float32", torch.float32, 8, 23), ("float16", torch.float16, 5, 10),
                       ("bfloat16", torch.bfloat16, 8, 7)]:
    fi = torch.finfo(dt)
    print(f"{name:10s} {fi.bits:5d} {e:4d} {m:5d} {fi.eps:12.2e} {fi.max:10.2e} {fi.tiny:12.2e}")

format      bits  exp  mant  machine eps        max   min normal
float32       32    8    23     1.19e-07   3.40e+38     1.18e-38
float16       16    5    10     9.77e-04   6.55e+04     6.10e-05
bfloat16      16    8     7     7.81e-03   3.39e+38     1.18e-38



float16 has more mantissa bits than bfloat16 (finer resolution) but a small range: it overflows above 65,504 and underflows below \(6\times10^{-5}\) (normal) or \(6\times10^{-8}\) (subnormal).
bfloat16 has the same range as float32 but coarse resolution (about 2–3 decimal digits). It rarely overflows. It rounds aggressively.


34.5.1 Accumulation error
Adding many small numbers to a large running sum loses them. Once the sum is large, each small term is below half the spacing between representable numbers and is rounded away.

total16 = np.float16(0.0); total32 = np.float32(0.0)
for _ in range(100_000):
    total16 = np.float16(total16 + np.float16(1e-4))
    total32 = np.float32(total32 + np.float32(1e-4))
print(f"sum of 100,000 × 1e-4 (true value 10.0):  float16 {float(total16):.4f},  float32 {float(total32):.4f}")

sum of 100,000 × 1e-4 (true value 10.0):  float16 0.2500,  float32 10.0063


The float16 sum stalls near 0.25, where \(10^{-4}\) is smaller than half the spacing of float16 numbers. This is why matrix-multiply hardware accumulates in float32 even when inputs are 16-bit, and why softmax, normalisation, and loss sums are done in float32.


34.5.2 Gradient underflow and loss scaling
Gradients can be tiny. In float16, values below about \(6\times10^{-8}\) become exactly zero. Loss scaling multiplies the loss by a large factor (e.g. \(2^{16}\)) before the backward pass, which scales all gradients by the same factor, and divides afterwards in float32.

g_true = np.array([1e-9, 1e-8, 1e-7, 1e-6, 1e-4], dtype=np.float64)
plain = g_true.astype(np.float16)
S = 2.0 ** 16
scaled = (g_true * S).astype(np.float16).astype(np.float32) / S
print("true gradients     :", g_true)
print("float16            :", plain.astype(np.float64))
print("with loss scaling  :", scaled.astype(np.float64))
print("exp(12) in float16 :", np.exp(np.float16(12.0)), " (overflow: max is 65504)")

true gradients     : [1.e-09 1.e-08 1.e-07 1.e-06 1.e-04]
float16            : [0.00000000e+00 0.00000000e+00 1.19209290e-07 1.01327896e-06
 1.00016594e-04]
with loss scaling  : [1.00044417e-09 9.99716576e-09 1.00000761e-07 1.00024045e-06
 1.00016594e-04]
exp(12) in float16 : inf  (overflow: max is 65504)


bfloat16 does not need loss scaling, because its range equals float32’s. That is a main reason it became the default for large-model training.


34.5.3 Mixed precision in practice
A standard recipe keeps a float32 master copy of the weights and optimiser state, runs the forward and backward passes in bfloat16, and accumulates in float32. Memory per parameter with Adam: 2 bytes (bf16 weight) + 4 (fp32 master) + 4 + 4 (Adam moments) + 2 (gradient) = 16 bytes.

for N in (7e9, 70e9):
    bytes_per_param = 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 2
    print(f"{N / 1e9:4.0f} B parameters: weights+optimiser state ≈ {N * bytes_per_param / 2**30:,.0f} GiB "
          f"(excluding activations)")

   7 B parameters: weights+optimiser state ≈ 104 GiB (excluding activations)
  70 B parameters: weights+optimiser state ≈ 1,043 GiB (excluding activations)

text:
34.6 Production
PyTorch’s autocast runs selected operations in lower precision while keeping others (softmax, normalisation, reductions) in float32. We check the effect on one layer.

torch.manual_seed(0)
lin = nn.Linear(512, 512)
x = torch.randn(64, 512)
ref = lin(x)
with torch.autocast("cpu", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    y = lin(x)
rel = ((y.float() - ref).norm() / ref.norm()).item()
print(f"output dtype under autocast: {y.dtype};  relative error vs float32: {rel:.1e}")
print("bf16 resolution near 1.0:", torch.tensor(1.0, dtype=torch.bfloat16).item(),
      "→ 1 + 2^-8 rounds to", float(torch.tensor(1.0 + 2 ** -8, dtype=torch.bfloat16)))

output dtype under autocast: torch.bfloat16;  relative error vs float32: 2.9e-03
bf16 resolution near 1.0: 1.0 → 1 + 2^-8 rounds to 1.0

title: 34  Mixture-of-Experts, Scale and Numerical Precision
text:
34.7 Failure modes
Expert collapse. The router sends most tokens to a few experts. The others never train. Remedies: a balance loss, noise in the router, expert capacity limits.
Router instability. Router logits can grow large, making routing erratic and softmax saturate. A small penalty on the log-sum-exp of the router logits (a “z-loss”) keeps them bounded.
Token dropping. With a fixed expert capacity, tokens routed to a full expert may be dropped. This changes the output between training and inference.
Loss spikes. Large runs show sudden loss increases, often linked to rare large gradients, overflow in attention logits, or optimiser state in low precision. Gradient clipping and careful normalisation reduce them.
Overflow and underflow. Float16 needs loss scaling and float32 for softmax. Check for inf and nan.
Non-determinism. Summing in a different order gives different rounding. Two runs on the same data may differ in the last digits, then diverge.
Extrapolating scaling laws. A power law fitted on a narrow range may fail outside it. Laws depend on how data, learning rate, and architecture are scaled together.

title: 35  Convolutional Vision in Depth
text:
35.2 Receptive fields
A unit in layer \(l\) depends on a patch of the input. Its size is the receptive field \(r_l\). Let \(j_l\) be the jump: the distance in input pixels between adjacent units of layer \(l\). For a layer with kernel \(k\), stride \(s\), and dilation \(\delta\):
\[
r_l=r_{l-1}+(k-1)\,\delta\,j_{l-1},\qquad
j_l=j_{l-1}\,s,\qquad r_0=1,\ j_0=1.
\tag{35.1}\]






TipDerivation



A kernel of width \(k\) spans \(k\) units of the previous layer. Adjacent units of the previous layer are \(j_{l-1}\) input pixels apart. So the kernel spans \((k-1)\,\delta\,j_{l-1}\) input pixels between its first and last unit, which adds to the receptive field of the previous layer. A stride multiplies the spacing of all later units. \(\blacksquare\)



def receptive_field(layers):
    r, j, out = 1, 1, []
    for k, s, dil in layers:
        r += (k - 1) * dil * j
        j *= s
        out.append(r)
    return out

L = 12
plain = [(3, 1, 1)] * L
strided = [(3, 2 if i % 2 == 1 else 1, 1) for i in range(L)]
dilated = [(3, 1, 2 ** (i % 5)) for i in range(L)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
for layers, name, c in [(plain, "3×3, stride 1", PALETTE["data"]), (strided, "stride 2 every 2nd layer", PALETTE["model"]),
                        (dilated, "dilation 1, 2, 4, …", PALETTE["grad"])]:
    ax.semilogy(range(1, L + 1), receptive_field(layers), "o-", color=c, label=name)
ax.set_xlabel("layer"); ax.set_ylabel("receptive field (pixels)"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()
print("receptive field after 12 layers — plain:", receptive_field(plain)[-1],
      " strided:", receptive_field(strided)[-1], " dilated:", receptive_field(dilated)[-1])







Figure 35.2: Receptive field against depth for three designs. Stacked 3×3 convolutions with stride 1 grow linearly (2 pixels per layer). Downsampling by 2 every second layer makes the growth exponential. Dilation 1, 2, 4, 8 also grows exponentially without downsampling.





receptive field after 12 layers — plain: 25  strided: 253  dilated: 131


A \(224\times224\) image needs a receptive field of that order at the deepest layer, so that the final features can see the whole object. Plain stacking would need over 100 layers. Downsampling gets there with a few.

title: 35  Convolutional Vision in Depth
text:
35.3 Cheaper convolutions
A full convolution mixes space and channels in one step, at a cost of \(k^2C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}}\) weights.
\(1\times1\) convolution. Kernel size 1. It does no spatial mixing. It applies the same linear layer (Chapter 9) to the channel vector at every pixel.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0)
x = torch.randn(2, 8, 5, 5)                          # (B, C_in, H, W)
conv = nn.Conv2d(8, 4, kernel_size=1, bias=False)
W = conv.weight.squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1)              # (C_out, C_in)
manual = torch.einsum("oc,bchw->bohw", W, x)         # same linear map at every pixel
print("1×1 conv equals a per-pixel linear layer:", torch.allclose(conv(x), manual, atol=1e-6))

1×1 conv equals a per-pixel linear layer: True


Depthwise-separable convolution splits the work in two: a depthwise \(k\times k\) convolution (each channel on its own, groups=C_in) for spatial mixing, followed by a \(1\times1\) convolution for channel mixing.
\[
\text{params}:\quad k^2C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}}\;\longrightarrow\;k^2C_{\text{in}}+C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}},\qquad
\text{ratio}=\frac1{C_{\text{out}}}+\frac1{k^2}.
\tag{35.2}\]

Cin, Cout, k = 128, 128, 3
full = nn.Conv2d(Cin, Cout, k, padding=1, bias=False)
sep = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(Cin, Cin, k, padding=1, groups=Cin, bias=False),
                    nn.Conv2d(Cin, Cout, 1, bias=False))
n_full = sum(p.numel() for p in full.parameters()); n_sep = sum(p.numel() for p in sep.parameters())
print(f"full 3×3: {n_full:,} weights;  separable: {n_sep:,} weights;  ratio {n_sep / n_full:.3f}"
      f"  (formula {1 / Cout + 1 / k ** 2:.3f})")
H = W_ = 56
print(f"FLOPs at {H}×{W_}: full {2 * n_full * H * W_ / 1e6:.0f} M, separable {2 * n_sep * H * W_ / 1e6:.0f} M")

full 3×3: 147,456 weights;  separable: 17,536 weights;  ratio 0.119  (formula 0.119)
FLOPs at 56×56: full 925 M, separable 110 M


Mobile-friendly architectures (MobileNet, EfficientNet) rely on this factorisation to cut cost by about an order of magnitude.

title: 35  Convolutional Vision in Depth
text:
35.4 Residual networks
Stacking more convolutions ought not to hurt: extra layers could learn the identity. In practice, plain deep stacks are harder to train than shallow ones. Residual blocks fix this by computing a correction to the input:
\[
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}+F(\mathbf{x}),\qquad F=\text{conv}\to\text{BN}\to\text{ReLU}\to\text{conv}\to\text{BN}.
\tag{35.3}\]
The identity path gives the gradient a direct route (Chapters 18, 31). If \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(F(\mathbf{x})\) have different shapes (stride or more channels), the shortcut uses a \(1\times1\) convolution to match them.
We compare four designs on the digits (Chapter 11): plain and residual stacks of basic blocks (two \(3\times3\) convolutions each), with and without batch normalisation (next section). Same width, optimiser, and seed. We vary the depth.

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
D = load_digits()
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(D.data / 16.0, D.target, test_size=0.25,
                                      random_state=0, stratify=D.target)
Xt = torch.tensor(Xtr, dtype=torch.float32).view(-1, 1, 8, 8)
Xv = torch.tensor(Xte, dtype=torch.float32).view(-1, 1, 8, 8)
yt, yv = torch.tensor(ytr), torch.tensor(yte)

class Unit(nn.Module):
    """Basic block: conv-(BN)-ReLU-conv-(BN), with or without a skip around both convs."""
    def __init__(self, w, residual, bn):
        super().__init__()
        self.residual = residual
        self.c1, self.c2 = nn.Conv2d(w, w, 3, padding=1), nn.Conv2d(w, w, 3, padding=1)
        self.b1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(w) if bn else nn.Identity()
        self.b2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(w) if bn else nn.Identity()
    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.b2(self.c2(F.relu(self.b1(self.c1(x)))))
        return F.relu(x + h) if self.residual else F.relu(h)

class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, blocks, residual, bn, width=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.inp = nn.Conv2d(1, width, 3, padding=1)
        self.blocks = nn.Sequential(*[Unit(width, residual, bn) for _ in range(blocks)])
        self.fc = nn.Linear(width, 10)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc(self.blocks(F.relu(self.inp(x))).mean((2, 3)))      # global average pooling

def fit(model, steps=300, lr=0.05, bs=128):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr, momentum=0.9)
    for _ in range(steps):
        idx = torch.randint(0, len(Xt), (bs,), generator=g)
        opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(model(Xt[idx]), yt[idx]).backward(); opt.step()
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return F.cross_entropy(model(Xt), yt).item(), (model(Xv).argmax(1) == yv).float().mean().item()

designs = {"plain": (False, False), "residual": (True, False),
           "plain + BN": (False, True), "residual + BN": (True, True)}
print(f"{'convolutions':>12s} | " + " | ".join(f"{n:>22s}" for n in designs))
results = {}
for blocks in (1, 4, 8):
    row = []
    for name, (res, bn) in designs.items():
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        loss, acc = fit(Net(blocks, res, bn)); results[(blocks, name)] = (loss, acc)
        row.append(f"loss {loss:5.3f}, acc {acc:5.3f}")
    print(f"{2 * blocks:12d} | " + " | ".join(f"{r:>22s}" for r in row))

convolutions |                  plain |               residual |             plain + BN |          residual + BN
           2 |  loss 1.692, acc 0.342 |  loss 0.861, acc 0.736 |  loss 0.034, acc 0.982 |  loss 0.051, acc 0.973
           8 |  loss 2.304, acc 0.100 |  loss 2.304, acc 0.100 |  loss 0.001, acc 0.993 |  loss 0.001, acc 0.998
          16 |  loss 2.304, acc 0.100 |  loss 2.303, acc 0.100 |  loss 0.086, acc 0.951 |  loss 0.000, acc 0.991


Read the table carefully, because it is not what the legend of a textbook ResNet figure suggests.

Without normalisation, every design fails (loss stays at \(\ln10=2.30\), chance accuracy) once the stack is 8 convolutions deep, residual or not. With default initialisation and plain SGD, the signal does not survive. The skip alone does not rescue it.
With batch normalisation, both trainable. At depth 16, the residual network is clearly better than the plain one.
The benefit of the skip appears at depth, and is one ingredient of a recipe. It works together with normalisation and sensible initialisation (Chapter 20).

title: 35  Convolutional Vision in Depth
text:
35.5 Batch normalisation
Batch normalisation (BN) standardises each channel using statistics computed over the batch and over all spatial positions:
\[
\hat{x}_{nchw}=\frac{x_{nchw}-\mu_c}{\sqrt{\sigma_c^2+\epsilon}},\qquad
y_{nchw}=\gamma_{c}\hat{x}_{nchw}+\beta_c,
\tag{35.4}\]
with \(\mu_c,\sigma_c^2\) the mean and variance of channel \(c\) over \((n,h,w)\). During training the batch statistics are used (and a running average is stored). During evaluation the stored averages are used, so that one example gives the same output whatever the batch.

torch.manual_seed(0)
x = torch.randn(16, 4, 6, 6) * 3 + 2
bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(4, eps=1e-5)
bn.train(); y = bn(x)
mu = x.mean((0, 2, 3), keepdim=True); var = x.var((0, 2, 3), keepdim=True, unbiased=False)
manual = (x - mu) / torch.sqrt(var + 1e-5)
print("train mode equals the formula:", torch.allclose(y, manual, atol=1e-5))
print("per-channel mean and std of the output:", y.mean((0, 2, 3)).abs().max().item() < 1e-5,
      y.std((0, 2, 3), unbiased=False).round(decimals=3).tolist())
bn.eval()
single = bn(x[:1])
print("eval mode uses the running averages (output for one example differs from batch-stat output):",
      not torch.allclose(single, manual[:1], atol=1e-3))

train mode equals the formula: True
per-channel mean and std of the output: True [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
eval mode uses the running averages (output for one example differs from batch-stat output): True

title: 35  Convolutional Vision in Depth
text:
35.6 Upsampling: transposed convolution
Many vision models must go up in resolution: segmentation, image generation (Chapters 40–42). Transposed convolution does this. If a convolution is a matrix \(\mathbf{M}\) (Chapter 12), the transposed convolution multiplies by \(\mathbf{M}^{\intercal}\). It is also the operation that appears in the backward pass of a convolution (Chapter 18).
For input size \(n\), kernel \(k\), stride \(s\), padding \(p\):
\[
n_{\text{out}}=(n-1)\,s-2p+k.
\tag{35.5}\]

n, k, s = 8, 3, 1
kern = torch.randn(1, 1, k)                                  # (C_out, C_in, k)
# matrix of the convolution: (n - k + 1) × n
M = torch.zeros(n - k + 1, n)
for i in range(n - k + 1):
    M[i, i:i + k] = kern[0, 0]
v = torch.randn(1, 1, n - k + 1)
via_matrix = (M.T @ v[0, 0]).view(1, 1, n)
via_transposed = F.conv_transpose1d(v, kern)                 # kernel is applied in the same orientation
print("conv_transpose1d equals multiplication by Mᵀ:", torch.allclose(via_matrix, via_transposed, atol=1e-6))
up = nn.ConvTranspose2d(4, 4, kernel_size=4, stride=2, padding=1)
print("ConvTranspose2d(k=4, s=2, p=1): 16×16 ->", tuple(up(torch.randn(1, 4, 16, 16)).shape[2:]),
      "  formula:", (16 - 1) * 2 - 2 * 1 + 4)

conv_transpose1d equals multiplication by Mᵀ: True
ConvTranspose2d(k=4, s=2, p=1): 16×16 -> (32, 32)   formula: 32


A well-known artefact: with a kernel size not divisible by the stride, transposed convolutions produce a checkerboard pattern. Many models upsample by interpolation followed by an ordinary convolution instead.

title: 35  Convolutional Vision in Depth
text:
35.7 Spatial transformations as matrices
A rotation, scale, shear, or translation of an image is an affine map of pixel coordinates. In homogeneous coordinates, with a point \((x,y)\) written as \((x,y,1)\), all of them are one \(3\times3\) matrix, and they compose by matrix product (Chapter 5):
\[
\begin{pmatrix}x'\\y'\\1\end{pmatrix}=
\begin{pmatrix}a&b&t_x\\c&d&t_y\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{35.6}\]
To warp an image we use the inverse map. For each output pixel we compute where it comes from in the input (using \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\)) and read the value there, interpolating between the four nearest pixels (bilinear interpolation). Using the forward map would leave holes.

def bilinear(img, rr, cc):
    """Sample img at float coordinates (rr, cc); zero outside."""
    H, W = img.shape
    r0, c0 = np.floor(rr).astype(int), np.floor(cc).astype(int)
    fr, fc = rr - r0, cc - c0
    def px(r, c):
        ok = (r >= 0) & (r < H) & (c >= 0) & (c < W)
        return np.where(ok, img[np.clip(r, 0, H - 1), np.clip(c, 0, W - 1)], 0.0)
    return ((1 - fr) * (1 - fc) * px(r0, c0) + (1 - fr) * fc * px(r0, c0 + 1)
            + fr * (1 - fc) * px(r0 + 1, c0) + fr * fc * px(r0 + 1, c0 + 1))

def warp(img, A):
    """Warp img by the 3×3 affine matrix A (acts on (row, col, 1))."""
    H, W = img.shape
    rr, cc = np.meshgrid(np.arange(H), np.arange(W), indexing="ij")
    src = np.linalg.inv(A) @ np.stack([rr.ravel(), cc.ravel(), np.ones(H * W)])
    return bilinear(img, src[0].reshape(H, W), src[1].reshape(H, W))

def rot_scale_about_centre(theta, scale, shape, shift=(0.0, 0.0)):
    H, W = shape; c = np.array([(H - 1) / 2, (W - 1) / 2])
    R = scale * np.array([[np.cos(theta), -np.sin(theta)], [np.sin(theta), np.cos(theta)]])
    A = np.eye(3); A[:2, :2] = R
    A[:2, 2] = c - R @ c + np.array(shift)           # rotate/scale about the centre, then shift
    return A

from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image
photo = load_sample_image("china.jpg").astype(float).mean(axis=2)[50:210, 150:390]     # (160, 240)
A = rot_scale_about_centre(np.deg2rad(20), 0.8, photo.shape, shift=(10, 20))
warped = warp(photo, A)

from scipy.ndimage import affine_transform
Ainv = np.linalg.inv(A)
ref = affine_transform(photo, Ainv[:2, :2], offset=Ainv[:2, 2], order=1, mode="grid-constant", cval=0.0)
print("matches scipy.ndimage.affine_transform:", np.allclose(warped, ref, atol=1e-6))
print(f"largest difference: {np.abs(warped - ref).max():.1e}")

matches scipy.ndimage.affine_transform: True
largest difference: 6.8e-12



shear = np.eye(3); shear[0, 1] = 0.4
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.2))
for ax, im, t in zip(axes, [photo, warped, warp(photo, shear)], ["original", "rotate 20°, scale 0.8, shift", "shear"]):
    ax.imshow(im, cmap="gray"); ax.set_title(t); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 35.3: Affine warps as 3×3 matrices. Left: the original. Middle: rotation by 20°, scale 0.8, and a shift, as one matrix. Right: a shear. Each is computed by looking up, for every output pixel, where it came from in the input.






35.7.1 Augmentation fixes what architecture does not
In Chapter 12, a model trained on centred digits lost much of its accuracy when the test images were shifted by one pixel. Convolution is equivariant to shifts, but the classifier is not invariant. Data augmentation addresses this by training on randomly transformed copies. We close the loop on that experiment.

class SmallCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.c, self.l = nn.Conv2d(1, 8, 3), nn.Linear(72, 10)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.l(F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.c(x)), 2).flatten(1))

def train_cnn(augment, steps=800, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed); rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    m = SmallCNN(); opt = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), lr=0.5)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x = Xt
        if augment:
            dy, dx = rng.integers(-1, 2, 2)
            x = torch.roll(Xt, (int(dy), int(dx)), (2, 3))          # random shift by up to 1 pixel
        opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(m(x), yt).backward(); opt.step()
    return m

acc = lambda m, X: (m(X).argmax(1) == yv).float().mean().item()
print(f"{'training':12s} {'original':>9s} {'shifted +1 col':>15s} {'shifted (−1, +1)':>17s}")
for aug in (False, True):
    m = train_cnn(aug)
    print(f"{'augmented' if aug else 'plain':12s} {acc(m, Xv):9.3f} "
          f"{acc(m, torch.roll(Xv, (0, 1), (2, 3))):15.3f} {acc(m, torch.roll(Xv, (-1, 1), (2, 3))):17.3f}")

plain            0.973           0.498             0.293
augmented        0.944           0.929             0.856

title: 35  Convolutional Vision in Depth
text:
35.8 Failure modes
Aliasing. Strided convolution and pooling subsample without low-pass filtering, so small input shifts can change the output unpredictably (Chapter 12). Blur-pool and anti-aliased downsampling reduce it.
Border effects. Padding adds artificial context at the image border. Zero padding can leak absolute position information into the features.
Shortcut mismatch. A residual add needs equal shapes. A stride or channel change without a projection shortcut is a shape error.
Batch-norm and small batches. Statistics from a batch of 2 are noisy. In evaluation mode, the running statistics may not match the test distribution. Group or layer normalisation avoids this.
Train/eval mode. Forgetting model.eval() changes BN (and dropout) behaviour and silently changes results.
Large receptive field is not large effective receptive field. The theoretical field is a bound. In trained networks, the units that matter lie mostly near the centre.
Interpolation artefacts. Repeated resampling blurs images. Augmentation composed from many warps should compose the matrices first, and warp once.

title: 35  Convolutional Vision in Depth

35.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



System A can now be built deep and efficient: the receptive field is under control, convolutions can be made cheap, residual paths make depth trainable, and spatial transformations are matrices that augment the data. It also has the upsampling operator that generative models need.
All of the spatial reasoning here is built into the convolution. The next chapter replaces it with attention: instead of a sliding kernel, an image becomes a sequence of patches, and the Transformer of Chapter 31 reads it (Chapter 36).

title: 35  Convolutional Vision in Depth
text:
Chapter summary

Receptive field: \(r_l=r_{l-1}+(k-1)\delta j_{l-1}\), \(j_l=j_{l-1}s\). Stride and dilation make it grow exponentially.
\(1\times1\) convolution is a per-pixel linear layer. Separable convolution costs \(\frac1{C_{\text{out}}}+\frac1{k^2}\) of a full one.
\(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}+F(\mathbf{x})\) makes deep CNNs trainable.
BN uses batch statistics in training and running averages in evaluation.
Transposed convolution is multiplication by \(\mathbf{M}^{\intercal}\). \(n_{\text{out}}=(n-1)s-2p+k\).
An affine transformation is a \(3\times3\) matrix. Warps use the inverse map and interpolation.
Augmentation supplies the invariance that convolution alone does not.

title: 36  Vision Transformers
text:
36.3 Patches and patch embedding
Split an \(H\times W\) image with \(C\) channels into non-overlapping \(P\times P\) patches. There are \(N=HW/P^2\) of them. Flatten each to a vector of length \(P^2C\) and apply one linear map \(\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times P^2C}\):
\[
\mathbf{z}_i=\mathbf{E}\,\text{vec}(\text{patch}_i)+\mathbf{b},\qquad i=1,\dots,N.
\tag{36.1}\]
Reshaping does the cutting (Chapter 6). The linear map is a layer of Chapter 9. Together they are one convolution (Chapter 12) with kernel size \(P\) and stride \(P\): each output position sees exactly one patch.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0)
B, C, H, W, P, d = 2, 3, 16, 24, 4, 10
img = torch.randn(B, C, H, W)

# 1. reshape: (B, C, H, W) -> (B, N, P*P*C)
patches = (img.reshape(B, C, H // P, P, W // P, P)
              .permute(0, 2, 4, 3, 5, 1)                     # (B, H/P, W/P, P, P, C)
              .reshape(B, (H // P) * (W // P), P * P * C))
lin = nn.Linear(P * P * C, d)
z_linear = lin(patches)                                      # (B, N, d)

# 2. the same as a strided convolution
conv = nn.Conv2d(C, d, kernel_size=P, stride=P)
with torch.no_grad():                                        # copy the weights across layouts
    conv.weight.copy_(lin.weight.view(d, P, P, C).permute(0, 3, 1, 2))
    conv.bias.copy_(lin.bias)
z_conv = conv(img).flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)                # (B, N, d)
print("tokens:", z_linear.shape[1], " (", H // P, "×", W // P, ")")
print("linear-on-patches equals Conv2d(kernel = stride = P):", torch.allclose(z_linear, z_conv, atol=1e-5))
unf = F.unfold(img, P, stride=P)                         # PyTorch's own patch extraction
print("F.unfold gives (B, P·P·C, N):", tuple(unf.shape), "  N =", unf.shape[2])

tokens: 24  ( 4 × 6 )
linear-on-patches equals Conv2d(kernel = stride = P): True
F.unfold gives (B, P·P·C, N): (2, 48, 24)   N = 24

title: 36  Vision Transformers
text:
36.4 The class token and positions
After embedding, we have \(N\) tokens and no summary of the whole image. A learned class token \(\mathbf{z}_0\) is prepended. Through attention it can gather information from every patch. Its output after the last block is fed to the classifier.
Attention has no notion of position (Chapter 30), so we add positional embeddings \(\mathbf{p}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^d\). In a basic ViT they are learned parameters, one per position. Nothing tells the model that patch 5 is next to patch 6 or above patch 9: the geometry must be learned.
The input to the encoder is
\[
\mathbf{Z}_0=\bigl[\mathbf{z}_{\text{cls}};\ \mathbf{z}_1;\ \dots;\ \mathbf{z}_{N}\bigr]+\bigl[\mathbf{p}_0;\ \mathbf{p}_1;\ \dots;\ \mathbf{p}_{N}\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d}.
\tag{36.2}\]
The encoder is the block of Chapter 31, without the causal mask: every patch may attend to every other.

36.5 Cost: tokens and resolution
Attention builds an \(N\times N\) matrix per head per layer. Doubling the image side multiplies \(N\) by 4 and the attention cost by 16.

for side, P in [(224, 16), (384, 16), (224, 8), (512, 16), (1024, 16)]:
    N = (side // P) ** 2
    mb = 12 * N * N * 2 / 2 ** 20

title: 36  Vision Transformers
text:
36.6 A small ViT in PyTorch
We apply the ViT to the \(8\times8\) digits, with \(2\times2\) patches: \(N=16\) tokens. The model has width 48, 4 heads, 2 blocks.

import math
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
D = load_digits()
Xall, Xte, yall, yte = train_test_split(D.data / 16.0, D.target, test_size=0.25,
                                        random_state=0, stratify=D.target)
Xv = torch.tensor(Xte, dtype=torch.float32).view(-1, 1, 8, 8); yv = torch.tensor(yte)

class EncoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, h):
        super().__init__()
        self.h = h
        self.ln1, self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.qkv, self.o = nn.Linear(d, 3 * d), nn.Linear(d, d)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 2 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(2 * d, d))
    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, d = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(self.ln1(x)).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        sp = lambda t: t.view(B, T, self.h, d // self.h).transpose(1, 2)
        q, k, v = sp(q), sp(k), sp(v)
        A = (q @ k.transpose(-1, -2) / math.sqrt(d // self.h)).softmax(-1)     # (B, h, T, T), no mask
        x = x + self.o((A @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, d))
        return x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x)), A

class ViT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, patch=2, d=48, heads=4, layers=2, classes=10, side=8):
        super().__init__()
        n = (side // patch) ** 2
        self.embed = nn.Conv2d(1, d, patch, stride=patch)               # patch embedding
        self.cls = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1, d))
        self.pos = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, n + 1, d) * 0.02)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([EncoderBlock(d, heads) for _ in range(layers)])
        self.ln, self.head = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.Linear(d, classes)
    def forward(self, x, return_attn=False):
        t = self.embed(x).flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)                    # (B, N, d)
        t = torch.cat([self.cls.expand(len(t), -1, -1), t], dim=1) + self.pos
        attn = []
        for b in self.blocks:
            t, A = b(t); attn.append(A)
        out = self.head(self.ln(t[:, 0]))                               # class token only
        return (out, attn) if return_attn else out

class SmallCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.c, self.l = nn.Conv2d(1, 8, 3), nn.Linear(72, 10)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.l(F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.c(x)), 2).flatten(1))

def train_eval(model, n, steps=600, lr=3e-3, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); idx = rng.choice(len(Xall), n, replace=False)
    X = torch.tensor(Xall[idx], dtype=torch.float32).view(-1, 1, 8, 8); y = torch.tensor(yall[idx])
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=0.01)
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    for _ in range(steps):
        i = torch.randint(0, n, (min(128, n),), generator=g)
        opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(model(X[i]), y[i]).backward(); opt.step()
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (model(Xv).argmax(1) == yv).float().mean().item()

torch.manual_seed(0)
vit = ViT()
print("ViT parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in vit.parameters()),
      "  CNN parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in SmallCNN().parameters()))
acc_full = train_eval(vit, len(Xall))
print(f"ViT test accuracy with all {len(Xall)} training images: {acc_full:.3f}")

ViT parameters: 39610   CNN parameters: 810
ViT test accuracy with all 1347 training images: 0.967



36.6.1 Data hunger
A CNN has locality and translation structure built in. A ViT must discover it. We compare both on training sets of different size (three random subsets each).

sizes = [50, 150, 500, len(Xall)]
res = {"ViT": [], "CNN": []}
for n in sizes:
    for name, mk in [("ViT", ViT), ("CNN", SmallCNN)]:
        accs = []
        for seed in range(3):
            torch.manual_seed(seed)
            accs.append(train_eval(mk(), n, seed=seed))
        res[name].append((np.mean(accs), min(accs), max(accs)))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6))
for name, c in [("ViT", PALETTE["model"]), ("CNN", PALETTE["data"])]:
    m = np.array(res[name])
    ax.errorbar(sizes, m[:, 0], yerr=[m[:, 0] - m[:, 1], m[:, 2] - m[:, 0]], fmt="o-", color=c, capsize=3, label=name)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("training images"); ax.set_ylabel("test accuracy"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
print(f"{'training images':>16s} {'ViT':>8s} {'CNN':>8s}")
for n, v, c in zip(sizes, res["ViT"], res["CNN"]):
    print(f"{n:16d} {v[0]:8.3f} {c[0]:8.3f}")

With little data, the CNN’s built-in assumptions help a lot. As data grows, the gap narrows (to about 1.5 points at the full set here). The same pattern, at a much larger scale, is seen when ViTs are trained on small or large image collections.

36.7 What the model learned
Where does the class token look? We average the last block’s attention from the class token to the 16 patches and display it on the \(4\times4\) patch grid, for six test digits. We should not assume it looks at the ink.

vit.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    logits, attn = vit(Xv[:6], return_attn=True)
cls_att = attn[-1].mean(1)[:, 0, 1:].reshape(-1, 4, 4)         # (6, 4, 4): CLS -> patches
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 6, figsize=(10, 3.4))
for i in range(6):
    axes[0, i].imshow(Xv[i, 0], cmap="gray_r"); axes[0, i].set_title(f"label {yv[i].item()}", fontsize=9)
    axes[1, i].imshow(cls_att[i], cmap="viridis")
    for r in (0, 1): axes[r, i].set_xticks([]); axes[r, i].set_yticks([]); axes[r, i].grid(False)
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("image"); axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("CLS attention")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
border = np.zeros((4, 4), bool); border[[0, 3], :] = True; border[:, [0, 3]] = True
print(f"mean attention on border patches {cls_att[:, border].mean():.3f}  vs interior patches {cls_att[:, ~border].mean():.3f}"
      f"  (uniform would be {1 / 16:.3f})")







Figure 36.4: Attention of the class token over the 4 × 4 patch grid in the last block (average over heads), for six test digits. Each map is placed under its digit. The pattern differs between digits, but it is not simply ‘look at the strokes’: on average the border patches receive more attention than the interior ones (numbers below).





mean attention on border patches 0.063  vs interior patches 0.038  (uniform would be 0.062)


Did it learn the geometry? The positional embeddings were initialised randomly and nothing told the model about neighbours. We check whether patches that are close in the image have similar learned embeddings. If so, similarity should fall with distance.

pos = vit.pos.detach()[0, 1:]                                  # (16, d)
posn = pos / pos.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True)
S = (posn @ posn.T).numpy()
coords = np.array([(r, c) for r in range(4) for c in range(4)])
dist = np.linalg.norm(coords[:, None] - coords[None], axis=-1)
iu = np.triu_indices(16, 1)
corr = np.corrcoef(S[iu], dist[iu])[0, 1]
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
im = ax1.imshow(S, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1); ax1.grid(False)
ax1.set_xlabel("patch"); ax1.set_ylabel("patch")
ax2.scatter(dist[iu], S[iu], s=14, color=PALETTE["model"], alpha=0.7)
ax2.set_xlabel("distance between patches (grid units)"); ax2.set_ylabel("cosine similarity")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"correlation between similarity and distance: {corr:+.2f}   (a learned grid would give a clearly negative value)")







Figure 36.5: Cosine similarity between the learned positional embeddings of the 16 patches (rows and columns ordered row by row). The scatter shows similarity against the distance between patches. In this small model, trained on 1,347 images, there is no clear spatial structure: the embeddings did not learn that neighbouring patches are close.

title: 36  Vision Transformers

36.8 Changing the resolution
A ViT trained at one resolution has a fixed number of positional embeddings. To run it on a larger image, the grid of embeddings is interpolated to the new grid size (bilinear or bicubic), treating it as a small image with \(d\) channels.

def resize_pos(pos, old_g, new_g):
    """pos: (1, 1 + old_g², d) -> (1, 1 + new_g², d); the class position is kept."""
    cls, grid = pos[:, :1], pos[:, 1:]
    d = grid.shape[-1]
    g = grid.reshape(1, old_g, old_g, d).permute(0, 3, 1, 2)            # (1, d, g, g)
    g = F.interpolate(g, size=(new_g, new_g), mode="bicubic", align_corners=False)
    return torch.cat([cls, g.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).reshape(1, new_g * new_g, d)], dim=1)

new_pos = resize_pos(vit.pos.detach(), 4, 8)
print("positional embeddings:", tuple(vit.pos.shape), "->", tuple(new_pos.shape))
print("neighbouring patches remain similar after interpolation:",
      F.cosine_similarity(new_pos[0, 1], new_pos[0, 2], dim=0).item() >
      F.cosine_similarity(new_pos[0, 1], new_pos[0, 40], dim=0).item())

neighbouring patches remain similar after interpolation: True

title: 36  Vision Transformers
text:
36.10 Failure modes
Data hunger. Without locality and translation structure built in, a ViT trained on little data under-performs a CNN (Figure 36.3). Large-scale pre-training, strong augmentation, and regularisation close the gap.
Resolution change. Positional embeddings must be interpolated. A model run at another resolution without adaptation sees patches at scales and positions it did not learn.
Quadratic cost. Attention grows as \(N^2\). High resolution needs larger patches, windowed or hierarchical attention, or token pruning.
Patch size trade-off. Large patches lose fine detail within a patch. Small patches mean more tokens and cost.
Class token versus pooling. Some designs drop the class token and average the patch outputs. Both work. They differ in what is trained to hold the summary.
Position encoding shortcuts. A model with learned absolute positions can overfit to absolute locations. Augmentation by shifts and crops is important. In our small model the learned positions carried no visible grid structure (Figure 36.5); large models trained on large datasets do learn it, and fixed 2D sinusoidal embeddings provide it from the start.

title: 37  Detection and Structured Prediction
text:
37.2 Boxes and overlap
An axis-aligned box is stored as corners \((x_1,y_1,x_2,y_2)\) or as centre and size \((c_x,c_y,w,h)\). The two are related by \(x_1=c_x-w/2\), \(x_2=c_x+w/2\), and similarly for \(y\). Coordinates are usually divided by the image size, so that they lie in \([0,1]\).
The intersection of two boxes is a box (or empty). Its width is the overlap of the two \(x\)-intervals, clipped at zero:
\[
w_\cap=\max\bigl(0,\ \min(x_2,x_2')-\max(x_1,x_1')\bigr),\qquad
A_\cap=w_\cap\,h_\cap.
\tag{37.1}\]
The intersection over union is
\[
\text{IoU}(A,B)=\frac{A_\cap}{A_A+A_B-A_\cap}\in[0,1].
\tag{37.2}\]
It is 1 for identical boxes and 0 for disjoint ones. \(1-\text{IoU}\) is a metric (Chapter 13): it is the Jaccard distance of the two regions.

def box_area(b):
    return np.clip(b[..., 2] - b[..., 0], 0, None) * np.clip(b[..., 3] - b[..., 1], 0, None)

def iou_giou(a, b):
    """a: (..., 4), b: (..., 4) in x1,y1,x2,y2 -> IoU and GIoU (elementwise)."""
    lt = np.maximum(a[..., :2], b[..., :2]); rb = np.minimum(a[..., 2:], b[..., 2:])
    inter = np.prod(np.clip(rb - lt, 0, None), axis=-1)
    union = box_area(a) + box_area(b) - inter
    iou = inter / np.maximum(union, 1e-12)
    clt = np.minimum(a[..., :2], b[..., :2]); crb = np.maximum(a[..., 2:], b[..., 2:])
    enclose = np.prod(crb - clt, axis=-1)                       # smallest enclosing box
    giou = iou - (enclose - union) / np.maximum(enclose, 1e-12)
    return iou, giou

A = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 2.0])
for name, B in [("identical", [0, 0, 2, 2]), ("shifted by 1", [1, 0, 3, 2]),
                ("touching", [2, 0, 4, 2]), ("far away", [5, 0, 7, 2]), ("contained", [0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 1.5])]:
    i, g = iou_giou(A, np.array(B, float))
    print(f"{name:14s} IoU = {i:5.3f}   GIoU = {g:6.3f}")

identical      IoU = 1.000   GIoU =  1.000
shifted by 1   IoU = 0.333   GIoU =  0.333
touching       IoU = 0.000   GIoU =  0.000
far away       IoU = 0.000   GIoU = -0.429
contained      IoU = 0.250   GIoU =  0.250



37.2.1 Why IoU is a poor loss, and GIoU
If two boxes do not overlap, \(\text{IoU}=0\) whatever the distance between them. The loss \(1-\text{IoU}\) is then flat and gives no gradient to move the prediction towards the target (Chapters 14, 18).
The generalised IoU subtracts the fraction of the smallest enclosing box \(C\) that is not covered by the union:
\[
\text{GIoU}(A,B)=\text{IoU}(A,B)-\frac{|C|-|A\cup B|}{|C|}\in(-1,1].
\tag{37.3}\]
For far-apart boxes the enclosing box is large and mostly empty, so GIoU is close to \(-1\), and it rises smoothly as the boxes approach.

offsets = np.linspace(-8, 8, 400)
A = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 2.0, 2.0])
Bs = np.stack([offsets, np.zeros_like(offsets), offsets + 2, np.full_like(offsets, 2.0)], axis=1)
iou_v, giou_v = iou_giou(np.broadcast_to(A, Bs.shape), Bs)
l1 = np.abs(Bs - A).sum(axis=1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.6))
ax.plot(offsets, iou_v, color=PALETTE["data"], lw=2, label="IoU")
ax.plot(offsets, giou_v, color=PALETTE["grad"], lw=2, label="GIoU")
ax.plot(offsets, 1 - l1 / l1.max() * 2, color=PALETTE["neutral"], ls="--", label="1 − scaled L1")
ax.axhline(0, color="#9CA3AF", lw=0.6)
ax.set_xlabel("horizontal offset of B relative to A"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
print("IoU at offset −6 and −4:", np.round(iou_v[np.argmin(np.abs(offsets + 6))], 3), np.round(iou_v[np.argmin(np.abs(offsets + 4))], 3))
print("GIoU at offset −6 and −4:", np.round(giou_v[np.argmin(np.abs(offsets + 6))], 3), np.round(giou_v[np.argmin(np.abs(offsets + 4))], 3))







Figure 37.2: A box B slides horizontally past a fixed box A. IoU (blue) is exactly zero until the boxes touch, so it has no gradient there. GIoU (green) is negative and increases as B approaches A: it still points the way. An L1 distance between the box coordinates (grey, scaled) also works, but ignores overlap.





IoU at offset −6 and −4: 0.0 0.0
GIoU at offset −6 and −4: -0.5 -0.332

title: 37  Detection and Structured Prediction
text:
37.3 Duplicates and non-maximum suppression
Classic detectors predict a box at thousands of positions. Several boxes land on the same object. Non-maximum suppression (NMS) keeps the highest-scoring box and removes any other whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold, then repeats.

def nms(boxes, scores, thr=0.5):
    order = np.argsort(-scores); keep = []
    while len(order):
        i = order[0]; keep.append(int(i))
        if len(order) == 1:
            break
        ious, _ = iou_giou(np.broadcast_to(boxes[i], (len(order) - 1, 4)), boxes[order[1:]])
        order = order[1:][ious <= thr]
    return keep

boxes = np.array([[10, 10, 50, 50], [12, 12, 52, 52], [8, 14, 48, 54],       # three boxes on object 1
                  [100, 20, 140, 70], [102, 22, 138, 68]], float)             # two on object 2
scores = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.6, 0.95, 0.7])
print("kept boxes:", nms(boxes, scores, 0.5), "  (one per object)")
print("threshold 0.95 keeps:", nms(boxes, scores, 0.95), "  (too lax: duplicates survive)")

kept boxes: [3, 0]   (one per object)
threshold 0.95 keeps: [3, 0, 1, 4, 2]   (too lax: duplicates survive)


NMS is a hand-made post-processing step with a threshold that must be tuned. It fails for crowded scenes, where real objects overlap.

title: 37  Detection and Structured Prediction
text:
37.4 Set prediction and matching
An alternative (DETR) predicts a fixed number \(N\) of boxes (one per learned query), each with a class, including a special “no object” class, and compares the set with the target set directly. Duplicates are discouraged by the loss, so no NMS is needed.
The comparison needs a correspondence: which prediction answers which target? The loss is computed after finding the best one-to-one assignment \(\hat\sigma\) between predictions and targets:
\[
\hat\sigma=\arg\min_{\sigma}\sum_{i}\mathcal{C}\bigl(i,\sigma(i)\bigr),
\tag{37.4}\]
with a cost matrix \(\mathcal{C}_{ij}\) combining, for prediction \(j\) and target \(i\): the negative probability of the correct class, an L1 box distance, and \(1-\text{GIoU}\).

37.4.1 The Hungarian algorithm
Enumerating all assignments costs \(n!\). The Hungarian algorithm solves the assignment problem exactly in \(O(n^3)\). We check it against brute force for \(n=6\) (720 assignments).

from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Cm = rng.random((6, 6))
r, c = linear_sum_assignment(Cm)
best_h = Cm[r, c].sum()
best_b = min(sum(Cm[i, p[i]] for i in range(6)) for p in itertools.permutations(range(6)))
print(f"Hungarian optimum {best_h:.6f};  brute force over {math.factorial(6)} permutations {best_b:.6f}")

print(f"{'n':>4s} {'n! assignments':>20s} {'n³':>12s}")
for n in (5, 10, 20, 100):
    print(f"{n:4d} {float(math.factorial(n)):20.3e} {n ** 3:12,d}")

Hungarian optimum 1.173202;  brute force over 720 permutations 1.173202
   n       n! assignments           n³
   5            1.200e+02          125
  10            3.629e+06        1,000
  20            2.433e+18        8,000
 100           9.333e+157    1,000,000




37.4.2 Matching in pictures

title: 37  Detection and Structured Prediction
text:
37.5 The set loss
After matching, the loss has three parts: classification of each query (matched queries must predict the object class; unmatched ones must predict “no object”), and box regression on matched pairs only:
\[
\mathcal{L}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Bigl[-\ln p_j(c_{\hat\sigma^{-1}(j)})\Bigr]+\sum_{i\in\text{targets}}\Bigl[\lambda_{1}\lVert b_i-\hat b_{\hat\sigma(i)}\rVert_1+\lambda_{2}\bigl(1-\text{GIoU}(b_i,\hat b_{\hat\sigma(i)})\bigr)\Bigr].
\tag{37.5}\]
The matching is a discrete step with no gradient. It selects which pairs the (differentiable) losses apply to. The class term is weighted down for “no object”, since most queries are unmatched.

title: 37  Detection and Structured Prediction
text:
37.6 A small detector
We build the smallest set-prediction detector. The data: \(24\times24\) images containing one to three bright rectangles. The model: a small CNN to a feature vector, then one linear head that outputs, for each of \(N=4\) queries, two class logits (object / no object) and a box (four numbers in \([0,1]\), passed through a sigmoid). The loss is Equation 37.5, with matching by the Hungarian algorithm for every image.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
S, NQ = 24, 4
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def make_images(B):
    imgs = np.zeros((B, 1, S, S), np.float32); gts = []
    for b in range(B):
        boxes = []
        for _ in range(rng.integers(1, 4)):
            w, h = rng.integers(4, 9, 2); x, y = rng.integers(0, S - w), rng.integers(0, S - h)
            imgs[b, 0, y:y + h, x:x + w] = 1.0
            boxes.append([x / S, y / S, (x + w) / S, (y + h) / S])
        gts.append(np.array(boxes, np.float32))
    return torch.tensor(imgs), gts

def giou_t(a, b):                                   # torch version, (n,4) x (m,4) -> (n,m)
    lt = torch.max(a[:, None, :2], b[None, :, :2]); rb = torch.min(a[:, None, 2:], b[None, :, 2:])
    inter = (rb - lt).clamp(min=0).prod(-1)
    aa = ((a[:, 2] - a[:, 0]) * (a[:, 3] - a[:, 1]))[:, None]; bb = ((b[:, 2] - b[:, 0]) * (b[:, 3] - b[:, 1]))[None]
    union = aa + bb - inter
    clt = torch.min(a[:, None, :2], b[None, :, :2]); crb = torch.max(a[:, None, 2:], b[None, :, 2:])
    enc = (crb - clt).prod(-1)
    return inter / (union + 1e-9) - (enc - union) / (enc + 1e-9)

class Detector(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.f = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(1, 16, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                               nn.Conv2d(16, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                               nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(32 * 6 * 6, 256), nn.ReLU())
        self.cls, self.box = nn.Linear(256, NQ * 2), nn.Linear(256, NQ * 4)
    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.f(x)
        return self.cls(h).view(len(x), NQ, 2), self.box(h).view(len(x), NQ, 4).sigmoid()

def set_loss(logits, boxes, gts):
    total = 0.0
    for b, g in enumerate(gts):
        g = torch.tensor(g); p = boxes[b]; logp = logits[b].log_softmax(-1)
        cost = -logp[:, 1][:, None] + 5 * torch.cdist(p, g, p=1) + 2 * (1 - giou_t(p, g))
        r, c = linear_sum_assignment(cost.detach().numpy())          # Hungarian matching
        tgt = torch.zeros(NQ, dtype=torch.long); tgt[r] = 1          # matched queries are "object"
        l_cls = F.cross_entropy(logits[b], tgt, weight=torch.tensor([0.5, 1.0]))
        l_box = (5 * (p[r] - g[c]).abs().sum(-1) + 2 * (1 - giou_t(p[r], g[c]).diagonal())).mean()
        total = total + l_cls + l_box
    return total / len(gts)

torch.manual_seed(0)
det = Detector(); opt = torch.optim.Adam(det.parameters(), lr=2e-3)
hist, t0 = [], time.time()
for step in range(1500):
    x, g = make_images(32)
    lg, bx = det(x)
    loss = set_loss(lg, bx, g)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); hist.append(loss.item())
print(f"trained in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s;  loss {hist[0]:.2f} -> {np.mean(hist[-20:]):.2f}")

trained in 21 s;  loss 7.54 -> 1.03



x, g = make_images(300)
with torch.no_grad():
    lg, bx = det(x)
counts_ok, ious = 0, []
for b in range(300):
    keep = lg[b].argmax(-1) == 1
    n_pred = int(keep.sum()); counts_ok += int(n_pred == len(g[b]))
    if n_pred:
        M = giou_t(bx[b][keep], torch.tensor(g[b]))
        iou_m = np.array([[iou_giou(p, t)[0] for t in g[b]] for p in bx[b][keep].numpy()])
        r, c = linear_sum_assignment(-iou_m); ious += list(iou_m[r, c])
ious = np.array(ious)
print(f"images where the number of detections equals the true count: {counts_ok / 300:.2f}")
print(f"matched detections: mean IoU {ious.mean():.2f};  fraction with IoU > 0.5: {(ious > 0.5).mean():.2f}")

matched detections: mean IoU 0.74;  fraction with IoU > 0.5: 0.91

for b, ax in enumerate(axes):
    ax.imshow(x[b, 0], cmap="gray", extent=(0, 1, 1, 0))

        ax.add_patch(Rectangle(t[:2], t[2] - t[0], t[3] - t[1], fill=False, ec=PALETTE["grad"], lw=2.2))

            p = bx[b, j].numpy()
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle(p[:2], p[2] - p[0], p[3] - p[1], fill=False, ec=PALETTE["loss"], lw=1.2, ls="--"))

title: 37  Detection and Structured Prediction
text:
37.7 From first principles to production
Real detectors differ in scale, not in principle. DETR replaces our CNN feature vector with a CNN or ViT backbone producing a grid of feature tokens (Chapter 36). A Transformer decoder takes \(N\) learned query vectors and uses cross-attention over the image tokens (Chapter 30) to produce one output vector per query. A small feed-forward head turns each into a class and a box. The loss is Equation 37.5. Libraries provide box_iou, generalized_box_iou, and nms operators, and the Hungarian solver is the one used here.

title: 37  Detection and Structured Prediction
text:
37.9 Failure modes
IoU has no gradient for disjoint boxes. It is a poor training loss for boxes far apart. Use GIoU, or L1 on coordinates, or a combination.
Duplicates and thresholds. NMS thresholds trade missed objects in crowds against duplicate detections.
Class imbalance. Most queries (or anchors) match nothing. Without a lower weight on “no object”, the model predicts “no object” everywhere.
Unstable matching early in training. At the start, predictions are random and the assignment changes from step to step. Training is slow to start and needs patience.
Small objects. A box of few pixels has noisy IoU: one pixel of error changes IoU a lot. Evaluation therefore reports average precision at several IoU thresholds.
Fixed number of queries. If there are more objects than queries, some cannot be detected.
Evaluation is not the loss. Detection is scored by mean average precision, which depends on ranking by confidence and on IoU thresholds. It is not differentiable. The loss is a surrogate.

title: 37  Detection and Structured Prediction
text:
37.11 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now output structured, variable-size predictions and be trained on them. The new ingredients are a geometric overlap measure (IoU and GIoU), a differentiable surrogate for it, and an optimal matching step that turns “compare two unordered sets” into a well-defined loss.
So far, every model was trained with labels. Labels are expensive. Chapter 38 shows how models learn useful representations without them.

title: 37  Detection and Structured Prediction
text:
Chapter summary

A detection is a class and a box. A detector outputs a set of them.
\(\text{IoU}=A_\cap/(A_A+A_B-A_\cap)\). It is flat at 0 for disjoint boxes. GIoU subtracts the uncovered share of the enclosing box and remains informative.
NMS removes duplicates by IoU thresholding. Set prediction avoids duplicates through one-to-one matching.
The Hungarian algorithm finds the optimal assignment in \(O(n^3)\).
The set loss is computed after matching: classification for all queries, box losses for matched ones.

Every method in this chapter has the same shape:

fig = box_flow(["input x", "two views\nv₁, v₂ (augment)", "encoders\nf(v₁), f(v₂)", "representations\nz₁, z₂", "similarity /\nalignment\nobjective", "learned\nrepresentation\nspace"],

               figsize=(11, 1.9), fontsize=8)
plt.show()







Figure 38.2: The recurring self-supervised system. Two views of the same input (augmentations, or a masked version) go through encoders. A similarity or alignment objective on the representations defines the loss. No label is used.






import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

D = load_digits(); X, y = D.data / 16.0, D.target
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y)
Xt = torch.tensor(Xtr, dtype=torch.float32); Xe = torch.tensor(Xte, dtype=torch.float32)

def probe(Ztr, Zte, n_labels=100, seed=0):
    """Linear probe: logistic regression on frozen embeddings, trained on n_labels labels."""
    idx = np.random.default_rng(seed).choice(len(Ztr), n_labels, replace=False)
    return LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000).fit(Ztr[idx], ytr[idx]).score(Zte, yte)

print("probe accuracy on raw pixels:",
      {n: round(probe(Xtr, Xte, n), 3) for n in (10, 30, 100)})

title: 38  Representation and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
38.3 Autoencoders
An autoencoder compresses the input to a short code \(\mathbf{z}=f(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^k\) and reconstructs it, \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}=g(\mathbf{z})\). The loss is the reconstruction error \(\lVert\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2\). The label is the input itself.
With linear \(f,g\), the optimum is exactly the PCA solution of Chapter 7: the best rank-\(k\) approximation of the data (Eckart–Young) is obtained by projecting onto the top \(k\) principal directions. The autoencoder may use any basis of that subspace, but it must span the same one.

from scipy.linalg import subspace_angles
k = 8
torch.manual_seed(0)
enc, dec = nn.Linear(64, k), nn.Linear(k, 64)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(list(enc.parameters()) + list(dec.parameters()), lr=1e-2)
for _ in range(3000):
    i = torch.randint(0, len(Xt), (256,))
    loss = F.mse_loss(dec(enc(Xt[i])), Xt[i]); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
with torch.no_grad():
    mse_ae = F.mse_loss(dec(enc(Xt)), Xt).item()
pca = PCA(k).fit(Xtr)
mse_pca = np.mean((pca.inverse_transform(pca.transform(Xtr)) - Xtr) ** 2)
angles = np.degrees(subspace_angles(dec.weight.detach().numpy(), pca.components_.T))
print(f"reconstruction MSE (k = {k}): linear autoencoder {mse_ae:.5f},  PCA {mse_pca:.5f}")
print(f"largest angle between the decoder subspace and the PCA subspace: {angles.max():.1f}°")

# nonlinear autoencoder with the same code size
torch.manual_seed(0)
nenc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, k))
ndec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(k, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(list(nenc.parameters()) + list(ndec.parameters()), lr=3e-3)
for _ in range(3000):
    i = torch.randint(0, len(Xt), (256,))
    loss = F.mse_loss(ndec(nenc(Xt[i])), Xt[i]); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
with torch.no_grad():
    print(f"nonlinear autoencoder, same code size: MSE {F.mse_loss(ndec(nenc(Xt)), Xt).item():.5f}")

reconstruction MSE (k = 8): linear autoencoder 0.02388,  PCA 0.02375
largest angle between the decoder subspace and the PCA subspace: 9.0°
nonlinear autoencoder, same code size: MSE 0.01134


The linear autoencoder reaches the PCA error (to within 0.6%), and its decoder spans nearly the same subspace (largest principal angle 9°, the remainder being finite training). A nonlinear one does about twice as well at the same code size, because it can follow curved structure (the failure of PCA in Chapter 7).
Reconstruction has a weakness as a representation objective. To reconstruct pixels, the code must preserve everything, including noise and details irrelevant to meaning. Contrastive objectives avoid this.

title: 38  Representation and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
38.4 Contrastive learning
Take an example \(\mathbf{x}\). Create two views by random augmentation (shift, crop, noise, intensity change): \(\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\). They show the same underlying object. Their embeddings should be similar. Views of different examples should be different.
For a batch of \(K\) examples, embed both views and normalise to unit length (Chapter 4). Let \(s_{ij}=\mathbf{z}_i^{(1)}\cdot\mathbf{z}_j^{(2)}\) be the cosine similarity between view 1 of example \(i\) and view 2 of example \(j\). The InfoNCE loss for example \(i\) is
\[
\ell_i=-\ln\frac{\exp(s_{ii}/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(s_{ij}/\tau)}.
\tag{38.1}\]
Look at it carefully. It is the cross-entropy loss (Chapter 14) of a \(K\)-way classification: given view 1 of example \(i\), which of the \(K\) view-2 embeddings is its partner? The logits are the similarities divided by the temperature \(\tau\), and the softmax is that of Chapter 24. The true class is \(j=i\).

38.4.1 Why this learns something






TipInfoNCE bounds mutual information (sketch)



Let the “true” partner be drawn from the joint distribution and the \(K-1\) others from the marginal. Using the optimal critic, which is proportional to the density ratio \(p(\mathbf{z}^{+}\mid\mathbf{z})/p(\mathbf{z}^{+})\), one can show \[
I(\mathbf{z};\mathbf{z}^{+})\;\ge\;\ln K-\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}.
\] Minimising the loss therefore maximises a lower bound on the mutual information (Chapter 15) between the two views. The bound cannot exceed \(\ln K\): a larger batch (more negatives) allows a tighter bound. \(\blacksquare\)


The temperature \(\tau\) controls how sharply the loss focuses on the hardest negatives: a small \(\tau\) amplifies differences in similarity (Chapter 24).


38.4.2 A small contrastive learner
The encoder is an MLP from 64 pixels to a 32-dimensional embedding. Augmentation: a random one-pixel shift, random intensity scaling, and Gaussian noise. The loss is symmetrised InfoNCE.

def augment(x):
    B = len(x); im = x.view(B, 1, 8, 8)
    dy, dx = torch.randint(-1, 2, (2,)).tolist()
    im = torch.roll(im, (dy, dx), (2, 3))
    im = im * (0.7 + 0.6 * torch.rand(B, 1, 1, 1)) + 0.1 * torch.randn_like(im)
    return im.view(B, 64)

def make_encoder(out=32):
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, out))

def train_contrastive(tau=0.2, use_negatives=True, steps=600, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    f = make_encoder(); opt = torch.optim.AdamW(f.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        i = torch.randint(0, len(Xt), (128,))
        a = F.normalize(f(augment(Xt[i])), dim=1); b = F.normalize(f(augment(Xt[i])), dim=1)
        if use_negatives:
            logits = a @ b.T / tau; t = torch.arange(len(a))
            loss = (F.cross_entropy(logits, t) + F.cross_entropy(logits.T, t)) / 2
        else:
            loss = -(a * b).sum(1).mean()                     # pull positives together only
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return f(Xt).numpy(), f(Xe).numpy(), loss.item()

def mean_pair_cosine(Z):
    Zn = Z / np.linalg.norm(Z, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    S = Zn @ Zn.T
    return (S.sum() - len(Z)) / (len(Z) * (len(Z) - 1))

torch.manual_seed(7)
rand_f = make_encoder()
with torch.no_grad():
    Z_rand = (rand_f(Xt).numpy(), rand_f(Xe).numpy())
Z_nce = train_contrastive(0.2, True)
Z_pos = train_contrastive(0.2, False)
rows = {"raw pixels": (Xtr, Xte), "random encoder": Z_rand, "contrastive (InfoNCE)": Z_nce[:2],
        "positives only (no negatives)": Z_pos[:2]}
print(f"{'representation':30s} {'10 labels':>10s} {'30':>7s} {'100':>7s}   mean cosine between random pairs")
for name, (a, b) in rows.items():
    accs = [probe(a, b, n) for n in (10, 30, 100)]
    print(f"{name:30s} {accs[0]:10.3f} {accs[1]:7.3f} {accs[2]:7.3f}   {mean_pair_cosine(a):+.3f}")

representation                  10 labels      30     100   mean cosine between random pairs
raw pixels                          0.398   0.678   0.896   +0.689
random encoder                      0.189   0.129   0.653   +0.789
contrastive (InfoNCE)               0.236   0.578   0.851   +0.009
positives only (no negatives)       0.098   0.104   0.124   +1.000


Read the table with care.

Collapse. Training with only positive pairs finds a trivial solution: every input mapped to the same direction. The loss is \(-1\) (perfect agreement), the average cosine between random pairs is \(+1\), and the probe is at chance. Without negatives nothing stops the representation from ignoring its input.
Contrastive learning works, far above a random encoder.
Raw pixels are a very strong baseline here. The digits are tiny, clean, and almost linearly separable in pixel space. Self-supervised learning pays when labels are scarce and the raw input is a poor representation: photographs, audio, text. Here the 32-dimensional learned embedding does not beat the 64 raw pixels at any of the three label budgets (for example 0.85 against 0.90 with 100 labels). It is far above a random encoder, which shows that something useful was learned, and below the baseline, which shows that on this data there was little left to learn.



38.4.3 The temperature

taus = [0.02, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 2.0]
accs_tau = []
for t in taus:
    a, b, _ = train_contrastive(t, True, steps=600)
    accs_tau.append(probe(a, b, 100))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.2))
ax.bar([str(t) for t in taus], accs_tau, color=PALETTE["model"])
ax.set_xlabel("temperature τ"); ax.set_ylabel("probe accuracy (100 labels)"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
plt.show()
print({t: round(a, 3) for t, a in zip(taus, accs_tau)})

title: 38  Representation and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
38.5 Teacher–student methods and DINO
Contrastive learning needs many negatives. A different family needs none: a student network is trained to match the output of a teacher network on a different view. The teacher is not trained by gradient descent. It is an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student:
\[
\theta_{\text{teacher}}\leftarrow m\,\theta_{\text{teacher}}+(1-m)\,\theta_{\text{student}},\qquad m\approx0.99\text{–}0.999.
\tag{38.2}\]
In DINO, both networks output a vector of \(K\) scores. The loss is the cross-entropy between the teacher’s softmax (a target) and the student’s softmax:
\[
\mathcal{L}=-\sum_kp^{\text{teacher}}_k\,\ln p^{\text{student}}_k,
\qquad
p^{\text{teacher}}=\text{softmax}\!\Bigl(\frac{\mathbf{o}_t-\mathbf{c}}{\tau_t}\Bigr),\quad
p^{\text{student}}=\text{softmax}\!\Bigl(\frac{\mathbf{o}_s}{\tau_s}\Bigr).
\tag{38.3}\]
Two operations prevent the two ways a method without negatives can collapse:








Collapse
Cause
Prevented by




One output dimension always wins
all inputs get the same one-hot target
centering: subtract a running mean \(\mathbf{c}\) of teacher outputs


Uniform output for every input
softmax of a constant
sharpening: low teacher temperature \(\tau_t\)



The two are balanced. Centering pushes towards uniform. Sharpening pushes away from it.

def train_dino(center=True, sharpen=True, steps=600, seed=0, K=32):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    student = make_encoder(K); teacher = copy.deepcopy(student)
    for p in teacher.parameters():
        p.requires_grad_(False)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(student.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
    c = torch.zeros(K)
    for _ in range(steps):
        i = torch.randint(0, len(Xt), (128,))
        va, vb = augment(Xt[i]), augment(Xt[i])
        with torch.no_grad():
            o_t = teacher(va)
            target = F.softmax((o_t - (c if center else 0)) / (0.04 if sharpen else 0.5), dim=-1)
        loss = -(target * F.log_softmax(student(vb) / 0.1, dim=-1)).sum(-1).mean()
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        with torch.no_grad():
            for pt, ps in zip(teacher.parameters(), student.parameters()):
                pt.mul_(0.99).add_(ps, alpha=0.01)                 # EMA update
            c = 0.9 * c + 0.1 * o_t.mean(0)                       # centering statistic
    with torch.no_grad():
        return teacher(Xt).numpy(), teacher(Xe).numpy(), loss.item()

print(f"uniform-collapse loss would be ln K = {math.log(32):.3f}")
print(f"{'variant':26s} {'final loss':>10s} {'probe (100 labels)':>19s}")
for name, kw in [("centering + sharpening", dict()), ("no centering", dict(center=False)),
                 ("no sharpening", dict(sharpen=False))]:
    a, b, l = train_dino(**kw)
    print(f"{name:26s} {l:10.3f} {probe(a, b, 100):19.3f}")

uniform-collapse loss would be ln K = 3.466
variant                    final loss  probe (100 labels)
centering + sharpening          1.974               0.571
no centering                    0.000               0.311
no sharpening                   3.466               0.104


Without sharpening, the loss sits at exactly \(\ln K\): the teacher’s output is uniform for every input, a total collapse, and the probe is at chance. With both operations, training avoids the two collapses, but in 600 steps on this tiny dataset the representation is not good: its probe accuracy (about 0.57) is below that of a random encoder (0.65). We do not claim that DINO-style learning works well at this scale. The experiment shows the two collapse modes, which are real, and which the two operations control.

title: 38  Representation and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
38.6 Masked modelling
A third route hides part of the input and predicts it from the rest. BERT masks tokens of a sentence. Masked autoencoders (MAE) mask a large fraction (about 75%) of image patches (Chapter 36) and reconstruct them. Language models are the same idea in one direction: the hidden part is the next token (Chapter 33). The signal is again the data itself, and the loss is cross-entropy or squared error.
crumbs: Part VIII — Putting the Mathematical Systems Together

title: 38  Representation and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
38.7 Evaluating representations
The standard test is the linear probe: freeze the encoder, train only a linear classifier on top, and report accuracy for several numbers of labels (as above). A representation is good if a simple classifier suffices with few labels. Other tests: \(k\)-NN accuracy (Chapter 13), transfer to other tasks, and fine-tuning.

38.8 Production
PyTorch has everything used here. The one detail to check is that our InfoNCE equals a library cross-entropy over a similarity matrix.

torch.manual_seed(0)
a = F.normalize(torch.randn(6, 8), dim=1); b = F.normalize(torch.randn(6, 8), dim=1)
tau = 0.2
S = a @ b.T / tau
manual = torch.stack([-(S[i, i] - torch.logsumexp(S[i], 0)) for i in range(6)]).mean()
print("InfoNCE equals cross_entropy over the similarity matrix:",
      torch.allclose(manual, F.cross_entropy(S, torch.arange(6))))
print(f"ln K = {math.log(6):.3f}; the loss of random embeddings is about this: {F.cross_entropy(S * tau, torch.arange(6)).item():.3f}")

InfoNCE equals cross_entropy over the similarity matrix: True
ln K = 1.792; the loss of random embeddings is about this: 1.746

title: 38  Representation and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
38.9 Failure modes
Collapse. All inputs map to one point (@code-simclr) or to a uniform output (@code-dino). The loss looks excellent while the representation is useless. Always monitor the variance of embeddings and a probe, not just the loss.
Dimensional collapse. Embeddings occupy a few dimensions of the available space. They are not constant, but they are low-rank. Check the singular values of the embedding matrix (Chapter 7).
False negatives. Two different images of the same class are treated as negatives and pushed apart. Larger batches make this more frequent for categories with few classes.
Augmentation is the supervision. The representation becomes invariant to exactly the transformations used, and sensitive to what they preserve. A bad augmentation (colour jitter that destroys the signal, or none that hides a shortcut such as image borders) gives a bad representation.
Batch size. InfoNCE’s bound is at most \(\ln K\). Small batches limit it.
Temperature. Needs tuning (Figure 38.3).
Probe protocol. A probe trained on many labels hides weaknesses. Report several label budgets.

title: 38  Representation and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
38.11 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now learn representations from unlabelled data. It has three objectives: reconstruction (autoencoders, equal to PCA when linear), contrast (InfoNCE, a classification of partners, a bound on mutual information), and teacher–student matching (DINO, with centering and sharpening against collapse). It also has a way to judge them: the linear probe.
These were all trained on one modality. The next step is to put two modalities in one space: images and text. That is the subject of Chapter 39.

title: 38  Representation and Self-Supervised Learning
text:
Chapter summary

A linear autoencoder spans the PCA subspace. Nonlinear ones go further.
InfoNCE is \(K\)-way cross-entropy on similarities. \(I\ge\ln K-\mathcal{L}\).
Without negatives, representation learning collapses. DINO uses an EMA teacher, centering, and sharpening.
Evaluate with a linear probe at several label budgets.
Raw pixels are a strong baseline on easy data: here neither contrastive nor DINO-style embeddings beat them. Self-supervision pays where raw inputs are poor and labels scarce.

39  CLIP and Multimodal Language Models

title: 39  CLIP and Multimodal Language Models
text:
39.3 The CLIP objective
Take a batch of \(B\) matched pairs \((\text{image}_i,\text{text}_i)\). The encoders give unit vectors \(\mathbf{z}_I^{(i)},\mathbf{z}_T^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^d\). The similarity matrix is
\[
S_{ij}=\frac{\mathbf{z}_I^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{z}_T^{(j)}}{\tau}.
\tag{39.1}\]
The diagonal holds the true pairs. Row \(i\) asks: which text belongs to image \(i\)? Column \(j\) asks: which image belongs to text \(j\)? Each is a \(B\)-way classification (Chapter 24) and the loss is the average of the two cross-entropies, the symmetric InfoNCE of Chapter 38:
\[
\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12\Bigl[\text{CE}(S,\ \mathbf{I})+\text{CE}(S^{\intercal},\ \mathbf{I})\Bigr],
\tag{39.2}\]
where the targets are the diagonal, \(0,1,\dots,B-1\). The temperature \(\tau\) is itself learned, as \(\tau=e^{-s}\) with \(s\) a trainable scalar.

39.3.1 A synthetic image–caption problem
Real CLIP trains on hundreds of millions of web image–text pairs. We use a synthetic version that fits in seconds. The images are the \(8\times8\) digits. The caption is two words: an attribute (thin or thick, from the total ink of the image) and the digit name. So “thick seven” describes a seven with a lot of ink. The text encoder embeds the words and averages them (Chapter 3). The data is synthetic and the language trivial: the aim is to see the mechanism, not to reproduce CLIP’s quality.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
D = load_digits(); X, y = D.data / 16.0, D.target
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y)

names = ["zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine"]
vocab = names + ["thin", "thick"]                              # token ids 0..9 digit names, 10 thin, 11 thick
thr = np.median(Xtr.sum(1))
def captions(Xs, ys):                                          # (N, 2) token ids: attribute, name
    attr = np.where(Xs.sum(1) > thr, 11, 10)
    return torch.tensor(np.stack([attr, ys], 1))
Ttr, Tte = captions(Xtr, ytr), captions(Xte, yte)
Xt, Xe = torch.tensor(Xtr, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(Xte, dtype=torch.float32)
print("example captions:", [" ".join(vocab[t] for t in Ttr[i].tolist()) for i in range(4)])
print("distinct captions in the data:", len({tuple(r) for r in Ttr.tolist()}))

example captions: ['thin seven', 'thick three', 'thick six', 'thick six']
distinct captions in the data: 20


Only 20 distinct captions exist for 1,347 images. In a batch of 128, many images share the same caption. Plain InfoNCE treats those matching texts as negatives: a false-negative problem (Chapter 38). A standard remedy is a multi-positive target: all texts identical to text \(i\) count as correct, and the target is spread equally over them.

class ImageEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=32):
        super().__init__(); self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, d))
    def forward(self, x): return F.normalize(self.net(x), dim=-1)

class TextEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, V=12, d=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.emb = nn.Embedding(V, 64)                         # token lookup (Chapter 3)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, d))
    def forward(self, tok):                                    # tok: (B, T) ids
        return F.normalize(self.mlp(self.emb(tok).mean(1)), dim=-1)     # bag of words, then MLP

def clip_loss(zi, zt, logit_scale, tok, multi_positive):
    S = logit_scale.exp().clamp(max=100) * zi @ zt.T           # (B, B)
    if multi_positive:
        same = (tok[:, None, :] == tok[None, :, :]).all(-1).float()    # texts identical to text i
        target = same / same.sum(1, keepdim=True)
        li = -(target * S.log_softmax(1)).sum(1).mean()
        lt = -(target * S.T.log_softmax(1)).sum(1).mean()
    else:
        t = torch.arange(len(S))
        li, lt = F.cross_entropy(S, t), F.cross_entropy(S.T, t)
    return (li + lt) / 2

def train_clip(multi_positive, steps=800, B=128, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    ie, te = ImageEncoder(), TextEncoder()
    ls = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(math.log(1 / 0.07)))
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(list(ie.parameters()) + list(te.parameters()) + [ls], lr=3e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        i = torch.randint(0, len(Xt), (B,))
        loss = clip_loss(ie(Xt[i]), te(Ttr[i]), ls, Ttr[i], multi_positive)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return ie, te, ls

def zero_shot_accuracy(ie, te):
    """Class text embedding = mean of the 'thin' and 'thick' captions of that digit."""
    with torch.no_grad():
        cls_tok = torch.tensor([[a, c] for c in range(10) for a in (10, 11)])        # (20, 2)
        zt = te(cls_tok).view(10, 2, -1).mean(1)
        zt = F.normalize(zt, dim=-1)
        pred = (ie(Xe) @ zt.T).argmax(1)
    return (pred.numpy() == yte).mean()

for mp in (False, True):
    ie, te, ls = train_clip(mp)
    print(f"multi-positive targets = {mp!s:5s}: zero-shot accuracy {zero_shot_accuracy(ie, te):.3f}   "
          f"learned temperature τ = {math.exp(-ls.item()):.3f}")

multi-positive targets = False: zero-shot accuracy 0.987   learned temperature τ = 0.059
multi-positive targets = True : zero-shot accuracy 0.987   learned temperature τ = 0.058


Both variants reach the same accuracy here. In this synthetic problem the “false negatives” share the same class, so they pull the embeddings in the same direction as the true positives, and little harm is done. The issue matters more when texts that are treated as negatives are in fact good descriptions of the image but differ from it in some important detail. We keep the multi-positive form as the more careful default.
Zero-shot classification used no class labels as such. It only used the caption text of each class, embedded by the text encoder, and the nearest one in the joint space. A new class could be added by writing a new caption.


39.3.2 The joint space

ie, te, ls = train_clip(True)
with torch.no_grad():
    Zi = ie(Xe).numpy()
    cls_tok = torch.tensor([[a, c] for c in range(10) for a in (10, 11)])
    Zt = te(cls_tok).numpy()
    Zc = F.normalize(te(cls_tok).view(10, 2, -1).mean(1), dim=-1).numpy()
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
pca = PCA(2).fit(np.vstack([Zi, Zt]))
P_i, P_c = pca.transform(Zi), pca.transform(Zc)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.6))
sc = ax.scatter(*P_i.T, c=yte, cmap="tab10", s=8, alpha=0.7)
ax.scatter(*P_c.T, marker="*", s=240, color="black")
for c, p in enumerate(P_c):
    ax.annotate(names[c], p, xytext=(4, 4), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("PC 1"); ax.set_ylabel("PC 2")
plt.show()
d_match = np.mean([Zi[i] @ Zc[yte[i]] for i in range(len(Zi))])
d_all = np.mean(Zi @ Zc.T)
print(f"mean cosine of an image with its own class text: {d_match:.2f};  with all class texts: {d_all:.2f}")







Figure 39.3: The joint embedding space, projected to 2D with PCA fitted on both modalities together. Dots: test-image embeddings coloured by digit. Stars: the text embeddings of the ten class captions. Each star lies in or next to its digit’s cluster: images and text are aligned.





mean cosine of an image with its own class text: 0.70;  with all class texts: 0.04




39.3.3 The modality gap
Reported analyses of large trained CLIP models find that image embeddings and text embeddings occupy different regions of the sphere, even though matched pairs are close relative to mismatched ones. A measure is the distance between the centroids of the two groups, relative to the spread within each. In our small synthetic model the gap is small, as the numbers below show.

with torch.no_grad():
    Zt_all = te(torch.tensor(Tte.numpy())).numpy()               # one caption per test image
    Zi_all = ie(Xe).numpy()
cen_i, cen_t = Zi_all.mean(0), Zt_all.mean(0)
gap = np.linalg.norm(cen_i - cen_t)
spread_i = np.linalg.norm(Zi_all - cen_i, axis=1).mean()
spread_t = np.linalg.norm(Zt_all - cen_t, axis=1).mean()
print(f"centroid distance {gap:.2f};  average distance to own centroid: images {spread_i:.2f}, texts {spread_t:.2f}")
print(f"mean cosine of matched image–text pairs {np.mean(np.sum(Zi_all * Zt_all, 1)):.2f}")

centroid distance 0.19;  average distance to own centroid: images 0.98, texts 0.97
mean cosine of matched image–text pairs 0.79
