title: 39  CLIP and Multimodal Language Models
section: 39.4 From CLIP to multimodal language models
text:
39.4 From CLIP to multimodal language models
A CLIP model compares an image with text. A multimodal language model conditions text generation on an image: it answers questions and describes. The usual design reuses a pre-trained vision encoder and a pre-trained language model, and connects them with a small projector:

fig = box_flow(["image", "vision encoder\n(ViT)\nN × d_v", "projector\nN × d_LM", "[visual tokens ; text tokens]\n(N + T) × d_LM", "decoder-only\nLLM", "next-token\ndistribution"],
               colors=[PALETTE["data"], PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["prob"], PALETTE["data"], PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["loss"]],
               figsize=(11, 2.0), fontsize=7.8)
plt.show()







Figure 39.4: Level 1: a multimodal LLM. A vision encoder turns the image into patch tokens. A projector maps them into the language model’s embedding space. They are placed in the same sequence as the text tokens, and the decoder (Chapter 32) predicts the answer token by token.





The projector is a linear map or a small MLP: \(\mathbf{H}_{\text{vis}}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{W}_p\), with \(\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_v}\) and \(\mathbf{W}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{\text{LM}}}\). The result lives in the same space as word embeddings (Chapter 3), so the language model treats image patches as if they were unusual tokens.

d_v, d_lm, N_vis, T_txt = 1024, 4096, 576, 32
torch.manual_seed(0)
V = torch.randn(1, N_vis, d_v)                                  # vision-encoder output
Wp = nn.Linear(d_v, d_lm)                                       # projector
text_emb = torch.randn(1, T_txt, d_lm)                          # embedded text prompt
seq = torch.cat([Wp(V), text_emb], dim=1)
print("visual tokens:", tuple(Wp(V).shape), "  full sequence:", tuple(seq.shape))
print(f"projector parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in Wp.parameters()):,}")
print(f"attention score matrix per head and layer: {seq.shape[1]}² = {seq.shape[1] ** 2:,} entries "
      f"(vs {T_txt ** 2:,} for text alone)")

visual tokens: (1, 576, 4096)   full sequence: (1, 608, 4096)
projector parameters: 4,198,400
attention score matrix per head and layer: 608² = 369,664 entries (vs 1,024 for text alone)


Each image adds hundreds of tokens, and attention cost grows with the square of the sequence (Chapters 30, 34).

39.4.1 Cross-attention and resamplers
An alternative to concatenation keeps the language model’s input as text only and lets its layers read the image through cross-attention (Chapter 30): queries come from the text states, keys and values from the image tokens.
A resampler reduces the number of image tokens first. A fixed set of \(M\) learned query vectors attends over the \(N\) image tokens (the same device as the detection queries of Chapter 37), and the \(M\) outputs are passed on:
\[
\mathbf{H}_{\text{vis}}=\text{softmax}\!\Bigl(\frac{\mathbf{Q}_{\text{learned}}\,\mathbf{K}_{\text{img}}^{\intercal}}{\sqrt{d}}\Bigr)\mathbf{V}_{\text{img}}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d},\qquad M\ll N.
\tag{39.3}\]

class Resampler(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d, n_queries):
        super().__init__()
        self.q = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n_queries, d) * 0.02)          # learned queries
        self.k, self.v = nn.Linear(d_in, d, bias=False), nn.Linear(d_in, d, bias=False)
    def forward(self, tokens):                                            # (B, N, d_in)
        K, Vv = self.k(tokens), self.v(tokens)
        A = (self.q @ K.transpose(1, 2) / math.sqrt(K.shape[-1])).softmax(-1)   # (B, M, N)
        return A @ Vv, A

res = Resampler(d_v, 512, n_queries=32)
out, A = res(V)
print(f"image tokens {V.shape[1]} -> {out.shape[1]} tokens of width {out.shape[2]}")
print("attention rows sum to 1:", torch.allclose(A.sum(-1), torch.ones(1, 32)))
print(f"cost of the language model's attention per layer: {(32 + T_txt) ** 2:,} entries "
      f"instead of {(N_vis + T_txt) ** 2:,}")

image tokens 576 -> 32 tokens of width 512
attention rows sum to 1: True
cost of the language model's attention per layer: 4,096 entries instead of 369,664

title: 39  CLIP and Multimodal Language Models
text:
39.5 Training recipes
A common recipe has stages:

Pre-train the vision encoder (CLIP-style, Chapter 38, or self-supervised).
Start from a pre-trained language model.
Train the projector only, on image–caption pairs, with the next-token loss (Chapter 33) on the caption.
Then train projector and language model (often with LoRA, Chapter 7) on instruction data with images.

The loss throughout is the language-model cross-entropy on text tokens, computed with the image tokens as part of the conditioning prefix. Nothing new is added to the mathematics of Chapters 32–33.

title: 39  CLIP and Multimodal Language Models
text:
39.7 Failure modes
False negatives. Images and texts that match are treated as mismatches (@code-clip). In large datasets, duplicates and near-duplicates are frequent.
Batch size. The loss compares each item with \(B-1\) others. The mutual-information bound is at most \(\ln B\). Real CLIP training uses very large batches (tens of thousands).
Bag-of-words behaviour. With a mean-pooled text encoder, word order is lost: “thick seven” and “seven thick” give the same embedding. Many CLIP-style models are weak at relations (“a dog chasing a cat” versus the reverse).

with torch.no_grad():
    a = te(torch.tensor([[11, 7]])); b = te(torch.tensor([[7, 11]]))
print("embedding of 'thick seven' equals that of 'seven thick':", torch.allclose(a, b, atol=1e-6))

embedding of 'thick seven' equals that of 'seven thick': True


Modality gap. In large models the two groups stay apart on the sphere (not seen in our toy model). This affects the use of image and text embeddings interchangeably, for example mixing image–text similarity with image–image similarity.
Hallucination. A language model with weak grounding generates fluent text that is not supported by the image. The image is one prefix among many and may be underweighted.
Cost of visual tokens. Hundreds of tokens per image dominate the context. Resamplers and token pruning reduce them at some loss of detail.
Prompt sensitivity of zero-shot. The class text matters. Averaging several prompts (as we did with thin and thick) improves robustness.

39.9 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The three running systems are now one. Images and text share an embedding space (System B’s retrieval works across modalities), a language model can read image tokens (System C sees), and a classifier can be specified in words. crumbs: Part VIII — Putting the Mathematical Systems Together

title: 40  Latent-Variable Models and VAEs
text:
40.2 Latent-variable models
Suppose a handwritten digit is determined by a few hidden factors: which digit, slant, thickness. We never observe them. A latent-variable model says:
\[
\mathbf{z}\sim p(\mathbf{z}),\qquad
\mathbf{x}\sim p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z}).
\tag{40.1}\]
The prior \(p(\mathbf{z})\) is simple (a standard Gaussian). The decoder \(p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\) is a neural network that turns a latent code into a distribution over data. Generating is easy: sample \(\mathbf{z}\), decode.
Training by maximum likelihood (Chapter 25) needs the marginal likelihood
\[
p_\theta(\mathbf{x})=\int p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\,p(\mathbf{z})\,d\mathbf{z}.
\tag{40.2}\]
The integral runs over all latent codes and has no closed form for a neural-network decoder. We cannot compute \(\ln p_\theta(\mathbf{x})\), let alone its gradient.
crumbs: Part VIII — Putting the Mathematical Systems Together

title: 40  Latent-Variable Models and VAEs
text:
40.3 The evidence lower bound
We introduce an approximate posterior \(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\), the encoder: a distribution over codes that plausibly produced \(\mathbf{x}\).






TipDerivation: the ELBO



Multiply and divide inside the integral by \(q_\phi\), and use Jensen’s inequality for the concave \(\ln\) (Chapter 15): \[
\ln p_\theta(\mathbf{x})=\ln\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})}\!\Bigl[\frac{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\,p(\mathbf{z})}{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})}\Bigr]
\;\ge\;\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}\!\bigl[\ln p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\bigr]-D_{\text{KL}}\bigl(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\,\Vert\,p(\mathbf{z})\bigr).
\] The right side is the ELBO. The gap is exact: expanding with Bayes’ rule, \[
\ln p_\theta(\mathbf{x})=\text{ELBO}+D_{\text{KL}}\bigl(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\,\Vert\,p_\theta(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\bigr).
\] The KL divergence is non-negative (Gibbs, Chapter 15), so the ELBO is a lower bound, and it is tight when \(q_\phi\) equals the true posterior. \(\blacksquare\)


The ELBO has two terms with clear meanings:








Term
Meaning
Pulls towards




\(\mathbb{E}_q[\ln p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})]\)
reconstruction: can the decoder rebuild \(\mathbf{x}\) from the code?
informative codes


\(-D_{\text{KL}}(q_\phi\Vert p)\)
regularisation: stay close to the prior
an organised, samplable space



Maximising the ELBO over \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) trains the model.
crumbs: Part VIII — Putting the Mathematical Systems Together

title: 40  Latent-Variable Models and VAEs
text:
40.4 Making it trainable
Encoder. A neural network outputs the mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}(\mathbf{x})\) and log-variance \(\ln\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2(\mathbf{x})\) of a diagonal Gaussian: \(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\text{diag}\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2)\).
KL term, in closed form. For this Gaussian and the prior \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\) (Chapter 23):
\[
D_{\text{KL}}=\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\mu_k^2+\sigma_k^2-1-\ln\sigma_k^{2}\bigr).
\tag{40.3}\]
Reconstruction term, by sampling. The expectation over \(q_\phi\) is estimated with one sample. To let gradients reach the encoder, the sample is reparameterised (Chapter 23):
\[
\mathbf{z}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\sigma}\odot\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\qquad\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}).
\tag{40.4}\]
Decoder likelihood. With a Gaussian \(p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})=\mathcal{N}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{z}),s^{2}\mathbf{I})\), the log-likelihood is a squared error (Chapter 25): \(-\frac{\lVert\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2}{2s^2}-\frac D2\ln(2\pi s^2)\).
The loss to minimise is then (a negative ELBO, up to a constant):
\[
\mathcal{L}=\frac{\lVert\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2}{2s^2}+\beta\,D_{\text{KL}},\qquad\beta=1\text{ for the true ELBO}.
\tag{40.5}\]

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
D = load_digits(); X, y = D.data / 16.0, D.target
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y)
Xt, Xe = torch.tensor(Xtr, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(Xte, dtype=torch.float32)
S_DEC = 0.25                                                   # decoder standard deviation s

class VAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, k=2, h=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, h), nn.ReLU())
        self.mu, self.logvar = nn.Linear(h, k), nn.Linear(h, k)
        self.dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(k, h), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h, 64), nn.Sigmoid())
    def encode(self, x):
        h = self.enc(x); return self.mu(h), self.logvar(h)
    def forward(self, x):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x)
        z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)        # reparameterisation
        return self.dec(z), mu, logvar

def parts(model, x):
    xh, mu, logvar = model(x)
    rec = ((x - xh) ** 2).sum(1) / (2 * S_DEC ** 2)                    # -ln p(x|z) up to a constant
    kl = 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + logvar.exp() - 1 - logvar).sum(1)
    return rec.mean(), kl.mean()

def train_vae(beta=1.0, k=2, steps=1500, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = VAE(k); opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=2e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        i = torch.randint(0, len(Xt), (128,))
        rec, kl = parts(m, Xt[i]); loss = rec + beta * kl
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return m

vae = train_vae(beta=1.0)
with torch.no_grad():
    rec, kl = parts(vae, Xe)
print(f"test set: reconstruction term {rec:.1f}, KL {kl:.2f} nats")

test set: reconstruction term 19.8, KL 3.92 nats

40.5 What the latent space looks like
With a 2-dimensional latent space we can see it directly.

with torch.no_grad():
    mu_te, _ = vae.encode(Xe)
g = np.linspace(-2.5, 2.5, 10)
grid = torch.tensor([[a, b] for b in g[::-1] for a in g], dtype=torch.float32)
with torch.no_grad():
    imgs = vae.dec(grid).view(10, 10, 8, 8).numpy()
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1]})
sc = ax1.scatter(*mu_te.numpy().T, c=yte, cmap="tab10", s=8)
ax1.set_xlabel("z₁"); ax1.set_ylabel("z₂")
ax1.legend(*sc.legend_elements(), title="digit", fontsize=7, ncol=2, loc="upper right")
canvas = np.block([[imgs[r, c] for c in range(10)] for r in range(10)])
ax2.imshow(canvas, cmap="gray_r", aspect="equal"); ax2.set_xticks([]); ax2.set_yticks([]); ax2.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 40.2: The learned 2D latent space. Left: encoder means of the test images, coloured by digit (no labels were used in training). Some digits form their own regions (0, 1, 4); others overlap heavily, as two numbers cannot separate ten classes. Right: the decoder applied to a regular grid of latent points, from −2.5 to 2.5 in each direction. Moving through the space changes the output gradually, and every point decodes to something digit-like.






40.5.1 Sampling
To generate, sample \(\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\) and decode. The KL term is what makes this work: it keeps the aggregate of the encoder’s outputs close to the prior, so that prior samples land where the decoder has been trained.

torch.manual_seed(1)
with torch.no_grad():
    samples = vae.dec(torch.randn(16, 2)).view(16, 8, 8).numpy()
    recon = vae(Xe[:16])[0].view(16, 8, 8).numpy()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 16, figsize=(12, 2.4))
for r, (imgs_, lab) in enumerate([(samples, "prior samples"), (Xe[:16].view(16, 8, 8).numpy(), "test images"),
                                  (recon, "reconstructions")]):
    for c in range(16):
        axes[r, c].imshow(imgs_[c], cmap="gray_r"); axes[r, c].axis("off")
    axes[r, 0].set_title(lab, fontsize=8, loc="left")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 40.3: Generated digits. Top: decoder output for 16 samples from the prior. Middle and bottom: test images and their reconstructions (encode, then decode). Samples are recognisable but blurry: the Gaussian decoder outputs the average of the many images consistent with a code. With only two latent numbers, the reconstruction is often a different digit from the input: the code cannot carry enough information (an 8-dimensional code, below, reconstructs far better).
crumbs: Part VIII — Putting the Mathematical Systems Together

title: 40  Latent-Variable Models and VAEs
text:
40.6 Checking the bound
The ELBO is a lower bound on \(\ln p_\theta(\mathbf{x})\). We can estimate the true log-likelihood of one image by importance sampling: draw many codes from \(q_\phi\) and average the ratios \(p(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})p(\mathbf{z})/q(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\) (Chapter 26). If our derivation is right, the estimate must lie above the ELBO.

def log_normal(x, mu, var):                                    # sum over the last dimension
    return (-0.5 * (math.log(2 * math.pi) + var.log() + (x - mu) ** 2 / var)).sum(-1)

@torch.no_grad()
def elbo_and_logp(model, x, n_samples=5000):
    mu, logvar = model.encode(x[None]); std = torch.exp(0.5 * logvar)
    z = mu + std * torch.randn(n_samples, mu.shape[1])
    xh = model.dec(z)
    log_px_z = log_normal(x[None], xh, torch.full_like(xh, S_DEC ** 2))     # normalised Gaussian
    log_pz = log_normal(z, torch.zeros_like(z), torch.ones_like(z))
    log_qz = log_normal(z, mu, std ** 2)
    w = log_px_z + log_pz - log_qz                              # log importance weights
    logp = torch.logsumexp(w, 0) - math.log(n_samples)
    elbo = w.mean()                                             # E_q[log p(x|z) + log p(z) − log q(z|x)]
    return elbo.item(), logp.item()

print(f"{'image':>6s} {'ELBO':>10s} {'log p(x) (IS)':>14s} {'gap':>8s}")
for i in range(5):
    e, lp = elbo_and_logp(vae, Xe[i])
    print(f"{i:6d} {e:10.2f} {lp:14.2f} {lp - e:8.2f}")

 image       ELBO  log p(x) (IS)      gap
     0     -14.96         -10.90     4.05
     1      19.85          20.65     0.80
     2       7.32           7.45     0.13
     3       3.76           3.84     0.08
     4      11.11          11.65     0.54


The importance-sampled \(\ln p(\mathbf{x})\) is above the ELBO in every row. The gap is \(D_{\text{KL}}(q\Vert p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x}))\): how far the encoder is from the true posterior.

section: 40.7 The role of the KL weight
text:
40.7 The role of the KL weight
We train the same model with different weights \(\beta\) on the KL term (\(\beta=1\) is the true ELBO). We record the test reconstruction error and the KL, and the active dimensions: latent coordinates whose encoder mean varies across inputs.

betas = [0.0, 0.1, 1.0, 5.0, 20.0, 100.0]
rows = []
for b in betas:
    m = train_vae(beta=b, k=8, steps=1500)
    with torch.no_grad():
        rec_, kl_ = parts(m, Xe)
        mu_, _ = m.encode(Xe)
        active = int((mu_.var(0) > 0.05).sum())
    rows.append((b, rec_.item(), kl_.item(), active))
print(f"{'beta':>6s} {'recon error':>12s} {'KL':>8s} {'active dims (of 8)':>19s}")
for b, r_, k_, a_ in rows:
    print(f"{b:6.1f} {r_:12.1f} {k_:8.2f} {a_:19d}")
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
bs = [max(b, 0.02) for b, *_ in rows]
ax1.semilogx(bs, [r[1] for r in rows], "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"], label="reconstruction error")
ax1.set_xlabel("β (KL weight; 0 plotted at 0.02)"); ax1.set_ylabel("reconstruction error", color=PALETTE["loss"])
ax2 = ax1.twinx(); ax2.semilogx(bs, [r[2] for r in rows], "s-", color=PALETTE["data"])
ax2.set_ylabel("KL (nats)", color=PALETTE["data"])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

  beta  recon error       KL  active dims (of 8)
   0.0          6.6    99.63                   8
   0.1          7.1    19.13                   8
   1.0         11.3     7.76                   8
   5.0         25.0     1.81                   4
  20.0         38.1     0.00                   0
 100.0         38.1     0.00                   0








Figure 40.4: Effect of the KL weight β, in a model with an 8-dimensional latent space. As β grows, the KL falls (the code carries less information) and the reconstruction error rises. For β = 20 the KL is almost zero: the encoder ignores the input and every code equals the prior. This is posterior collapse: the decoder then outputs the same average image for everything.





The trade-off is the rate–distortion trade-off of information theory (Chapter 15): the KL is the rate (information the code carries about the input) and the reconstruction error is the distortion.

40.8 Production
torch.distributions provides the Gaussian, its rsample, and the KL. We check that our closed form and our sampling agree.

from torch.distributions import Normal, kl_divergence
torch.manual_seed(0)
mu_t, logvar_t = torch.randn(5, 4), torch.randn(5, 4)
q = Normal(mu_t, torch.exp(0.5 * logvar_t)); p = Normal(torch.zeros(5, 4), torch.ones(5, 4))
kl_lib = kl_divergence(q, p).sum(1)
kl_mine = 0.5 * (mu_t ** 2 + logvar_t.exp() - 1 - logvar_t).sum(1)
print("closed-form KL equals torch.distributions:", torch.allclose(kl_lib, kl_mine, atol=1e-5))
z = q.rsample()
print("rsample keeps the graph (gradients can flow):", z.requires_grad or mu_t.requires_grad is False)

title: 40  Latent-Variable Models and VAEs
text:
40.10 Failure modes
Posterior collapse. The encoder outputs the prior for every input. The KL is near zero and the decoder ignores \(\mathbf{z}\). It occurs with large \(\beta\) or a very powerful decoder (an autoregressive decoder can model the data without the code). Remedies: KL annealing (increase \(\beta\) gradually), free bits, weaker decoders.
Holes. With \(\beta\to0\), the model is an autoencoder. Codes of different inputs sit far apart and the space between them decodes to nonsense. Samples from the prior fall in the holes.
Blurry samples. A Gaussian decoder with fixed variance reconstructs the mean of all images that fit a code. Fine detail is averaged away. Better likelihoods or adversarial and diffusion decoders (Chapters 41, 42) address it.
Wrong decoder variance. The scale \(s\) sets the balance between reconstruction and KL: it plays the role of \(\beta\). A poor choice looks like a poor \(\beta\).
Looseness of the bound. The ELBO may be far below \(\ln p(\mathbf{x})\) if the encoder family is too simple (diagonal Gaussian).
Latent dimension. Too few dimensions limit capacity. Too many go unused (inactive dimensions).

title: 40  Latent-Variable Models and VAEs
text:
40.12 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now generate: it has a probabilistic model with hidden causes, a trainable bound on the likelihood (the ELBO), an encoder that infers causes, and a sampler (prior, then decoder). It also has a language for the trade-off between how much a code says and how well it reconstructs.
One latent step generates blurry samples. Chapter 41 chains many small latent steps, each denoising, and obtains sharp ones.

title: 40  Latent-Variable Models and VAEs
text:
Chapter summary

A latent-variable model: \(\mathbf{z}\sim p(\mathbf{z})\), \(\mathbf{x}\sim p_\theta(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})\). The marginal is intractable.
\(\text{ELBO}=\mathbb{E}_q[\ln p(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{z})]-D_{\text{KL}}(q\Vert p)\le\ln p(\mathbf{x})\), with gap \(D_{\text{KL}}(q\Vert p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x}))\).
VAE: Gaussian encoder, reparameterisation \(\mathbf{z}=\boldsymbol{\mu}+\boldsymbol{\sigma}\odot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\), closed-form KL.
Sampling: \(\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})\), decode.
\(\beta\) trades rate for distortion. Large \(\beta\) collapses the posterior. \(\beta=0\) gives holes.

title: 40  Latent-Variable Models and VAEs
text:
Exercises

Compute. For \(\boldsymbol{\mu}=(1,0)\), \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}=(0.5,1)\), compute the KL divergence to \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\).
Derive. Show that the ELBO equals \(\ln p(\mathbf{x})\) when \(q(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})=p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathbf{x})\).
Derive. Show that with a Gaussian decoder of variance \(s^2\), the loss \(\lVert\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2/(2s^2)+D_{\text{KL}}\) is equivalent to \(\lVert\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\rVert^2+2s^2D_{\text{KL}}\). What is \(\beta\) in terms of \(s\)?
Derive. Show that the gradient of the KL term with respect to \(\sigma_k\) is \(\sigma_k-1/\sigma_k\). Where is it zero?
Code. Train with a 16-dimensional latent space and \(\beta=1\). How many dimensions are active?
Code. Add KL annealing (linearly increase \(\beta\) from 0 to 1 in the first 500 steps). Compare with the plain run.
Code. Interpolate between the codes of two test digits and decode eight points. Plot them.
Code. Replace the Gaussian decoder by a Bernoulli one (binary cross-entropy). Compare samples.
Diagnose. A VAE reconstructs well, but samples from the prior are noise. Which term and which \(\beta\) would you suspect?
Explain. Why does the ELBO need an encoder at all? What would happen if we sampled \(\mathbf{z}\) from the prior to estimate the marginal likelihood?

title: 41  Diffusion Models
text:
41.3 The forward process
At each step, shrink the signal a little and add Gaussian noise:
\[
q(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t-1})=\mathcal{N}\bigl(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t-1},\ \beta_{t}\mathbf{I}\bigr),\qquad t=1,\dots,T,
\tag{41.1}\]
with small noise levels \(\beta_t\). Write \(\alpha_t=1-\beta_t\) and \(\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s\le t}\alpha_s\).






TipDerivation: the closed form



One step is \(\mathbf{x}_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t-1}+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t\) with \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\) (Chapter 23). Substitute the previous step: \[
\mathbf{x}_t=\sqrt{\alpha_{t}\alpha_{t-1}}\,\mathbf{x}_{t-2}+\sqrt{\alpha_t(1-\alpha_{t-1})}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t-1}+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t.
\] The two noise terms are independent Gaussians. Their sum is Gaussian with variance (variances add, Chapter 21) \(\alpha_t(1-\alpha_{t-1})+(1-\alpha_t)=1-\alpha_{t}\alpha_{t-1}\). So the sum equals \(\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t}\alpha_{t-1}}\,\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\) for a single standard normal \(\bar{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\). Repeating the argument down to \(\mathbf{x}_0\): \[
\boxed{\;q(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_0)=\mathcal{N}\bigl(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbf{x}_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_t)\mathbf{I}\bigr),\qquad
\mathbf{x}_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbf{x}_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\;}\ \blacksquare
\]


This is the key convenience: any noise level can be sampled directly, without running the chain. We check it by simulating the chain step by step.

T = 100
betas = np.linspace(1e-3, 0.12, T)
alphas = 1 - betas
abar = np.cumprod(alphas)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x0 = 1.7                                                          # a scalar "data point"
x = np.full(200_000, x0)
for t in range(40):                                               # run 40 noising steps
    x = np.sqrt(alphas[t]) * x + np.sqrt(betas[t]) * rng.normal(size=x.shape)
print(f"after 40 steps (chain):   mean {x.mean():.3f}, std {x.std():.3f}")
print(f"closed form at t = 40:    mean {np.sqrt(abar[39]) * x0:.3f}, std {np.sqrt(1 - abar[39]):.3f}")
print(f"signal left at the final step: sqrt(abar_T) = {np.sqrt(abar[-1]):.3f}")

after 40 steps (chain):   mean 1.032, std 0.794
closed form at t = 40:    mean 1.034, std 0.794
signal left at the final step: sqrt(abar_T) = 0.043



41.3.1 Schedules
The sequence \(\beta_t\) is the noise schedule. Its effect is best seen through \(\bar\alpha_t\) (signal fraction) and the signal-to-noise ratio \(\text{SNR}(t)=\bar\alpha_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)\).

s = 0.008
tt = np.arange(T + 1) / T
f = np.cos((tt + s) / (1 + s) * np.pi / 2) ** 2
abar_cos = (f / f[0])[1:]
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))
for ab, name, c in [(abar, "linear β", PALETTE["data"]), (abar_cos, "cosine", PALETTE["model"])]:
    ax1.plot(np.sqrt(ab), color=c, lw=2, label=name)
    ax2.plot(np.log(ab / (1 - ab + 1e-12)), color=c, lw=2, label=name)
ax1.set_xlabel("step t"); ax1.set_ylabel("√ᾱ_t  (signal coefficient)"); ax1.legend()
ax2.set_xlabel("step t"); ax2.set_ylabel("log SNR(t)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 41.3: Two noise schedules over T = 100 steps. Left: the signal coefficient √ᾱ_t falls from 1 towards 0. Right: the log signal-to-noise ratio. The linear schedule (blue) destroys the signal early. The cosine schedule (orange) removes it more evenly. At the last step, a small residual signal remains for both.

title: 41  Diffusion Models
text:
41.4 The reverse process
To generate, we need to go backwards: \(p(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_t)\). That distribution depends on the whole data distribution, and is unknown. But if we also condition on \(\mathbf{x}_0\), it is a Gaussian that we can write down exactly. By Bayes’ rule (Chapter 22), applied to Gaussians (Chapter 23):
\[
q(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_t,\mathbf{x}_0)=\mathcal{N}\bigl(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t(\mathbf{x}_t,\mathbf{x}_0),\ \tilde\beta_{t}\mathbf{I}\bigr),
\tag{41.2}\]
\[
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\mathbf{x}_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\mathbf{x}_t,\qquad
\tilde\beta_t=\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\beta_t.
\tag{41.3}\]






TipWhy this form



By Bayes, \(q(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_t,\mathbf{x}_0)\propto q(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t-1})\,q(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\mid\mathbf{x}_0)\): a product of two Gaussians in \(\mathbf{x}_{t-1}\). The exponent of a product of Gaussians is a sum of quadratics, which is again quadratic. Completing the square gives a precision (inverse variance) that is the sum of the two precisions, \(1/\tilde\beta_t=\alpha_t/\beta_t+1/(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\), and a mean that is the precision-weighted average of the two means. Simplifying yields Equation 41.3. \(\blacksquare\)


We check the formulas numerically on scalar data: simulate pairs \((\mathbf{x}_{t-1},\mathbf{x}_t)\) from the forward chain, and compare the empirical conditional mean and variance given \(\mathbf{x}_t\) with the formula.

t = 30                                                             # index into arrays (step t+1 in 1-based)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x0 = 1.7
x_prev = np.sqrt(abar[t - 1]) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - abar[t - 1]) * rng.normal(size=2_000_000)   # x_{t-1}
x_t = np.sqrt(alphas[t]) * x_prev + np.sqrt(betas[t]) * rng.normal(size=x_prev.shape)         # x_t
# empirical regression of x_{t-1} on x_t (conditioned on the fixed x0)
A = np.cov(x_prev, x_t)[0, 1] / x_t.var()
resid = x_prev - (x_prev.mean() + A * (x_t - x_t.mean()))
mu_coef_xt = np.sqrt(alphas[t]) * (1 - abar[t - 1]) / (1 - abar[t])
mu_const = np.sqrt(abar[t - 1]) * betas[t] / (1 - abar[t]) * x0
var_formula = (1 - abar[t - 1]) / (1 - abar[t]) * betas[t]
print(f"coefficient of x_t in the posterior mean: empirical {A:.4f}, formula {mu_coef_xt:.4f}")
print(f"posterior variance:                       empirical {resid.var():.5f}, formula {var_formula:.5f}")
mid = np.argmin(np.abs(x_t - x_t.mean()))
print(f"posterior mean at x_t = {x_t[mid]:.2f}: formula {mu_const + mu_coef_xt * x_t[mid]:.4f}")

coefficient of x_t in the posterior mean: empirical 0.9346, formula 0.9351
posterior variance:                       empirical 0.03532, formula 0.03532
posterior mean at x_t = 1.26: formula 1.2857

title: 41  Diffusion Models
text:
41.5 Training: predict the noise
We do not know \(\mathbf{x}_0\) at generation time. We estimate it. From the closed form, \(\mathbf{x}_0=(\mathbf{x}_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\). So knowing the noise \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) is equivalent to knowing \(\mathbf{x}_0\). Substituting into Equation 41.3 gives a mean in terms of \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\):
\[
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Bigl(\mathbf{x}_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\Bigr).
\tag{41.4}\]
A network \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t)\) is trained to predict the noise that was added:
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_0,\ t,\ \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\Bigl[\bigl\lVert\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta\bigl(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mathbf{x}_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\ t\bigr)\bigr\rVert^{2}\Bigr].
\tag{41.5}\]
This is a squared-error regression (Chapter 14). It follows from the ELBO of Chapter 40 (the chain of latents \(\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_T\)), where each KL term between two Gaussians reduces to a squared difference of means. Dropping the per-step weights gives Equation 41.5, which works well in practice.
The training algorithm is three lines: sample a data point, a step \(t\), and noise; form \(\mathbf{x}_t\); take a gradient step on the squared error.

41.5.1 The link to the score
The score of a distribution is the gradient of its log-density, \(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\ln p(\mathbf{x})\). For the Gaussian \(q(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_0)\),
\[
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_t}\ln q(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_0)=-\frac{\mathbf{x}_t-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mathbf{x}_0}{1-\bar\alpha_t}=-\frac{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}.
\tag{41.6}\]
So the noise prediction is, up to the factor \(-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\), an estimate of the score of the noisy data distribution: the direction in which the density increases most. Denoising is moving up the density.

title: 41  Diffusion Models
section: 41.6 A diffusion model on a 2D distribution
text:
41.6 A diffusion model on a 2D distribution
We train a diffusion model on the two-moons distribution. The network is an MLP with inputs \((\mathbf{x}_t,t)\) (the step is given a sinusoidal embedding, as in Chapter 31), and output \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta\in\mathbb{R}^2\).

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons

def sample_data(n, seed=None):
    X, _ = make_moons(n, noise=0.06, random_state=seed)
    return torch.tensor((X - np.array([0.5, 0.25])) * 2.0, dtype=torch.float32)

class EpsNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden=128, temb=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.temb = temb
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 + temb, hidden), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.SiLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, 2))
    def forward(self, x, t):                                   # t: (B,) integer steps
        f = torch.exp(-math.log(1000) * torch.arange(self.temb // 2) / (self.temb // 2))
        a = t[:, None].float() * f[None]
        return self.net(torch.cat([x, a.sin(), a.cos()], dim=1))

abar_t = torch.tensor(abar, dtype=torch.float32)
alphas_t = torch.tensor(alphas, dtype=torch.float32); betas_t = torch.tensor(betas, dtype=torch.float32)

torch.manual_seed(0)
net = EpsNet(); opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=2e-3)
losses, t0 = [], time.time()
for step in range(20000):
    x0 = sample_data(256)
    t = torch.randint(0, T, (256,))
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    xt = abar_t[t].sqrt()[:, None] * x0 + (1 - abar_t[t]).sqrt()[:, None] * eps      # closed form
    loss = F.mse_loss(net(xt, t), eps)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); losses.append(loss.item())
print(f"trained in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; loss {np.mean(losses[:50]):.3f} -> {np.mean(losses[-200:]):.3f}")

trained in 13 s; loss 0.553 -> 0.333



41.6.1 Sampling
DDPM sampling starts from pure noise \(\mathbf{x}_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\) and applies the learned reverse step \(T\) times:
\[
\mathbf{x}_{t-1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Bigl(\mathbf{x}_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t)\Bigr)+\sigma_{t}\mathbf{z},\qquad\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}).
\tag{41.7}\]
DDIM sampling removes the fresh noise and jumps between a sparse subset of steps. First estimate the clean sample, then re-noise it deterministically to the next step:
\[
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_0=\frac{\mathbf{x}_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}},\qquad
\mathbf{x}_{t'}=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t'}}\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t'}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta.
\tag{41.8}\]

@torch.no_grad()
def ddpm_sample(n, seed=0, record=False):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    x = torch.randn(n, 2, generator=g); traj = [x.clone()]
    for t in reversed(range(T)):
        tt = torch.full((n,), t)
        eps = net(x, tt)
        mean = (x - betas_t[t] / (1 - abar_t[t]).sqrt() * eps) / alphas_t[t].sqrt()
        if t > 0:
            sigma = ((1 - abar_t[t - 1]) / (1 - abar_t[t]) * betas_t[t]).sqrt()
            x = mean + sigma * torch.randn(n, 2, generator=g)
        else:
            x = mean
        if record: traj.append(x.clone())
    return (x, traj) if record else x

@torch.no_grad()
def ddim_sample(n, steps, seed=0):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    x = torch.randn(n, 2, generator=g)
    ts = np.linspace(T - 1, 0, steps).round().astype(int)
    for k, t in enumerate(ts):
        eps = net(x, torch.full((n,), int(t)))
        x0_hat = (x - (1 - abar_t[t]).sqrt() * eps) / abar_t[t].sqrt()
        if k + 1 < len(ts):
            a_next = abar_t[ts[k + 1]]
            x = a_next.sqrt() * x0_hat + (1 - a_next).sqrt() * eps
        else:
            x = x0_hat
    return x

def sliced_wasserstein(a, b, n_proj=200, seed=0):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    dirs = g.normal(size=(n_proj, 2)); dirs /= np.linalg.norm(dirs, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    pa, pb = np.sort(a.numpy() @ dirs.T, axis=0), np.sort(b.numpy() @ dirs.T, axis=0)
    return np.abs(pa - pb).mean()

ref = sample_data(2000, seed=123)
samples = {"DDPM, 100 steps": ddpm_sample(2000)}
for k in (20, 10, 5, 2):
    samples[f"DDIM, {k} steps"] = ddim_sample(2000, k)
noise = torch.randn(2000, 2)
print(f"{'sampler':20s} {'sliced Wasserstein distance to the data':>40s}")
print(f"{'pure noise':20s} {sliced_wasserstein(noise, ref):40.3f}")
print(f"{'fresh data (floor)':20s} {sliced_wasserstein(sample_data(2000, seed=7), ref):40.3f}")
for name, s_ in samples.items():
    print(f"{name:20s} {sliced_wasserstein(s_, ref):40.3f}")

sampler               sliced Wasserstein distance to the data
pure noise                                              0.430
fresh data (floor)                                      0.016
DDPM, 100 steps                                         0.061
DDIM, 20 steps                                          0.076
DDIM, 10 steps                                          0.101
DDIM, 5 steps                                           0.202
DDIM, 2 steps                                           0.553



x0 = sample_data(1500, seed=5)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(12, 4.8))
for ax, t in zip(axes[0], [0, 10, 30, 60, 99]):
    ab = abar[t - 1] if t > 0 else 1.0
    xt = math.sqrt(ab) * x0 + math.sqrt(1 - ab) * torch.randn_like(x0)
    ax.scatter(*xt.numpy().T, s=3, alpha=0.5, color=PALETTE["data"]); ax.set_title(f"x_t, t = {t}", fontsize=9)
for ax, (name, pts) in zip(axes[1], [("data", ref), ("DDPM 100", samples["DDPM, 100 steps"]),
                                      ("DDIM 20", samples["DDIM, 20 steps"]), ("DDIM 10", samples["DDIM, 10 steps"]),
                                      ("DDIM 2", samples["DDIM, 2 steps"])]):
    ax.scatter(*pts.numpy().T, s=3, alpha=0.5, color=PALETTE["model"] if name != "data" else PALETTE["grad"])
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=9)
for ax in axes.ravel():
    ax.set_xlim(-3.5, 3.5); ax.set_ylim(-3.5, 3.5); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 41.4: Top: the forward process on the two-moons data at steps 0, 10, 30, 60, and 99. The shape dissolves into a Gaussian blob. Bottom: samples from the trained model. Left to right: real data, DDPM with 100 steps, DDIM with 10 steps, DDIM with 2 steps. DDPM (100 steps) and DDIM with 20 or 10 steps reproduce the two moons with similar quality (sliced Wasserstein distance about 0.10, against 0.43 for pure noise and 0.016 for fresh data). Two steps give only a rough approximation (0.36).







41.6.2 The learned vector field
For each step, the network’s output points from a noisy point towards higher density. We draw the field \(-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x},t)\) at a medium and a low noise level.

gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3, 3, 18), np.linspace(-3, 3, 18))
pts = torch.tensor(np.c_[gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()], dtype=torch.float32)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.2))
for ax, t in zip(axes, [80, 10]):
    with torch.no_grad():
        v = -net(pts, torch.full((len(pts),), t)).numpy()
    ax.scatter(*ref.numpy().T, s=2, color="#D1D5DB")
    ax.quiver(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], v[:, 0], v[:, 1], color=PALETTE["model"], angles="xy")
    ax.set_title(f"t = {t}"); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 41.5: The learned denoising direction −ε_θ(x, t) on a grid, at a high noise level (t = 80) and a low one (t = 10), with the data in grey. At high noise, the arrows point towards the centre of mass of the data. At low noise, they point to the nearest crescent: the field follows the shape in detail.

title: 41  Diffusion Models
text:
41.8 Failure modes
Residual signal at the last step. If \(\bar\alpha_T\) is not near zero, \(\mathbf{x}_T\) is not pure noise, but sampling starts from pure noise. The mismatch shows up as washed-out or biased samples. Check \(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_T}\) (it was \(0.05\) here).
Slow sampling. DDPM needs one network evaluation per step, typically hundreds to a thousand. DDIM and higher-order solvers cut this to 10–50 (here, 10 steps were as good as 100 DDPM steps). Very few steps (2 here) degrade quality badly.
Exposure bias. Training sees true noisy inputs. Sampling feeds the model its own outputs. Errors can compound.
Schedule. The noise schedule decides how training effort is spread over noise levels. A linear schedule can spend many steps at nearly pure noise. Cosine schedules and loss re-weighting help.
Prediction target. Predicting \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) is unstable at very low and very high noise. Alternatives are \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_0\)-prediction and “velocity” prediction.
Mode coverage versus fidelity. A model that matches the density well is not necessarily the one that looks best. Guidance (Chapter 42) trades diversity for fidelity.
Compute. Training and sampling cost grow with image resolution. This is the reason for latent diffusion (Chapter 42).

title: 41  Diffusion Models
text:
41.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now generate sharp samples by many small steps. The ingredients are all familiar: Gaussian algebra gives the forward process in closed form, Bayes’ rule gives the reverse step, the loss is a squared-error regression, and a score is a gradient of a log-density. Sampling can be accelerated by deterministic samplers.
The cost is the number of network evaluations, and the size of the images. Chapter 42 makes diffusion cheap by running it in a compressed latent space (the VAE of Chapter 40) and makes it controllable with text through guidance.

title: 41  Diffusion Models
text:
Chapter summary

Forward: \(\mathbf{x}_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mathbf{x}_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\).
Reverse posterior given \(\mathbf{x}_0\) is Gaussian with mean \(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_t\) and variance \(\tilde\beta_t\).
Training: predict \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) with a squared-error loss on random \((\mathbf{x}_0,t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\).
\(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta\approx-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla\ln q(\mathbf{x}_t)\): the score.
DDPM samples with fresh noise at each step. DDIM is deterministic and uses fewer steps.

title: 42  Latent Diffusion and Diffusion Transformers
text:
42.3 Why latents: the arithmetic
An autoencoder (Chapter 40) compresses an image to a small tensor. A typical design maps \(512\times512\times3\) to \(64\times64\times4\): a factor of 8 per side, with 4 latent channels.

def n_values(h, w, c): return h * w * c
pixel = n_values(512, 512, 3); latent = n_values(64, 64, 4)
print(f"pixel space : {pixel:,} values;  latent space: {latent:,} values;  ratio {pixel / latent:.0f}x")

patch = 2
tok_pixel = (512 // patch) ** 2; tok_latent = (64 // patch) ** 2
print(f"tokens for a Transformer denoiser with {patch}×{patch} patches: pixels {tok_pixel:,}, latents {tok_latent:,}")
print(f"attention score entries per layer: pixels {tok_pixel ** 2:,}, latents {tok_latent ** 2:,} "
      f"(ratio {tok_pixel ** 2 / tok_latent ** 2:,.0f}x)")

pixel space : 786,432 values;  latent space: 16,384 values;  ratio 48x
tokens for a Transformer denoiser with 2×2 patches: pixels 65,536, latents 1,024
attention score entries per layer: pixels 4,294,967,296, latents 1,048,576 (ratio 4,096x)


The attention cost grows with the square of the number of tokens (Chapter 30), so the latent space is thousands of times cheaper in that part, and tens of times cheaper elsewhere. The autoencoder is trained once, separately, and then frozen. Diffusion is trained on its latents.

42.3.1 A digit-scale demonstration
We repeat the idea at small scale. A VAE with an 8-dimensional latent space (Chapter 40) compresses the \(8\times8=64\)-value digits. We train the same class-conditional denoiser network twice: once on the 64 pixels, once on the 8 latent values (standardised).

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

D = load_digits(); X, y = D.data / 16.0, D.target
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y)
Xt, yt = torch.tensor(Xtr, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(ytr)
judge = LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000).fit(Xtr, ytr)                 # independent classifier as a judge
print(f"judge classifier accuracy on real test digits: {judge.score(Xte, yte):.3f}")

class VAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, k=8, h=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, h), nn.ReLU())
        self.mu, self.lv = nn.Linear(h, k), nn.Linear(h, k)
        self.dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(k, h), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h, 64), nn.Sigmoid())
    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.enc(x); mu, lv = self.mu(h), self.lv(h)
        return self.dec(mu + torch.exp(0.5 * lv) * torch.randn_like(mu)), mu, lv

torch.manual_seed(0)
vae = VAE(); opt = torch.optim.Adam(vae.parameters(), lr=2e-3)
for _ in range(3000):
    i = torch.randint(0, len(Xt), (128,)); xh, mu, lv = vae(Xt[i])
    loss = ((Xt[i] - xh) ** 2).sum(1).div(2 * 0.25 ** 2).mean() + 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + lv.exp() - 1 - lv).sum(1).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
with torch.no_grad():
    Z = vae.mu(vae.enc(Xt)); z_mean, z_std = Z.mean(0), Z.std(0)
    recon_err = F.mse_loss(vae.dec(Z), Xt).item()
Zs = (Z - z_mean) / z_std
print(f"autoencoder: 64 -> 8 values, reconstruction MSE {recon_err:.4f} per pixel")

judge classifier accuracy on real test digits: 0.969
autoencoder: 64 -> 8 values, reconstruction MSE 0.0115 per pixel



T = 100
betas = torch.linspace(1e-3, 0.12, T); alphas = 1 - betas; abar = torch.cumprod(alphas, 0)

class CondNet(nn.Module):
    """Denoiser for data of dimension k, conditioned on a class (label 10 = 'no condition')."""
    def __init__(self, k, h=256, temb=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.temb = temb; self.cls = nn.Embedding(11, 16)
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(k + temb + 16, h), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(h, h), nn.SiLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(h, h), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(h, k))
    def forward(self, x, t, c):
        f = torch.exp(-math.log(1000) * torch.arange(self.temb // 2) / (self.temb // 2))
        a = t[:, None].float() * f[None]
        return self.net(torch.cat([x, a.sin(), a.cos(), self.cls(c)], dim=1))

def train_denoiser(data, k, steps=15000, p_uncond=0.15, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    net = CondNet(k); opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=2e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        i = torch.randint(0, len(data), (256,)); x0 = data[i]; c = yt[i].clone()
        c[torch.rand(256) < p_uncond] = 10                       # condition dropout (for guidance)
        t = torch.randint(0, T, (256,)); eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
        xt = abar[t].sqrt()[:, None] * x0 + (1 - abar[t]).sqrt()[:, None] * eps
        loss = F.mse_loss(net(xt, t, c), eps)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return net

@torch.no_grad()
def ddim(net, n, k, cls, w=1.0, steps=25, seed=0):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    x = torch.randn(n, k, generator=g); ts = np.linspace(T - 1, 0, steps).round().astype(int)
    c, u = torch.full((n,), cls), torch.full((n,), 10)
    for j, t in enumerate(ts):
        tt = torch.full((n,), int(t))
        e_c, e_u = net(x, tt, c), net(x, tt, u)
        e = e_u + w * (e_c - e_u)                                # classifier-free guidance
        x0 = (x - (1 - abar[t]).sqrt() * e) / abar[t].sqrt()
        if j + 1 < len(ts):
            an = abar[ts[j + 1]]; x = an.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - an).sqrt() * e
        else:
            x = x0
    return x

t0 = time.time()
net_lat = train_denoiser(Zs, 8)
net_pix = train_denoiser(Xt * 2 - 1, 64)                         # pixels scaled to [-1, 1]
print(f"trained both denoisers in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s (same architecture, 15,000 steps)")

@torch.no_grad()
def to_pixels_lat(z):
    return vae.dec(z * z_std + z_mean)
def to_pixels_pix(x):  return (x + 1) / 2

def evaluate(net, k, decode, w=1.5, n=100):
    acc, out_range, dist = [], [], []
    for cls in range(10):
        im = decode(ddim(net, n, k, cls, w, seed=cls)).numpy()
        out_range.append(np.mean((im < -0.05) | (im > 1.05)))
        acc.append((judge.predict(np.clip(im, 0, 1)) == cls).mean())
        d = np.linalg.norm(np.clip(im, 0, 1)[:, None] - Xtr[None, :1000], axis=-1).min(1)
        dist.append(d.mean())
    return np.mean(acc), np.mean(out_range), np.mean(dist)

print(f"{'space':10s} {'judge accuracy':>15s} {'pixels out of [0,1]':>20s} {'dist. to nearest train image':>30s}")
for name, net, k, dec in [("latent", net_lat, 8, to_pixels_lat), ("pixel", net_pix, 64, to_pixels_pix)]:
    a, o, d = evaluate(net, k, dec)
    print(f"{name:10s} {a:15.3f} {o:20.3f} {d:30.2f}")

trained both denoisers in 33 s (same architecture, 15,000 steps)
space       judge accuracy  pixels out of [0,1]   dist. to nearest train image
latent               0.994                0.000                           0.84
pixel                0.975                0.182                           1.25


Read the table. With the same network and the same training, the latent model produces digits the judge recognises almost always (0.994 against 0.975), its outputs stay inside the valid pixel range (no values outside \([-0.05,1.05]\), against 18% for pixel-space diffusion), and its samples are closer to real digits (mean distance to the nearest training image 0.84 against 1.25). The pixel-space model has to learn, from scratch and with a small network, which of the 64 numbers go together. The decoder already knows this. The small scale makes the difference modest in absolute terms, but it is the same effect that makes latent diffusion practical for large images.

def grid(net, k, decode, per=8):
    rows = []
    for cls in range(10):
        im = decode(ddim(net, per, k, cls, 1.5, seed=100 + cls)).clamp(0, 1).view(per, 8, 8).numpy()
        rows.append(np.concatenate(list(im), axis=1))
    return np.concatenate(rows, axis=0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5.2))
for ax, (title, net, k, dec) in zip(axes, [("latent diffusion (8 values)", net_lat, 8, to_pixels_lat),
                                           ("pixel diffusion (64 values)", net_pix, 64, to_pixels_pix)]):
    ax.imshow(grid(net, k, dec), cmap="gray_r"); ax.set_title(title); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 42.3: Class-conditional samples (guidance w = 1.5, 25 DDIM steps). Each row is one class, 0 to 9. Left: denoising in the 8-dimensional latent space, then decoding. Right: denoising directly in 64-dimensional pixel space with the same architecture.

title: 42  Latent Diffusion and Diffusion Transformers
text:
42.4 Conditioning and classifier-free guidance
We want samples from \(p(\mathbf{x}\mid c)\). By Bayes’ rule (Chapter 22),
\[
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\ln p(\mathbf{x}\mid c)=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\ln p(\mathbf{x})+\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\ln p(c\mid\mathbf{x}).
\tag{42.1}\]
The first term is the unconditional score. The second says: move in the direction that makes the condition more likely. We can amplify that second term with a weight \(w\):
\[
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\ln p(\mathbf{x})+w\,\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\ln p(c\mid\mathbf{x})
=(1-w)\,\nabla\ln p(\mathbf{x})+w\,\nabla\ln p(\mathbf{x}\mid c).
\tag{42.2}\]
Since the noise prediction is proportional to the (negative) score (Chapter 41), the same combination applies to \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\):
\[
\tilde{\boldsymbol\epsilon}=\boldsymbol\epsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t,\varnothing)+w\bigl(\boldsymbol\epsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t,c)-\boldsymbol\epsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t,\varnothing)\bigr).
\tag{42.3}\]
This is classifier-free guidance: one network is trained with the condition randomly replaced by a null token (here, 15% of the time), so that it can produce both \(\boldsymbol\epsilon_c\) and \(\boldsymbol\epsilon_u\). At \(w=0\) the sample ignores the condition. At \(w=1\) it is the plain conditional model. For \(w>1\) it is pushed further along the direction that distinguishes the condition.

ws = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 8.0]
accs, divs = [], []
for w in ws:
    a, d = [], []
    for cls in range(10):
        im = to_pixels_lat(ddim(net_lat, 100, 8, cls, w, seed=cls)).numpy()
        a.append((judge.predict(im) == cls).mean())
        dd = np.linalg.norm(im[:, None] - im[None], axis=-1); d.append(dd.sum() / (100 * 99))
    accs.append(np.mean(a)); divs.append(np.mean(d))
real_div = np.mean([np.linalg.norm(Xtr[ytr == c][:100][:, None] - Xtr[ytr == c][:100][None], axis=-1).sum() / (100 * 99)
                    for c in range(10)])
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))
ax1.plot(ws, accs, "o-", color=PALETTE["grad"]); ax1.set_xlabel("guidance weight w"); ax1.set_ylabel("judge accuracy")
ax2.plot(ws, divs, "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"]); ax2.axhline(real_div, ls="--", color="black")
ax2.set_xlabel("guidance weight w"); ax2.set_ylabel("within-class diversity")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"{'w':>5s} {'accuracy':>9s} {'diversity':>10s}")
for w, a, d in zip(ws, accs, divs):
    print(f"{w:5.1f} {a:9.3f} {d:10.3f}")
print(f"real data within-class diversity: {real_div:.3f}")







Figure 42.4: Effect of the guidance weight w on class-conditional latent diffusion. Left: the fraction of generated digits that the independent judge assigns to the requested class. At w = 0 (condition ignored) it is at chance. It rises to nearly 1 by w = 2. Right: the diversity of samples within a class (mean pairwise pixel distance). It falls steadily with w: guidance buys fidelity with variety. The dashed line is the diversity of real digits of one class.

  0.5     0.699      1.747
  1.0     0.968      1.553

42  Latent Diffusion and Diffusion Transformers

title: 42  Latent Diffusion and Diffusion Transformers
text:
42.6 Diffusion Transformers
The denoiser of Chapter 41 was an MLP. For images, early latent diffusion models used a U-Net: a convolutional encoder–decoder with skip connections and attention (Chapter 35). A Diffusion Transformer (DiT) replaces it with the Transformer of Chapter 31, applied to the sequence of patch tokens of the latent (Chapter 36).
The condition (time step and class or pooled text) is injected by adaptive layer norm with zero initialisation (adaLN-Zero). A small network maps the condition \(c\) to six vectors: a scale \(\boldsymbol\gamma\), shift \(\boldsymbol\beta\), and gate \(\boldsymbol\alpha\) for each of the attention and MLP sub-layers:
\[
\mathbf{h}\leftarrow\mathbf{h}+\boldsymbol\alpha_1(c)\odot\text{Attn}\bigl(\boldsymbol\gamma_1(c)\odot\text{LN}(\mathbf{h})+\boldsymbol\beta_1(c)\bigr),
\] \[
\mathbf{h}\leftarrow\mathbf{h}+\boldsymbol\alpha_2(c)\odot\text{MLP}\bigl(\boldsymbol\gamma_2(c)\odot\text{LN}(\mathbf{h})+\boldsymbol\beta_2(c)\bigr).
\tag{42.4}\]
The gates \(\boldsymbol\alpha\) are initialised to zero. At the start of training every block is the identity map (Chapter 31, residual path), which makes training of a deep stack stable.

import math
class DiTBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, heads=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.h = heads
        self.ln1, self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d, elementwise_affine=False), nn.LayerNorm(d, elementwise_affine=False)
        self.qkv, self.o = nn.Linear(d, 3 * d), nn.Linear(d, d)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * d, d))
        self.ada = nn.Linear(d, 6 * d)                             # condition -> γ1, β1, α1, γ2, β2, α2
        nn.init.zeros_(self.ada.weight); nn.init.zeros_(self.ada.bias)      # adaLN-Zero
    def forward(self, x, c):                                       # x: (B, N, d) tokens; c: (B, d)
        g1, b1, a1, g2, b2, a2 = self.ada(c)[:, None].chunk(6, dim=-1)
        B, N, d = x.shape
        h = (1 + g1) * self.ln1(x) + b1
        q, k, v = self.qkv(h).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        sp = lambda t: t.view(B, N, self.h, d // self.h).transpose(1, 2)
        att = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(sp(q), sp(k), sp(v)).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, N, d)
        x = x + a1 * self.o(att)
        h = (1 + g2) * self.ln2(x) + b2
        return x + a2 * self.mlp(h)

torch.manual_seed(0)
blk = DiTBlock(d=64)
tokens = torch.randn(2, 16, 64); cond = torch.randn(2, 64)           # 16 latent patches, one condition vector
print("output shape:", tuple(blk(tokens, cond).shape))
print("at initialisation the block is the identity map:", torch.allclose(blk(tokens, cond), tokens))
with torch.no_grad():
    blk.ada.weight.add_(0.05 * torch.randn_like(blk.ada.weight))
print("after perturbing the adaLN weights the block changes the tokens:",
      not torch.allclose(blk(tokens, cond), tokens, atol=1e-4))

The condition modulates every layer: scale, shift, and gate vary with the time step and the class or text. That gives the network a strong way to change its behaviour with the noise level, which is crucial in diffusion, where the right operation at \(t=90\) (mostly noise) differs from that at \(t=5\) (fine detail).

title: 42  Latent Diffusion and Diffusion Transformers
text:
42.8 Failure modes
Autoencoder limits. The decoder bounds quality: fine detail lost in compression cannot be restored by diffusion. Text and small faces suffer first.
Latent scale. The latent should be standardised (we did) or multiplied by a fixed factor, so that its variance matches the noise schedule’s assumptions. A mismatch changes the effective signal-to-noise ratio.
Over-guidance. Large \(w\) gives over-saturated, high-contrast, repetitive images and mode collapse. In our digits, the accuracy saturates while diversity continues to fall.
Missing condition dropout. Without null-condition training, classifier-free guidance has no \(\boldsymbol\epsilon_u\).
Prompt encoding. The image model sees only what the text encoder encodes: bag-of-words behaviour (Chapter 39) shows up as errors in counting and relations.
Sampling cost. Tens of denoiser evaluations per image, each on thousands of tokens. Distillation methods reduce the step count.

NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The generative pipeline is complete: text → condition → denoiser over a compressed latent → decoder → image. title: 43  Flow Matching
text:
43.2 Flows and ODEs
A velocity field \(\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)\) assigns to every position and time a direction and speed. Place a point at \(\mathbf{x}(0)=\mathbf{x}_0\) and let it drift:
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt}=\mathbf{v}\bigl(\mathbf{x}(t),t\bigr),\qquad t\in[0,1].
\tag{43.1}\]
The solution is a trajectory. Because \(\mathbf{v}\) is a function of position, two trajectories never cross, and each starting point has exactly one path. The map from \(\mathbf{x}(0)\) to \(\mathbf{x}(1)\) is the flow. If the starting points are noise, the end points are samples; the field is chosen so that they follow the data distribution.

43.2.1 Numerical integration
An ODE is solved by small steps. Euler’s method follows the tangent for a step \(\Delta=1/N\):
\[
\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta}=\mathbf{x}_t+\Delta\,\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}_t,t).
\tag{43.2}\]
Heun’s method (a second-order method) takes the tangent, looks at the tangent at the predicted end point, and uses the average:
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{x}_t+\Delta\,\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}_t,t),\qquad
\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta}=\mathbf{x}_t+\frac\Delta2\Bigl[\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}_t,t)+\mathbf{v}(\tilde{\mathbf{x}},t+\Delta)\Bigr].
\tag{43.3}\]
Euler’s error per unit time falls like \(\Delta\) (first order). Heun’s falls like \(\Delta^2\) at the cost of two field evaluations per step. We check on \(\dot{x}=-x\), whose exact solution from \(x(0)=1\) is \(x(t)=e^{-t}\).

def integrate(method, N):
    x, dt, f = 1.0, 1.0 / N, lambda x, t: -x
    for k in range(N):
        t = k * dt
        if method == "euler":
            x = x + dt * f(x, t)
        else:
            xp = x + dt * f(x, t)
            x = x + dt / 2 * (f(x, t) + f(xp, t + dt))
    return x
Ns = np.array([2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128])
err_e = [abs(integrate("euler", n) - math.exp(-1)) for n in Ns]
err_h = [abs(integrate("heun", n) - math.exp(-1)) for n in Ns]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 3.5))
ax.loglog(1 / Ns, err_e, "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"], label="Euler")
ax.loglog(1 / Ns, err_h, "o-", color=PALETTE["grad"], label="Heun")
ax.set_xlabel("step size Δ"); ax.set_ylabel("error at t = 1"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
slope = lambda e: np.polyfit(np.log(1 / Ns), np.log(e), 1)[0]
print(f"fitted orders: Euler {slope(err_e):.2f}, Heun {slope(err_h):.2f}")







Figure 43.2: Error at t = 1 of Euler and Heun integration of dx/dt = −x, against the step size. Euler’s error falls with slope 1 on a log-log plot (first order). Heun’s falls with slope 2 (second order). Halving the step cuts the Euler error by 2 and the Heun error by 4.

title: 43  Flow Matching
text:
43.3 Learning the field: flow matching
We want \(\mathbf{v}_\theta\) such that integrating it from \(\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\) gives \(\mathbf{x}_{1}\sim p_{\text{data}}\). There are many such fields. Choose the simplest path: for a noise point \(\mathbf{x}_0\) and a data point \(\mathbf{x}_1\), move on the straight line
\[
\mathbf{x}_t=(1-t)\,\mathbf{x}_0+t\,\mathbf{x}_1,\qquad
\frac{d\mathbf{x}_t}{dt}=\mathbf{x}_1-\mathbf{x}_0.
\tag{43.4}\]
The velocity along this particular path is the constant \(\mathbf{x}_1-\mathbf{x}_0\). The conditional flow matching loss regresses the network onto it:
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\ \mathbf{x}_0,\ \mathbf{x}_1}\Bigl[\bigl\lVert\mathbf{v}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,t)-(\mathbf{x}_1-\mathbf{x}_0)\bigr\rVert^{2}\Bigr].
\tag{43.5}\]

43.3.1 Why this works
A given point \(\mathbf{x}\) at time \(t\) can be reached from many \((\mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{x}_1)\) pairs, with different velocities \(\mathbf{x}_1-\mathbf{x}_0\). A network sees only \((\mathbf{x},t)\). A squared-error regression has the conditional mean as its minimiser (Chapter 14):
\[
\mathbf{v}^*(\mathbf{x},t)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{x}_1-\mathbf{x}_0\ \big|\ \mathbf{x}_t=\mathbf{x}\bigr].
\tag{43.6}\]
This is exactly the marginal velocity field: the field whose flow carries the distribution of \(\mathbf{x}_t\) (noise at \(t=0\), data at \(t=1\)) correctly in time (by the continuity equation, whose derivation we omit). So regressing on the easy per-pair target recovers the field that transports \(p_0\) to \(p_1\). The loss Equation 43.5 and the loss of the marginal field differ only by a constant, and have the same gradient with respect to \(\theta\).


43.3.2 An exact check in one dimension
Take data concentrated at two points, \(x_{1}\in\{-2,+2\}\) with equal probability, and \(x_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). Given \(x_t=x\), we have \(x_0=(x-tx_1)/(1-t)\), so the velocity is \((x_1-x)/(1-t)\). The only unknown is \(\mathbb{E}[x_{1}\mid x_t=x]\), which Bayes gives in closed form: the likelihood of \(x\) given \(x_1\) is \(\mathcal{N}(x;\,t\,x_1,(1-t)^2)\). Hence
\[
v^*(x,t)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[x_{1}\mid x]-x}{1-t},\qquad
\mathbb{E}[x_{1}\mid x]=2\tanh\!\Bigl(\frac{2tx}{(1-t)^2}\Bigr).
\tag{43.7}\]
We train a small network by Equation 43.5 and compare it with Equation 43.7.

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0)

class VNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in=1, h=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d_in + 1, h), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(h, h), nn.SiLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(h, h), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(h, d_in))
    def forward(self, x, t):
        return self.net(torch.cat([x, t[:, None]], dim=1))

net1 = VNet(1); opt = torch.optim.Adam(net1.parameters(), lr=2e-3)
for _ in range(6000):
    x1 = (torch.randint(0, 2, (512, 1)) * 4 - 2).float()               # data: ±2
    x0 = torch.randn(512, 1); t = torch.rand(512)
    xt = (1 - t[:, None]) * x0 + t[:, None] * x1
    loss = F.mse_loss(net1(xt, t), x1 - x0)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

for t_ in (0.2, 0.5, 0.8):
    x1 = (torch.randint(0, 2, (20000, 1)) * 4 - 2).float()
    xt = (1 - t_) * torch.randn(20000, 1) + t_ * x1               # points the network sees in training
    t = torch.full((20000,), t_)
    with torch.no_grad():
        learned = net1(xt, t)[:, 0]
    analytic = (2 * torch.tanh(2 * t_ * xt[:, 0] / (1 - t_) ** 2) - xt[:, 0]) / (1 - t_)
    rms = ((learned - analytic) ** 2).mean().sqrt()
    print(f"t = {t_}: RMS error {rms:.3f} on training-distribution points   (field RMS {analytic.pow(2).mean().sqrt():.2f})")

t = 0.2: RMS error 0.123 on training-distribution points   (field RMS 0.16)
t = 0.5: RMS error 0.073 on training-distribution points   (field RMS 1.97)
t = 0.8: RMS error 0.068 on training-distribution points   (field RMS 2.23)



xg = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 200)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.2), sharey=True)
for ax, t_ in zip(axes, [0.2, 0.5, 0.8]):
    t = torch.full((200,), t_)
    with torch.no_grad():
        ax.plot(xg, net1(xg[:, None], t)[:, 0], color=PALETTE["model"], lw=2, label="learned")
    ax.plot(xg, (2 * torch.tanh(2 * t_ * xg / (1 - t_) ** 2) - xg) / (1 - t_), "--", color="black", label="exact")
    ax.axhline(0, color="#9CA3AF", lw=0.6); ax.set_title(f"t = {t_}"); ax.set_xlabel("x")
axes[0].set_ylabel("v(x, t)"); axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 43.3: The velocity field for two-point data, at three times. Dashed: the exact marginal field (Bayes). Solid: the field learned by the regression. At t = 0.2 the field points towards the middle (the data mean is 0): every point is far from either mode. At t = 0.8 it splits: points on the right move to +2, points on the left to −2. At t = 0.5 and 0.8 the curves agree where the data are (RMS error 0.07 against a field RMS of about 2). At t = 0.2 the true field is weak (RMS 0.16) and the network error (0.12) is almost as large, so the shape there is only roughly right. They differ in the tails, where few training points fall, and at t = 0.8 near the sharp switch at x = 0.

title: 43  Flow Matching
text:
43.4 Flow matching on a 2D distribution
We train the same kind of model on the two-moons data used in Chapter 41, with the same network size. Sampling now integrates the ODE from noise.

from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
def sample_data(n, seed=None):
    X, _ = make_moons(n, noise=0.06, random_state=seed)
    return torch.tensor((X - np.array([0.5, 0.25])) * 2.0, dtype=torch.float32)

torch.manual_seed(0)
net = VNet(2, h=128); opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=2e-3)
t0 = time.time(); hist = []
for step in range(20000):
    x1 = sample_data(256); x0 = torch.randn_like(x1); t = torch.rand(256)
    xt = (1 - t[:, None]) * x0 + t[:, None] * x1
    loss = F.mse_loss(net(xt, t), x1 - x0)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); hist.append(loss.item())
print(f"trained in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; loss {np.mean(hist[:50]):.3f} -> {np.mean(hist[-500:]):.3f}")

@torch.no_grad()
def integrate_net(n, steps, method="euler", seed=0, return_path=False):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    x = torch.randn(n, 2, generator=g); dt = 1.0 / steps; path = [x.clone()]; nfe = 0
    for k in range(steps):
        t = torch.full((n,), k * dt)
        v = net(x, t); nfe += 1
        if method == "euler":
            x = x + dt * v
        else:
            xp = x + dt * v
            v2 = net(xp, t + dt); nfe += 1
            x = x + dt / 2 * (v + v2)
        path.append(x.clone())
    return (x, path, nfe) if return_path else (x, nfe)

def sliced_wasserstein(a, b, n_proj=200, seed=0):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    dirs = g.normal(size=(n_proj, 2)); dirs /= np.linalg.norm(dirs, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return np.abs(np.sort(a.numpy() @ dirs.T, axis=0) - np.sort(b.numpy() @ dirs.T, axis=0)).mean()

ref = sample_data(2000, seed=123)
print(f"{'method':14s} {'steps':>6s} {'net evaluations':>16s} {'sliced Wasserstein':>19s}")
print(f"{'pure noise':14s} {'-':>6s} {'-':>16s} {sliced_wasserstein(torch.randn(2000, 2), ref):19.3f}")
print(f"{'fresh data':14s} {'-':>6s} {'-':>16s} {sliced_wasserstein(sample_data(2000, seed=7), ref):19.3f}")
results = {}
for method in ("euler", "heun"):

        x, nfe = integrate_net(2000, steps, method)
        results[(method, steps)] = (nfe, sliced_wasserstein(x, ref))
        print(f"{method:14s} {steps:6d} {nfe:16d} {results[(method, steps)][1]:19.3f}")

title: 43  Flow Matching
text:
43.5 Relation to diffusion
Flow matching with the straight path is a special case of a general recipe: choose any path \(\mathbf{x}_t=a_{t}\mathbf{x}_1+b_{t}\mathbf{x}_0\), and regress on its velocity \(\dot a_{t}\mathbf{x}_1+\dot b_{t}\mathbf{x}_0\). A diffusion model uses a different path (\(a_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\), \(b_t=\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\), with \(\mathbf{x}_0\) as noise) and a different parametrisation. The quantities are interchangeable. For the straight path, with \(\mathbf{x}_0=\boldsymbol\epsilon\):
\[
\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{x}_1-\boldsymbol\epsilon,\qquad
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1=\mathbf{x}_t+(1-t)\,\mathbf{v},\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}=\mathbf{x}_t-t\,\mathbf{v}.
\tag{43.8}\]

x1 = torch.randn(5, 2); eps = torch.randn(5, 2); t = 0.37
xt = (1 - t) * eps + t * x1
v = x1 - eps
print("x1 recovered from v:", torch.allclose(xt + (1 - t) * v, x1, atol=1e-6))
print("ε  recovered from v:", torch.allclose(xt - t * v, eps, atol=1e-6))

x1 recovered from v: True
ε  recovered from v: True


The DDIM sampler of Chapter 41 is an Euler discretisation of an ODE of this family (the “probability-flow ODE” of the diffusion process). The difference between the methods is the path and the training weights, not a different kind of model.
An important contrast: DDPM sampling is a stochastic differential equation (noise is injected at each step). The flow is deterministic. Given the starting noise, the output is fixed. That allows exact likelihoods (by integrating the divergence of the field) and clean interpolation between samples.

title: 43  Flow Matching
text:
43.6 Production
An adaptive solver can integrate the learned field accurately. We use SciPy’s RK45 as a reference, and check that our 100-step Euler is close.

from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
n = 200
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(11)
x_init = torch.randn(n, 2, generator=g)

def rhs(t, y):
    x = torch.tensor(y.reshape(n, 2), dtype=torch.float32)
    with torch.no_grad():
        return net(x, torch.full((n,), float(t))).numpy().ravel()

sol = solve_ivp(rhs, (0.0, 1.0), x_init.numpy().ravel().astype(np.float64), method="RK45", rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-6)
x_ref = sol.y[:, -1].reshape(n, 2)
print(f"RK45 used {sol.nfev} function evaluations (each on the whole batch)")
for steps in (4, 16, 100):
    x = x_init.clone(); dt = 1.0 / steps
    with torch.no_grad():
        for k in range(steps):
            x = x + dt * net(x, torch.full((n,), k * dt))
    print(f"Euler, {steps:3d} steps: mean distance to the RK45 solution {np.linalg.norm(x.numpy() - x_ref, axis=1).mean():.4f}")

title: 43  Flow Matching
text:
43.8 Failure modes
Too few steps. With one Euler step, every noise point moves along the initial field, which points towards the mean of the data. The result is a blob at the centre. The error of Euler is first order (Figure 43.2). Heun and other higher-order solvers help.
Curved flows. The marginal field is generally not straight, even though each conditional path is. Where the data has several modes, the field must curve to split the noise between them. Re-training on the model’s own pairs (“reflow”) straightens the paths and allows fewer steps.
Time sampling. Sampling \(t\) uniformly in training may spend effort on times where the task is easy. Other time distributions or loss weights help.
Data scale. The straight path assumes data and noise have comparable scales. Standardise the data.
Stiffness. Where the field changes rapidly (near the end for sharp modes), a fixed step size is inaccurate. Adaptive solvers or non-uniform time grids are used.
Conditioning. As in Chapter 42, guidance is applied by combining conditional and unconditional velocities.

43.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The generative systems now share a single view. Generation is transport: a velocity field carries simple noise to complex data. Training is a regression on a velocity (a squared error, Chapter 14). Sampling is numerical integration of an ODE (Euler, Heun). Diffusion models are the same idea with a particular path and parametrisation.
All the pieces of the book’s mathematics have now appeared in at least one modern system. The last chapter puts them together.

title: 43  Flow Matching
text:
Chapter summary

A flow integrates \(d\mathbf{x}/dt=\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)\). Trajectories do not cross.
Euler has first-order error and Heun second-order.
Flow matching: \(\mathbf{x}_t=(1-t)\mathbf{x}_0+t\mathbf{x}_1\), target \(\mathbf{x}_1-\mathbf{x}_0\), squared-error loss.
The regression minimiser is the marginal velocity \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_1-\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{x}_t]\).
Velocity, \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_1\), and \(\hat{\boldsymbol\epsilon}\) are interchangeable parametrisations.
Fewer steps need straighter paths and better solvers.

Exercises

Compute. For \(\mathbf{x}_0=(1,0)\), \(\mathbf{x}_1=(3,2)\), give \(\mathbf{x}_{0.25}\) and the target velocity.

title: 44  One AI System, All the Mathematics
text:
44.2 The smallest complete system
A classifier for two-dimensional points. The chain is
\[
\mathbf{x}\ \xrightarrow{\ \mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}_1\ }\ \mathbf{z}\ \xrightarrow{\ \sigma\ }\ \mathbf{h}\ \xrightarrow{\ \mathbf{w}_2^{\intercal}\mathbf{h}+b_2\ }\ s\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{sigmoid}\ }\ \hat y\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{cross-entropy}\ }\ L\ \xrightarrow{\ \nabla\ }\ \nabla_\theta L\ \xrightarrow{\ -\eta\nabla\ }\ \theta'.
\tag{44.1}\]
Each arrow is a chapter: matrix-vector product (Chapter 5), a nonlinearity (Chapters 10 and 11), a probability (Chapter 24), a loss (Chapters 14 and 25), the chain rule (Chapters 16 and 18), and the update (Chapter 19). We write the backward pass by hand and check it against finite differences.

from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X, y = make_moons(400, noise=0.15, random_state=0)
H = 16
params = {"W1": rng.normal(0, 0.7, (H, 2)), "b1": np.zeros(H),
          "w2": rng.normal(0, 0.7, H), "b2": np.array(0.0)}

def forward(p, X):
    z = X @ p["W1"].T + p["b1"]          # (n, H)   affine
    h = np.tanh(z)                       # (n, H)   nonlinearity
    s = h @ p["w2"] + p["b2"]            # (n,)     score
    yhat = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-s))          # (n,)     probability
    return z, h, s, yhat

def loss_fn(p, X, y):
    yhat = forward(p, X)[3]
    return -np.mean(y * np.log(yhat + 1e-12) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - yhat + 1e-12))

def backward(p, X, y):
    z, h, s, yhat = forward(p, X); n = len(y)
    ds = (yhat - y) / n                                  # d loss / d score (sigmoid + cross-entropy)
    g = {"w2": h.T @ ds, "b2": ds.sum()}
    dh = np.outer(ds, p["w2"])                           # (n, H)
    dz = dh * (1 - h ** 2)                               # tanh'
    g["W1"] = dz.T @ X; g["b1"] = dz.sum(0)
    return g

# gradient check against central finite differences
g = backward(params, X, y); worst = 0.0
for name, arr in params.items():
    a = np.atleast_1d(arr)
    for idx in np.ndindex(a.shape):
        old = a[idx]
        a[idx] = old + 1e-5; lp = loss_fn(params, X, y)
        a[idx] = old - 1e-5; lm_ = loss_fn(params, X, y)
        a[idx] = old
        num = (lp - lm_) / 2e-5
        ana = np.atleast_1d(g[name])[idx]
        worst = max(worst, abs(num - ana) / (abs(num) + abs(ana) + 1e-12))
print(f"gradient check: worst relative error over all {sum(np.size(v) for v in params.values())} parameters = {worst:.1e}")

eta = 0.5
for step in range(2001):
    g = backward(params, X, y)
    for k in params: params[k] = params[k] - eta * g[k]
    if step in (0, 100, 500, 2000):
        acc = ((forward(params, X)[3] > 0.5) == y).mean()
        print(f"step {step:5d}  loss {loss_fn(params, X, y):.3f}  accuracy {acc:.3f}")

gradient check: worst relative error over all 65 parameters = 4.2e-09
step     0  loss 0.848  accuracy 0.285
step   100  loss 0.231  accuracy 0.905
step   500  loss 0.079  accuracy 0.973
step  2000  loss 0.039  accuracy 0.988


Every quantity in the chain is a named array with a shape. We use this habit for the rest of the chapter.
