text:
44.3 A tiny GPT, from explicit operations
The language model of Chapters 31–33, written without nn.Module for attention. Every operation is a line. The parameters are one flat dictionary of tensors.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X}_0&=\mathbf{E}[\text{ids}]+\mathbf{P}\\
\mathbf{X}_{\ell+1}&=\mathbf{X}_\ell'+\text{MLP}\bigl(\text{LN}(\mathbf{X}_\ell')\bigr),\quad
\mathbf{X}_\ell'=\mathbf{X}_\ell+\text{MHA}\bigl(\text{LN}(\mathbf{X}_\ell)\bigr)\\
\text{logits}&=\text{LN}(\mathbf{X}_L)\,\mathbf{E}^{\intercal}
\end{aligned}
\tag{44.2}\]

import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from pydoc_data import topics

raw = " ".join(topics.topics[k] for k in sorted(topics.topics)).lower()
keep = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz .,\n")
text = " ".join("".join(c if c in keep else " " for c in raw).split())[:200_000]
chars = sorted(set(text)); V = len(chars); ix = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(chars)}
data = torch.tensor([ix[c] for c in text]); n_tr = int(0.9 * len(data))
train_data, val_data = data[:n_tr], data[n_tr:]

def init_params(V, T, d, L, dtype=torch.float32, seed=0):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    rn = lambda *s: (torch.randn(*s, generator=g) * 0.02).to(dtype).requires_grad_()
    z = lambda *s: torch.zeros(*s, dtype=dtype).requires_grad_()
    o = lambda *s: torch.ones(*s, dtype=dtype).requires_grad_()
    p = {"E": rn(V, d), "P": rn(T, d), "lnf_g": o(d), "lnf_b": z(d)}
    for l in range(L):
        p.update({f"{l}.ln1_g": o(d), f"{l}.ln1_b": z(d), f"{l}.Wqkv": rn(d, 3 * d), f"{l}.bqkv": z(3 * d),
                  f"{l}.Wo": rn(d, d), f"{l}.bo": z(d), f"{l}.ln2_g": o(d), f"{l}.ln2_b": z(d),
                  f"{l}.W1": rn(d, 4 * d), f"{l}.b1": z(4 * d), f"{l}.W2": rn(4 * d, d), f"{l}.b2": z(d)})
    return p

def layer_norm(x, g, b, eps=1e-5):
    mu = x.mean(-1, keepdim=True); var = ((x - mu) ** 2).mean(-1, keepdim=True)
    return (x - mu) / torch.sqrt(var + eps) * g + b

def gpt_forward(p, ids, L, n_heads):
    B, T = ids.shape; d = p["E"].shape[1]; dh = d // n_heads
    x = p["E"][ids] + p["P"][:T]                                    # (B, T, d)
    mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool))
    for l in range(L):
        h = layer_norm(x, p[f"{l}.ln1_g"], p[f"{l}.ln1_b"])
        q, k, v = (h @ p[f"{l}.Wqkv"] + p[f"{l}.bqkv"]).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        sp = lambda t: t.reshape(B, T, n_heads, dh).transpose(1, 2)  # (B, H, T, dh)
        scores = (sp(q) @ sp(k).transpose(-1, -2)) / math.sqrt(dh)   # (B, H, T, T)
        att = torch.softmax(scores.masked_fill(~mask, float("-inf")), dim=-1)
        o = (att @ sp(v)).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, d)
        x = x + o @ p[f"{l}.Wo"] + p[f"{l}.bo"]
        h = layer_norm(x, p[f"{l}.ln2_g"], p[f"{l}.ln2_b"])
        x = x + F.gelu(h @ p[f"{l}.W1"] + p[f"{l}.b1"]) @ p[f"{l}.W2"] + p[f"{l}.b2"]
    return layer_norm(x, p["lnf_g"], p["lnf_b"]) @ p["E"].T          # (B, T, V)

def lm_loss(p, batch, L, n_heads):
    logits = gpt_forward(p, batch[:, :-1], L, n_heads)
    return F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, logits.shape[-1]), batch[:, 1:].reshape(-1))


44.3.1 Check the gradient
Autograd computes the gradient of a very long chain. We check it against central differences, in 64-bit arithmetic, on a very small instance (so that finite differences are affordable). We test three random entries of every tensor.

Vt, Tt, dt_, Lt, ht = 7, 6, 8, 2, 2
pc = init_params(Vt, Tt, dt_, Lt, dtype=torch.float64, seed=1)
for t in pc.values():                      # larger random values so no gradient is trivially zero
    t.data += 0.3 * torch.randn_like(t)
batch = torch.randint(0, Vt, (3, Tt + 1))
loss0 = lm_loss(pc, batch, Lt, ht); loss0.backward()
gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(5); worst = 0.0; checked = 0
for name, t in pc.items():
    flat = t.data.view(-1); gflat = t.grad.view(-1)
    for j in torch.randint(0, flat.numel(), (3,), generator=gen).tolist():
        old = flat[j].item(); e = 1e-6
        flat[j] = old + e; lp = lm_loss(pc, batch, Lt, ht).item()
        flat[j] = old - e; lm_v = lm_loss(pc, batch, Lt, ht).item()
        flat[j] = old
        num = (lp - lm_v) / (2 * e); ana = gflat[j].item()
        worst = max(worst, abs(num - ana) / (abs(num) + abs(ana) + 1e-12)); checked += 1
print(f"{len(pc)} tensors, {checked} entries checked; worst relative error {worst:.1e}")

28 tensors, 84 entries checked; worst relative error 5.2e-05




44.3.2 Train it

T_ctx, d, n_layers, n_heads = 64, 64, 2, 4
torch.manual_seed(0)
p = init_params(V, T_ctx, d, n_layers)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(p.values(), lr=3e-3)

def batch_from(src, B=32):
    s = torch.randint(0, len(src) - T_ctx - 1, (B,))
    return torch.stack([src[i:i + T_ctx + 1] for i in s])

t0 = time.time(); hist = []
for step in range(1500):
    loss = lm_loss(p, batch_from(train_data), n_layers, n_heads)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); hist.append(loss.item())
with torch.no_grad():
    val = np.mean([lm_loss(p, batch_from(val_data, 64), n_layers, n_heads).item() for _ in range(20)])
counts = torch.bincount(train_data, minlength=V).float(); pr = counts / counts.sum()
unigram = -(pr * torch.log(pr)).sum().item()
print(f"trained {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; train loss {hist[0]:.3f} -> {np.mean(hist[-50:]):.3f}")
print(f"validation loss {val:.3f} nats  (perplexity {math.exp(val):.2f})")
print(f"baselines: uniform ln V = {math.log(V):.3f};  unigram entropy = {unigram:.3f}")

@torch.no_grad()
def sample(prompt, n=200, temp=0.8, seed=0):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    ids = [ix[c] for c in prompt]
    for _ in range(n):
        ctx = torch.tensor([ids[-T_ctx:]])
        logits = gpt_forward(p, ctx, n_layers, n_heads)[0, -1] / temp
        ids.append(torch.multinomial(torch.softmax(logits, -1), 1, generator=g).item())
    return "".join(chars[i] for i in ids)
print(repr(sample("the function ")))

text:
44.4 Counting: parameters, FLOPs, memory
Shapes alone tell us what a model costs. We derive the counts and then check them against the code.
Parameters. With vocabulary \(V\), context \(T\), width \(d\), \(L\) layers (the formula of Chapter 31):
\[
N=Vd+Td+L\,(12d^2+13d)+2d.
\tag{44.3}\]
FLOPs of one forward pass over a sequence of \(T\) tokens, counting a multiply-add as 2 FLOPs and including only matrix products. Per layer: the QKV projection \(2T\cdot d\cdot3d\), the scores \(2T^2d\), the weighted values \(2T^2d\), the output projection \(2Td^2\), and the MLP \(2\cdot2T\cdot d\cdot4d\):
\[
F_{\text{layer}}=24\,Td^2+4\,T^2d,\qquad
F=L\,F_{\text{layer}}+2TdV.
\tag{44.4}\]
Memory. Training with Adam in 32-bit floats holds the parameters, the gradients, and two Adam moments: \(4N\) numbers, \(16N\) bytes. Activations come in addition and scale with batch size.

from torch.utils.flop_counter import FlopCounterMode
N_actual = sum(t.numel() for t in p.values())
N_formula = V * d + T_ctx * d + n_layers * (12 * d * d + 13 * d) + 2 * d
print(f"parameters: counted {N_actual:,}   formula {N_formula:,}")

T = T_ctx
F_formula = n_layers * (24 * T * d * d + 4 * T * T * d) + 2 * T * d * V
ids = torch.randint(0, V, (1, T))
with FlopCounterMode(display=False) as fc, torch.no_grad():
    gpt_forward(p, ids, n_layers, n_heads)
print(f"forward FLOPs for one sequence of {T} tokens: counted {fc.get_total_flops():,}   formula {F_formula:,}")
print(f"training step (forward + backward ≈ 3× forward), batch 32: {3 * 32 * F_formula / 1e9:.2f} GFLOP")
print(f"weights + gradients + Adam state: {16 * N_actual / 1e6:.2f} MB")

training step (forward + backward ≈ 3× forward), batch 32: 1.43 GFLOP

The same formulas, applied to larger shapes, give the figures quoted in Chapter 34. For a Llama-class model with \(d=4096\), \(L=32\), the ratio of the attention-score term to the projection term is \(4T^2d/(24Td^2)=T/(6d)\), which is small for \(T\ll6d\approx24{,}500\) and grows past one only for very long contexts.

44.7 Decompose this architecture
Here is a description of a model the book has not discussed:

Model Z. An audio clip is turned into a spectrogram (a 2-D array, frequency × time). The spectrogram is cut into non-overlapping 16×16 patches, each flattened and projected linearly to a vector. title: 45  Systems Thinking: Components, Interfaces and Contracts
text:
If every component is good, is the system good? And if the system fails, which component do we repair?



Systems thinking. We describe the whole as parts, interfaces, feedback and requirements. This chapter and the next one do that.
Performance characterisation. We measure how a component or a system behaves as its input and its parameters change, and we give the answer as a distribution with a stated confidence, not as one number. Chapters 47 to 50 do that. The approach follows the work of Robert M. Haralick and Visvanathan Ramesh in computer vision (see the references at the end of Chapter 47).

title: 45  Systems Thinking: Components, Interfaces and Contracts
text:
45.2 What a system is
A system is a set of components \(\{C_1,\dots,C_m\}\), a set of interfaces that join them, and a purpose. We write a chain of components as a composition (Chapter 8):
\[
y = (C_m\circ C_{m-1}\circ\cdots\circ C_1)(x).
\tag{45.1}\]
This is the same idea as a neural network (Chapter 11). The difference is that the components are not all differentiable layers. Some are cameras, thresholds, look-up tables, rules, queues and people. We cannot back-propagate through a human review step, so we must characterise it by measurement.
Three questions describe any component.







Question
Answer is called




What input does it accept?
Pre-condition (its input domain)


What output does it produce?
Post-condition (its output range)


How well, and under which conditions?
Performance characterisation



The third row is the subject of the next chapters. The first two rows are the contract.

title: 45  Systems Thinking: Components, Interfaces and Contracts
text:
45.3 Requirements first
A requirement is a statement that a test can decide. “The detector must be accurate” is not a requirement. “On daytime highway images with rain, at most 1 in 10,000 vehicles is missed and at most 1 in 100 frames contains a false alarm, with 95% confidence” is one.
A good requirement has four parts:

an operating condition (which inputs),
a measure (which quantity),
a level (which number), and
a confidence (how sure we must be that we met it).

Part 4 is the one most often left out. It decides how much test data we need (Chapter 49).

title: 45  Systems Thinking: Components, Interfaces and Contracts
section: 45.4 Series reliability and the correlation trap
text:
45.4 Series reliability and the correlation trap
Suppose stage \(k\) gives a correct result with probability \(p_k\). If a correct final answer needs every stage to be correct, and stage failures are independent, then
\[
P(\text{system correct})=\prod_{k=1}^{m}p_k.
\tag{45.2}\]
Three stages with \(p=(0.95,\,0.90,\,0.92)\) give \(0.95\times0.90\times0.92=0.787\). The system is worse than its worst stage. This is the first system effect: more components, less reliability, unless the interfaces repair errors.
Equation 45.2 assumes independence. Real stages are not independent. A blurred, dark or unusual input is hard for all stages. We model this with one shared latent “difficulty” per input. The inputs that are hard (30% of them) fail 2.5 times as often as average at every stage. The marginal success rate of each stage stays the same.

rng = np.random.default_rng(45)
N = 200_000
p = np.array([0.95, 0.90, 0.92])
print("product of stage accuracies      ", p.prod().round(4))

independent = (rng.random((N, 3)) < p).all(1).mean()
print("simulated, independent failures  ", independent.round(4))

hard = rng.random(N) < 0.30          # 30% of inputs are hard for every stage
k_hard = 2.5                          # hard inputs fail 2.5x as often as average
k_easy = (1 - 0.30 * k_hard) / 0.70   # keeps the average failure rate unchanged
q = 1 - p
p_stage = np.where(hard[:, None], 1 - q * k_hard, 1 - q * k_easy)
ok = rng.random((N, 3)) < p_stage

print("stage success rates              ", ok.mean(0).round(4))
print("simulated, shared difficulty     ", ok.all(1).mean().round(4))

product of stage accuracies       0.7866
simulated, independent failures   0.7868
stage success rates               [0.9502 0.8994 0.9186]
simulated, shared difficulty      0.8004


Each stage keeps its measured success rate. The system is more reliable than the product predicts: \(0.800\) against \(0.787\). Failures cluster on the same inputs, so fewer inputs fail overall.
This is not a reason to relax. The same effect hides the worst case. The failures are concentrated on the hard 30% of the inputs, where the system is much less reliable than its average.

succ = ok.all(1)
vals = [p.prod(), independent, succ[~hard].mean(), succ[hard].mean()]
names = ["product\nformula", "independent\nsimulation", "easy inputs\n(shared difficulty)", "hard inputs\n(shared difficulty)"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
ax.bar(names, vals, color=[PALETTE["neutral"], PALETTE["neutral"], PALETTE["grad"], PALETTE["loss"]])
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(i, v + 0.01, f"{v:.3f}", ha="center")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05); ax.set_ylabel("P(system correct)")
plt.show()
print("easy:", succ[~hard].mean().round(3), " hard:", succ[hard].mean().round(3))







Figure 45.2: System success with three stages. Left: the product formula and a simulation with independent failures agree. Right: with a shared difficulty, the average rises but the success on hard inputs is much lower than on easy inputs.





easy: 0.92  hard: 0.523


The lesson: the average hides the structure. Characterise performance by condition (Chapter 47), not only by its mean.

title: 45  Systems Thinking: Components, Interfaces and Contracts
text:
45.5 Locating a failure
An end-to-end score tells us that the system fails. It does not tell us where. To find the stage, we need a test for each stage with known good input. The data above shows how the information is distributed.

failed = ~ok.all(1)
share = (~ok)[failed].mean(0)
for k, s in enumerate(share, 1):
    print(f"stage {k}: fails in {s:.1%} of the system failures")
print("stage shares sum to", share.sum().round(3), "(a failure can involve more than one stage)")

stage 1: fails in 25.0% of the system failures
stage 2: fails in 50.4% of the system failures
stage 3: fails in 40.8% of the system failures
stage shares sum to 1.161 (a failure can involve more than one stage)


Stage 2 is involved in about half of all system failures, although its accuracy of \(0.90\) is only a little worse than the others. The share depends on the accuracy and on how often the stage runs with a bad input from an earlier stage. A stage-by-stage report with a fixed, trusted input gives the stage’s own accuracy. A report from the running system gives the conditional accuracy. Both are needed.

title: 45  Systems Thinking: Components, Interfaces and Contracts
text:
45.6 Interface contracts
An interface passes data between components. The data has a shape, a type, a unit, a range and a distribution. If the producer and the consumer disagree on any of these, no exception is raised in most numerical code. The result is a plausible but wrong number.
We make the contract executable. The check costs little and it turns a silent error into a loud one.

import numpy as np

class Contract:
    """Pre/post-condition for an array that crosses an interface."""
    def __init__(self, name, shape, lo, hi, dtype=np.floating):
        self.name, self.shape, self.lo, self.hi, self.dtype = name, shape, lo, hi, dtype
    def check(self, a):
        a = np.asarray(a)
        if a.ndim != len(self.shape) or any(s is not None and s != d for s, d in zip(self.shape, a.shape)):
            raise ValueError(f"{self.name}: shape {a.shape}, expected {self.shape}")
        if not np.issubdtype(a.dtype, self.dtype):
            raise ValueError(f"{self.name}: dtype {a.dtype}, expected {self.dtype.__name__}")
        if np.isnan(a).any():
            raise ValueError(f"{self.name}: contains NaN")
        if a.min() < self.lo or a.max() > self.hi:
            raise ValueError(f"{self.name}: values in [{a.min():.3g}, {a.max():.3g}], expected [{self.lo}, {self.hi}]")
        return a

image_in = Contract("normalised image", (None, None), 0.0, 1.0)

good = np.random.default_rng(0).random((4, 4))        # already in [0, 1]
bad = (good * 255).round()                            # an upstream stage forgot to rescale

print("good input accepted:", image_in.check(good).shape)
try:
    image_in.check(bad)
except ValueError as e:
    print("bad input rejected :", e)

good input accepted: (4, 4)
bad input rejected : normalised image: values in [1, 238], expected [0.0, 1.0]


The second call fails with a message that names the interface and the violated condition. Without the contract, the model would run on values in \([0,255]\) and return an output with no error.






NoteWhere to place checks



Put a contract at every interface that crosses a team, a language, a process or a network. Inside one function, a test suite is enough.

45.7 Feedback to the designer
The chain in Equation 45.1 looks one-directional. A real project is a loop: requirements lead to a design, the design is characterised, the characterisation shows whether the requirement is met, and the result changes the design or the requirement. Chapter 46 treats the loops that exist inside the running system. Chapter 50 gives the protocol for the design loop.

title: 45  Systems Thinking: Components, Interfaces and Contracts
text:
45.8 Failure modes
Metric of the part, not of the whole. A component is optimised for its own score. The system score falls. Example: a detector tuned for recall floods the next stage with false alarms.
Silent contract breach. Units, colour order, normalisation and tensor layout differ between training code and serving code (Chapter 6).
Average-only reporting. The mean hides the hard condition where the system is not safe (Figure 45.2).
Test of parts without test of the whole. Every unit passes. The interfaces are wrong.
Test of the whole without test of parts. The system fails and nobody can say which stage to repair.

46.1 The system problem
Chapter 45 treated the system as a chain: input in, answer out. Real AI systems have loops. A recommender shows items, users click, the clicks become training data. A language model writes text, the text goes to the web, the web becomes training data. A controller measures a state, acts, and measures again.
This chapter has three parts: how errors move along a chain, how they move around a loop, and how a loop with delay can oscillate.

title: 46  Feedback, Coupling and Stability
text: When the output of a system affects its next input, what stays stable and what does not?
crumbs: Part IX — Systems Thinking and Performance Characterisation

title: 46  Feedback, Coupling and Stability
text:
46.2 Errors along a chain: gain
Take a chain \(y=C_m\circ\cdots\circ C_1(x)\) and add a small error \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\) to \(x\). To first order, the output error is the Jacobian of the chain times \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\) (Chapter 17). The chain rule (Chapter 18) gives
\[
\Delta\mathbf y\approx\mathbf J_m\mathbf J_{m-1}\cdots\mathbf J_1\,\boldsymbol\epsilon .
\tag{46.1}\]
For the norm, the submultiplicative rule gives a bound:
\[
\|\Delta\mathbf y\|\le\Bigl(\prod_{k=1}^{m}\|\mathbf J_k\|_2\Bigr)\|\boldsymbol\epsilon\|.
\tag{46.2}\]
Each factor \(\|\mathbf J_k\|_2\) is the gain of one stage: the largest stretch it applies to any error. If every gain is below 1, errors shrink. If one gain is above 1, a bad input can grow. The bound is loose: a random error does not usually point along the worst direction.

rng = np.random.default_rng(46)
n = 20
def stage(scale):
    """A random linear stage whose largest singular value is `scale`."""
    A = rng.normal(size=(n, n))
    return A * (scale / np.linalg.norm(A, 2))

for scale in (0.9, 1.0, 1.2):
    ratios, bounds = [], []
    for trial in range(200):
        Ms = [stage(scale) for _ in range(8)]
        eps = rng.normal(size=n)
        e = eps.copy()
        for M in Ms:
            e = M @ e
        ratios.append(np.linalg.norm(e) / np.linalg.norm(eps))
        bounds.append(np.prod([np.linalg.norm(M, 2) for M in Ms]))
    print(f"stage gain {scale}: bound {np.mean(bounds):8.3f}   actual mean {np.mean(ratios):8.3f}   "
          f"actual / bound {np.mean(ratios) / np.mean(bounds):.3f}")

stage gain 0.9: bound    0.430   actual mean    0.003   actual / bound 0.006
stage gain 1.0: bound    1.000   actual mean    0.006   actual / bound 0.006
stage gain 1.2: bound    4.300   actual mean    0.026   actual / bound 0.006


Eight stages with gain \(1.2\) have a bound of \(1.2^8\approx4.3\). The actual mean growth is \(0.026\), about \(0.6\%\) of the bound. A random matrix stretches only a few directions by its largest gain, and a random error is not aligned with them. Even with gain \(1.2\) the typical error shrinks. The bound is still the right warning: it says what can happen if the error is aligned. Adversarial inputs (Chapter 20) are the aligned case.






NoteGain and conditioning



The ratio of the largest to the smallest stretch of a matrix is its condition number (Chapter 5). A stage with a large condition number loses information in the squeezed directions and amplifies noise when the stage is inverted.
crumbs: Part IX — Systems Thinking and Performance Characterisation

title: 46  Feedback, Coupling and Stability
text:
46.3 Errors around a loop: feedback
In a loop, the output of generation \(g\) is the input of generation \(g+1\). Take the simplest case. A model is a Gaussian \(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\). At each generation we draw \(n\) samples from the current model and refit the mean and standard deviation to them. The original data are never seen again.
The maximum-likelihood estimate of the variance is biased low by the factor \((n-1)/n\) (Chapter 25). The sample mean also moves by chance. Each generation adds an estimation error and no generation corrects it.

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n_samples, n_gen, n_runs = 20, 100, 400
std = np.empty((n_runs, n_gen + 1)); std[:, 0] = 1.0
for r in range(n_runs):
    mu, sd = 0.0, 1.0
    for g in range(1, n_gen + 1):
        x = rng.normal(mu, sd, n_samples)
        mu, sd = x.mean(), x.std()          # maximum likelihood refit
        std[r, g] = sd
for g in (0, 10, 25, 50, 100):
    print(f"generation {g:3d}: mean std {std[:, g].mean():.3f}   median std {np.median(std[:, g]):.3f}")

generation   0: mean std 1.000   median std 1.000
generation  10: mean std 0.650   median std 0.568
generation  25: mean std 0.334   median std 0.252
generation  50: mean std 0.127   median std 0.068
generation 100: mean std 0.013   median std 0.004


The standard deviation drifts toward zero. The tails disappear first. Rare cases (large \(|x|\)) are the first to be lost, and the loss is not visible in the training loss of any single generation.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
for r in range(25):
    ax.plot(std[r], color=PALETTE["data"], alpha=0.25, lw=0.8)
ax.plot(np.median(std, axis=0), color=PALETTE["loss"], lw=2.4, label="median of 400 runs")
ax.set_xlabel("generation"); ax.set_ylabel("fitted standard deviation"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.legend()
plt.show()







Figure 46.2: A Gaussian refitted on 20 of its own samples, generation after generation. Thin lines are single runs, the heavy line is the median over 400 runs. The spread shrinks toward zero: the model forgets the tails.





A remedy is to keep contact with the world: mix fresh real data into every generation. The next code cell mixes in a fraction \(\alpha\) of the original distribution.

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
def final_std(alpha, n_gen=100, n_runs=300):
    out = []
    for _ in range(n_runs):
        mu, sd = 0.0, 1.0
        for _ in range(n_gen):
            k = int(round(alpha * n_samples))
            x = np.concatenate([rng.normal(mu, sd, n_samples - k), rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, k)])
            mu, sd = x.mean(), x.std()
        out.append(sd)
    return np.mean(out)
for a in (0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5):
    print(f"fresh real data fraction {a:4.2f}: mean std after 100 generations {final_std(a):.3f}")

fresh real data fraction 0.00: mean std after 100 generations 0.018
fresh real data fraction 0.10: mean std after 100 generations 0.841
fresh real data fraction 0.25: mean std after 100 generations 0.913
fresh real data fraction 0.50: mean std after 100 generations 0.962


Without fresh data the mean spread after 100 generations is \(0.018\). With 10% fresh data it is \(0.84\), and with 50% it is \(0.96\). The true value is \(1\). A small fraction of real data is enough to stop most of the loss, but it does not remove the bias completely. The principle applies to any loop: an anchor to ground truth keeps the loop from drifting. In production, the anchor is a flow of fresh, independently labelled examples.

title: 46  Feedback, Coupling and Stability
text:
46.4 Delay and gain: oscillation
Feedback control corrects an error in proportion to its size. Let \(x_t\) be the deviation from a target. We apply a correction of strength \(k\), but the measurement is late by one step:
\[
x_{t+1}=x_t-k\,x_{t-1}.
\tag{46.3}\]
The solutions of Equation 46.3 grow like \(z^t\), where \(z\) solves \(z^2-z+k=0\). For \(k>1/4\) the roots are complex with \(|z|^2=k\). So the deviation decays if \(k<1\) and grows if \(k>1\). A correction that is too strong, applied with a delay, overshoots and makes the error larger.

def run(k, T=40):
    x = np.zeros(T); x[0] = x[1] = 1.0
    for t in range(1, T - 1):
        x[t + 1] = x[t] - k * x[t - 1]
    return x
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.4))
for k, c in [(0.5, PALETTE["grad"]), (1.0, PALETTE["model"]), (1.2, PALETTE["loss"])]:
    ax.plot(run(k), color=c, lw=2, label=f"gain k = {k}")
ax.set_xlabel("time step t"); ax.set_ylabel("deviation $x_t$"); ax.set_ylim(-4, 4)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()
for k in (0.5, 1.0, 1.2):
    r = np.roots([1, -1, k])
    print(f"k={k}: largest root magnitude {np.abs(r).max():.3f}   |x_40| = {abs(run(k, 41)[-1]):.3f}")







Figure 46.3: The loop of the equation with one step of delay. Gain 0.5 settles with a decaying oscillation. Gain 1.0 oscillates for ever. Gain 1.2 grows without limit. The stability boundary is at gain 1, as the root analysis predicts.





k=0.5: largest root magnitude 0.707   |x_40| = 0.000
k=1.0: largest root magnitude 1.000   |x_40| = 1.000
k=1.2: largest root magnitude 1.095   |x_40| = 35.951


The numbers agree with the analysis: the largest root has magnitude \(\sqrt k\).
The same pattern appears far from control engineering. A learning rate that is too high (Chapter 19) is a gain above the stability limit. An autoscaler that reacts to a slow metric oscillates. A pricing model that reacts to its own effect on demand overshoots.

title: 46  Feedback, Coupling and Stability
text:
46.5 Coupling
Two components are coupled when a change in one changes the correct setting of the other. Chapter 45 named one form: an upstream threshold tuned for recall changes the downstream workload. Coupling makes local tuning unsafe. Each team improves its own score and the whole gets worse.
We handle coupling in three ways.

Decouple with an interface that hides the change (a stable contract, Chapter 45).
Tune jointly against the system measure (Chapter 50).
Monitor the interface distribution, so that a drift is seen when it starts (Chapter 27).
crumbs: Part IX — Systems Thinking and Performance Characterisation

title: 46  Feedback, Coupling and Stability
text:
46.6 Failure modes
Self-training drift. A system trains on its own labels or outputs. Diversity and tails vanish (Figure 46.2).
Popularity loops. A recommender shows what is clicked. What is shown is clicked more. Items never shown cannot be measured.
Over-correction. A controller or a tuner reacts to noise as if it were signal. Gain with delay gives oscillation (Figure 46.3).
Hidden coupling. One team changes a pre-processing step. A downstream model silently loses accuracy.
Aligned perturbation. A small error aligned with a high-gain direction is amplified (Equation 46.2). Natural noise rarely does this. An adversary does.

NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now be analysed as a dynamic object. We have a bound on how a chain amplifies a small error, a worked example of a loop that forgets its tails, a rule for when a delayed correction turns into oscillation, and a name for coupling.
All of this reasoning used qualitative tools and small simulations. We still lack a standard procedure to say, for a given component, how its output error depends on its input noise and its parameters. That is performance characterisation. Chapter 47 gives its paradigm.

title: 47  Performance Characterisation: The Paradigm
text:
47.1 The system problem
In the 1980s and 1990s, computer vision had many algorithms for edges, corners, lines, regions and motion. Each paper showed a few images where the new method looked better. R. M. Haralick pointed out that this is not engineering. A bridge builder gives a load limit and a safety factor. An algorithm designer gave a picture.
The work of Haralick and of V. Ramesh and co-authors answers with a method: performance characterisation. This chapter presents the method in its simplest setting, one component and one number of noise. Chapters 48 to 50 extend it to pipelines, to confidence statements and to experimental protocols.

title: 47  Performance Characterisation: The Paradigm
text:
How well does this algorithm work, under which conditions, with which settings, and how do we know?








NoteSources



The ideas in Part IX follow the programme described in R. M. Haralick, “Performance characterization in computer vision”, CVGIP: Image Understanding 60(2), 1994, and in the papers of V. Ramesh and R. M. Haralick on random perturbation models, covariance propagation and parameter tuning for vision algorithm sequences (early 1990s to the late 1990s). The examples in this book are my own small constructions in that spirit, not reproductions of their experiments. Check details against the original papers before citing them.

title: 47  Performance Characterisation: The Paradigm
text:
47.2 The paradigm in four steps

box_flow(["Input +\nperturbation\nmodel", "Algorithm\n+ parameters", "Output\ndistribution", "Validate on\nreal data"],
         colors=[PALETTE["data"], PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["prob"], PALETTE["grad"]], figsize=(9, 1.9))
plt.show()







Figure 47.1: The characterisation loop. Model the ideal input and the perturbation. Run the algorithm with parameters. Describe the output as a distribution. Compare with real data and correct the model.






Model the input. State an ideal input \(\mathbf x_0\) (the clean world: a step edge of height \(h\) at position \(s\)). State how the real input differs: \(\mathbf x=\mathbf x_0+\boldsymbol\epsilon\), with \(\boldsymbol\epsilon\) drawn from a perturbation model, for example independent Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\). This is a random perturbation model.
Define the algorithm as a mapping \(\mathbf y=A(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\theta)\) with tuning parameters \(\boldsymbol\theta\) (a window size, a threshold).
Describe the output. The output \(\mathbf y\) is a random variable because \(\mathbf x\) is. Find its distribution, or its relevant moments, as a function of \((h,\sigma,\boldsymbol\theta)\). Do it by derivation where possible and by simulation otherwise.
Validate. Compare the predicted behaviour with the behaviour on real, labelled data. If they differ, the perturbation model is wrong, not the data.

The result is an operating characteristic: a table, curve or formula that says what the algorithm does for each condition.

title: 47  Performance Characterisation: The Paradigm
section: 47.3 A worked component: a step-edge detector
text:
47.3 A worked component: a step-edge detector
We take a one-dimensional signal with a step of height \(h\) at position \(s\), plus independent noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\). The algorithm has one structural parameter, the window width \(w\), and one threshold \(\tau\). For each position \(i\) it computes the mean of the \(w\) samples after \(i\) minus the mean of the \(w\) samples before \(i\):
\[
D_i=\frac1w\sum_{j=0}^{w-1}x_{i+j}-\frac1w\sum_{j=1}^{w}x_{i-j}.
\tag{47.1}\]
It reports an edge where \(|D_i|\) is the largest value and exceeds \(\tau\).

47.3.1 What theory predicts
For a clean step, the filter peaks at the step with value exactly \(h\). For noise only, \(D_i\) is a difference of two window means, so it is Gaussian with variance
\[
\sigma_D^2=\sigma^2\Bigl(\frac1w+\frac1w\Bigr)=\frac{2\sigma^2}{w}.
\tag{47.2}\]
Larger windows reduce noise by \(\sqrt{2/w}\). At one sample, a threshold \(\tau\) gives a false alarm probability
\[
P_{\text{FA}}^{(1)}(\tau)=2\,Q\!\left(\frac{\tau}{\sigma_D}\right),
\tag{47.3}\]
where \(Q\) is the upper tail of the standard normal. So we can set the threshold from a required false alarm rate: \(\tau=\sigma_D\,Q^{-1}\!\bigl(P_{\text{FA}}^{(1)}/2\bigr)\). This is the central benefit of an analytic model.
At the true edge, \(D=h+\text{noise}\) with standard deviation \(\sigma_D\). The probability that it exceeds \(\tau\) is \(Q\bigl((\tau-h)/\sigma_D\bigr)\) (plus a negligible term for the other side). It depends on the signal-to-noise ratio \(h/\sigma_D\) and the threshold only.


47.3.2 Measuring
We now measure the detector, to test the prediction. A detection is a trial where the largest response exceeds \(\tau\) and lies within \(\pm2\) samples of the true edge. A false alarm is a response above \(\tau\) at a place far from the edge. We use \(\sigma=1\) and set \(\tau\) for a per-sample false alarm probability of \(0.001\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(47)
Ls, s0 = 200, 100

def diff_filter(x, w):
    c = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(x)])
    i = np.arange(w, len(x) - w + 1)
    return i, (c[i + w] - c[i]) / w - (c[i] - c[i - w]) / w

def run_trials(h, sigma, w, tau, n=3000):
    det = loc = 0
    errs = []
    for _ in range(n):
        x = rng.normal(0, sigma, Ls); x[s0:] += h
        i, d = diff_filter(x, w)
        a = np.abs(d); k = a.argmax()
        if a[k] > tau and abs(i[k] - s0) <= 2:
            det += 1; errs.append(i[k] - s0)
    return det / n, (np.std(errs) if errs else np.nan)

sigma, pfa1 = 1.0, 1e-3
print(" w  sigma_D   tau   per-sample FA (measured)")
for w in (3, 5, 9):
    sD = sigma * np.sqrt(2 / w)
    tau = sD * norm.isf(pfa1 / 2)
    fa = np.mean([(np.abs(diff_filter(rng.normal(0, sigma, Ls), w)[1]) > tau).mean() for _ in range(3000)])
    print(f"{w:2d}   {sD:.3f}  {tau:.3f}   {fa:.5f}")

 w  sigma_D   tau   per-sample FA (measured)
 3   0.816  2.687   0.00102
 5   0.632  2.081   0.00090
 9   0.471  1.551   0.00097


The measured false alarm rate matches the design value \(0.001\) within noise. The model predicted a number and the experiment confirmed it. Now the detection probability as a function of the edge height, with the theory curve \(Q\bigl((\tau-h)/\sigma_D\bigr)\) for comparison.

hs = np.linspace(0.5, 5, 10)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.7))
cols = {3: PALETTE["loss"], 5: PALETTE["model"], 9: PALETTE["grad"]}
table = {}
for w in (3, 5, 9):
    sD = sigma * np.sqrt(2 / w); tau = sD * norm.isf(pfa1 / 2)
    meas = np.array([run_trials(h, sigma, w, tau, n=1500)[0] for h in hs])
    theo = norm.sf((tau - hs) / sD)
    table[w] = (meas, theo)
    ax.plot(hs, theo, color=cols[w], lw=1.8, label=f"w = {w}")
    ax.plot(hs, meas, "o", color=cols[w], ms=4)
ax.set_xlabel("edge height h (noise σ = 1)"); ax.set_ylabel("P(detect)")
ax.legend(); plt.show()
w = 5
print("w=5: largest |measured - theory| =", np.abs(table[w][0] - table[w][1]).max().round(3))







Figure 47.2: Detection probability against edge height for three window widths, at fixed false alarm rate 0.001 per sample. Dots are measured over 3,000 trials. Lines are the one-sample prediction. A wider window detects weaker edges.





w=5: largest |measured - theory| = 0.07


The theory is the one-sample formula. It ignores competing noise peaks elsewhere in the signal and it is therefore slightly optimistic at low heights. The largest gap between measurement and theory for \(w=5\) is \(0.07\), near the knee of the curve. A characterisation reports both: the clean formula for design, and the measured curve for the truth.


47.3.3 Localisation
A detector must also say where the edge is. We measure the standard deviation of the position error over correct detections.

print("edge height 4, sigma 1:  window  P(detect)  location std (samples)")
for w in (3, 5, 9, 15):
    sD = sigma * np.sqrt(2 / w); tau = sD * norm.isf(pfa1 / 2)
    p, s = run_trials(4.0, sigma, w, tau, n=3000)
    print(f"                         {w:6d}  {p:9.3f}  {s:9.2f}")

edge height 4, sigma 1:  window  P(detect)  location std (samples)
                              3      0.960       0.35
                              5      0.996       0.39
                              9      0.999       0.37
                             15      0.995       0.37


At height 4 the detection probability rises from \(0.960\) (\(w=3\)) to about \(0.995\) or more, and the location error stays near \(0.4\) samples for every window. We counted only detections within \(\pm2\) samples, so this number is truncated. The window width does not matter much for one clean edge. It matters when a second edge is near.

def two_edge_resolution(gap, w, n=1500, h=4.0):
    """P(both edges of a bar of width `gap` are detected, each within +-2 samples)."""
    sD = sigma * np.sqrt(2 / w); tau = sD * norm.isf(pfa1 / 2)
    ok = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        x = rng.normal(0, sigma, Ls); x[s0:s0 + gap] += h
        i, d = diff_filter(x, w); a = np.abs(d)
        found = lambda c: a[np.abs(i - c) <= 2].max() > tau
        ok += found(s0) and found(s0 + gap)
    return ok / n
print("both edges of a bar found, P(resolve) by window w and bar width (samples):")
print("bar width:   " + "  ".join(f"{g:5d}" for g in (3, 6, 12, 24)))
for w in (3, 9, 15):
    print(f"w = {w:2d}:      " + "  ".join(f"{two_edge_resolution(g, w):5.2f}" for g in (3, 6, 12, 24)))

both edges of a bar found, P(resolve) by window w and bar width (samples):
bar width:       3      6     12     24
w =  3:       0.92   0.92   0.93   0.91
w =  9:       0.21   1.00   1.00   1.00
w = 15:       0.02   0.85   1.00   1.00


A bar of width 3 is found by \(w=3\) in 92% of trials, by \(w=9\) in 21%, and by \(w=15\) in 2%. A wide window averages across a narrow bar, so the response at each edge is weak. In the other direction, \(w=3\) has a lower detection probability at the single edge (Figure 47.2), and it never reaches 1.00 on the wider bars, because its threshold is higher. The window width is a tuning parameter with a trade-off: noise rejection against resolution. A characterisation shows the trade-off. It does not hide it behind one “accuracy” number.

title: 47  Performance Characterisation: The Paradigm
text:
47.4 What to report
A characterisation report for a component states:







Item
Content




Input domain
the ideal inputs and the perturbation model, with ranges


Parameters
each tuning parameter and its tested range


Measures
detection, false alarm, localisation, with the definition of each


Results
the measure as a function of condition and parameter, with confidence (Chapter 49)


Validation
agreement between the model and real data, and where it fails


Operating rule
for a stated requirement, which parameters to use (Chapter 50)

title: 47  Performance Characterisation: The Paradigm
text:
47.5 Failure modes
Wrong perturbation model. Real noise is correlated, heavy-tailed or signal-dependent. The formula is exact for the model and wrong for the world. Chapter 50 tests this by deliberately mismatching the model.
One number for a function. The detector has a curve, not a score.
Definition drift. “Detection” must be defined (how near is near enough?). A different definition changes the curve.
Condition coverage. The test set contains only easy inputs. The operating characteristic is silent about the hard ones.
Tuning on the test set. The parameters were selected on the data used to report performance (Chapter 27).

title: 48  Random Perturbation and Error Propagation
text:
48.1 The system problem
Chapter 47 characterised one component against noise on its input. In a pipeline, the input of stage 2 is the output of stage 1. Its noise is not an assumption any more. It is a result.
This is the second step in the programme of Haralick and Ramesh: carry the perturbation model through the whole sequence of operations, so that the uncertainty at the end is predicted from the uncertainty at the start (see the sources in Chapter 47).
fig = box_flow(["Noisy\npoints", "Line fit\n(a, b)", "Two lines", "Intersection\n(x, y)"],
               colors=[PALETTE["data"], PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["prob"]],
               figsize=(9, 1.9))
ax = fig.axes[0]
for x, lab in [(1.0, r"$\Sigma_{ab}$"), (2.0, r"$\Sigma_{a_1b_1a_2b_2}$"), (3.0, r"$\Sigma_{xy}$")]:
    ax.text(x - 0.02, 0.06, lab, ha="center", fontsize=10, color="#374151")
plt.show()







Figure 48.1: A three-stage measurement. Noisy points go into a line fit. Two fitted lines go into an intersection. The covariance at each arrow is computed from the covariance at the previous arrow.

title: 48  Random Perturbation and Error Propagation
text:
48.2 Propagating a covariance
Let \(\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^n\) be a random vector with mean \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and covariance \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) (Chapter 23). Let \(\mathbf v=f(\mathbf u)\). The first-order (Taylor) expansion around \(\boldsymbol\mu\) is
\[
\mathbf v\approx f(\boldsymbol\mu)+\mathbf J\,(\mathbf u-\boldsymbol\mu),\qquad
\mathbf J=\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mathbf u}\right|_{\boldsymbol\mu}.
\tag{48.1}\]
Taking the covariance of both sides gives the propagation rule:
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf v)\approx\mathbf J\,\boldsymbol\Sigma\,\mathbf J^{\intercal}.
\tag{48.2}\]
It is exact if \(f\) is linear. It is the covariance form of the chain rule (Chapter 18). For a chain \(f_2\circ f_1\) we apply it twice, which multiplies the Jacobians (Equation 46.1).
We implement the rule with a numerical Jacobian, so that it works for any function we can call.

def jacobian(f, u, h=1e-6):
    u = np.asarray(u, float); f0 = np.atleast_1d(f(u))
    J = np.empty((f0.size, u.size))
    for j in range(u.size):
        d = np.zeros_like(u); d[j] = h
        J[:, j] = (np.atleast_1d(f(u + d)) - np.atleast_1d(f(u - d))) / (2 * h)
    return J

def propagate(f, mu, Sigma):
    J = jacobian(f, mu)
    return J @ Sigma @ J.T

# a check on a function whose answer is known: v = u1 * u2 with u independent
mu = np.array([3.0, 2.0]); S = np.diag([0.01, 0.04])
print("propagated variance of u1*u2:", propagate(lambda u: u[0] * u[1], mu, S)[0, 0].round(4))
print("by hand: u2^2 var1 + u1^2 var2 =", (2.0**2 * 0.01 + 3.0**2 * 0.04))

propagated variance of u1*u2: 0.4
by hand: u2^2 var1 + u1^2 var2 = 0.39999999999999997

section: 48.3 Stage 1: the covariance of a fitted line
text:
48.3 Stage 1: the covariance of a fitted line
We observe \(y_i=a x_i+b+\epsilon_i\) at fixed positions \(x_i\) with independent noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\). Least squares gives \((\hat a,\hat b)\). Write the design matrix \(\mathbf X\) with rows \((x_i,1)\). Then, exactly (Chapter 25),
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\begin{pmatrix}\hat a\\\hat b\end{pmatrix}=\sigma^2\,(\mathbf X^{\intercal}\mathbf X)^{-1}.
\tag{48.3}\]
The matrix \(\mathbf X^{\intercal}\mathbf X\) depends on where we sample. Points that spread widely in \(x\) give a precise slope. Points that cluster give an uncertain one. The uncertainty is partly a design property, not only a noise property.

rng = np.random.default_rng(48)
sigma = 0.3
def cov_ab(x, sigma):
    X = np.column_stack([x, np.ones_like(x)])
    return sigma**2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)

x_wide = np.linspace(0, 10, 20)
x_narrow = np.linspace(4, 6, 20)
for name, x in [("x in [0,10]", x_wide), ("x in [4,6] ", x_narrow)]:
    C = cov_ab(x, sigma)
    print(f"{name}: std(a) = {np.sqrt(C[0,0]):.4f}   std(b) = {np.sqrt(C[1,1]):.4f}")

# confirm by simulation
a_true, b_true = 0.5, 1.0
est = []
for _ in range(20000):
    y = a_true * x_wide + b_true + rng.normal(0, sigma, x_wide.size)
    est.append(np.polyfit(x_wide, y, 1))
est = np.array(est)
print("simulated std(a), std(b) for x in [0,10]:", est.std(0).round(4))

x in [0,10]: std(a) = 0.0221   std(b) = 0.1293
x in [4,6] : std(a) = 0.1105   std(b) = 0.5566
simulated std(a), std(b) for x in [0,10]: [0.022  0.1283]


Squeezing the sample positions into \([4,6]\) makes the slope five times less certain. The simulation agrees with Equation 48.3.

section: 48.4 Stage 2: the intersection of two lines
text:
48.4 Stage 2: the intersection of two lines
Two lines \(y=a_1x+b_1\) and \(y=a_2x+b_2\) meet at
\[
x^*=\frac{b_2-b_1}{a_1-a_2},\qquad y^*=a_1x^*+b_1.
\tag{48.4}\]
The denominator \(a_1-a_2\) explains the behaviour: when the lines are nearly parallel, a small slope error moves \(x^*\) a long way. We compute the predicted covariance with Equation 48.2 and compare with a Monte Carlo experiment for two configurations: lines crossing at a wide angle and at a narrow angle. Both cross at \((5,\,3.5)\).

def intersect(p):
    a1, b1, a2, b2 = p
    x = (b2 - b1) / (a1 - a2)
    return np.array([x, a1 * x + b1])

configs = {
    "wide angle   (slopes  0.5, -0.5)": (0.5, 1.0, -0.5, 6.0),
    "narrow angle (slopes  0.5,  0.4)": (0.5, 1.0, 0.4, 1.5),
}
x = x_wide
rows = {}
for name, (a1, b1, a2, b2) in configs.items():
    # block-diagonal covariance of the four line parameters (the two fits are independent)
    C = cov_ab(x, sigma)
    S = np.block([[C, np.zeros((2, 2))], [np.zeros((2, 2)), C]])
    p0 = np.array([a1, b1, a2, b2])
    pred = propagate(intersect, p0, S)
    # Monte Carlo
    pts = []
    for _ in range(20000):
        pa = np.polyfit(x, a1 * x + b1 + rng.normal(0, sigma, x.size), 1)
        pb = np.polyfit(x, a2 * x + b2 + rng.normal(0, sigma, x.size), 1)
        pts.append(intersect([pa[0], pa[1], pb[0], pb[1]]))
    pts = np.array(pts)
    rows[name] = (pred, pts)
    print(name)
    print("   predicted std (x, y):", np.sqrt(np.diag(pred)).round(3))
    print("   simulated std (x, y):", pts.std(0).round(3))

wide angle   (slopes  0.5, -0.5)
   predicted std (x, y): [0.095 0.047]
   simulated std (x, y): [0.095 0.048]
narrow angle (slopes  0.5,  0.4)
   predicted std (x, y): [0.949 0.43 ]
   simulated std (x, y): [2.887 1.334]


At the wide angle, theory and simulation agree: \(0.095\) against \(0.095\) for \(x^*\). At the narrow angle the prediction is \(0.949\), ten times larger, and the simulation gives \(2.887\), about three times larger again. The narrow angle is a different regime, and the first-order prediction is too optimistic there, because \(x^*\) is a ratio whose denominator \(a_1-a_2\) can come close to zero. We look at the distribution, not only at the standard deviation.

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.6))
t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
for ax, (name, (pred, pts)) in zip(axs, rows.items()):
    ax.plot(*pts[:1500].T, ".", ms=2, alpha=0.4, color=PALETTE["data"])
    mu = intersect(configs[name])
    w, V = np.linalg.eigh(pred)
    E = mu[:, None] + V @ (2 * np.sqrt(w)[:, None] * np.array([np.cos(t), np.sin(t)]))
    ax.plot(*E, color=PALETTE["loss"], lw=2, label="predicted 2σ ellipse")
    ax.plot(*mu, "k+", ms=10)
    ax.set_title(name.split("(")[0].strip()); ax.set_xlabel("x*"); ax.set_ylabel("y*")
    ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="datalim"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()
for name, (pred, pts) in rows.items():
    mu = intersect(configs[name])
    inside = []
    Pinv = np.linalg.inv(pred)
    d2 = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", pts - mu, Pinv, pts - mu)
    print(f"{name.split('(')[0].strip():13s}: share of points inside the predicted 2-sigma ellipse "
          f"(Mahalanobis² < 4): {(d2 < 4).mean():.3f}   (Gaussian: 0.865)")







Figure 48.2: Simulated intersection points (dots) and the predicted 2-sigma ellipse from the covariance propagation rule (line). Left: wide crossing angle. Right: narrow crossing angle, where the cloud is much larger and the ellipse is a poorer description of its tails.





wide angle   : share of points inside the predicted 2-sigma ellipse (Mahalanobis² < 4): 0.863   (Gaussian: 0.865)
narrow angle : share of points inside the predicted 2-sigma ellipse (Mahalanobis² < 4): 0.810   (Gaussian: 0.865)


For a Gaussian cloud, 86.5% of points fall inside the 2-sigma ellipse in two dimensions. The wide-angle cloud gives \(0.863\). The narrow-angle cloud gives \(0.810\), with a much longer tail than the model. The predicted covariance understates the probability of a large error. The correct statement is that first-order propagation is a design tool, valid where noise is small compared with the scale on which the function curves.

title: 48  Random Perturbation and Error Propagation
text:
48.5 When does first order break?
We repeat the narrow-angle case with increasing noise and compare the predicted standard deviation of \(x^*\) with the simulated one.

a1, b1, a2, b2 = configs["narrow angle (slopes  0.5,  0.4)"]
sig_list = [0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5]
ratio, rob = [], []
for sg in sig_list:
    C = cov_ab(x, sg); S = np.block([[C, np.zeros((2, 2))], [np.zeros((2, 2)), C]])
    pred = np.sqrt(propagate(intersect, np.array([a1, b1, a2, b2]), S)[0, 0])
    sims = []
    for _ in range(8000):
        pa = np.polyfit(x, a1 * x + b1 + rng.normal(0, sg, x.size), 1)
        pb = np.polyfit(x, a2 * x + b2 + rng.normal(0, sg, x.size), 1)
        sims.append(intersect([pa[0], pa[1], pb[0], pb[1]])[0])
    sims = np.array(sims)
    ratio.append(sims.std() / pred)
    # a robust width (IQR / 1.349) is not affected by the rare extremes
    q1, q3 = np.percentile(sims, [25, 75]); rob.append((q3 - q1) / 1.349 / pred)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.4))
ax.plot(sig_list, ratio, "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"], label="std ratio")
ax.plot(sig_list, rob, "s--", color=PALETTE["data"], label="robust (IQR) ratio")
ax.axhline(1, color="gray", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("noise σ"); ax.set_ylabel("simulated / predicted"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
for sg, r1, r2 in zip(sig_list, ratio, rob):
    print(f"sigma {sg:4.2f}: std ratio {r1:5.2f}   robust ratio {r2:5.2f}")







Figure 48.3: Ratio of simulated to predicted standard deviation of the intersection abscissa for the narrow-angle case, against the noise level. At small noise the ratio is near 1. As noise grows the ratio rises: the prediction becomes too optimistic.





sigma 0.02: std ratio  1.00   robust ratio  1.00
sigma 0.05: std ratio  1.00   robust ratio  1.00
sigma 0.10: std ratio  1.02   robust ratio  1.01
sigma 0.20: std ratio  1.08   robust ratio  1.01
sigma 0.30: std ratio 18.21   robust ratio  1.03
sigma 0.50: std ratio 26.40   robust ratio  1.07


The ratio is \(1.00\) to \(1.08\) for \(\sigma\le0.2\), which confirms the rule in its range of validity. At \(\sigma=0.3\) and \(0.5\) the standard deviation ratio jumps to \(18\) and \(26\). In some trials \(a_1-a_2\) is close to zero and \(x^*\) explodes. A ratio of two Gaussians has no finite variance, so this sample standard deviation is not even stable: the same case gave a ratio of about \(3\) in the 20,000-trial run above and \(18\) here. The robust width (interquartile range) stays at \(1.03\) and \(1.07\). So the bulk of the distribution is predicted well and the tails are not. A report should state the regime where the first-order rule holds, and give quantiles for the tails.

title: 48  Random Perturbation and Error Propagation
text:
48.6 An error budget
Propagation gives more than a total. The contribution of each input to the output variance is the sum of the terms \(J_{ij}\,\Sigma_{jj}\,J_{ij}\) (for uncorrelated inputs). For the wide-angle configuration we split the variance of \(x^*\) by line parameter.

a1, b1, a2, b2 = configs["wide angle   (slopes  0.5, -0.5)"]
C = cov_ab(x, sigma)
S = np.block([[C, np.zeros((2, 2))], [np.zeros((2, 2)), C]])
p0 = np.array([a1, b1, a2, b2])
J = jacobian(intersect, p0)
# contributions include correlation inside each line's (a, b) pair, so group by line
line1 = J[0, :2] @ C @ J[0, :2]
line2 = J[0, 2:] @ C @ J[0, 2:]
total = line1 + line2
print(f"variance of x*: {total:.4f}   line 1 share {line1/total:.2f}   line 2 share {line2/total:.2f}")
print("Jacobian row for x* with respect to (a1, b1, a2, b2):", J[0].round(3))

variance of x*: 0.0090   line 1 share 0.50   line 2 share 0.50
Jacobian row for x* with respect to (a1, b1, a2, b2): [-5. -1.  5.  1.]


The two lines contribute equally here, as the symmetric design suggests. If one line were fitted from fewer points, the budget would show that line as the one to improve. This is the engineering use of propagation: it says where to spend measurement effort.

title: 48  Random Perturbation and Error Propagation
text:
48.7 Failure modes
Linearisation outside its range. The rule holds for small noise and mild curvature. Narrow angles, near-singular matrices and ratios break it (Figure 48.3).
Ignoring correlation. The outputs of one stage are usually correlated (here \(\hat a\) and \(\hat b\) are). Treating them as independent gives the wrong covariance.
Input noise model wrong. The rule propagates the model, whatever it is. If the model is wrong at the input, the result is exact and meaningless.
Bias ignored. First-order propagation gives the covariance. It does not give the bias of a non-linear transform. The mean of the output is not \(f(\boldsymbol\mu)\) in general.
Standard deviation as tail guarantee. A heavy-tailed output needs a quantile, not a standard deviation. Here the sample standard deviation differed by a factor of six between two runs.

48.9 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now predict the uncertainty of a pipeline output from the uncertainty of its input. We have a general propagation rule, an exact result for the fitted-line covariance that depends on the sampling design, a worked non-linear stage, a test that shows where the rule fails, and a budget that points to the dominant contributor.
Everything so far was about the spread of continuous errors. Many components make decisions: detect or not, accept or reject. Their quality is measured by two kinds of error at once, and the trade-off between them is the subject of Chapter 49, with the confidence that comes with a finite test set.

49.1 The system problem
The detector of Chapter 47 outputs a score and compares it with a threshold. A low threshold finds more true cases and raises more false alarms. A high threshold does the opposite. We cannot say how good the detector is without saying at which threshold.
The answer needs three tools: the ROC curve, a confidence interval and a paired test.

title: 49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence
text: We have two detectors and a test set of 400 items. Detector B scores higher. Is B better, and by how much, and how sure are we?
crumbs: Part IX — Systems Thinking and Performance Characterisation
49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence

title: 49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence
text:
49.2 Two errors and one curve
For a score \(s\) and a threshold \(\tau\), we declare “positive” if \(s>\tau\). Four counts follow: true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN), false negatives (FN). Two rates describe the detector:
\[
\text{TPR}(\tau)=\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FN}},\qquad
\text{FPR}(\tau)=\frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP}+\text{TN}}.
\tag{49.1}\]
TPR is the detection rate (also recall or sensitivity). FPR is the false alarm rate (one minus specificity). The ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic) is the set of points \((\text{FPR}(\tau),\text{TPR}(\tau))\) for all \(\tau\).
The area under the curve (AUC) has a simple meaning: it is the probability that a randomly chosen positive item has a higher score than a randomly chosen negative item. This is the Mann–Whitney statistic (Chapter 26).
We use a model where we know the truth. Negatives have scores \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). Positives have scores \(\mathcal N(d,1)\). The separation \(d\) (“d-prime”) sets the difficulty. In this model the ROC and AUC are known exactly: \(\text{TPR}=Q\bigl(Q^{-1}(\text{FPR})-d\bigr)\) and \(\text{AUC}=\Phi(d/\sqrt2)\).

rng = np.random.default_rng(49)

def roc(scores, labels):
    order = np.argsort(-scores)
    l = labels[order]
    tpr = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(l) / l.sum()])
    fpr = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(1 - l) / (1 - l).sum()])
    return fpr, tpr

def auc_rank(scores, labels):
    # Mann-Whitney: P(score_pos > score_neg), ties count one half
    pos, neg = scores[labels == 1], scores[labels == 0]
    return ((pos[:, None] > neg[None, :]).mean() + 0.5 * (pos[:, None] == neg[None, :]).mean())

d_A, d_B = 1.5, 1.8
print("exact AUC  A:", norm.cdf(d_A / np.sqrt(2)).round(4), "  B:", norm.cdf(d_B / np.sqrt(2)).round(4))

n_pos = n_neg = 200
labels = np.r_[np.ones(n_pos, int), np.zeros(n_neg, int)]
# a SHARED latent per item makes the two detectors' errors correlated, as real detectors are
shared = rng.normal(size=labels.size)
sA = labels * d_A + 0.7 * shared + np.sqrt(1 - 0.49) * rng.normal(size=labels.size)
sB = labels * d_B + 0.7 * shared + np.sqrt(1 - 0.49) * rng.normal(size=labels.size)
print("test set (400 items) AUC  A:", auc_rank(sA, labels).round(3), "  B:", auc_rank(sB, labels).round(3))

exact AUC  A: 0.8556   B: 0.8985
test set (400 items) AUC  A: 0.874   B: 0.896


On this one test set, B has the higher AUC: \(0.896\) against \(0.874\). The exact values are \(0.899\) and \(0.856\), so the measured gap (\(0.022\)) is about half of the true gap (\(0.043\)). That is sampling noise at work. We quantify it.

title: 49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence
section: 49.3 A confidence interval for an operating point
text:
49.3 A confidence interval for an operating point
At one threshold, TPR is a proportion: \(k\) detections out of \(n\) positives. The sampling distribution of \(k\) is binomial (Chapter 23). The exact (Clopper–Pearson) interval at confidence \(1-\alpha\) uses the beta distribution:
\[
\bigl[\,B^{-1}(\tfrac\alpha2;\,k,\,n-k+1),\;B^{-1}(1-\tfrac\alpha2;\,k+1,\,n-k)\,\bigr].
\tag{49.2}\]

def clopper_pearson(k, n, alpha=0.05):
    lo = 0.0 if k == 0 else beta.ppf(alpha / 2, k, n - k + 1)
    hi = 1.0 if k == n else beta.ppf(1 - alpha / 2, k + 1, n - k)
    return lo, hi

# operating point: threshold at which A gives FPR about 5%
tau = np.sort(sA[labels == 0])[::-1][int(0.05 * n_neg) - 1]
kA = int((sA[labels == 1] > tau).sum()); fa = int((sA[labels == 0] > tau).sum())
lo, hi = clopper_pearson(kA, n_pos)
print(f"detector A at tau={tau:.2f}: TPR {kA}/{n_pos} = {kA/n_pos:.3f}   95% CI [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]")
lo, hi = clopper_pearson(fa, n_neg)
print(f"                        FPR {fa}/{n_neg} = {fa/n_neg:.3f}   95% CI [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]")

detector A at tau=1.70: TPR 98/200 = 0.490   95% CI [0.419, 0.561]
                        FPR 9/200 = 0.045   95% CI [0.021, 0.084]


With 200 positives, the detection rate \(0.490\) is known to within about \(\pm0.07\). The false alarm rate \(0.045\) has an interval from \(0.021\) to \(0.084\). It is wide relative to its size, because only 9 events were counted.

49.3.1 A zero is not a zero
If a detector makes no false alarm in \(n\) trials, the 95% upper bound on the false alarm rate is about \(3/n\) (the “rule of three”). Exactly, it is \(1-0.05^{1/n}\).

for n in (100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000):
    exact = 1 - 0.05 ** (1 / n)
    print(f"n = {n:6d} negatives, 0 false alarms: upper 95% bound {exact:.5f}   (3/n = {3/n:.5f})")

n =    100 negatives, 0 false alarms: upper 95% bound 0.02951   (3/n = 0.03000)
n =    300 negatives, 0 false alarms: upper 95% bound 0.00994   (3/n = 0.01000)
n =   1000 negatives, 0 false alarms: upper 95% bound 0.00299   (3/n = 0.00300)
n =   3000 negatives, 0 false alarms: upper 95% bound 0.00100   (3/n = 0.00100)
n =  10000 negatives, 0 false alarms: upper 95% bound 0.00030   (3/n = 0.00030)


A requirement of “at most 1 false alarm in 1,000” with 95% confidence needs about 3,000 clean negative samples with no false alarm at all. If the detector makes some, the test set must be larger still. This is why Section 45.3 in Chapter 45 includes a confidence statement: it fixes the data size.

title: 49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence
section: 49.4 Confidence on a curve and on a score: the bootstrap
text:
49.4 Confidence on a curve and on a score: the bootstrap
For AUC there is no simple closed form that is exact. The bootstrap (Chapter 26) resamples the test items with replacement and recomputes the statistic. We resample positives and negatives separately, so that each replicate keeps the class counts.

def boot_auc(s, y, B=2000, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pos, neg = s[y == 1], s[y == 0]
    out = np.empty(B)
    for b in range(B):
        p = pos[r.integers(0, pos.size, pos.size)]
        q = neg[r.integers(0, neg.size, neg.size)]
        out[b] = (p[:, None] > q[None, :]).mean()
    return out

bA = boot_auc(sA, labels)
print(f"A: AUC {auc_rank(sA, labels):.3f}   95% bootstrap CI [{np.percentile(bA, 2.5):.3f}, {np.percentile(bA, 97.5):.3f}]")
bB = boot_auc(sB, labels, seed=1)
print(f"B: AUC {auc_rank(sB, labels):.3f}   95% bootstrap CI [{np.percentile(bB, 2.5):.3f}, {np.percentile(bB, 97.5):.3f}]")

A: AUC 0.874   95% bootstrap CI [0.838, 0.905]
B: AUC 0.896   95% bootstrap CI [0.864, 0.925]


The two intervals overlap. It is tempting to conclude “no difference”. That conclusion is wrong in general, because both detectors were scored on the same items. Their errors are correlated, and the intervals of the separate scores ignore this.
crumbs: Part IX — Systems Thinking and Performance Characterisation
49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence

title: 49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence
text:
49.5 Paired comparison
We resample the items, and compute for each replicate the difference of the two AUCs. A paired analysis uses the correlation between the detectors.

def boot_diff(sA, sB, y, B=2000, seed=2):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    ip, in_ = np.where(y == 1)[0], np.where(y == 0)[0]
    out = np.empty(B)
    for b in range(B):
        p = ip[r.integers(0, ip.size, ip.size)]
        q = in_[r.integers(0, in_.size, in_.size)]
        a = (sA[p][:, None] > sA[q][None, :]).mean()
        c = (sB[p][:, None] > sB[q][None, :]).mean()
        out[b] = c - a
    return out

dd = boot_diff(sA, sB, labels)
print(f"AUC(B) - AUC(A) = {auc_rank(sB, labels) - auc_rank(sA, labels):+.3f}   "
      f"95% paired CI [{np.percentile(dd, 2.5):+.3f}, {np.percentile(dd, 97.5):+.3f}]")
print("independent-style width of the difference CI:",
      (np.sqrt(bA.var() + bB.var()) * 2 * 1.96).round(3), "   paired width:",
      (np.percentile(dd, 97.5) - np.percentile(dd, 2.5)).round(3))
print("share of bootstrap replicates with B > A:", (dd > 0).mean().round(3))

AUC(B) - AUC(A) = +0.022   95% paired CI [-0.010, +0.056]
independent-style width of the difference CI: 0.092    paired width: 0.066
share of bootstrap replicates with B > A: 0.91


The paired interval has width \(0.066\). The one that treats the scores as independent has width \(0.092\). The paired interval still contains zero: \([-0.010,\,+0.056]\). In \(91\%\) of the replicates B beats A. So the data suggest that B is better and do not establish it. We know from the simulation that B is better, with a gap of \(0.043\). The experiment, with 400 items, is too small to show a gap of this size with confidence. A report must say this, and not “B is better” or “no difference”.

title: 49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence
section: 49.6 How big must the test set be?
text:
49.6 How big must the test set be?
The width of an interval shrinks like \(1/\sqrt n\). We estimate the AUC interval width as a function of the number of test items, using the model where the truth is known.

ns = [25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600]
widths = []
r = np.random.default_rng(3)
for n in ns:
    ws = []
    for rep in range(6):
        y = np.r_[np.ones(n, int), np.zeros(n, int)]
        s = r.normal(size=2 * n) + d_A * y
        b = boot_auc(s, y, B=300, seed=int(r.integers(1e6)))
        ws.append(np.percentile(b, 97.5) - np.percentile(b, 2.5))
    widths.append(np.mean(ws))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
ax.loglog(ns, widths, "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"], label="measured width")
ref = widths[0] * np.sqrt(ns[0] / np.array(ns))
ax.loglog(ns, ref, "--", color="gray", label=r"$\propto 1/\sqrt{n}$")
ax.set_xlabel("items per class n"); ax.set_ylabel("95% CI width of AUC"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
for n, w in zip(ns, widths):
    print(f"n = {n:5d} per class: mean width {w:.3f}")







Figure 49.2: Width of the 95% bootstrap interval for AUC (detector A, d = 1.5) against the number of items per class. Quadrupling the data halves the width. The dashed line shows the 1/sqrt(n) trend.





n =    25 per class: mean width 0.209
n =    50 per class: mean width 0.148
n =   100 per class: mean width 0.097
n =   200 per class: mean width 0.070
n =   400 per class: mean width 0.050
n =   800 per class: mean width 0.035
n =  1600 per class: mean width 0.025


A rule of thumb: AUC near 0.85 needs about 100 items per class for a width near \(0.1\), and about 1,600 per class for a width near \(0.025\). For a difference between two detectors with a gap of \(0.02\), the sample must be large enough that the paired interval is narrower than the gap.

49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence

title: 49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence
text:
49.7 Operating points are requirements
A production system works at one threshold. The ROC curve lets us choose it from a requirement: the largest TPR subject to \(\text{FPR}\le\alpha\), or the lowest cost under stated costs of the two errors.
For costs \(c_{FN}\) and \(c_{FP}\) and prior probability \(\pi\) of a positive, the expected cost at a threshold is \(\pi\,c_{FN}(1-\text{TPR})+(1-\pi)\,c_{FP}\,\text{FPR}\). The best point on the ROC curve is where its slope equals \(\frac{(1-\pi)c_{FP}}{\pi\,c_{FN}}\). The threshold depends on \(\pi\). If the prevalence of positives in deployment differs from the test set, the best threshold moves (Chapter 27).

fprA, tprA = roc(sA, labels); fprB, tprB = roc(sB, labels)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 4.2))
ax.plot(fprA, tprA, color=PALETTE["model"], lw=2, label=f"A  (AUC {auc_rank(sA, labels):.3f})")
ax.plot(fprB, tprB, color=PALETTE["data"], lw=2, label=f"B  (AUC {auc_rank(sB, labels):.3f})")
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="gray", lw=1, ls="--")
ax.plot(fa / n_neg, kA / n_pos, "ko"); ax.annotate("operating point of A", (fa / n_neg + 0.02, kA / n_pos - 0.07))
ax.set_xlabel("false alarm rate FPR"); ax.set_ylabel("detection rate TPR"); ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.show()
at = 0.01
print("TPR at FPR <= 0.01:  A", tprA[fprA <= at].max().round(3), "  B", tprB[fprB <= at].max().round(3),
      "  (one false alarm = 0.005 in FPR with 200 negatives)")







Figure 49.3: ROC curves of detectors A and B on the 400-item test set, with the operating point of A at 5% false alarm marked. The grey line is chance. At a false alarm rate of 1%, B detects 38% and A detects 23%, but only two false-alarm items decide that point.





TPR at FPR <= 0.01:  A 0.23   B 0.38   (one false alarm = 0.005 in FPR with 200 negatives)


The curve values at FPR \(0.01\) rest on two false-alarm items. Any claim made at such a point has a very wide interval. For this reason ROC plots in a report should show the interval band, or the claim should be restricted to the region where the data are dense.

title: 49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence
text:
49.8 Failure modes
One score for a curve. AUC averages over operating points that nobody will use. Report the point of the requirement.
Rate without count. “0% false alarms” with no number of trials.
Unpaired comparison. Separate intervals for two systems tested on the same items. This is conservative and can hide a real improvement.
Test set reuse. Choosing a threshold, a model and a report from one set (Chapter 27).
Prevalence mismatch. Precision depends on the share of positives. A detector with TPR 0.9 and FPR 0.05 has precision \(0.5\) when positives are 5% of items. It is \(0.95\) when they are 50%.
Interval on the wrong unit. If several frames come from one video, the independent unit is the video. Resample by video.

title: 49  Operating Curves, ROC and Confidence
text:
49.10 System connection






NoteWhat the system gained in this chapter



The system can now make a claim with a stated confidence. We have the two-error picture, the ROC curve, an exact interval for a rate, a bootstrap for a score, a paired comparison of two detectors, and a way to compute the data size from the requirement.
What remains is a protocol: how to choose conditions and parameters to test, how to separate tuning data from reporting data, how to test the model when its assumptions are wrong, and how to write the result. Chapter 50 gives the protocol. Chapter 51 applies it to large models.

Chapter summary

TPR and FPR are the two error rates. The ROC curve shows every operating point.
AUC is the probability that a positive outscores a negative.
A rate from \(n\) trials has an interval of width about \(1/\sqrt n\). Zero events in \(n\) trials gives an upper bound near \(3/n\).

title: 50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting
text:
50.1 The system problem
Chapters 45 to 49 gave the parts: a system view, loops, a paradigm, error propagation, operating curves with confidence. Each can be done well and the whole can still be wrong, if the experiment is badly planned. We close the book with the plan.
We use the edge detector of Chapter 47 as a running example, because every step can be checked against known truth. The same protocol applies to a vision model, a language model or a sensor chain.
box_flow(["Require-\nment", "Design of\nconditions", "Tune on\ntuning data", "Measure on\nfresh data", "Stress +\nreport"],
         colors=[PALETTE["neutral"], PALETTE["data"], PALETTE["model"], PALETTE["grad"], PALETTE["prob"]],
         figsize=(9.4, 1.8))
plt.show()







Figure 50.1: The characterisation protocol. Requirements fix the conditions and the measures. Tuning data choose parameters. Fresh data measure the result. A stress step tests the model assumptions. The report states limits.

title: 50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting
text: We must deliver a detector that meets a requirement. Which experiments do we run, in which order, on which data, and what do we write down?

50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting

title: 50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting
text:
50.2 Step 1: the requirement
A requirement in the form of Chapter 45 for our detector:

For a step edge of height 2 in additive noise of standard deviation 1, in a signal of 200 samples, find the edge within \(\pm2\) samples in as many cases as possible, with at most 5% of noise-only signals raising any false alarm.

The constraint is on a per-signal false alarm rate of \(5\%\). The objective is the detection probability. The condition is \((h,\sigma)=(2,1)\). We now know what the experiment must measure.
crumbs: Part IX — Systems Thinking and Performance Characterisation
50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting

title: 50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting
crumbs: Part IX — Systems Thinking and Performance Characterisation
50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting

title: 50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting
text:
50.4 Step 3: tune on tuning data
The window \(w\) is a tuning parameter. For each candidate \(w\), the threshold \(\tau\) is set from the noise-only data so that the requirement on false alarms is met: \(\tau\) is the 95th percentile of the largest absolute response in noise-only signals. Then the detection probability is measured. We choose the \(w\) with the highest detection probability.

sigma, h = 1.0, 2.0
rows = []
for w in (3, 5, 9, 15, 25):
    tau = np.quantile(max_noise_response(sigma, w, 1000), 0.95)
    rows.append((w, tau, detect_prob(h, sigma, w, tau, 600)))
print(" w    tau    P_detect (tuning data)")
for w, tau, p in rows:
    print(f"{w:2d}  {tau:6.3f}   {p:.3f}")
w_best, tau_best, p_tune = max(rows, key=lambda r: r[2])
print("chosen: w =", w_best, "  tau =", round(tau_best, 3))

 w    tau    P_detect (tuning data)
 3   2.945   0.138
 5   2.292   0.380
 9   1.622   0.807
15   1.256   0.885
25   0.955   0.875
chosen: w = 15   tau = 1.256


The detection probability rises with \(w\) up to \(15\) and then flattens. The values for \(w=15\) and \(w=25\) differ by \(0.01\), which is within sampling noise for 600 trials (about \(\pm0.013\)). The choice between them is not supported by the data. A characterisation should say so, and pick the smaller window if resolution matters (Chapter 47).
crumbs: Part IX — Systems Thinking and Performance Characterisation
50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting

title: 50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting
text:
50.5 Step 4: measure on fresh data
The score on the tuning data was used to select. It carries the optimiser’s curse (Chapter 27). We generate new signals and measure again.

n = 4000
fa_hits = int((max_noise_response(sigma, w_best, n) > tau_best).sum())
det_hits = int(round(detect_prob(h, sigma, w_best, tau_best, n) * n))

def clopper_pearson(k, n, a=0.05):
    return (0.0 if k == 0 else beta.ppf(a / 2, k, n - k + 1),
            1.0 if k == n else beta.ppf(1 - a / 2, k + 1, n - k))

print(f"false alarm per signal : {fa_hits/n:.3f}   95% CI {np.round(clopper_pearson(fa_hits, n), 3)}   (requirement 0.05)")
print(f"detection probability  : {det_hits/n:.3f}   95% CI {np.round(clopper_pearson(det_hits, n), 3)}   (tuning data: {p_tune:.3f})")

false alarm per signal : 0.057   95% CI [0.05  0.064]   (requirement 0.05)
detection probability  : 0.875   95% CI [0.865 0.886]   (tuning data: 0.885)


On fresh data the false alarm rate is \(0.057\), with an interval from \(0.050\) to \(0.064\). The requirement was \(0.05\). The requirement is not shown to be met: the whole interval is at or above the limit. The threshold was set from only 1,000 noise-only signals, so the threshold itself carries sampling error, and the realised rate landed above the target. Two remedies exist: more tuning data, or a margin (aim at \(0.04\) so that the interval falls below \(0.05\)). The detection probability on fresh data, \(0.875\), is slightly below the tuning value \(0.885\), as the optimiser’s curse predicts.

50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting

title: 50  A Characterisation Protocol: Experimental Design and Reporting
text:
50.6 Step 5: stress the model
So far the test noise came from the same family as the tuning noise. A characterisation is only as good as the model of the world. We now violate the model on purpose, in two ways.
Noise type. The threshold was derived for Gaussian noise. Real noise can have heavier tails. We keep the variance and change the shape. We use the Gaussian design of Chapter 47: \(\tau=\sigma_D\,Q^{-1}(0.0005)\).

sD = sigma * np.sqrt(2 / w_best)
tau_g = sD * norm.isf(1e-3 / 2)
print("noise shape (same variance)   per-sample false alarm   design value 0.001")
for kind in ("gauss", "laplace", "t3"):
    fa = np.mean([(np.abs(dfilt(noise(kind, sigma, Ls), w_best)[1]) > tau_g).mean() for _ in range(1500)])
    print(f"  {kind:8s}                    {fa:.5f}")
print()
print("error in the noise estimate:   per-sample false alarm")
for f in (0.8, 1.0, 1.2):
    fa = np.mean([(np.abs(dfilt(noise('gauss', sigma, Ls), w_best)[1]) > f * tau_g).mean() for _ in range(1500)])
    print(f"  threshold from sigma x {f:3.1f}   {fa:.5f}")

noise shape (same variance)   per-sample false alarm   design value 0.001
  gauss                       0.00094
  laplace                     0.00140
  t3                          0.00529

error in the noise estimate:   per-sample false alarm
  threshold from sigma x 0.8   0.00784
  threshold from sigma x 1.0   0.00102
  threshold from sigma x 1.2   0.00009


Heavy tails (Student \(t\) with 3 degrees of freedom) raise the false alarm rate by a factor of about \(5\) at the same variance. An error of \(20\%\) in the noise level moves the false alarm rate up by a factor of about \(8\) (noise underestimated) or down by a factor of about \(11\) (overestimated). The threshold is sensitive to the noise level, because it lives on the tail of the distribution. A small error in the model becomes a large error in a rare-event rate. This is the most important practical lesson of the paradigm: tail rates are fragile.
Noise level. The threshold was tuned at \(\sigma=1\). In the field, the noise level may differ. We compare two policies over a range of \(\sigma\): a fixed threshold (tuned at \(\sigma=1\)) and an adaptive threshold that scales with an estimate of \(\sigma\) from the data. The estimate uses the median absolute deviation (MAD) of first differences, which is hardly affected by a single edge.

def sigma_hat(x):
    d = np.diff(x)
    return np.median(np.abs(d - np.median(d))) / 0.6745 / np.sqrt(2)

# adaptive threshold factor: percentile of max response / estimated sigma, calibrated once at sigma = 1
ratio = []
for _ in range(1500):
    x = noise("gauss", 1.0, Ls)
    ratio.append(np.abs(dfilt(x, w_best)[1]).max() / sigma_hat(x))
c_adapt = np.quantile(ratio, 0.95)

sig_grid = [0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0]
fixed, adapt = [], []
for sg in sig_grid:
    fx = ad = 0
    for _ in range(1500):
        x = noise("gauss", sg, Ls)
        m = np.abs(dfilt(x, w_best)[1]).max()
        fx += m > tau_best
        ad += m > c_adapt * sigma_hat(x)
    fixed.append(fx / 1500); adapt.append(ad / 1500)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
ax.plot(sig_grid, fixed, "o-", color=PALETTE["loss"], label="fixed threshold")
ax.plot(sig_grid, adapt, "s-", color=PALETTE["grad"], label="adaptive threshold")
ax.axhline(0.05, color="gray", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("true noise σ"); ax.set_ylabel("false alarm per signal"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
for sg, f, a in zip(sig_grid, fixed, adapt):
    print(f"sigma {sg:4.2f}:  fixed {f:.3f}   adaptive {a:.3f}")







Figure 50.2: Per-signal false alarm probability against the true noise level. The fixed threshold was tuned at sigma = 1. The adaptive threshold scales with the noise estimated from each signal. The requirement is 0.05.





sigma 0.50:  fixed 0.000   adaptive 0.040
sigma 0.75:  fixed 0.001   adaptive 0.053
sigma 1.00:  fixed 0.057   adaptive 0.053
sigma 1.50:  fixed 0.702   adaptive 0.049
sigma 2.00:  fixed 0.987   adaptive 0.044


The fixed threshold holds the requirement only at the noise level where it was tuned: its false alarm rate is \(0.70\) at \(\sigma=1.5\) and \(0.99\) at \(\sigma=2\). The adaptive threshold stays between \(0.040\) and \(0.053\) over the whole range. The cost of adaptation is the estimation step, which is itself a component to characterise (it assumes that most differences contain only noise). This is the closing of the loop that Haralick and Ramesh described: the characterisation shows what the parameter must depend on, and the algorithm is redesigned so that it does.
